Plants vs. Zombies developed by PopCap (the makers of the infamous game Bejeweled) and released on the PC platform on May 5, 2009. It is also available on iPhone/iPad, PlayStation 3, PlayStation Vita, Xbox 360.
According to Metacritic,
it:

Plants vs.Zombies (PVZ in short), is awesome. Go get it. The End. ^_^
How I wish I could submit such writing and call it a day but this will not do it any justice. Even after 8 years, this is a treasure to behold. Hugs PVZ. My PRECIOUSZ!

What is Plants vs.Zombies about:
PVZ is a single player, 2D, tower defense game. Basically, you plant plants (towers) to defend your home from the waves of hungry zombies. That's it.
PVZ offers players:

On top of that, you get to plant 3 types of potted plants (3 maps; Day, Night, Water) that earns coins for you and a map to plant a Wisdom tree that grows up to a 100 feet.
You get all that variety of game modes in a fraction of what you would normally pay for a AAA title. Even after 8 years.
and that's not even the best part yet.
Visuals, Audio, Controls:
Let me start off with the easy part first. The controls uses mouse. Nothing more. Everything you do in PVZ uses the mouse; digging, planting, collecting coins/suns.
Audio, normally, I don't give audio much attention but in PVZ, its well made. It's very distinct. Anyone who has played PVZ will know that tune if they heard it in the middle of a supermarket. It's become a trademark. lol.
Every action you make, has a feedback sound. Every zombies that appear or animate will have unique sound to them. Even blowing up the zombies with your potatoes sound so satisfying. Or the comb rocket of death. Kapow. I mean Kaboom.
Music is well made. It's kinda soothing actually and It add's to the tension of the game. It changes when the horde comes with higher tempo notes. Credit to the audio team +1
Visually, its simple, cute, child friendly, very colorful - depending on your day/night setting. It's flat coloring so not a lot of texture to see. The main hero for PVZ is in it's plant and zombies. Everything has been crafted beautifully. Every plant and zombie is unique and wacky.
Exploding potatos, exploding cherries, wallnuts? PEA shooters?! plant eating zombies, Pumpkin armour?!?, bungee jumping zombies, a zombie that resembles MJ, a mining zombie, snow sledge zombies?! zombies on a vehicle lobbing coconuts?!?! a YETI ZOMBIE>!>#@ WT# lol.
Yup, Character design +1 to the team. Kudo's. Great job on the overall product with the visual, audio, animation and story wise.
I nearly forgot, Crazy Dave. Crazy Dave as his name suggest, is kinda crazy. He's your neighborhood buddy? His role is more or less the narrator, the person that ushers you from level to level. and He sells upgrades, pots to you. The introduction of Crazy Dave to the story mode is really interesting and lightens up the mood from time to time. You never know what crazy thing he's gonna put you through from bowling zombies to tiny zombies and more. +1 Another point to the team/writing department.
Game Mechanics:
Your goal is to protect your house from the zombie invasion. Generally, as you progress through the game (in adventure mode/story mode) you will earn other types of plants. Some of them however, you will need to purchase from Crazy Dave.
The Game add's a little twist to the environment:
Day, Night, Water, Roof. Each setting has consequences and forces player to rethink their strategy because of the different zombies/availability of plants.
I'll give a quick example:
Day time: Sun flower generates normal sun energy - where you will use the sun energy to purchase your choice of plants.
Night time: Sun flower will not be able to generate the normal amount of sun energy. You have to use mushrooms. The shroom that procudes sun energy for you will start off tiny, producing half the normal sun energy you get. but after a certain amount of time, it will grow in full size and give you the normal amount of sun energy.
What this makes you do is to change your concept/strategy for night games because of the lack of resources.
If you want to use a day time plant in a night game, sure. You have to have a "bean" that costs 75 sun.
Water levels@pool has some water plants and introduces some crazy zombies riding on dolphins. The most distinct water plant is the nine tails. Awesome. You need to play lily on the 2 water titles. The rest are land. So this is a combination of land and water plants.
There's a lot more to say, but I fear steam word count limit. So i'll sum up the game mechanic as creative, innovative design that turns Tower Defense(TD) game fun. Crazy.
My personal thoughts:
I have completed PVZ many, many times since it's launch. I've never experience any performance issues, crashes or even bugs.
It took me many years later on to purchase it on STEAM. (blame the other steam games xD) This is one of the few games that successfully innovate the product with creativity & wackiness to deliver a memorable fun product. I wish there were more games like this on STEAM.
For those who love TD games, this is a must to try. I haven't covered the mini games or puzzles yet. There's just so many variety of games to keep you engaged in PVZ. Of course the ultimate battle would be the endless waves. Test your skill and put your best plant combo to see how far you can go and earn steam achievement while doing it =)
I nearly forgot, a must mention: you have a boss fight. It's epic. There's a twist in the level and with what the boss can do (smash your plants with a truck x_x) you are in for an epic fight. The reward? An epic song featuring all the plants and zombies.
My Summary:
With that, it's time for the finale. I would like to gather all the plants and zombies for a group photo. If possible, I would love to have a group photo with the devs too. I'll hang them in my bedroom - the hallmark of a great game. In 50 years time, i'll pass this photo to my children and tell them: Eat your veges... I mean, if you have not played PVZ, you haven't lived your life to the FULLEST! Don't you dare go kicking the bucket without trying this !!!
Drums please sun flower!  *drum rolls*
So, on the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for Plants vs. Zombies is a CRAZY DAVE in GOLDEN Blings-Blings worth 9/10.
PVZ exceeds all expectations of a traditional TD product. It is one of the few Great games to date in the market.
must buy. I'll be waiting for PVZ 2 to come on steam even if it makes me wait for another 8 years. xD

I had bought PvZ GOTY when it was on sale for around $1 USD, and even still it is only $5 USD by default. Although, I'm going to state why you shouldn't buy this.
First off, if you have a 16:9 aspect ratio screen, instead of a 4:3
, you're going to be very disapointed, as the game only supports it's native 4:3 aspect ratio, even in full screen. There is no fix for widescreen mode, so if you are on a widescreen (16:9 aspect ratio), and you put the game in full screen mode, it will just stretch the hell out of the game, and make it look disgusting. This doesn't affect gameplay, but I'm still disapointed that they couldn't enable even a fix for it, since the console version is in 720p and allows for both 16:9 and 4:3 aspect ratios, and looks great on either.
The game seems to perform alright most of the time, but has a lot of moments where it will just randomly dip. No matter your specs, this game is bound to just be at an inconsistent FPS.
Even better is the "3D Acceleration option", which is made to supposedly boost frames by using your GPU. Unfortunately, this comes at the cost of the games visuals, as the game will either become blurry, or more pixelated.  And if you'd rather looks over framerate, and you're using your GPU to connect to your display, you can't disable it. Disabling it will cause a  'blue-screen' from Windows (Something like
) .
You may be asking, "Why does this game have so many problems?", well, it's actually because it's a port. Not a console port, a flash game port. Capcom were really just that lazy, and they expect people to pay $5 USD for something that you could
play for free, with just as much love and care put into it. I mean, they could've easily ported the all new neato console version (Even if it was released after this), and just added in the PC exclusive minigames, which would've been a much better idea.
The gameplay is fun, but can be boring, well, when you're playing the story. Every other game mode is amazing, and offers you so much to do that will make you satisfied. But, unfortunately, the story acts as a restrictive parent, and won't let you play any other game mode until you do your chores. I was never fond of this idea, and never have been
The controls are perfect, and allow you to be a master planter with ease. The mouse is a far better choice than a controller in my opinion, but it still would've been nice to have some controller support for those lazy moments, where you just want to lie down or something.
I could talk about the story, but there's no point. I understand that this wasn't meant to be a story rich game, and I definitely wouldn't want more of a story in a game such as this.
Now, is it the worst game out there? No. Not at all. Although, should it be fixed if they want to keep charging $5 USD for this?

Me and my boyfriend played Resident Evil 5 coop where the first player controls Chris and the second player controls Sheva. We had many fun moments but also many frustrating moments. I was very unsure if I should recommend it to you or not.
Let's start with the positive things. It's a really good coop action game, one of those where you have to stay together and really cooperate. The game has many environments, cool combat music and great variety of bosses! You and your partner can tease each other with your character's voice commands. We were shouting at each other a lot and it was very entertaining.
In my short clips video you can see all the good things I was writting about. We were really having fun and laughing a lot:
And here comes all the criticism I need to share with you. The Steam PC version of Resident Evil 5 has many bugs and complicated mouse+keyboard controls. I don't like quick time events very much. But the weird combinations of buttons in RE5 are unbelievable. Sometimes A+D and sometimes F+V with very short time to react to that. I watched some gameplay on consoles and they only had to press one button on their controllers. It's even more annoying during cutscenes when you sit back, enjoy and don't expect anything.
Another unpleasant moment is when you find out that you as Sheva won't get the steam achivement for finishing a chapter if your partner's game crashes or if you decide to stop playing in the middle of a chapter, save the progress and finish later. Only Chris, the player who host the game, will get it then.
It happened to us that an important enemy with a keycard we needed spawned in an inaccessible area, I was locked in a cage and my boyfriend spent quite long time trying to get there while I was waiting and waiting for ages. We tried it again and this time we only saw his shadow on the floor. I tried to use explosives so we got him down from that unknown place this time and luckily it was on the right side.
Another very annoying moment was the final boss fight where you have to press F as Sheva for almost a minute. Not just that but you have to do it SUPER fast. You kind of need to be like The Flash! I played this game 6 years ago as well and I remember I had to give up back then. It was not possible. On my last playthrough I tried it so many times and I managed to do it only once.. My finger really hurt, so I had to ignore the pain and was lucky my boyfriend didn't mess it up after that so we could continue. Uffff! These moments definitely made us want to ragequit..
RE5 Bosses in general can be very annoying. When you are not doing the right thing - shooting the right spots at the right moments , you are basically wasting your ammo and the game won't give you any more and it won't make you fail either even when you clearly can't do it. You just have to decide for yourself to restart from the last checkpoint.. But in case you somehow manage to do it but you already wasted all your ammo before, good luck to you, because you can't buy ammo directly. However you can buy weapons and sell them so you keep the ammo they had.
Final verdict: Partly recommended! Overall I am very hesitant in case of Resident Evil 5. I am a fan of RE games. I like the coop option of it. But all the bugs are breaking the full enjoyment of it for me. I believe the console version is much better! If you love Resident Evil games and you have the patience to deal with it, go for it! Wait for a sale, please. Don't pay the full price for something what couldn't have bugs fixed since 2009.
Thank you for reading my review! In case you have some questions feel welcome to ask me :)

Loot Hero DX is a hard game to review.
Occupying a niche alongside so-called "clicker" games, there isn't any gameplay to speak of. You merely hold right and your tiny knight dashes at incredible speeds into the enemy army. Monsters explode like obedient loot pinatas and then you spend some gold giving your knight incremental upgrades (hint: defense beats all).
That's the complete summation of the game. The problem is that the developer(s) obviously put a lot of effort into the visuals and the engine. It's incredibly smooth despite the crazy speeds our metal covered hero sprints around at and the sprite work makes has a consistent and very pleasing look. Even the backgrounds have some serious polish.
I'm recommending this game only for those who like "clicker" games and to support and encourage the developer to do more with this games art assets. Please spin this into maybe a side-scrolling RPG or something.

While I only have a few hours recorded here on Steam, I have quite a few more on the X-Box 360 version of this game. Despite the "okay" voice-acting, the really stupid friendly A.I., accidental racism, and the few poorly-visioned cinematic scenes, I loved this game. I loved the variety of weapons I could use and unlock, and how much more fun it was to play this game with a friend! (Seriously, f*** the friendly A.I.) I bought the Steam version, as I don't really want to keep buying a yearly subscription just to play online anymore.
This version of the game has a few quirks, however. The very first one I found was with the Anti-Ailising. At first the game was grand, but as the game progressed, I noticed quite a bit of screen-tearing, and soon it escelated to the point where the game was virtually unplayable. Luckily, AA can be modified at run-time, and after I turned off this nightmare, it worked just fine.
The next bug is the issue of the timers. Normally, at the level results screen or the mission prep screen, if one is playing with another person, and they select that they are ready to move on, you have 60 seconds to finish
what you are doing and move on to the next thing. Once, I didn't press this in time, and my game froze, and my parner's game said they were waiting for mine to load. One
forced reboot later, all is well again.
All in all, this is still the goofy wonder it was on the X-box 360, only now with a few more blemishes.
8/10 if you are playing alone.
9/10 with a friend. Seriously. Don't play with the friendly A.I. It's not worth the hit to your sanity, even if they are a better shot than your friend.

Alright folks, the game doesn't deserve all the hate. Well, ummm, actually it does, but not to this extent. I originally bought the game at version 8 (now it's version 14e), so yeah, I'm amongst those who were "cheated" by early promises, and I will still give this game a thump up.
Why it does deserve the hate? Because it's clearly unfinished.
-Several in-game features are clunky, for example ordering your troops around: you can't simply say "go there", you can only place patrol points. So exploring the dungeons beneath the surface is like: right-click somewhere, place waypoint, wait until they get there, right-click on waypoint, remove waypoint, right-click somewhere else, place waypoint, wait until they get there, etc. Since there's no other option I can live with it, but I'm not lovin' it.
-Poor pathfinding. The townies may just ignore the roads, although they walk parallel with them only one square away.
-AI is lacking. The haulers tend to choose stuff to pick up far, far away, instead of that exact same thing they are standing on. And, please, don't go to sleep or eat when several dozens of spiders are besieging the town. Also, don't try to gather loot in the middle of the battlefield, because it's dangerous to your health.
-The variety of stuff to build is a bit underwhelming, although not always. For example you can build one type of wooden chair (not counting that one which needs gold besides wood), but at the same time there are like twenty stone wall styles. So building homes is not on Sims level.
I think these are the negatives worth mentioning, may update if I encounter something I haven't written here yet. Umm, okay, others may say the music is repetitive, but I don't mind, it's not horrible.
Why it does not deserve this much hate:
- Contrary to a lot of other reviews, I have not encountered _any_ bugs, at least not apparent ones. No memory leaks. No hangups, no slowdowns, no CTDs. I don't really get what others mean when they describe this game as "buggy as ****". There were a lot of them in earlier versions, but right now this is one of the most bug-free games I ever played.
I will not make a list about other pros, because they are subjective. I just leave here this: I still prefer Towns way over Gnomoria, and if it was a terrible game I wouldn't have come close to play it for 270 hours. Not many of my games can boast that much playtime.
Thus, I dare to say, if you like building towns from blocks, and if Towns is on sale, try it.

I admit, this game doesn't have much replay value at all (even with the 100 level achievement to snag).  It is fun in short spurts and can be used as a decent, mindless way to get out some frustration after a long day.  The music is wonderful and the art style is rather nice to look at as well.  As others have mentioned the miners, while a nice touch, are mostly pointless since the amount of gold they give you can easily be picked up with a single run through a level.  The game says that they continue to earn gold even while you are away, but if you've done much of what you need to on the first playthrough (like I did), the gold they bring won't benefit you much at all.  Keep in mind that it took me about 3.5 hours to run the game dry.  If the developer adds more later on, I would re-visit it (and might here and there for a quick run through of a level... with speed boosts, it can take as little as 6 seconds to complete a level for me now).
Worth noting is that the DX version on Steam does add a few new levels, enemies in those levels and the concept of the miners to rescue after killing each dragon.  It's a small upgrade from previous versions found on Desura, but it is nice to see that they are adding a bit of extra content.
While I do reccmmend it, it's a borderline pass.  It's certainly cheap enough and can sometimes be found in a bundle, so keep your eyes open for that, but for the current price of 2.99, it's hard to say that you're getting an amazing value for your money.

Absolute Drift, herein abbreviated as AD, is essentially a minimalistic casual driving game. You play from a 3D, third person “top-down” perspective, as you traverse 7 worlds completing various drifting tasks. The goal? Become a master drifter, sliding over water and doing donuts around Ferris Wheels. Here are a few things worth noting.
The elegant contrast of white landscapes against bright red obstacles is the key idea behind the art style of AD. The graphics look gorgeous with their minimalistic textures and subtle physics. As you drive through stacks of blocks, you’ll be blown away at how the particles just seem to fall away without hesitation. The soundtrack is perfectly suited for the game, and huge props to the artists for their great work in that department.
The game seems simple at first – get your car sideways, countersteer, and you’re set. It’s not quite that easy. In free roam you will learn how to stay in drifts and exit the drift whenever you need to. Meanwhile, you can use various events to hone your skills on-track. There’s no difficulty toggle here – in events you are ranked against other players in global and friend-based rankings.
One of the only gripes I had with this game was the length of the free roam world. There are seven “worlds” you go through before having to resort to replaying tracks over and over just to beat your own times. I would love to see a co-op or even online 1-on-1 game mode in this, and it would definitely give it a bit more reason to play beyond free-roam.
AD runs phenomenally on my rig, as I expected. However, as with all my reviews, I tested the game on Intel Integrated Graphics to see how well it would do for casual gamers. It ran at a solid 35 or so fps, definitely within a playable range. You could likely push it to 50 by playing 1280x720 windowed.
Do I like this game? Absolutely. (Pardon the pun) I would recommend it to anyone looking for a game that they can complete with 100% achievements in less than 5 hours.

Resident Evil 5 is designed to be played cooperatively from start to finish. For good or ill, you're either ideally playing with a human partner or you have an AI companion in tow throughout the entire game. This affects every aspect of the followup to the masterpiece, RE4: from the inventory system, the level design, the difficulty, the puzzles... it all revolves around two characters in play. It's a very different game from previous entries, veering more towards monster arena shooter than any type of horror or traditional tense atmosphere.
 
  It's a very “brown” game, released in an era when that was generally used as an insult toward generic shooters with limited color pallets. Here it's fitting, with the majority of your time spent out in the sun bleached African slums and savanna. Playing as Chris Redfield with your partner Sheva, you're almost immediately assaulted by hordes of a new strain of infected locals. The enemies are numerous and nimble, testing your aim and keeping you on your toes as you try to avoid getting trapped in a corner. You still do not have the ability to aim and shoot simultaneously, so combat is a test of pinpoint accuracy and situational awareness. The first two thirds or so of the game feels very monotone in both look and action; you're fighting similar enemies in brown arenas, broken up only by the occasional on-rails shooting setpiece or boss fight.
 
  The action isn't bad, just on the repetitive side and it doesn't hold up particularly well compared to newer titles that have improved and iterated on the formula. Most encounters boil down to popping some shots off while standing still, running away, doing a quick turn, repeat. Thankfully, the last two chapters add some variety and make the entire game better by proxy. Exploring a brightly lit, futuristic underground lab and a well realized cargo ship are nice visual changes of pace. Your tactics also get a major shakeup as armed infected now start to regularly shoot back at you with automatic weapons and come in armored forms, causing you to really think about where you aim before wasting ammunition. Mechanics like taking cover behind walls are also introduced, and the stop and pop pace is threatened by cattle prod carrying psychos slowly encroaching. The urgency and intensity explodes in the final act, moving the game's needle from fairly generic third person shooter to something definitely worth playing.
 
  Resident Evil 5 would be unplayable if your AI companion sucked, but for the most part Sheva does what you expect her to do. While she does have the habit of getting in the way of your aiming laser from time to time or thinks it's a good idea to be up your♥♥♥♥♥when fighting a boss with an obvious weak spot on it's back, she's more or less competently autonomous. You have full control over her inventory, so equipping her with a sniper rifle and loading her up with ammo is a good idea as she'll provide decent cover support. The concessions to cooperative play actually streamlines the inventory system in a good way; the game does not want you to pause at any time, so hitting the inventory button brings up an easily accessible grid. Once you understand the options, using, dropping, combining, and swapping items between characters is ultra snappy and intuitive. If it went back to a Resident Evil Zero style system this game would have been a ♥♥♥♥ing disaster.
 
  Like most games in the series, Resident Evil 5 is built to be replayed multiple times. Along with a New Game Plus mode that let's you play as Sheva in single player, experiencing her point of view during the limited times she splits up from Chris, there's also the straight arena, score based Mercenaries Mode. You earn points for playing the game in most modes which can then be spent to unlock characters for Mercenaries, costumes for the main game, collectible figures, visual filters, etc. There's quite a bit of game here. There's even a versus multiplayer mode, but that was garbage even when the game was in it's prime.
 
  Included in the “Gold Edition” is two single player (well, coop...) DLC missions; one has Jill and Chris returning to the Spencer mansion from the first Resident Evil. If that sounds great, hold your horses; for some reason they took the time to model almost the entire mansion in the RE5 engine, then did almost nothing with it. You fight a total of four enemies... the same type of enemies... then have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Wesker boss fight and the whole thing is over in an hour. That's disappointing. The other DLC mission, Desperate Escape, is better though not really essential. It's a side story with Jill and some helicopter pilot that was in the main game for two minutes, and you're bombarded with enemies the entire time. It culminates in a Horde Mode-style defense where you're tasked with holding out against increasingly difficult enemies while waiting for a timer to tick down. It's not bad.

Resident Evil 5 is the tragic tale of a good friendship gone bad.
During their adolescent years, Chris Redfield and Albert Wesker were the best of friends. This always surprised people because personality wise, they were almost polar opposites. Whereas Chris was sombre, Albert was frivolous and a serial prankster. But they were inseparable and would often attend wild fraternity parties together. Albert always wore his "I'm with Stupid" T-shirt and people would laugh and laugh.
When they were young adults, they formed the Backdoor Boys, a R&B boy band that became popular in Beaver City. They were renowned for hits like "Kiss Me, Thrill Me, Bite Me", "Don't Drop The Soap", "Who Put The Toilet Seat Down?", and the worldwide #1 "Backdoor's Back (Tonight)".
For awhile life was good, but it didn't last.
The truth was, Albert had a dark secret that he kept from everyone, even his best friend Chris. He had a grim and melancholic side, and was prone to bouts of depression that often lasted days, the legacy of a dysfunctional relationship with his estranged father that had haunted him since childhood.
When Albert was 7 years old, he wanted a LEGO Star Wars X-Wing Fighter for Christmas. He cut out pictures from toy catalogues and stuck them on the family fridge so his dad would see it everytime he went for a beer. He behaved himself all year and was as good as gold. On Christmas day, Albert was terribly excited. He woke up at dawn, ran to the Christmas Tree and ripped open his present, but instead of a LEGO Star Wars X-Wing Fighter, it was some cheap LEGO-compatible knock off that was Made in China. It didn't even look like an X-Wing. Poor Albert was crushed.
A few years later when Albert was 10 years old, he wanted to go to Disneyland for his birthday. Albert had always dreamed of visiting Disneyland, the place where dreams come true and money disappears. He dreamed of going on all the exciting rides, overpaying for cheap junk food, and buying overpriced merchandise from glamorous gift shops. Unfortunately, family finances were extremely tight. Beleaguered by a huge sub-prime mortgage and unremitting expenses, Albert's father couldn't afford to take him.
For months Albert pleaded and cajoled incessantly. Finally, on the day of his 10th birthday, his overwrought and exasperated father drove him to an old burnt out warehouse and told him Disneyland burnt down. Albert cried and cried, and was inconsolable for weeks. Even after he got over it, Albert was never the same again. This singular event had scarred him emotionally for life, and would cement his later inevitable slide into villainy. Unable to tolerate the overbearing boy anymore, Albert's father eventually abandoned him and eloped with a waitress from Hooters.

Resident Evil 5 is set in Africa where the nefarious Umbrella is once again up to no good. Leon Kennedy is nowhere to be seen because he's currently embroiled in a nasty scandal involving Ashley Graham and teenage pregnancy, although the White House has strongly denied the rumours.
This time Chris Redfield and his new partner Sheba have been sent to investigate. Sheba is a local, but she was educated overseas and speaks English fluently. She also told Chris that she's the Queen of the Jungle and can talk to animals, and that he should address her as 'Your Majesty' in line with local custom.
Although Chris doesn't speak the local African lingo, he insists on doing all the talking anyway, speaking English slowly and loudly in a typically American touristy way. When the natives can't understand him, he gets agitated and
them. It doesn't really help, but at least it keeps the beggars away.
Because the BSAA doesn't pay him very well, Chris will happily take any gold and tribal artifacts lying around. Chris is also quite the snazzy trader, always looking for opportunities to make a deal. One time, he offered to trade his "Magic Number Machine" for a priceless Solid Gold Wachuti Fertility Idol, but nobody wanted his digital watch. Another time, he offered to "Bring back the Sun" for a modest fee in Gold bullion, but the natives opted to wait out the solar eclipse.
It wouldn't be a Resident Evil game without epic boss fights, and Resident Evil 5 has plenty, but the biggest innovation to the series is the addition of a co-op mode. The AI partner is competent, if not a little trigger happy. However, there's no substitute for a human player when it comes to truely ♥♥♥♥ing up a boss fight.

After the amazing Resident Evil 4, expectations for Resident Evil 5 were very high and many people were subsequently disappointed. By all means, Resident Evil 5 isn't a great port, glitches still exist and patches are required for the best experience. But the recent removal of GfWL and addition of Steamworks is a step in the right direction. Although Resident Evil 5 doesn't surpass the high bar set by Resident Evil 4, it is a good game that stands on its own merits and a worthy addition to the Resident Evil family.

I could not possibly fly the pixilated flag of this love letter to those NES days any higher. It's a side scrolling platformer that would have been etched in our memories as a timeless classic if it came out in the late 80s. It looks and sounds amazing, every sprite has a high level of detail, every background looks impressive, it's colourful, exciting, and the music is just spot on. It's an utter joy to play too, the controls feel just right, the levels are fun and the bosses top even some of the best of Megaman's Robot Masters. There is a simple story to tie it all together peppered with some humour and references to the era that inspired it.
It's not the most difficult game, though there is enough of a challenge there though to keep you interested. However should you feel like the need for NES like difficulty there is a harder New Game+, tricky achievements, the ability to destroy checkpoints for gold rather than use them as a safety net and a huge amount of cheat codes that can really alter the gameplay.
If you haven't got it, do so as soon as you can as it's something not to be missed.

This game is one the BEST retro platformers out there, even one of the best platformers in general! This game is perfection, not one thing about this game is bad. The controls are easy to understand and fluent. The levels are extremely unique and fun to play through. The bosses are great fun, and all of them have completely different ways to beat them, so you never feel like you're doing the same thing over. There's plenty of money and jewels hidden throughout levels (Including numerous music sheets for you to find and give back to the Bard for money.) so you can spend them on shovel upgrades, different armor, health and relic upgrades, and more. As for the difficulty, that really depends on your personal skill with games like this. I, personally, thought the game, while hard in certain points, made me slam my controller on the floor. (BTW, I recommend an Xbox 360 controller to play with, trust me it's worth it.) So, for me, the difficulty is really good. But if you're a novice platformer, I'd say maybe pass this one up if you aren't good at them. As for anything I disliked... That's a tough one. Yacht Club Games did a phenomenal job with this game, and I wish them more in the future. Really, there isn't anything I can think that I personally didn't like. Some people say it's too short, or it's too hard. But really, I found both of those things false. So, in conclusion, GET THIS GAME! I was a little skeptical at first, but I absolutely ADORE this game. It's totally in my top 10 best platformers of all time. So, again, get this game, you will not regret it!

Specter of Torment Review: This is by far my favorite DLC yet (and I'm not just saying that because Specter Knight is my favorite)! With a new story and tons of new mechanics, this DLC really gives the player a lot of options when deciding on how to deal with your foes. The wall jumping mechanic is fairly simple to use, and is a lot easier to use than I originally thought it would be. The bosses are also changed up, so it won't be like you're just replaying the game for a third time. Also, as usual, there are plenty of achievements and easter eggs to find, so there is plenty of content. In addition to Specter Knight's story, this DLC included local co-op and a gender swap mode for the Shovel Knight story. I just want to make this clear: the local co-op and gender swap mode are ONLY for the Shovel Knight story, not the other stories. Anyway, great expansion and I can't wait for King Knight's story!

Rating 8/10
This game has improved a lot over its predecessor.
The rep system blocking you from story missions is removed and instead, it is used for unlocking upgrades for you, your weapons, and your gang.
Activities are still around and are introduced as one time quests as part of the main story and then optional, more difficult missions to earn more rep and cash.
The vehicle controls are more stable and the navigation to waypoints improved allowing you to speed through the city easily.
One thing I didn't like was not being able to store vehicles I found while on a mission in my garage.
I also was able to buy this game along with much of the DLC heavily discounted, so I don't know how much that content improved the game experience beyond what is in the base game.
If you'd like to try a more humorous version of GTA, this is one to go for.
It's a great game to kill some time.

Game review:
Loot Hero is your standard generic MMORPG / RPG endcontent grindfest in a nutshell.
"Just 200 boars more then my hunting rank is 9001!
"Just 20 more raids and i will get my purple armor!"
"Doing this dungeon run 3 more times and i will have the armor set complete!"
You know, it's always about grinding, always about numbers, always about loot.
Loot Hero offers you exactly that, without downtimes, without emptying your inventory,
without lengthy boss fights, without having to deal with kill stealers, just pure grind.
You like MMORPGs, don't read the quest stories anyways and just love slaughtering
hordes of mobs to see your level increase and loot flying all over the place?
Then get Loot Hero ;)

Like many of us, I love Arma.  Yes, it has problems, framerate issues, bugs, and all the things you may have heard are indeed true.  However, over the nearly 3 years that I've been playing Arma (since June of 2014), the performance, quality and content of Arma 3 has done nothing but improve.  For me, Bohemia has never disappointed as far as Arma is concerned, and I hope that they never do.  User created content is the thing that keeps this game alive and well.  Total conversions (such as Red Hammer Studios' Armed forces of the United States, Russian Federation and Green Forces), gameplay mods (such as the Advanced Combat Environment) and user made missions using the Eden editor (the days of the 2D editor are gone!).
Arma isn't just about Mil-Sim missions and Units either, there are a ton of other things, such as several different survival modes, and RPG modes.  While I am not a fan of these modes, many people are and they've certainly formed their own community.
If you do want mil-sim, there are tons of Units and great communities for that as well, just go to the Find A Unit subreddit and start looking into one you might like to join!  Arma isn't just a game, it's a platform, and that's why you often see so many people with a ridiculous amount of hours.  There are so many games, and so many mods, you can have completely different experiences every timeyou boot up the game.
If you have the extra money, or the game is on sale, definitely get the Apex edition! It's totally worth it.  Tanoa is a great map, the Apex firearms are great, and I believe the Apex edition comes with Karts, Marksman and Helicopters as well!

text:
Kickstarter gets a bad rap sometimes, and for good reason, but if the service creates more games like this, I will die defending it, because Shovel Knight is one of the finest platformers I have ever played. The market is flooded with mediocre retro-style indie platformers that do little more than pander to people's nostalgia for a quick buck, but Shovel Knight stands out as a game that truly feels like an 8-bit game, from the color palatte to the sound design to the two-button control scheme, and would stand tall as a classic even alongside 8-bit titans like Mega Man and Castlevania. Controls are tight and fluid, giving you perfect control and making the simple actions you perform fun in their own right, which is essential for a platformer. The level design in on par with the best of the NES era, teaching the player about it's mechanics without ever shoving it in their face, and offering some amazingly creative ideas and mechanics. The combat is very fun, with several oppurtunities to test your shoveling skills against enemies that take more than one hit to fell, allowing you to chain attacks together in a smooth and satisfying fashion. The boss battles in particular are fantastic, offering massive challenge and forcing you to think on your feet, since they have set attacks, but don't always do those attacks in the same order. They're the best bosses I've ever seen in a 2D platformer. Despite it's purposeful limitations, the game looks great, and the music is some of the best chiptune work I've ever heard. It even has a story, and a good one at that, with some great interactive storytelling and a genuinely touching ending. It's no masterpiece, but it's more than I'd expect from a game like this, especially when so many higher-budget games with more focus on story get it so wrong.
What impresses me most about Shovel Knight, though, is how well it captures the true essenece of nostalgia. Most retro indie games' defintion of nostalgia is to say "hey, remember game X? Wasn't game X great?" which is misguided admiration at best and manipulative design at worst. Instead, Shovel Knight builds the elements that create nostalgia into the core of it's design, rather than merely reminding us of games that incited those same feelings. It does this through a combination of discovery and safety. Shovel Knight, while playing on familiar tropes, has many incredibly unique and surprising moments that play with our expectations to create something new, and even when they're not setting us up the level and mechanic design is so utterly inspired you just can't help but be in awe of it. However, there isn't too much new. The game is presented in a style familar to nearly everyone who plays games, and the simple traditions that underscore this discovery, like returning to the town to give music sheets to the bard and buy health upgrades, give the game a safe haven, a sense of security that prevents the influx of new mechanics from becoming overwhelming and threatening. Discovery and security are the things that made childhood great: being able to experience so many things for the first time, but always having a sense of security in the feeling that you would come inside and mom would cook you dinner at the end of the day. So in other words, Shovel Knight evokes emotions that reflect a positive view of childhood, and what word describes a positive view of the past? Nostalgia. People often use nostalgia as a negative, but they have to realize that for a game to invoke nostalgia, the memories of it have to be positive. The same techniques that make people remember games like Zelda so fondly are replicated perfectly in Shovel Knight, and that is no small feat.
Admittedly, the game isn't perfect. The biggest problem is that it's a bit on the easy side. Checkpoints are frequent, magic items are too powerful, and magic refills are far too common. While this does suit the game's intent, which is more about having simple fun than massive challenges, it left me wanting more when I completed the quest. The New Game + mode does address these problems by increasing damage, removing health power-ups, and giving you less checkpoints, but it would have been nice if that was selectable from the start as hard difficulty. Additionally, there isn't nearly enough to spend your money on, and all the treasure you get from the pleathora of well-hidden secrets this game doesn't take long to become worthless. Finally, there's a bit too much knockback for my liking, as I fell into several pits simply by being knocked into them by an enemy. The overarching theme of this game seems to be to take the good bits of retro games and leave the bad stuff behind, so it's inclusion is perplexing and occasionally frustrating. There is an armor which reduces knockback, though, which I like. Also, the game is kind of short, though a short length suits this kind of game. Overall, though, these are just nitpicks. Shovel Knight is an amazingly fun. It's a spectacular experience that anyone who enjoys the classics of the NES era will love, and even if you don't, Shovel Knight may convince you that, despite their age, those old games still have a lot of merit, and the love people have for them shouldn't be dismissed as a rose-tinted view of the past and a resistance to change, but rather a celebration of everything those old games did so right that newer titles have forgotten.

This game is basically Clicker Heroes without the clicking. It also manages to be even simpler, with absolutely no strategy whatsoever.
Usually, the grinding in those games quickly becomes very addictive, and you're stuck in an endless loop where you're restarting from level 1 but much more powerful, letting you reach a few levels higher before you have to start over again.
Here, the grinding never pays off. You never feel stronger since you're forced to run the exact same 8-9 levels (that can be cleared in less than 10 seconds each, no joke), and the enemies also level up at around the same pace as you do. You only have a single character so it gets old fast, and you have absolutely nothing to do except pushing forward and increasing your stats whenever possible. There's no way to try a glass canon build or a tanking build, you have to level up everything all at once, and clearing the game's 20 achievements will take you less than 2 hours.
Even as a free mobile game, I wouldn't recommend this. Everything you do past the first 2-3 minutes is completely pointless, and that's coming from someone who has spent 100+ hours in Clicker Heroes.
Sure, the game has "Possibly infinite gameplay", but it's about as fun as holding the space bar in a Word document and creating an infinite number of pages...

...Eh... erm... nah.
I've played more than my share of "idle" and/or single-mechanic games.  Clicker Heroes, AdVenture Capatalist, Cookie Clicker, Tap Heroes, Anti Idle...  just to name a few.  Loot Hero DX is of the same lineage.
The basics are easy to grasp.  Hold right to smash into enemies, grab the money that falls out, upgrade any of four stats at the regularly spaced checkpoints positioned throughout the level, and get strong enough to take out the boss at the end.
...And that's it.  Either you've got the power and defense to beat your foes...  or you don't, which means you hold left to beat up more dudes.  Passing each checkpoint refills your health automatically, so if you're capable of beating the monsters in a stage you simply walk back and forth to grind some cash for more upgrades.
It's worth mentioning that it's very easy to earn all the achievements, albeit a couple of them are just time sinks and rather grindy.
I don't mind simple mechanics, but this game is really brainless.  ...REALLY brainless.  Yes, I've paid plenty more for games that I spent less time with.  That said, can I recommend it to people?
...Eh... erm... nah.

A lot of people seem to think of this game as the Messiah of all games - The peak of what we're capable of achieving. This has led to this game acquiring a somewhat over-the-top amount of praise.
Is the game good? Yes! Is it great? Yeah.. Is it the best thing ever? Not quite.
Let's be reasonable here: It's a fun retro-platformer offering a lot of challenge and bringing back a lot of mechanics from older titles that we haven't seen used in a larger and more popular mainstream title for a long time.
Please, do keep in mind that some of these mechanics were left behind for a reason though.
It's a good, fun game - Possibly even close to a masterpiece, but it is *not* 'the one game to rule them all'.
What does it do really well?
- Tight controls and Dualshock 4 compatibility without any outside tools needed.
- Even thought it's an old style, the visuals are nice if you enjoy pixel-art.
- A good sense of humor and a decent, if slightly confusing, story.
- It's got a great deal of content and, like most games in this genre, it's more or less infinitely replayable.
What does it do not-so-well?
- An absolutely minute amount of bugs that can ruin your day. These are extremely rare in my experience, but while the game is solid it's not bulletproof.
- Some of the mechanics are.. Well, not so fun. Rooms going completely dark, forcing you to go around not really sure of where you're going or what's up above or beneath you. Bosses that have a slightly tiresome amount of RNG and lack of control to them leading to some not always very fair deaths. Mechanics that take control away from the player and leaves you relying on luck more than skill, and some screens where a you run the possible risk of getting a setup of hazards that's unpassable. (It's rare, but it happens, and it basically means a reset/death.)
I'd recommend this game to any platform enthusiast, but at the same time.. If you're like me and don't like mechanics where you can't rely on skill, this game *will* frustrate you every now and again.
The difficulty curve towards the end also takes a rather sudden, massive leap, making the second half of the game far, far harder than the first half without really easing you into it.
Great game, definitely a classic, and something I'm going to play more of - It's not the best game I've ever seen, nor evne the best of this particular genre. Top 5, but not number 1.

Like many of us, I love Arma.  Yes, it has problems, framerate issues, bugs, and all the things you may have heard are indeed true.  However, over the nearly 3 years that I've been playing Arma (since June of 2014), the performance, quality and content of Arma 3 has done nothing but improve.  For me, Bohemia has never disappointed as far as Arma is concerned, and I hope that they never do.  User created content is the thing that keeps this game alive and well.  Total conversions (such as Red Hammer Studios' Armed forces of the United States, Russian Federation and Green Forces), gameplay mods (such as the Advanced Combat Environment) and user made missions using the Eden editor (the days of the 2D editor are gone!).
Arma isn't just about Mil-Sim missions and Units either, there are a ton of other things, such as several different survival modes, and RPG modes.  While I am not a fan of these modes, many people are and they've certainly formed their own community.
If you do want mil-sim, there are tons of Units and great communities for that as well, just go to the Find A Unit subreddit and start looking into one you might like to join!  Arma isn't just a game, it's a platform, and that's why you often see so many people with a ridiculous amount of hours.  There are so many games, and so many mods, you can have completely different experiences every timeyou boot up the game.
If you have the extra money, or the game is on sale, definitely get the Apex edition! It's totally worth it.  Tanoa is a great map, the Apex firearms are great, and I believe the Apex edition comes with Karts, Marksman and Helicopters as well!

Isnt it ironic when the negative reviewers for a game have the most play time? I mean, it is such a boring game, yet you kept playing it for 4 hours......This type of entitlement is exactly why games like this struggle to exist. It is becoming more and more difficult to find decent reviews for unique indie titles, when the player base expects every game to be "Skyrim with guns 9/11 IGN". To be honest this game isnt something you are going to dump a lot of time into. The repetitive nature of the game is more or less likely to net you a good 2 hours of playtime. More if you're like me, and like casual games. Less if you just want to enjoy a few playthroughs. Loot hero is actually not much different than the popular "One finger death punch". Its a single click game (minus the QTEs). The pixel art style and colorful nature of this game is worth the few dollars to hop on. Do not expect there to be an elaborate RPG system or anything on top of the base upgrades(speed, ATK, DEF and Crits). The game has been quite popular on mobile. Dont believe me; you might want to check its popularity with the Android userbase. You can literally do a full playthrough in about 20 minutes but that should be expected for what you're paying for. This game aims to please the people who want to make the most out of 20 minutes of their time. And if you dont have high expectations LOOT HERO DX is great for a quick fix.

Loot Hero DX is a side-scrolling action game that is all about grinding xp and coins. It's quite addicting and I find it very original and simple to play, It's a great casual game that anybody can play and enjoy within 30 seconds of opening the game.
The game has got a different soundtrack for each of the 9 stage types and the retro graphics are enjoyable. The game plays smoothly and it's very fast paced.
As you play you unlock a mine and whenever you kill the boss final level, you get a miner that gets you more gold overtime and you restart the game with greater difficulty and more loot! Of course, you also get the gold if you are offline, so the more you have progressed into the game, the more gold you get when you come back.
You can level up your attack, critical, defence and speed with gold and it seems like you can level up your hero very far.
The game is great overall, but after about an hour of playtime, it will get repetitive to most people. Then again, even if the game is short, it's well-made and the price tag of the game is extremely low, literally anybody that wants to try it out should purchase it! If you are into small indie games, I think you will like it. It's refreshing and it's fun to play.
If you want to get 100% achievements done, you will get a few more hours of playtime out of the game.

I actually really like this game.
I've always had a softspot for Pixel art, the Loot Hero DX ticks all the boxes. It's rather simple though, you run from side to side impaling enemies with your lance, collect the loot they drop, upgrade your items and speed and repeat. You do this over and over through different areas, and monsters until you finally reach the dragon and dispatch him.
Afterwards the game restarts and you continue on, with the same game, but more difficult each time. Killing the dragon does rescue a single miner though and it unlocks the mine. They'll slowly collect loot for you, but honestly it's not needed. As shown in the second half of my little video, you can become utterly god-like and just demolish everything.
Now the game does get extremely repetitive, unless you simply can't get enough, or you need all the achievements available; but I still enjoy it. The music and art is lovely, and I do hope the developer will expand on the game and later turn it into a platformer/sidescrolling adventure game. I would really enjoy it.
As it stands, is it worth the asking price? I personally think so. It's great for bouts of fun, and I couldn't help but giggle to myself as I essentially turned into an armour wearing jousting sonic of death.

Oh boy. Where do I start with this little gem? Guess I could do a simple pros and cons list.
Pros:
Good for about 5-10 minutes. Then you beat the game and get to start from the beginning all over again. With the same enemies, music, backdrops, etc. The only thing that changes is the enemies' damage and health.
Has fairly nice art style, although gets a bit tiring after a while seeing pixelly blurs zoom past your screen once you've upgraded your speed high enough.
Runs quite smoothly. (I'm looking at you, Batman: Arkham Knight.)
Not incredibly buggy.
Cons:
Incredibly short.
Incredibly repetitive.
No challenge
Prices of upgrades doesn't go above 9999 "loot" (currency of the game)
You can't have any more than 99, 999 "loot" at any one time. The number simply doesn't go any higher.
You can continue upgrading your critical hit chance past 100. Well, when I say upgrading, I really meaning pumping another 9, 999 "loot" into the button, only for nothing to change.
When you're ramming through a bunch of enemies, the enemies you just killed may spawn directly behind you when you ram into the enemy in front of you. When this happens, you can slam into the enemy behind you, which deals damage to you which could kill you. This only happens when you are running from right to left.
Not really much of a story to speak of. You're a hero. Go kill these things by charging at them.
Essentially a "one-button game".
Eventually, once you've beaten the dragon and gone through the difficulties several times, all you have to upgrade is your defense to continue progressing.
Despite all of the cons, I do feel as if I enjoyed it for a short while. Yet I can't quite get rid of the feeling that even with a small discount and a fairly small asking price, this game still wasn't worth the $2.70 I paid for it. I also feel as though, with the amount of work that seems to be put into the large amount of sprites for the game (which seem to be quite well done), the game could have been quite a bit larger and better than how it felt. Although, keeping in mind that this is essentially a phone game, I would still like for them to have added more content for the PC version.

Finally after getting around to enjoy all 3 kinds of experiences that the game has to offer, i can definately say im happy with this CoD.
The Singleplayer offers an incredibly stunning looking campaign experience, with various new gimicks and fun changes from the ordinary expected FPS gameplay. The Story is great, and you care for the characters, which are all very well played by the actors. Definately amongst the top entries of my CoD Campaign experiences.
The multiplayer offers the same addictive gameplay that you'd come to expect from any kind of CoD title, and i must say its great to be back on the ground for a change. The multiplayer brings many new cool aspects to the functional formular like Headquarters and War gamemode. The usual gamemodes like TDM seems less enjoyable than in previous titles, because the maps seem quite tight, but the addition of War, and some awesome objective based gamemodes, sure makes up for it.
And now the main reason i purchased this game, Zombies.
The Zombies experience is purely amazing. Being a veteran of the usual Treyarch style, gave me some advantages in how the very base of the gamemode functioned, but beyond that, everything felt challenging, new and fun. This is definately the style we need for Sledgehammers take on the Zombies Gamemode.
--The game has had its flaws at launch, with many frustrating resets, connection issues and stat-loss. BUT seeing the devs putting out everyday patches to improve and make it more stable, is very promising. So ill be sure that anyone reading this in the future will be able to experience a flawless and stable experience all around! :)

Since the Portal series is one of my favorite series of all time, when I heard about the development of this "mod" I wanted it instantly. When it did come out, I had a pretty meh PC and didn't want to play it at a low framerate, so I waited until I got a new computer to play it.
And oh my god.
This mod, which should be a standalone game, lived up to the Portal series in a way I didn't expect it to at all. The platforming is solid and the combat goes from just "okay" to "feels great" through quality upgrades across the game. (I recommend getting the double jump slash shovel upgrade first when you gain access to it.) That and an assortment of other upgrades really give you good reason to keep investing into your character.
The levels are well done with ample secrets throughout and only a small handful of spots that were lacking in the design department. You can tell the inconsistencies when looking at deaths per level as they spike across the levels instead of increasing steadily or remaining similar throughout (depending on what their intent for difficulty was).
The art is an homage to classic NES design with a nice palette and excellent animations for almost all characters in the game. The music is spot on and gets you into the feel of the game, though nothing stuck out to me as being "zomg amazeballs"; that is, I don't find myself humming any of the songs, but that doesn't mean they're not good.
Definitely check it out, there's a lot to discover and the game has some quality platforming that harkens back to yesteryear.

I will tell you my personal experience of the game instead of some "This was good and this was not"-kind of thing. First of all. I am twenty nine years old writing this. Some might wonder why a twenty nine year old play a platform game that might be more suited for an eleven year old? My brother wonders the same thing when he sees me playing these kind of games and I do too whenever I play a bad one in search of the good stuff.
Thing is. I spent a lot of hours on plattformers growing up especially most of the Mega Man games. In more recent years I been trying to find games that gives me a certain feeling that some of the old games gave me. I re-found it in Mega Man X (SNES), Donkey Kong Country (SNES) and Shatterhand (NES) for example. But most games just bores me after some time because they miss that certain something and I rather return to games more suitable for my age.. Say Red Dead Redemption (PS3) or The Walking Dead (PS3 and PC).
Shovel Knight is one of the very few games that has given me the feeling I got as a kid. Most new games which is built upon a old concept is either too easy or too hard. Often centers around being "fast" and have lots of enemies. I am not looking for a easy or hard game though. I'm looking for a good game and Shovel Knight is just that.
When I started playing it first looked like an old DOS-game and then as a cheap Mega Man rip-off but very soon I realized it was more to this game than meets the eye. As the game developed I see a whole nods to games I love.. Golden Axe, Super Mario 3, Duck Tales and even Link 2.
Between levels you choose for your own liking you can visit a town. Just as in Link 2. The difference? These towns are actually fun to walk into and is very well done.. Unlike those for Link 2. Man I hated those towns even as a kid haha. The characters you meet there actually has something useful to say and they can help you in ways that make the game easier and more enjoyable.
The Mega Man references are all over the place but they are never just "Hey, let's put this Mega Man-thing here". No. They reconstructe the ideas and make them unique. The bosses for example. In Mega Man you mostly just learn a pattern and then most are stupidly easy. These bosses, while some are easy, are much smarter and have a bunch of attacks. I have finished the game and I not even sure I saw all their moves. They just don't stand taking hits either. Put them in a dangerous position and they will eventually get out of it.
The level design is top notch. There are plenty enemies and it's the hasards that mostly kill you or offer a real challenge. You don't need to be a genius to "get" what you are supposed to do but it makes the whole experience more fun and the next scene is never too predictable. An overall great flow during the whole game.
Unlike Mega Man some unexpected things happens to the map.. Think of the axe-men in Super Mario 3. But better and offers variation. There was a "what the f**k"-moment for me in the game. Even that is explained in a good way later on. The game isn't just a one way street either. As I watched the end credits there are stuff I actually missed in the game.. Which makes a replay a welcomed experience.
So... Nothing bad to say? Well. The game is very slow... Still better than too fast. But it could have been a notch faster. And I saw myself fighting against the controls.. Those who played Duck Tales and Darkwing Duck (NES) knows what I am talking about.
In the end of the day the music drives the game forward, the level design is fantastic, the story is well done, the bosses are fun and while it reminds me of different games it still finds originality in a way most platform games don't.
To me this is right up there with all the classics in the genre. Very well done guys. Comes recommended. I'd love to see more games with a similar concept that is as well done. I'd buy that. You should too!

You wake up in a castle with a note you have written yourself. You cannot remember who or where you are, but your former self is not surprised. The note tells you that you have purposefully forgotten recent events, and that you now have one goal: find and kill a man named Alexander. You don’t know who Alexander is or why you wanted to kill him, but your note warns that you are being chased by a dark shadow that alters reality and that time will be short.
The dark shadow is a persistent threat that is never directly seen but its presence can always be felt. Earthquakes are tearing the castle apart, and odd noises can be heard coming from outside. However, these are the least of your worries as strange creatures walk the halls of the castle. The castle is impressive – a massive maze of twisting rooms  and corridors. The earthquakes are causing parts of the roof to collapse, blocking off passages and creating new ones as you play.
Light is in limited supply, as candles provide your only means of illuminating the darkness. Tinderboxes are scattered all over the castle, but you never seem to have enough. You also have a lantern that runs on oil, but even that is in limited supply. Staying in the darkness slowly drains your sanity, which is something that could easily be lost in a place like this. You need to treat light like a limited resource, otherwise you could lose your mind.
You have to stay focused and keep your wits about you. Keeping the darkness at bay is only part of the challenge, as every odd event you witness chews on your soul. Looking too long at the foul creatures could cause you to panic and reveal your position, forfeiting your only advantage: stealth.  You will find no weapons to use against the creatures in the castle. Your only choice when faced with one of them is to run or hide. You can close doors and barricade yourself in rooms, but that will only slow them down. Running fast and far away or hiding in closets or other dark corners will be your best bet for survival.
As you lose your sanity your vision becomes blurred. You might start seeing and hearing things that are not actually there. Depending on how far gone you are there might even be a delay between mouse inputs and you performing the action. Keeping your mind on the tasks at hand is the only way to preserve what little sanity you have left, as solving a puzzle completely restores your sanity.
Solving these puzzles is how you will spend a majority of your time. The castle is in very bad shape with areas that you need to get to currently inaccessible. Many of the puzzles work like classic point and click adventure games. You have to find the items that you need, combine them to create something useful, and then use the item on the environment. This might include mixing chemicals to produce an explosive to clear your path, or to fix a broken steam generator by properly setting levers and replacing gears and other broken parts. The puzzles are well designed and often make good use of the physics engine. They will require you to think things through, but are never so complicated that you will be stuck on any one for too long.
The physics engine makes interacting with the world feel pretty real. Using the mouse you actually grab on to items and move them around. Opening doors requires more than just a click, as you have to push or pull your mouse to swing the door open. Similarly, turning valves requires you to move the mouse in the correct circular motion. It creates a unique physical connection between you and the game that really helps to immerse you in its world. It also helps increase the tension a lot, especially when running from enemies where you actually have to stop and swing a door open in order to get away.
The presentation of the game is pretty solid, especially for an indie game. The graphics engine won’t necessarily impress if you have been playing a lot of big budget games, but by no means does the game look bad. The actual art in the game is pretty good. Objects have a good amount of detail, and feel authentic for the time period.  The lighting engine works well, creating believable shadows and the use of ambient occlusion adds depth to the scenes. However, the most impressive part of the presentation has to be the audio design. The audio designers clearly understand that what you cannot see is often scarier then what you can, and they provide you with some truly terrifying sounds to get your imagination working against you. The graphics and audio combine to create a game that is really rich in atmosphere.

Pros: By mod standards, this is amazing. Not glitchy, the story fits nicely into the canon for the most part, at least four hours of gameplay on your first time through (took me almost six and I consier myself a fairly competent player), and it even features original assets and its own soundtrack that are just as good as what you'd find in the official game. If you liked the original Portal Soundtrack, which is also free btw, I would recommend downloading this just for the music. Honestly, the pros should be longer, but I'm better at pointing out what could be improved than what was done right.
Cons: It didn't feel quite as polished as the original game. The loading was much more noticable, the voice acting was sub-par, it's technically not canon no matter how hard it tries to be, it had prerendered cutscenes scattered randomly throughout the story, too many achivements for dieing, and most of the test chamber solutions involved deactivating material emancipation grills.
The loading happened more frequently than the official game, and in less consistent locations. For the most part, Portal 2 had all its loading in elevators, and occasionally between weird airlock doors. It usually kept the location of the player consistent through the process, which the mod fails to do. While keeping the player's location consistent seems like it would be difficult, the level design could have been altered to smooth out the loading screens.
I didn't like the voices in this game. Virgil was kind of annoying, AEGIS was unthreatening, and, most importantly, Cave Johnson didn't sound like Cave Johnson.
The cutscenes really took me out of the moment. They were slow, often full of dialogue, and had noticably different graphics from the rest of the game. I think Portal did cutscenes way better simply by avoiding them almost completely.
Way too many achivements for dieing in specific ways. Some of them were obvious, but you really don't want more than two or three of these in a game.
In the official game, the emancipation grills are almost never shut down by the player. They are the ultimate obstacle to get around, so it's kind of strange to just be able to turn them off in most of the tests. It honestly feels like they're just padding the playtime with them, especially when the solution to so many chambers in a row is to figure out what turns them off.
Also, we had a token companion cube dropped unceremoniously into our laps.
As a final nitpick, I didn't believe Virgil when he said the water was rising. I'm not sure if it would have risen eventually, had it taken me a while to solve the test chambers, but I saw no indication that it was moving at all. It definitely needed some way to establish it as a threat. The obvious answer is a timed test chamber where the water visibly rises. It has to be obvious, even if it's slow enough to give less experienced players a fighting chance.
Overall: It's not perfect, but what do you want? It's a free DLC sized mod with a free soundtrack. If it weren't so good, I wouldn't bother pointing out what I thought could be better. Most stuff wouldn't even come close to the official game's quality, and this nearly made it.

Like many of us, I love Arma.  Yes, it has problems, framerate issues, bugs, and all the things you may have heard are indeed true.  However, over the nearly 3 years that I've been playing Arma (since June of 2014), the performance, quality and content of Arma 3 has done nothing but improve.  For me, Bohemia has never disappointed as far as Arma is concerned, and I hope that they never do.  User created content is the thing that keeps this game alive and well.  Total conversions (such as Red Hammer Studios' Armed forces of the United States, Russian Federation and Green Forces), gameplay mods (such as the Advanced Combat Environment) and user made missions using the Eden editor (the days of the 2D editor are gone!).
Arma isn't just about Mil-Sim missions and Units either, there are a ton of other things, such as several different survival modes, and RPG modes.  While I am not a fan of these modes, many people are and they've certainly formed their own community.
If you do want mil-sim, there are tons of Units and great communities for that as well, just go to the Find A Unit subreddit and start looking into one you might like to join!  Arma isn't just a game, it's a platform, and that's why you often see so many people with a ridiculous amount of hours.  There are so many games, and so many mods, you can have completely different experiences every timeyou boot up the game.
If you have the extra money, or the game is on sale, definitely get the Apex edition! It's totally worth it.  Tanoa is a great map, the Apex firearms are great, and I believe the Apex edition comes with Karts, Marksman and Helicopters as well!

I've had a lot of problems with this game.  Now I know why they were giving it away for free.  First off, the game starts out in a dinky window.  If you switch to 1080p resolution it's STILL in a window.  If you switch to fullscreen it starts off looking OK, and then winds up like the screen is zoomed in too far and you can only see about 80% of the game (which takes up 100% of the screen).
OK, so you think you should quit and start over.  CRASH.  Really Big Sky has stopped working.  Press this button to do nothing or press this other button to wait 30 seconds and THEN do nothing.  Start the game over... nope it's still zoomed in way too far.  There is just no resolution option that feels good so after a lot of fidgeting you switch back to the original windowed mode.
OK then, so let's try to actually play the game.  It gives some really hokey tutorial about how you can use one stick to move and the other stick to shoot (or alternately explains WASD and mouse) while being narrated in this really bland voice that barely stands out amongst the game's bland soundtrack.  The graphics themselves have a muted tone to them as well so it's like the whole game is trying really hard to be the visual equivalent of oatmeal or rice cakes.
I started this up thinking it would be another good shooter like Syder Arcade, but instead it came out like a really poor imitation of the genre.  Maybe I'll change my mind after more than 10 minutes with it but at the moment the game has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off so much that 10 minutes was more than enough.
EDIT:  Ok, so I have given it another run and... I still don't really recommend it.
For starters, the menu is actually kinda confusing.  There's a set of options that looks like you should be able to press a button to toggle it from one selection to the other, but any button you press will exit the menu.  Instead there's an arrow pointing in a direction and you have to press the analog stick in that direction to get it to change.  For some reason I expected it to be the opposite (that the arrow showed the current condition and pressing in the opposite direction would change it).
The game has this annoying game mechanic where you have to Drill through "planets" at random points in the game.  You accomplish this by pressing a button that brings the drill around to the front of the ship and while it's there you can't fire.
It seems like the only thing the drill is good for is certain planet sized stuff, so you can't drill through an enemy (unless it's taking up the whole screen), and in general the game has poor conveyance of what is something to be shot and what is something to be collected.  I wound up dying a few times because I thought it was a powerup to pick up and instead I collided with an enemy or something in the background.
The announcer is apparently going for the "I'm talking to you from a distance over a radio" type voice effects, but that actually made it quite hard to understand.  Combine that with the fact that he's British and sometimes I hear something that sounds like (to my American ears) "Cor Blimey, crikey he's gone off his nutter, knees up mother brown.  Off with his head, and mind your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for that barmy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Mate! Oy!" And that's if I understand anything he said at all.
The backgrounds in the game are nice to look at, but it's all quite distracting and it's hard to tell which are the important game elements and what is just scenery.  I died a couple of times to stuff I thought I should have been able to fly by.
The music is all technoish and the flashing lights are reminiscent of a rave, but it still seems very muted somehow.  So far nothing has made me feel psyched up to take on the enemy.
I don't know yet if there's a way to get the game to look good in full screen.  I didn't want to risk it crashing on me again so I made sure to play it windowed.
The game's only saving graces from what I can see are the unlockable game modes and the fact that you can use your points scored in the last game to buy stats for your ship.   At least this way you don't feel like your time was completely wasted and that you're somehow making progress.
That doesn't sound like enough to keep me interested in this game long term though.  It's good for a 10-15 minute game here and there.

Definitely check it out, there's a lot to discover and the game has some quality platforming that harkens back to yesteryear.
