I will tell you my personal experience of the game instead of some "This was good and this was not"-kind of thing. First of all. I am twenty nine years old writing this. Some might wonder why a twenty nine year old play a platform game that might be more suited for an eleven year old? My brother wonders the same thing when he sees me playing these kind of games and I do too whenever I play a bad one in search of the good stuff.
Thing is. I spent a lot of hours on plattformers growing up especially most of the Mega Man games. In more recent years I been trying to find games that gives me a certain feeling that some of the old games gave me. I re-found it in Mega Man X (SNES), Donkey Kong Country (SNES) and Shatterhand (NES) for example. But most games just bores me after some time because they miss that certain something and I rather return to games more suitable for my age.. Say Red Dead Redemption (PS3) or The Walking Dead (PS3 and PC).
Shovel Knight is one of the very few games that has given me the feeling I got as a kid. Most new games which is built upon a old concept is either too easy or too hard. Often centers around being "fast" and have lots of enemies. I am not looking for a easy or hard game though. I'm looking for a good game and Shovel Knight is just that.
When I started playing it first looked like an old DOS-game and then as a cheap Mega Man rip-off but very soon I realized it was more to this game than meets the eye. As the game developed I see a whole nods to games I love.. Golden Axe, Super Mario 3, Duck Tales and even Link 2.
Between levels you choose for your own liking you can visit a town. Just as in Link 2. The difference? These towns are actually fun to walk into and is very well done.. Unlike those for Link 2. Man I hated those towns even as a kid haha. The characters you meet there actually has something useful to say and they can help you in ways that make the game easier and more enjoyable.
The Mega Man references are all over the place but they are never just "Hey, let's put this Mega Man-thing here". No. They reconstructe the ideas and make them unique. The bosses for example. In Mega Man you mostly just learn a pattern and then most are stupidly easy. These bosses, while some are easy, are much smarter and have a bunch of attacks. I have finished the game and I not even sure I saw all their moves. They just don't stand taking hits either. Put them in a dangerous position and they will eventually get out of it.
The level design is top notch. There are plenty enemies and it's the hasards that mostly kill you or offer a real challenge. You don't need to be a genius to "get" what you are supposed to do but it makes the whole experience more fun and the next scene is never too predictable. An overall great flow during the whole game.
Unlike Mega Man some unexpected things happens to the map.. Think of the axe-men in Super Mario 3. But better and offers variation. There was a "what the f**k"-moment for me in the game. Even that is explained in a good way later on. The game isn't just a one way street either. As I watched the end credits there are stuff I actually missed in the game.. Which makes a replay a welcomed experience.
So... Nothing bad to say? Well. The game is very slow... Still better than too fast. But it could have been a notch faster. And I saw myself fighting against the controls.. Those who played Duck Tales and Darkwing Duck (NES) knows what I am talking about.
In the end of the day the music drives the game forward, the level design is fantastic, the story is well done, the bosses are fun and while it reminds me of different games it still finds originality in a way most platform games don't.
To me this is right up there with all the classics in the genre. Very well done guys. Comes recommended. I'd love to see more games with a similar concept that is as well done. I'd buy that. You should too!

What really sets this game apart is the use of audio-visual effects to simulate the feeling of uneasiness in the dark while having to light your own way as you descend further into darkness; it's pretty cool. I have to be honest, I was startled a couple times. I played it in the dark with headphones as recommended.
In all fairness, the ending was a let down. I anticipated more than what I got. I expected it to get more scary, more difficult to remain sane and keep yourself out of darkness. I was never at risk to run out of flint/oil as both were abundant and not actually necessary most of the time. Descension stopped before my own imagined darker depths came.
Despite my disappointments I would recommend this game to anyone who appreciates gaming. It's really obvious that Amnesia pioneers horror immersion. It showcases the potential for new games that could be scary as hell.

EDIT: a couple years after I gotta change my thumbs up for a solid not recommend, after rereading my own review. Guessing I gave it a yes because I paid £1 for it (normal asking price of £2), but even like that this game has nothing other than cute art and I don't wanna mislead anyone about Loot Hero DX. There's no content, no challenge, no mechanics, nothing. Any idle game out there will offer you more for free. A big fat no, get a coffee with whipped cream on top with that money instead.
ORIGINAL REVIEW: To make it perfectly clear, this game is recommendable if you like cute, extremely casual action with absolutely no depth nor complications. It's addictive and fun in short bursts, and the mechanics get repetitive in around 10 minutes. Loot Hero was born for android and many people, such as me, got it in cheap bundles or offers all over the Internet. But then again, for the price of an oreo milkshake you pretty much know that beforehand.
You run towards the right side of the screen automatically attacking enemies with your lance, until you make it to the boss and kill it the same way, repeteadly bouncing into it, then go to the next level. At points during the levels you'll find inns in which you'll be able to spend gold obtained by your kills in upgrading your stats. There's only 10 levels, the last one having as a boss a dragon; once you slay the dragon, everything sort of resets, only with tougher enemies and bosses, and you keep your stats. And so on and on and on, presumibly without and end.
So, long story short, Loot Hero DX will give you a few hours of fun, trading cards and an easy set of achievements, if you're interested in this kind of games and also in achievements that is. I  recommend it while making that very clear, as I'm a sucker for achievement hunting myself :p

A detour from the lackluster previous editions where the focus was placed on over the top futuristic weaponry. This Call of Duty takes you back to the beginning to what made the series great in the first place.
The campaign is forgetful, but no one buys this game for the campaign. The zombies mode calls for coordination between players, which is what it's meant to be in the first palce. You can't just expect to last long buy shooting everything that's in front of you. Extremely fun with a squad of friends.
The online multiplayer, however, is where this game shines above most. The nostalgia of the weapon selections really brings you back. The maps are a nice variety, and there really isn't a big learning curve on any of them. You just have to get over the fact that you'll always play against hackers, dropshotters, and people that carry MP-40s on every class. But it wouldn't be COD without them.
Highly recommended 10/10

Not my kind of music. Weird techno-pop-trance♥♥♥♥♥♥going on.
Several vehicles to choose from. They differ in speed and handling. You can paint cars and/or put stickers on them!
Absolutely perfect. In the main story (kind of) area, there are buildings, roads and objects scattered around for your pleasure. A lot of different objects to drift around, through, under and between. Then there are also drift tracks.
*Mountain drift: No laps, you just go downwards while drifting as much as you can.
*Driftkhana: No laps. A closed off area where you perform drift moves (donuts, jumps, slaloms, drifts) until the timer runs out.
*Drift curcuit: Run 3 laps around while performing drift moves.
Collect points for each drift move. More angle and more speed mean more points. You can chain drifts. Careful for if you lose control, you crash. When you crash, you bank your current points but lose your streak.
There 6 areas, each requiring you to complete a number of tasks before unlocking the gate to the next area. Tasks vary between collecting things, completing certain drift moves, jumping over obstacles and some other stuff.
There are online leaderboards for all tracks. Try to go higher on each track and see how you fare compared to the general Steam population.
For the lack of good drifting games out there, and my love for drifting games, I give this game a solid 8/10. The reason for the 8 is, the lack of a proper story/mission/campaign thing, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ music.

Though I'm old enough, I didn't grow up playing the sort of games that inspired Shovel Knight.  As a result, I have no particular nostalia for its aesthetics, but I found it damn charming anyway.  Great art and animation, and fantastic music.  The developers' choice to limit themselves to an 8-bit palette, while ignoring other technical limitations of the era, works well and I find the design more cohesive than pretty much any other throwback pixel art game I've played.
The game is difficult by modern standards, but certainly nowhere near a "masocore" platformer.  Ultimately, I really enjoyed how it played despite a few frustrating bits.  The fact that the character control feels just about perfect in terms of respoviness goes a long way to mitigating the challenge.  I'm guessing the game is actually quite forgiving in comparsion to many of the games it pays homage to, but I think it's just right in terms of proving a challenge that feels like it can be overcome without requiring so much practice it stops being entertainment.
Before buying, I was unsure about the game because of that difficulty and because I have no particular reverance for it's ancestors, but I'm very glad I gave it a shot.  While it's not a game that I think is going to be especially memorable for me, I ended up enjoying it a lot.

This game is like a typical Michael Bay movie. Your expectations aren't high but in the end you're still let down.
I was hoping for a more updated version of Call of Duty: World at War. This game however is a clear console port. The graphics are okay though and there's actually a lot of graphics options which surprised me. They’ve even included a FOV slider which is great. The headquarters lobby system and the different unlockable outfits, skins and whatever are a great way to keep you interesting. Were it not that the multiplayer is a complete shitefest. The maps are pretty much all horrible. Only in Call of Duty can there be a close quarter map with trenches where you’ll still able to walk around for minutes without finding someone to shoot at. Somehow Battlefield games run fine with 60 people on a single server. Call of Duty still uses the same horrible P2P hosting service and limits you to 6 versus 6 matches on maps that aren’t fit for it in my opinion. Enjoy getting shot around corners or getting killed by people teleporting around the map who look like they’re playing on a phone line out of the civil war affected part of Syria.
The ship map is probably the worst Call of Duty experience I’ve ever had, and that actually means a lot. It looks like they tried to recreate a map similar to Wet Work in MW1. However, they failed hilariously. Everyone just stays in spawn with their sniper rifle and is fine with ending a TDM getting 3 kills and 3 deaths total. This is probably the last Call of Duty I’ll ever buy. I think they’ve completely lost all the charm that made MW1, WaW and even MW2 great games. And I’m not playing on a console, give us dedicated servers if you want your playerbase to keep playing the game. It’s not that difficult.
And kindly take your season pass and shove it somewhere. I feel like I should be payed to keep playing this game in the future. Not the other way around. So if it wasn’t clear yet, I definitely do not recommend buying this game if you’re looking for a fun WW2 FPS. Furthermore, usually Call of Duty games have a simple but fun singleplayer campaign. The story is never great and all the action is scripted. Still it is a lot of fun to play through it. In this case there really isn't much of a story and there's no character development. I can remember Gaz or Ghost dying and being upset. In this campaign everyone is just a typical 2D American soldier without any depth or backstory besides the main character. The pre rendered cut scenes looked great though. So they do have that going for them.
You’re better off buying a cheap World at War key somewhere. 4/10, Activision can suk mi cok.

This is indeed the difinitive version of the game.  The iPad version had less levels and features (At least when I played it last.) and eventually with a fully powered up character it also suffered some bad framerate issues.  However, there is none of that in this STEAM version and it runs perfectly well and smooth.
What you see in the trailer is literally what you get.  You traverse maps unendingly slaying monsters and endlessly leveling up.  That feeling alone is intense and satisfying and of course watching the stats going up and the feeling of forever getting stronger is quite fun.
Yes the game is very basic.  It is esentially one large leveling treadmill, but, depending on who you are, you might really enjoy it.  I can tell you for sure that 100%-ing it will take you around 2.5 hours and after that the game does indeed go on for all intents and purposes -- infinitely.  So you can revisit it again and again and eventually you will become so strong that you cannot even see what is happening on the screen any longer.  Your little dude is basically his own Intercontinental Ballistic Missile at that point, and it is hilarious to watch.
So if you like leveling up for leveling up's sake, buy it.  If not, don't.  Simple math really.
It definitely is a shame that people are reviewing this mini-gem negatively and talking about refunds, because really, it's just a great little game that will take you no more than 2.5 hours to finish and that you may come back to and play again one day.  IT'S 2 DOLLARS PEOPLE!  Many shames-on-you if you're even THINKING about refunding it.  We are essentially talking about a bottle of pop here.  And really you're cheating the poor developer because their game costs next to nothing and can be beaten within the time limit that STEAM still allows for refunds.  Which is a pretty disturbing loophole as far as this game is concerned and if you end up abusing it -- that's pretty sick and rather low in perfect honesty.
Oh well.  I'll be KEEPING my copy because I actually LOVE THIS GAME!

Resident Evil 5 carries on what Resident Evil 4 brilliantly reinvented. Survival Horror with a more action focused twist. This time the story takes place in Africa following Resident Evil veteran, Chris Redfield and newbie, Sheva Alomar, as they intercept a black market bioweapon deal. What follows is the situation going from bad to worse as they encounter series antagonist Albert Wesker.
Where Resident Evil 5 differs from the previous games in the series is it's use of co-op.  You could play the game by yourself and rely on the AI partner, but that's more terrifying than anything you'll find in this game. The AI will recklessly use health and ammo without a care in the world leaving you in serious trouble when it comes down to a tough encounter with a pack of enemies. Where it shines is if you play it with a friend, Resident Evil 5 is probably one of the best co-op games out there with a challenging, and reasonably sized campaign which will see you and your friend constantly communicating and relying on each other to get over difficult challenges.
Even though the game came out in 2009, the graphics still hold up well today and the game's soundtrack is what you'd expect of a Resident Evil title. You've got your typical "creepy lab" track, but you also have tracks that fit the African setting. The game also comes with Mercenaries mode, where you (and a partner) have to kill as many enemies to gain points in a time limit, but it's probably one of the weaker parts of the game and not really worth spending much time on. Resident Evil 6's mercenaries mode is a lot better.
Summing up, if you have a friend to play Resident Evil 5 with, then you can't ask for a better experience, especially if you play it on one of the harder difficulties. Playing by yourself is frustrating and not a lot of fun, so perhaps you should try Resident Evil 4 if you're by yourself.

Written after two free roam playthroughs using a controller once and keyboard once:
After seeing this game on sale for the winter sale I decided that I should buy it. The two things that caught my eye were first, drifting. As someone who considers themself a fan of drifting I was really interested in the physics of how the drifting was especially in comparison to my favorite game to drift which is Forza.  The second thing is the art. The art behind the game is incredibly minimalist, the simplicity caught my eye because it rivals Mirrors Edge almost perfect in style and coloring.  That being said I took the dive on and indie game, which is something I do not do often.
Currently, I have spent most of my time playing the freeroam, and just want to address that as of now. I will certainly come back for an edit with more of my opinion based on the "events".  The freeroam alone is great. The settings within the game are really quite enjoyable while work perfectly with the concept of the game. The missions you do aren't to insane, most are easy and they are more of a relaxing type of fit for the game. As someone who generally likes games to be more difficult it was kind of disappointing, but it seems like that will really take affect later in the "event" section.
The physics of the game is amazing.  I really enjoyed how drifting felt from a top down view and found that it wasn't too difficult to grasp but was hard enough that I really liked to get to know the way it works.  I would say, that the physics are on par with other "simulation" games, like Forza. They are more forgiving certainly, but for this genre it works perfectly!
The other thing I would really like to talk about is the controls. I have seen some other reviews addressing them and say really this game is best with a controller and how the keyboard is definetly worse. So I started the game using a xbox one controller. I really enjoyed it and I found it was much easier to learn off the bat and was easily grasped.  The thing I would like to say is as great as the controller was, I personally enjoyed using my keyboard much more. For some reason, the controller felt much "slower" as in, i felt like the car it self was slow in response and speed (not in a bad way, it was just different than the keyboard), so when I played through a second time I decided to use the keyboard. The controls are extremely simple, the hardest thing is just getting used to how to multitask and use multiple buttons all at the same time.  For instance, it is weird using all of the arrow keys when counter-steering it is possible to oversteer or understeer so you have to make micro adjustments while still throttling and handbraking. So that was hard to grasp immediately, but after 10 minutes or so, it becomes great! I really enjoyed using the keyboard to play, actually even more than the controller.
The only con is the length of the game, it is quite easy to just zip right through the freeroam mode, but if you are someone who likes games that rely on leaderboards than this is certainly a good option.  Although it is short, I will say that replay value of free roam in my opinion is quite high because you wont remember all of the missions unless you have a photographic memory.
Overall, if you are looking for a good drifting game with a great physics engine and beautiful art (including music as well) you have found it right here.  I would say this is a must purchase driving game!

The retro aesthetic is interesting, and Shovel Knight strictly limits itself by sticking to authentic color, sound, and control layout limitations. It also strictly nails the gameplay, which is something not all retro-aesthetic indie games do these days. It doesn't rely on a quirk, twist, or gimmick: it's just sheer refined action platformer.
The gamecraft on display here is excellent, everything from the character design, limited but fun story, level design, and especially the original score are all among the very best even of games today, to say nothing of the old-school games it's meant to evoke.
Shovel Knight is a game that clearly knows what it's doing. It chose to be the best damn retro action platformer ever made - no more, no less - and it very well may have done just that.

I just finished the game for the first time, and took me almost exactly 6 hours.
Shovel Knight is a oldschool Sidescroller. Think of of a combination between the old Megaman, Castlevania and Ducktales Games. You have a Stage Selection, and each Stage features a unique Boss and has its own unique design. No stage feels the same, and i had tons of fun exploring everything. On your journey you will find several different items, like a magic wand that casts fireballs, or a special sword that allows a mid-air forward dash. These item function like the castlevania items, so each item consumes a different amount of magic - which can be refilled during the stage by finding restoration items. (Food for HP, Flasks for Mana)
The controlls and combat feels very fluid. You can reflect enemy projectiles with good timing, hack away or use your shovel as a pogo stick Ducktales style to get rid if your enemies. You will find a lot of gems, but instead of being just a means to reach a highscore, they are essentially a currency for certain upgrades. More HP and more Mana are nobrainers, but you can also upgrade your shovel and armor. For instance, you can unlock a charged slash.
Im a sucker for sidescrollers, so i absolutly loved this game. For those of you that are new to this genre, i can recommend it. Its not as unforgiving as the classic sidescrollers out there, while still offering a decent challenge. The Artstyle of course, is something you either love or hate. I for one, love it.
Soo, the gameplay is good, the graphics are pretty...sounds good, doesnt it? Yes. In fact, i only have three issues with this game. Nothing gamebreaking, but certainly worth mentioning.
First is the lenght. I dont know if its because im not that bad at these kind of games, but 6 hours feel kinda short. There is a NG+ Mode though.
Secondly, although challenging, most of the later bossfights are a lot easier than the stage itself. They can and will kill you if you dont pay attention, but they are by far not the biggest challenge in the game.
Last but certainly not least, being somewhat of a nod towards oldschool sidescrollers, the game suffers from "CKS. Castlevania Knockback Syndrom". Each hit will send you back a couple of inches, and - if youre unlucky - straight into a pit. To be fair, most of the time this is not a issue. Like, at all. That is expect for one part:
Disclaimer: This part of the review contains minor spoilers for the endboss
Other than that, i have no complaints. Its certainly worth its price.

This is the third game in the Assassin's Creed series; this time you pick Desmond's story where it was left in Assassin's Creed II by reliving Ezio's memories in Roma. This time you will be in one city carrying out quests all over Roma (which is huge, by the way).
Great additions/improvements for this game; let's start with:
- The combat system was improved, giving you the opportunity to see Ezio's fighting abilities giving an improved and rewarding experience, in other words was improved 4 or 5 times compared to the previous games in the series.
- Fast traveling is included as well, of course it's a big city, it will be really annoying to be running and running to travel from point A to point B and even though you can do it, you've the option to save minutes or even hours of travel.
- Lots and lots of content which will keep you busy; the main and side quest have an optional way to complete them in order to have full synchronization (if you want to complete the game 100%).
- and such much more (don't really want to spoil it for you)...
Unlike the previous games, this game have a multiplayer mode; a really fun and interesting one (when you find people to play it, because sometimes you can be waiting around 10 or 15 mins for people to join). I had fun hours playing multiplayer; which have several modes were in most of them is not how many people you kill, but the way you get the kills, the more sneaker is the way you do it, the more points you get.
In the end, I had a blast playing both single and multiplayer modes!! This is a good installment and recommended by me if you like the Assassin's Creed series!...

Were it not for the fact that I enjoy this game due to the potential it has, and how many little things can change the outcome of a game, I'd recommend against getting this game because of the scarcity of updates and its mostly communiity-based content being released, instead of actually new maps or weapons. Sure, the Jungle Inferno update dropped a few new weapons, and lets you get them for free through the use of the contract system that's been in the game for a while now, but it's relatively stale content with a new paintjob.
Don't get me wrong, I still enjoy playing Team Fortress 2. You've got your basic Quick Play games, which on their own are most of the time just as enjoyable as a rollercoaster (depending on who you are). You've also got your Jump servers, your Trade servers, your... ugh...
servers... You can even team up with friends and destroy hoards of robots! There's many things that you could do, even if you didn't want to jump into a game and murder aimlessly for fun.
That being said, it's a shame that from most of the time I've been playing this game, I've seen only a few scarce
updates. And I'm not talking about Scream Fortress, since that's an event. I'm talking about how hard the TF Dev team appears to be trying, but due to the man(n)power limits, they are unable to get as much done as other companies. I mean, it's just so... disheartening. Most of the updates either consist of skins, cosmetics, or  both. And yes, I'm aware of how redundant it is to complain about cosmetics in a game that has an entire
based around said cosmetics. I'm simply displeased with the amount of original-to-community content we get. I shouldn't be complaining about it, since the people whose items get put into the game work hard, almost excruciatlingly so, but I feel that it's only so often we get
items, not just another beard for Heavy or another edgy mask for Sniper.
Overall, though, I'd say get the game. My dissatisfaction is simply how I feel about the game's content and updates, but that alone shouldn't dissuade you from wanting to download and install. Most of the people you'll meet playing TF2 are insanely nice, and will make you want to continue to play, or get better, or perhaps both. If you enjoy having something to do in spare time, or something to do as a means of competitive play, I'd say this is a game you should definitely check out.

Frustrating at first... and then frustrating some more, but in a good way?  Rather than a case of easy to learn hard to master, this slightly fiddly, really quite accurate, drift simulator is tricky throughout.  As someone who sends a fair bit of time sideways in real life, I'd say these guys have made a really good job of capturing that feeling of desperately trying to maintain angle in order to snap the rear back the other way and transition into another drift.
The game relies heavily on the desire to achieve that perfect run of 3 laps of well timed transition and big fast sweeping drifts.  Great until you actually manage said run, and then you're left feeling a bit lost as you're unlikely to ever best it, by much at least.
A great toy, but requires something a little more in terms of aims/objectives/direction to make it into a truly great game.  If you like your sideways this is definietly worth a look, as long as you are prepared to persevere long enough to glean some satisfaction from neat drifts!

I just finished the game for the first time, and took me almost exactly 6 hours.
Shovel Knight is a oldschool Sidescroller. Think of of a combination between the old Megaman, Castlevania and Ducktales Games. You have a Stage Selection, and each Stage features a unique Boss and has its own unique design. No stage feels the same, and i had tons of fun exploring everything. On your journey you will find several different items, like a magic wand that casts fireballs, or a special sword that allows a mid-air forward dash. These item function like the castlevania items, so each item consumes a different amount of magic - which can be refilled during the stage by finding restoration items. (Food for HP, Flasks for Mana)
The controlls and combat feels very fluid. You can reflect enemy projectiles with good timing, hack away or use your shovel as a pogo stick Ducktales style to get rid if your enemies. You will find a lot of gems, but instead of being just a means to reach a highscore, they are essentially a currency for certain upgrades. More HP and more Mana are nobrainers, but you can also upgrade your shovel and armor. For instance, you can unlock a charged slash.
Im a sucker for sidescrollers, so i absolutly loved this game. For those of you that are new to this genre, i can recommend it. Its not as unforgiving as the classic sidescrollers out there, while still offering a decent challenge. The Artstyle of course, is something you either love or hate. I for one, love it.
Soo, the gameplay is good, the graphics are pretty...sounds good, doesnt it? Yes. In fact, i only have three issues with this game. Nothing gamebreaking, but certainly worth mentioning.
First is the lenght. I dont know if its because im not that bad at these kind of games, but 6 hours feel kinda short. There is a NG+ Mode though.
Secondly, although challenging, most of the later bossfights are a lot easier than the stage itself. They can and will kill you if you dont pay attention, but they are by far not the biggest challenge in the game.
Last but certainly not least, being somewhat of a nod towards oldschool sidescrollers, the game suffers from "CKS. Castlevania Knockback Syndrom". Each hit will send you back a couple of inches, and - if youre unlucky - straight into a pit. To be fair, most of the time this is not a issue. Like, at all. That is expect for one part:
Disclaimer: This part of the review contains minor spoilers for the endboss
Other than that, i have no complaints. Its certainly worth its price.

This game mirrors the classic Mega Man in gameplay, level design and enemies but comparisons end there as this game has its own fantasy mythos. Its self-imposed artistic limitations may make you question the asking price, but there is a fair amount of content hiding within Shovel Knight.
Your attack has a recoil, which will make enemies with lots of health the bane of your existence. You also move rather slowly. Default configuration for controllers may lead to you misusing your magic.
This game does not go on sale as often as you'd think, and is not as discounted as it probably should be. It has been a part of many off-site bundles, but the sales here are paltry. Before I say anything, I should probably mention that I've never played the first two installment of the Saints Row series. I tried but couldn't. It was odd in few ways. But I enjoyed Saints Row: The Third a lot. Now let me break it down brick by brick and explain you why.
You like Grand Theft Auto? Me too. This game is basically that. Open world, third-person shooter sandbox. But somehow it feels different. It's more enjoyable and fluent. And it's way more funnier than any other GTA game. Characters and voice acting are hilarious. Cutscenes and dialogs are amazing and rich, they have a lot of references to other stuff and well, they're really funny. I found myself smiling or cracking up in almost every cutscene.
It has a good map, fairly well story and great customization capability. You can customize your character's face, body, voice and special moves (dance and taunt move, they're really awesome as well). Also you can buy clothes and wear whatever you want. Talking about wearing a thong and a bra while playing a muscular bald guy with goatee beard. You can steal vehicles and store them in your garage. Later you can modify the cars by adding body parts, changing their color etc. It's really fun. There is a shortage of cars though. They're like ten cars around, maybe? But it's not a big deal, we're not playing a racing game after all. There are a lot of weapons and upgrades as well. Game also has experience and level system which anyone can easily like. As you progress and gain levels, you can upgrade your character and crew with paying in-game money that you earn from various ways.
Co-op is great. Although if you don't have any friends to play with, you can always play solo. It's not a big game changer. Also game has few bugs but nothing serious. Just some minor glitches and save issues.
To sum up I'll say that it is a great game.

Plants vs Zombies is an old game that still holds it's own. The setting is your house where you are in charge of planting mutant plants to defend your home from zombies. You meet only one other character called Crazy Dave, 'cause his shop is, "Crazy!" This tower defense game will challenge your mind as you progress to more difficult levels. What Pop Cap Games had created is a game that is one of the most addictive of it's kind.
You won't grow tired with Plants vs Zombies as there is a variety of plants (towers) to use. Each plant can be used tactically, like using a Hypno-Shroom against a zombie. Just as the plants name implies it hypnotizes the zombie to fight for your side, obviously recommended for tougher enemies . There are plenty of other plants of it's ilk in this game to meet your strategic need.
Plants vs Zombies has plenty of other challenges like, mini-games, puzzles and survival modes. The mini-games range from plant zombies that shoot back at you, to playing whack-a-zombie. The puzzle mode gives you a chance to play in different modes as the zombies or a breaking a pot game. (Where is Link when you need him?) Survival mode is similar to adventure mode; it just has more challenging levels. Then, there is a Zen Garden you can unlock as you progress through adventure mode. The goal there is to make a money farm for your grinding and to help grow a talking tree. So, yes plenty of other things to do long after you have finished adventure mode.
All in All

6 people go in, how many will come out? 2 people are infected with a disease that when they drink 6 units of blood located around the map area they can transform into a flesh deamon. These deamons can see in the dark and find the hiding people who would have been your friends had they been infected too. Instead, they're LUNCH! The other 4 must escape in a 3 stage maze of fuses and power loss. Go from one area to the next each phase offers a day phase where the infected people cannot transform. Once the lights go out, if they have enough blood power they can transform and kill one person. When the lights come back on, they transform back to normal and everyone can move up to the next stage. On the third stage, when the lights go out, you can open the escape hatch and then blood or not, the infected can transform on you and hunt you down until you escape or die.
How do you know who is infected? Simple, look for someone drinking blood. Wait... did he just drink blood? Can you convince your 4 other friends who aren't infected that he did and needs to be killed? Devices like scanners can tell you who is infected, but no one else can see what you see. You could be lying, you could be setting someone up because YOU are infected. Trackers will help you find people and watch when they transform, but maybe they don't transform. Instead they convince your friends that you must die...
The game possibilities are endless and entirely up to you how you.
Cons:
You will have a difficult time finding games until more people get the game.
You will ruin friendships over this game... just remember its a game. Grab a drink with your buddies and laugh at their expense later.

That's right, you might've guessed it: HEALTH DROPS!!!!!! I'm so happy this element has been reintroduced hah. Sledgehammer does it in a pretty nice way too, and I mean nice. Instead of only finding the drops on the map, and sometimes not for a long time - like in Finest Hour and the first CoD - you can have an ally that gives you some, and you can take them whenever you need them. I like this. It's not necessarily forgiving, but a better use, and introduction, of a "new" health system that replaces the slow regeneration.
Another thing I've noticed is that there are some callbacks to earlier games, either in the mission and map design, or in the plot, and that's awesome!
I have yet to play multiplayer, since I have always preferred to play the campaign before going into the extra features of a game. I will most likely update my review when the time comes.
For now though; excellent job Sledgehammer!

One of the best Resident Evil games to play with a friend or significant other. I highly recommend playing this game in co-op because that's where this game shines. I've been playing it since it came out on the xbox 360 and ps3, and still playing it to this day. This is one of those games that has aged rather well, the graphics still look great and the game is as fun as ever. The horror factor may be mostly gone, but it took the gameplay elements that made RE4 a masterpiece and improved on them. You may not get chills from playing this game, but you'll definitely get thrills.

Overall, I would recommend this game - it's not perfect, but it's a nice, refreshing take on those old-school, isometric-view racing games. As the name suggests, the focus is on drifting, not lap times. The controls are good with the Xbox 360 gamepad and getting used to the drifting mechanics are what's most difficult. From there, it's drifting accurately that becomes the game since many courses are tight and don't allow much room for error.
The soundtrack is great, the visuals are unique and refreshing, and it's easily one of those games where you can play a couple of quick sessions or play for hours trying to top your high score. There's no multiplayer, but there is a good leaderboard and after each session you'll know what you scored and how you rank worldwide.
My only problem is limited customization of the cars - you can change between a few basic paint colours and patterns, and there are only six cars. Each car has its own unique characteristics and chances are you'll only end up using a couple for the majority of your runs. Given the leaderboard system, I don't expect performance modifications, but greater visual customization would be nice, although it's far from being a gamebreaker.
The core game itself (the free-roam mode) can be finished very quickly (like, an hour), it's the pursuit of accuracy and precision that keeps you coming back. It's a casual game, but you need to play it more than casually if you want to link up sweet drifts through a complete tour of a track.

If you decide to pay for prem or dlcs you will be rewarded with a faster and easier leveling experience. This is standard for FTP games, and anyone who complains of pay to win, probably expects things to come easy in life.

Credits are rewarded for catching and keeping fish, the bigger the fish, the more money you get (this may be per fish species I am not sure at this point.) Kickstarter took off in 2012 when Double Fine announced a new adventure game from creator Tim Schafer. Everyone now had a way to directly fund games they were interested in without handing money over to greedy, faceless corporations. Double Fine faultered, though, and didn't manage to release their game for 2 years.
Many other developers went to Kickstarter with their ideas for titles and nothing came to fruition. It was seeming to be that indie devs found a way to bank off idealistic consumers. Why produce a full fledged product when you can just ask for money and run away?
Yacht Club Games came up with Shovel Knight and promptly went to Kickstarter. While the game took a year to develop, Yacht Club Games were intent on not deceiving their customers. They wanted to provide the best possible nostalgic throwback game that they could.
While not every stretch goal is currently included in the game, Shovel Knight is a rousing success for the indie dev. Not only is this better than most of it's inspirations, but it also trumps practically every game released in 2014. I can't think of the last time I had this much fun with an indie game.
Making liberal use of the Mega Man mold, Shovel Knight features 8 knights that stand in your way of saving your beloved, Shield Knight. The levels are constructed in a manner similar to the classic Capcom series with a bit more secret areas thrown in.
An interesting Dark Souls-esque death system is also in place. You can upgrade Shovel Knight with extra health, magic and new weapons, but that all requires gold. If you die in any level, you lose a decent chunk of gold that can be retrieved upon reaching the place of your burial. If you die before getting there, you can kiss that gold goodbye.
An overworld in the vein of Super Mario Bros 3 is also present. Random encounters occur and there are extra, bonus areas that lead to more gold and some upgrades. The amount of bonus stuff is pretty staggering. Considering it almost all has a point in furthering your character, it makes for some intense and engaging extra material.
The difficulty curve is also superbly handled. While I can't say the final area is the most difficult, the game progresses from fairly brainless to pixel perfect platforming while constantly giving you hints within the level design for what is coming next. There are no pointless, extraneous tutorials at all. This is gaming bliss.
The only downside I can think of is that none of the relics you use for weapons have much purpose. They certainly help, but bosses have no weaknesses and no level demands the use of them. You can beat the game without picking up a single one and nothing would change, apart from some platforming being harder.
The system used to change relics is also a little cumbersome. While a quick select has been patched in, pausing the action to pick a weapon a-la Mega Man just kind of breaks the flow up. I know the Wii U and 3DS versions allow you to simply tap the gamepad/touchscreen to swap without stopping, but there isn't much that can be done for the PC version.
Overall, you can't really go wrong with Shovel Knight. It's a fantastic platformer that more than deserves the praise it has gotten. Fantastic music and visuals and pristine controls make this game hard to put down. The achievements are even fun, which is rare now-a-days.

I got this game when it was offered for free and have no regrets.
If you like bullet hell, shoot-em-up style gameplay, then you will really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are wonderful, it reminds me a lot of geometry wars with all the crazy special effects. There is a lot of color and it can be overwhelming at times - the high activity on the screen can make it difficult to track where you are, enemy projectices, etc. The music is very good and adds to the intensity of the gameplay.
The controls are very simple, and the learning curve is minimal. There is a tutorial in the beginning of the game that is quick and very helpful. I find the narrator to be a bit annoying, but it is possible to turn the narration off.
Grinding in this game is actually quite easy because you can get a lot of credits very quickly with each game session (thanks to the score multipliers). The upgrading is simple, and they are mostly offensive-based.
There is a unique mechanic in this game where you will periodically encounter planets/asteroids. To pass them, you have to switch your weapon to your drill, allowing you to travel through to the other side. Inside the planets, there will be random bonuses like increased weapon spread, ship speed, score multiplier, etc - drilling through these will give you the bonuses. While your drill is active, your weapons will also charge, allowing you to shoot massive beams when you switch back to them.
As the game progresses, there will be times where your super boost activates, propelling you forward at a blinding speed. This is easily one of the most dangerous parts, because it is very easy to crash straight into an enemy projectile, or worse, any enemy ship.
The boss battles are not too difficult, but the game remains challenging, especially when the screen is filled with weapon effects.
Very fun game, pick it up if you like shoot-em-ups.

When compared to AC2, Sisterhood to a large extent is more of the same, although it brings back some elements from AC1 (flags, begging women, citizens tackling enemies, occasional trips out of animus to read other people's emails) and adds new things, too (most importantly, you're getting to be head of assassin's guild in single player campaing; and yes, there's multiplayer added).
Instead of segmentation into many smaller cities though, the majority of the action is on one huge map (Rome) with heaps of side missions to chose from at any single moment so it has more sandboxy feeling.
I actually liked this more than AC2. Mostly due to this game having more actual "game" in it. Gamification is above all present in the missions that sport an additional requirement for 100%ing it. Sometimes it gives real challenge like time trial, sometimes it actually limits your choices to specific weapons or angles of approach but sort of works to keep things varied. And the whole sandboxy aspect is also what I liked.
'Cause yeah lack of challenge, mostly in the fights (guards actually hit harder now and there's more of them, but conversely you get more efficient ways of killing them so it's still too easy), and feel of an interactive movie instead or something, is a beef I have with the series. I guess I embraced it though by now and even started to somewhat enjoy those overpowered fights. Still missing focus on stealth, but I don't mind it either anymore (I adjusted my expectations, eh? :D some missions ask you to remain undetected but stealth never seems to be the focus, really, you just charge head on or literally flick your fingers to kill every enemy on screen)
You still gotta love the parkour, rooftop jumping aspect, raiding tombs is fun too, there's a dash of puzzling involved tho not much, and story continuing present day and Ezio's day affairs still enjoyable, even though it doesn't really touch me deep on an emotional level.
About the story... The side missions don't directly connect to the main arc of retrieving the "magic apple", they have more to do with Ezio going all "I'm gonna pull the whole thing down. I'm gonna bring the whole f*n' diseased, corrupt temple down on your head" on the Borgias or, rather, living in denial that he fudged up royally and instead explaining to everyone that you gotta have more systemic approach rather than playing the cutting-down-hydra's-heads game. First and foremost, this game is free.  (Like all free games you CAN max out your items and gear, without paying a cent.)
If you decide to pay for prem or dlcs you will be rewarded with a faster and easier leveling experience. This is standard for FTP games, and anyone who complains of pay to win, probably expects things to come easy in life.
There are 2 currencies in game Gold and Credits
Gold cannot be purchased directly in game, It is rewarded for playing the game or issued with some of the dlcs, but not able to be purchased as a single item.
Gold gives you access to reels and rods and baits that are far better than most currency items.
Credits are rewarded for catching and keeping fish, the bigger the fish, the more money you get (this may be per fish species I am not sure at this point.) You are limited to how many fish you can keep per day by your fish stringer/net. Buy a dlc pack ($4.99) with a large keeper net and you can fish all day and make money by having a large amount of fish storage.
The Game:
If you are the type of person that wants to spend no money and rush and out level everyone as fast as possible in a fishing game, that is sad, and this game is not for you.
If you enjoy awesome visuals, lifelike water, the relaxing enjoyment of fishing, not expecting to catch a monster every cast, buy this game. It ROCKS!
Seriously, If you take the time to read about each rod and reel and bait and match them accordingly, you will catch more fish than someone who throws 30lb line on a reel made for 9lb line, with the wrong bobber, casting in the wrong areas, at the wrong time of day, and complains the game sux when thier reel breaks, you will rewarded with one hell of a fishing simulator.
There are some bugs, but none that are even close to gamebreaking at this point 6/10/16

Is Shovel Knight a good game? Certainly, there's almost no denying that. Is it a great game? ...not really.
Instead of the standard "omg so amazing" reviews that don't help anyone, I'm only going to focus on the problems, because everyone else has already pointed out the posititves.
The first problem is the over-reliance on instadeath prevalent in the second half of the game. By that point you have a lot of health and magic and presumably a lot of items. Thus, running out of HP becomes a lot rarer, especially since the frequency of full-heal chickens never decreases. The only way they can kill you with any efficiency in a standard run is to have lots of instadeath, INCLUDING in four boss fights. And instant death is about the only way any of those bosses are going to kill you too.
Basically, the game just ends up overly punishing. I understand needing to ramp up the difficulty but when an enemy comes out of nowhere you knock you off/push you off a platform into a pit/lava several times in the second half of the game, I don't feel like I did anything wrong as much as I was just screwed over by the game. Knockback is the biggest killer at that point, and the enemy placement is set up not so much to hurt you as to instakill you. The final tower levels feature almost nothing but instakill traps, including a long moving walls/crusher section, a long platform-riding section, and a long vertical autoscrolling section. Propeller Knight's stage suffers from this as well, and Polar Knight has quite a lot of spikes throughout his stage.
They're really good about keeping the difficulty balanced throughout most of the game but at this point it becomes too punishing and mostly about trial and error. Checkpoints are frequent enough and there's no lives or game over, which makes trial-and-error gameplay a bit less problematic, but doesn't excuse it entirely.
Spectre Knight's stage also has a few problems, namely the over-reliance on the darkness gimmick. Something around half the level has it, including the boss, which is a bit too much for that kind of gimmick, I feel, especially when it mostly serves to, again, instakill you. Not as frequent as later levels, but still. The stage is a bit of a difficulty spike compared to the intro stage and King Knight's stage, the only other level available at the time.
Plague Knight's fight is too intense and challenging for where it is in the game, I consider him the hardest boss even with full stats and you have to fight him before the halfway point of the game, where you don't have max HP or items.
The Wandering Traveller boss fights don't feel as polished as most of the game, either, which makes some sense given that they were made by kickstarter backers at least to some extent, but I feel they'd be more memorable and more fun with a bit more polish to them. Baz is especially bad, probably the worst boss in the game, but none of them I found as enjoyable as the main stage bosses.
The "lose money when you die" system is good in the sense that it rewards players for not dying, but it also overly punishes players who are struggling with the stage, preventing them from getting the tools necessary to make things easier on themselves. Arguably, there's a certain skill level where you're just not going to be able to beat the game at all, but it makes the game grindy when you have to keep replaying the easy levels just to buy upgrades and items to make the harder ones doable at all. This isn't a problem I faced myself but I can easily see many people getting frustrated over it.
I still would say I had a lot of fun with this game, but when all is said and done I'm going to remember it as "a good retro platformer" and not as "one of the greatest platformers of all time". I recommend it, certainly, but don't get overly hyped about it or you might end up disappointed.

Assassin’s Creed: Brotherhood is a direct continuation of Assassin’s Creed II, in pretty much every sense. The story picks up exactly where the last one left off (both in the past and the present), and the game mechanics are more or less identical. In some ways, the need for this game to exist seems a bit unnecessary (i.e. it feels more like the result of a corporate mandate to make an annual franchise than a creative decision). That said, it’s forgivable if only for the fact that it’s just as good as its predecessor, if not better. Part of what feels forced is the contrived story revolving around Ezio losing his Apple of Eden and having to retrieve it. But there you go... it is what it is - basically, a flimsy excuse to move to a new setting and do more cool things with a well-loved character.
The game takes place in the early 1500s, almost entirely in Rome. While that may sound like a reduced scope in setting from the prior games, it’s actually not. Rome is huge. Like, really huge. There are also a few other places that you get to explore in some of the main story missions as well, so there is plenty of variety in the environments. As usual, it’s a lot of fun just to explore the city and discover its secrets. Brotherhood also greatly expands the role of horses (you can ride them pretty much anywhere), and there are some fun combat mechanics added as well. The missions in the game are similar to those from AC2, so nothing major has changed on that front. The other primary mechanics introduced in AC2 (notoriety, blending, etc) all return here as well and are also just as good.
The main addition this game brings to the series is the titular Brotherhood. Ezio can now recruit citizens to the Assassin Brotherhood. As you progress through the game, more recruit slots are unlocked. Once recruited, you can call your Assassins to assist in combat or send them on missions in a sort of optional sub-game. Doing either of these things awards XP to the recruits and eventually they level up and become more powerful. Though hardly revelatory by any means, it’s a fun new aspect to the game and is a welcome addition.
While Assassin’s Creed: Brotherhood doesn’t really do anything groundbreaking or expand on the established formula in any major way, it is still worth playing if you enjoyed AC2. While it is essentially more of the same, at least it’s a *good* more of the same.
Grade: A-
Note: I don’t recommend playing any of the Assassin’s Creed games unless you have an Xbox360 controller (or equivalent-featured gamepad). The AC games have complicated control schemes and were clearly designed with controllers in mind, so proceed with mouse/keyboard at your own risk.

It's good in my opinion.
Multiplayer feels like it has a lot more to do now with new daily and weekly orders to do, awarding you with xp, credits and supply drops, collections to fill out by opening said supply drops and a lot of things to level up and prestiege (your soldier, guns and divisions).
Wait did I say supply drops? Yes, this game features them heavily, but before you grab your pitchforks, they are very generous with giving them out. I must have opened about 20 so far and I didn't spend any extra money on them. They also aren't too gamebreaking, you'll mostly want to open them for the collections as I mentioned earlier, but they'll also drop you some double xp in-game time (which gets used automatically, so no hoarding 1000 hours of dxp).
In terms of gameplay, it's COD, if you liked WaW and Black Ops 1 you'd like this. They got rid of the pick 10 system, so no longer do you feel like you need to give up your grenades just so you can get an extra perk. Speaking of perk, those are replaced with divisions and basic training. You pick one of each of those two, no more, no less. there are 5 divisions that you can level up 4 times each, getting new perks, then prestige them if you wish to unlock more items. Then there are roughly 28 basic training(s?) that give you a small boost, such as being able to reload faster and while sprinting, flinching less when shot or not letting enemies see skulls for your kills. Which coming from CS:GO, I appreciate since it make the playing field a bit more even, never did I feel like I missed out on a kill because I didn't have a specific division or basic training.
Zombies is a huge meh, I've only played 2 games so far, both solo, and without looking at gameplay beforehand and I already managed to make it to the final boss (died because I thought it was stunned when it wasn't). You're given a small journal in game and it tells you what step you're on, what you need to do and even outlines (through walls) what you need to interact with. I only need to search online for 1 step, the rest of it was easy. You also don't lose your perks when you go down. So if you're looking for the challenge that Black Ops 1, 2 and 3 zombies gave you with their tedious and very secret steps, this is a huge downgrade for you.
I've only played the first mission of the campaign and it's okay, but nothing I haven't seen before. Health doesn't regenerate and you can ask your squadmates for ammo and medkits, but that's about the only difference I could notice so far.

A fun little game with a GREAT soundtrack and a cool minimalist style.
The free-roam mode (the "story"-like mode) is about 90 minutes of play depending on how much you suck. Could probably be speedrun much faster. There's a bunch of drift and driftkhana tracks each with their own leaderboards, so the competitive leaderboard types of players will probably get much more than 90 minutes out of this game. The drift mechanics seem mildly accurate, for a really low-grip world.
Unfortunately the goal detection is kinda dodgy. Where you have to do donuts around an object, you actually just have to be drifting a certain angle, not even in the correct direction, within some radius of the object. You'll accidentally half-complete some objectives driving past it. Drifts to complete objectives don't have to be successful, you can slide past, tick off an objective, and then slam into the wall (the exception to this is that actually hitting clipping points doesn't give points, and donking donut objects sometimes resets them). The result of all this is that you can basically fumble your way through the whole game (you do gotta git gud for the leaderboard modes though).
Also there's a difficulty setting that seems to do nothing. I don't even know.
All up - it's a fun little toy, but it's not really a complete product.

Because the game has been abandoned doesn't mean the game is horrible just no additional patches, content, etc for this game.
Personally, I enjoy this game.  It took a bit to figure out but there's a wiki because what game doesn't have a wiki these days (
).  You can get most/all the information you need to be able to play the game here as well as access to mods or where to get mods.
I like how you're able to relocate/make resource areas to where you want them.  In a lot of these games, generally they just regrow in an area that you've already harvested or you have to craft a special/specific building to harvest any additional resources.  In this game, you can take saplings/seeds/fruit/etc and create an area where you'd like them to grow.  Flowers, trees, etc will still grow in other areas but this allows you to have say 5x5 of trees (for lumber) that will continually regrow in that exact same plot (after being chopped down, a sapling will begin to grow in it's place and after a few minutes you'll have a fully grown tree... this applies to wheat, fruit, etc.).  This makes your villagers much more efficient at gathering and better for your resource management.  It is also significantly safer than traversing the area filled with random monsters like brownies, goblins, ghosts, etc.
The big downside of the game is that a lot of people feel it isn't "finished" or "unpolished" and the lack of further development.  However, the game is fully functional and the balance may be a little off but that's easily adjustable via the xml files or mods.  Also, game can be pretty brutal at times such as when you expand a bit too early or get raided by monsters and your villagers have no armor nor weapons at their disposal in addition to their piddly health pool.
If you like these kinds of games (city building/resource management) and don't mind that there won't be able more updates then buy the game but I'd recommend waiting until it's on sale.  Even if development has stopped, there's a lot of mods for the game which add content or change texture packs, etc.

Another improvement over the previous game, and continues to wonderfully scratch the "Tomb Raider itch".  A huge amount of things to do and manage, a giant city to run around in, buildings to climb, etc, as well as a neat historic setting peppered with plenty of information on buildings, people and events.
There are problems of course, the controls don't always respond as quickly as you might like, the 100% synch challenges are more annoying than challenging, the investment system is a drag, and the scenes outside of the Animus continue to feel like irritating distractions to the "real" story of Ezio's adventures in Rome.  But they're minor problems in what is otherwise an extremely engaging game.

Lots of fun for not lots of money. Psudeo-isometric drifting game that is accessible to the beginner yet offers something for even the most experienced sim racer. This game forgoes the usual lisenced cars, awful bodykits and whiny community trying to organize endurance races for a more simple, beautific approach. A simple set of enviroments, with just enough car choices to make you feel like you have some options, is peppered with obstacles and objectives for you to slide your way around. The only shame is that there isn't more of everything - the few car choices are varied, the enviroments are different, and the original music is great background. If you grind and try to do everything, the whole "campaign" and all the achievements will still only take an experienced player ~5 hours or less. A more casual play gets maybe 10 before finishing the campaign and maybe another 3 for the remaining achievements.
Also, there's a reason they recommend a controller - it will make your life better. If you want the challenge or more gametime, you can try the keys, but if I were you I'd grab your handy dandy 360 pad you have sitting around.
Pros:
-Pick up and play
-Nice soundtrack
-Pretty to look at
-You can drift a van, which is pretty sweet
Cons:
-Easy to learn, hard to master, especially if you don't play a lot of driving games.
-Short. Like, sit down and play it straight through by accident short.
-Limited replayability.

This is one crazy game!!!! It reminds you of those classic shooters you played, but it's nothing like them at all!!!!
What you basically do is dive into infinite space with your tiny little ship with little wings. And you blast through enemies, collect power ups, drill through planets and asteroids, and save your hindquarters from nasty alien space ships. And it becomes increasingly difficult as you pass through hurdles!
The graphics are neon-ish. They look beautiful. 90% of the time you will see lasers on your screen. The rest 10% of the time you'll be drilling through planets, which do not house nasty alienses (that was Gollum, I swear!).
The game has a library of enemies which gets updated as you encounter them. The information is humorous. The devs who created this game did a great job!
So, the verdict? 10/10!! It will satisfy all your needs, whether they be shooting aliens, watching colorful lights in space, drilling through planets, or being mocked by the game via the "exit mode" button (You'll never see that text. One of the best games I've ever played. It's an actual horror game, where the horror comes from not knowing when it'll strike.
Amnesia is a first-person adventure game. Lantern oil and candles are limited and are used not only to see better but to keep yourself sane. Darkness causes you to go insane, but darkness also allows you to hide from the enemies, whom you are unable to fight. As you go insane, your vision warps, you begin to see things, and you'll hear enemies who might not actually be there. What's great is that they sound just like real enemies, so it keeps you on your toes. With fantastic gameplay and a great story, this is a 10/10.

GOTY 2015, without a doubt in my mind.
Absolute Drift is the best driving game on PC, period. If you're like me, poor and without a 180SX of you're own, fire up Absolute Drift and get sideways to an absolutely stellar soundtrack! Absolute has a really simplistic "indie" art style with a very Mirrors Edge color scheme, that just works and looks beautiful! For me this game filled a hole for a drifting game after Rockstar ruined GTA5's driving mechanics and didn't allow for drifting of any kind.
Pros:
- Best soundtrack in an indie game since Minecraft
- Best driving mechanics in any PC game EVER
- Realistic and awesome vehicle sounds and crash sounds
- Beautiful art style and color scheme
- Global leaderboards make for endless replayability!
- Good variety of vehicles, from a classic 180SX (missile) to the powerful WRX Wagon (hooniwagon)
- 5 worlds full of fun "missions" as well as a helpful tutorial
Cons:
- Only 5 worlds, even though they are all quite large, I would like to see more added. I would pay $10 for a DLC pack with 5 more worlds.
- Scoring mechanics are kinda iffy, often destroying your built-up multiplyer even when you are constantly drifting or just because you barely tap a wall.
9.5/10, HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!! For only CAD$12, how can you go wrong with a game like this?

I enjoy Absolute Drift. That's really the bottom line of this review. I enjoy it, but I wish it were longer. The game is, at its core, a top-down arcade-style drift game that reminds me of the Gymkhana bits in DIRT 3. Only this time, there's no "Go share it on YouTube!" Absolute Drift is a game that leaves you alone with your car, some blank-faced obstacles, some quiet drum and bass tracks, and tire tracks that follow you into the sky.
-----
Gameplay: It's a small, relaxing game that's more about you enjoying the driving mechanic than completing any objectives. I beat the game in about 2 hours, but beating the game is really just unlocking all areas to drive around aimlessly. With the recent addition of a sort of difficulty switch, you can make your car handle in a way that's either more challenging or forgiving, but either way it's tremendous fun.
Graphics/Visual Experience: This game is relaxing and the visuals are a big part of that. Being a simple top-down drifting game, there's very little pretending that any of the buildings or bridges are important as anything more than obstacles. Buildings and the ground are left the standard off-white color, while little details elsewhere are given a flourish to bring them a little more life (usually a shade of red). You have the option of 5 cars, each with their own ~5 colors and ~5 decals. The skidmarks follow you into the sky, which at first may seem like a silly detail but I felt it really added something to the game.
Sound: Previously, the sound of squealing tires was a tad too loud but it's been cranked down as of late, meaning the relaxing atmosphere the music creates is far more effective. My only complaint with it is one that's my own fault, which is that despite liking drum and bass music, I tire of it very quickly and it all starts sounding the same. I need to try it while playing with my own music, but I haven't tried that yet.
Replayability: It's one of those games that you have to be "in the mood" to play. While it's a fun game, the simplicity of the environment would work more as a strength should the world increase in size a little. In its current iteration, the world feels a little bare. However, should you find yourself liking the world, the gameplay will remain the same every time, and as I said before, "beating the game" isn't depriving you of any options or elements but merely recognition that you've unlocked all the parts of the open world.
How it Runs: The game is simple and is about as demanding as you would think. There's not much that's going to tax your computer should you decide to purchase this game.

One of the collective of Greenlight games that has been discontinued in its development.
The developers have backed away from it entirely, after having instilled new ones to take their place.
Though it has mods to take its replayability and value up a notch, it is not going anywhere beyond the most recent update.
The game itself offers an interesting idea, where you are given a group of individuals who've managed to get stranded in the middle of a wilderness where survival is bent upon preparation against attacks from waves native slime blobs, werebears, skeletons, goblin-like creatures, and other manners of mythical beings. Each of said creatures seems to inherently wish to destroy the little "Townies" that inhabit the locale.
Thus it is up to you to assign duties and crafts in order to farm, harvest, bake, mine, and provide a kind of economy of barter in order to sustain the townspeople from starving, or being slaughtered and eaten by local denizens.
After creating a working village, whether it be in a mountainside or under the ground, or whatever the case, townies can venture below, into the earth to unveil treasures from creatures, with or without the help of heroes attained from local taverns.
With certain mods, the game can be improved, but what with the care given to it, the modding community has very well moved on; it has been left aside and is a token of proof against the usefullness of buying games before their true completion.
Other games similar to this are Gnomoria, and Stonehearth, both of which brandish better Ai development and offer a team who is in love with the product they are creating.
I would only recommend trying this game if it were on sale at 80% off if you wish to give a town-simulator a try; but I personally would have preferred buying Gnomoria over this game.

I adore Towns. I know it's not the popular opinion here, but I have spent a happy 300+ hours building and exploring and fighting. It was well worth the $10 or so that I spent on it a few years ago.
In Towns, you are in charge of an idiotic band of Townies who you instruct to gather resources, build buidlings, craft luxuries, cook food, and defend the town both as soldiers and civilains. In addition to keeping you populace well-fed and happy, you must defend against raiding bands of villians while delving deep into the dangerous underground to find more stone, iron, and gold. You can entice heroes to come and help you or instead swarm the monsters with well-armed townsfolk. The gameplay is heavy in resource management and building but has a satisfying amount of fighting and exploring.
Why are the reviews so negative? This game long been public and under development, and that development stalled and then eventually halted. There are lists of features yet to be implemented and bugs to be fixed. Many believe that Towns is an unfinished game and are very angry about this. My interpretation is that the developers were just too ambitious about what to include and ended up with lots of great features that don't all function perfectly. I think it's finished, just not polished.
So despite my positive review, buyer beware. Play a demo if you can. Think about what bugs get under your skin and what you are happy to ignore while exploring the game mechanics. Think about how many hours or what level of gameplay you need to shell out some cash. But I would buy this game again, even in its current state. But do not buy it expecting additional development - that ship has sailed.

The successor is a worthy one, rife with changes.
Heavy weapons can now finally be bought, allowing you to weild big swords and axes whenever you please. You'll just not use them on a horse.
The setting is different now though. Largely, you'll spend your time in Rome. A confusing change. Not only for you, but your horse too it seems. Horse AI never needed to be very intelligent in past games, but here their intelligence' true nature seems to really surface. It's limited to silly situations, thankfully.
However, being one city, Rome is one big city to be in. You'll be busy renovating stores and freeing districts from Borgia influence. Which partly is entwined in the story.
That said, the story becomes quite a bit more interesting. A matured Ezio is becoming the driving force behind the goals of the Assassins, and will later on be able to command a handful of his own trainees. This forms a new method of approaching a problem. You'll have assassin signals assigned to you, which you can use to send one of your apprentices out of hiding, and attack your target.
Or, when you have enough signals saved up with enough aprentices, you can launch an arrow storm attack, killing almost all hostile in the vicinity. These signals slowly replenish over time.
If the story of AC2 engaged you, you will not be hard pressed to enjoy it here as well. Ezio is the child you've seen from birth, growing into a confident and strong man.

My 9th most played game on steam and one of the most entertaining games I've played in a long time.
+++ Steep learning curve. Modern games tend to be way too simplified in terms of mechanical skill required to play in order to appeal much casual audience as possible. Absolute drift is fairly hard to learn, harder to master while keeping it fun doing that.
+ Driving is really damn fun. Pulling out that perfect drift is reward in itself.
+ Leaderboards. The main reason of my game time.
+ Minimalistic Graphics. Result is a game that is not power hungry and looks nice and clean.
+ Soundtrack. Awesome and chill.
+ Initial D references and AE86. Love it.
-If you are looking for story, better go looking at other direction. There isn't one aside being told to become "Drifting master" at the beginning.
-Short campaign mode of 30-120 minutes depending how you play it.
-Even though having minimalistic graphics i'd really like seeing some scenery around the maps.
-Performance issues in couple of maps.
-For casual play the price point might not be justified for the reasons addressed above.

Shovel Knight is a love letter to the NES era that goes above and beyond the lazy references and sloppy pixel art that have become so common in "retro" games. It wears its influences on its sleeve - you'll quickly recognize bits of Mario, Mega Man, Castlevania, and more - but there's an obvious attention to detail in merging and updating them into a cohesive, modern game. With a plethora of retro style indie games, I honestly wasn't looking forward to this. With less than a minute I instantly fell in love with this game more so than any other of the style. It has that genuine spark of life classic games had that new style of retro games fail to capture time and time again. It is tough but fair while explaining concepts not with words but with gameplay. Then it has several tough achievements for masters to strive for that involves forgoing checkpoints and never dying. Aesthetically it is extremely pleasing to both ears and eyes. The stage songs are all catchy and their boss counterparts are faster and more intense. The sprites convey a lot of personality and everything was memorable. They may have set out to write a love letter about the Nintendo generation of gaming but it is so much more realized than just an homage. Everything from the button layout, color palette, and music is limited yet it still plays, looks, and sounds fantastic. Most of all, I could feel the developer's love put into everything and I had no choice but to embrace this for the wonderful game that it is.
