Longevity is tough for competitive shooters. Hardly a month goes by without new virtual arenas cropping up and enticing you into some fresh conflict, and only a few popular games manage to sustain active player bases even a year after their initial release. And then there's Team Fortress 2. Released in 2007, this class-based classic is still going strong well into its seventh year, thanks largely to its lively and creative community. Since GameSpot's original TF2 review, the game has benefited from numerous updates and made the jump to a free-to-play business model. So how well is Team Fortress 2 faring in 2014 among the current crop of competitors for your time and money?
The short answer is, it's holding up very well. The core action pits two teams of players against each other in a battle to capture points, move a cart, or steal a briefcase. The objective is always very straightforward; it's the interplay between the nine playable classes that makes things so varied and interesting. The speedy scout, the militant heavy, the diligent engineer, the conniving medic, the pesky sniper, the sneaky spy, the feisty pyro, the explosive soldier, and the even-more-explosive demoman all have unique weapons, attributes, and abilities that complement each other and clash in myriad ways. Encounters can vary widely depending on the match type and the makeup of each team, and this unpredictability is crucial to TF2's long-standing appeal.
When you come out of the gate as a heavy with a medic in tow, you're a formidable offensive force, but if a spy loops around to backstab the medic and you round the corner on a pyro, it can all come undone in a matter of seconds. Snipers can cover expected enemy paths, but rocket-jumping soldiers have a knack for finding alternative routes and raining explosive death from above. You may think you have a comparatively weak scout dead to rights, only to be stunned by a baseball and beaten to death. As you watch your giblets splatter on the ground and see a freeze-frame of your gleeful killer, it's hard not to chuckle at the sheer variety of ways you can meet an untimely demise. And the humorous quips, ridiculous outfits, and histrionic announcer help cultivate this lighthearted tone.
Of course, this core dynamic has persisted for most of TF2's life span, so if you stopped playing it a few years ago and come back for a few matches, you'll find things are very familiar. Learning the ropes and getting the hang of your chosen role is still a gratifying experience, and mastering advanced techniques doesn't just make you deadlier; it gives you more options for how to approach combat. Keeping your options open is still valuable too, because being flexible with your choice of character can help you avoid ending up on a catastrophically imbalanced squad. It is Team Fortress, after all.
But though there is much that has remained constant about the core game, there have been some notable changes over the years, as well as regular infusions of new weapons and items. Of the hundreds of things available in the online store, some can be unlocked through play, while others must be purchased with actual money. From small doodads that cost less than a dollar to massive bundles that cost hundreds, there's a wide range of ways to customize your experience.
No Caption Provided
Many of the items offer nothing more than a playful twist on the game's already cheeky cartoon aesthetic. You can buy hats, shirts, shoes, and other cosmetic gear to dress up like a character from Adult Swim or don spooky seasonal garb that you can wear only during Halloween or a full moon. Even if you don't fancy shelling out for any of this stuff, it's fun to see some visual variety as you try to light your opponents on fire.
Other weapons have more of an impact, like the ones that give your character a new chargeable and expendable power. The scout can build hype, which turns his usual double jump into a triple, quadruple, or quintuple jump, and the soldier can build rage, which allows him to rally his nearby teammates to do extra damage. Skills like these have more of a meaningful impact on the action, bringing something new to the table that your enemies must contend with. And then there are the totally out-there loadouts, like the one that turns the grenade-launching demoman into an extra from the movie Braveheart.In addition to the cosmetic options, there are a lot of weapons and items that offer small buffs or subtle tweaks to your attributes. Depending on which healing gun the medic equips, for example, he can imbue himself and his targeted ally with extra damage resistance or enable himself to match the speed of his target. Differences like these don't do much to change the core action, but they do give experienced players substantial room for strategic variation.
These options broaden the field of viable strategies, which helps keep combat lively and varied. And fortunately, none of the purchasable weapons or items tip the scales unfairly towards those willing to pay. Buffs and bonuses usually come with caveats, and the weapons that bestow new abilities are usually unlocked for free. For this review, I spent some money on goofy hats and some of the stranger weaponry on offer, like the pyro's flamethrower that actually shoots bubbles and rainbows. It was fun to play with the new gear, but I still found myself switching my loadout between free and paid weapons regularly to adapt to the match situation.
The biggest divergence from the game's origins comes in the cooperative mode, Mann vs. Machine. In it, you and a few other human players must prevent hordes of robotic incarnations of TF2's classes from delivering a bomb to your base. The money you earn from destroying robots can be spent on mid-match upgrades to your attributes and weaponry, which can be crucial to success. Even on the easiest level, the robot legions are fierce enough to test the mettle of an unorganized team. This is a mode where carefully planned weapon choices and defensive strategies can mean the difference between succeeding and having to try, try again. You can play this mode for free, but you won't be eligible to earn rare prizes or complete challenges unless you pay a dollar for a Tour of Duty ticket. Though it lacks the frenetic unpredictability of competitive play, the cooperative mode can still provide satisfaction for those dedicated enough to see it through.
But competition is the real draw, and the Team Fortress 2 community can certainly be competitive. On some servers, you might be berated for unwitting breaches of etiquette, while on others, you might be welcomed with helpful tips and ubercharges. You can even ask for help on certain servers and be paired up with another player who is willing to give you some tips through chat. The community around TF2 is an intriguing one, not just for their deep knowledge of and passion for the game, but for their creative efforts in designing new weapons, items, and maps that have since become part of the experience. It feels like a community of curators, without whom the game may well have dwindled away and passed into obsolescence years ago.
Staying relevant even a year after release is rare for a competitive shooter, and yet, here's Team Fortress 2, still lively after seven years in the business. At times it feels like the same game you could have played back then, and at other times it feels like no one will ever quite nail class-based shooter competition the way TF2 does. The experience has evolved over the years without compromising what made it so great in the first place, so though your free-to-play options may have increased considerably in the past few years, there are few that do it as well as Team Fortress 2.

You may think that this game is a mere hack-and-slash genre, like in Dynasty Warriors or Saints Row. No. Yall are wrong.
This game is just a commentary of Imperial Japan's military aggression against the United States during World War II. EDF = Japan. Opposition (Aliens, Bugs, etc,.) = USA. Like Imperial Japan, EDF lacked the advanced weaponry and the numbers of her opposition (aka USA). Thus, my fellow comrades were both heavily outgunned and outnumbered to the point where I became a lone survivor to this inevitable doom. Remember the mission where only merely-poor tanks and rangers must defend the beach against the superior alien robots (the one without the free bombing run)? Doesn't this mission ring a bell? If not, ignorance must be erradicated as this mission represents the US beachhead operation on Iwo Jima. Many of my fellow soldiers were swiftly rewarded a plane ticket to Yasakuni Shrine. How about the alien attacks on civilian in urban environments? That represents the US firebombing of Japan during the course of the war.
Despite our tremendous losses, I sense the Spirit of Yamato, the Essence of Bushido, and the Presence of the Samurai within the physical bodies of the EDF. Like the Imperial Japanese, the EDF fighting spirit will always outmatch the weapons of the foreign devils. Their arrogance only focus on material. We, EDF, focus on willpower. If I choose the side between Imperial Japan or USA, I'd obviously join Imperial Japan. The Emperor needs me. The white devils will never hinder me. The Yamato Race will live on to bring peace to the world through military unification like our Fore Fathers did during Sengoku Jidai, the invasions of Korea, the war against the Russians, and the conquest on the Chinese. OUR SPIRIT BULLETS ARE NO MATCH AGAINST THEIR LASERS, ACIDS, CLAWS, MANDIBLES, PHOTONS, SPIDER WEBS, ETC,. GUNS UP, MY NAKAMA! WE SHALL FIGHT WITH KATANAS DRAWN, DE ARIMASU!

An excellent retro platformer that shouldn’t be missed by anyone who’s a fan of the genre.
5-6 hours (Main game)
8.5/10
Shovel Knight is a retro platformer in the vein of many old NES games, and it’s pretty clear and unashamed that it draws its influences from such. As someone who grew up playing games of that sort, and still loves them to this day, Shovel Knight had me sold from the moment I first saw the trailer.
Gameplay-wise, it’s most similar to Mega Man in terms of its platforming, though it differs greatly in its combat. Instead of a buster cannon, you battle with the aid of your trust shovel, which functions as a short range melee weapon. There’s also an assortment of relic items that can be found and purchased to aid you in your quest, most functioning as additional combat weapons, though some serving other purposes. Gold (your currency) is accumulated by picking up gems, gold, coins, and the like throughout the levels. In addition to purchasing the relics, you can also use your gold to purchase armor, shovel upgrades, health upgrades, and magic upgrades (magic is consumed to use the relic items).
And of course what would a retro platformer be without 8-bit graphics and an old school style soundtrack? True to its influences, Shovel Knight has both in spades. The graphics look like a later era NES game, and will please anyone who’s a fan of that art style (I myself am quite fond of it). The music as well is pretty great.
The main difference I notice between this and the NES games it harkens back to is that it’s a far more reasonable difficulty than its ancestors, which were downright brutal at times. Now, I’ve never been one to mind a difficult game, and I do have an affinity for them even, but having less time to play games than I used to I must confess that I’m glad that the game’s difficulty is much more moderate. The game doesn’t utilize a life system, or limit your number of tries per level before forcing you to restart the whole level. Instead dying merely causes you to lose a portion of your gold (which can be regained by grabbing the floating bags of gold that hover by your place of death –so long as you manage to do so before dying again) and sending you back to the last checkpoint.
Though, many of those old games were so difficult simply to increase one’s playtime with them, as they were rather short. Shovel Knight itself is not a long game itself, as it’ll only take about 5-6 hours to complete the main game once through. Thankfully it’s a very fun 5-6 hours.
In the end, Shovel Knight is a stellar platformer that will be enjoyed by anyone who’s a fan of the genre, especially those who love the old NES games it emulates.

I fear that the English language doesn't yet have the words required to adequately describe this game, but I will make the attempt regardless.
tl;dr - CounterStrike's mentally-challenged half-brother. Get a friend, get voice and stop caring.
It feels like a version of CounteStrike that's been translated into Chinese and back about 300 times, all the way losing polish, gameplay and textures along with any hope of sense. There's nice ideas, like lugging around propane tanks to make crude traps, or kicking things out of the way with your mighty boot, but at the same time, there's no way to aim down the sights or, really, anything else you'll find in most shooters these days. You *can* raise your gun over your head and run around like a lunatic, however, and I strongly suggest you do.
Gun-wise, they are present in the game. Pistols may as well not be, because they kick like a mule, while SMGs are effective at all ranges. Shotguns are magic physics hoses that will sometimes kill, sometimes remove someone's entire upper torso and sometimes negate all physical constraints on the target and fling them screaming into the sky, presumably to orbit the earth forever. There are also sniper rifles, but this is not really the game for that. Not when first contact between T and CT can end in 10 seconds with a casualty rate similar to Passchendale.
Get a friend, stop caring and find driving and VIP missions, run around like tactical idiots with guns held tactically over your heads or drive a car (that feels like it's on ice) while crouched, navigating soley via the terrible mini-map or the yelling of your passenger. Haven't stopped laughing, especially thanks to the occasional team mate who's taking things far too seriously. God help me, but I have to recommend it, assuming you have friends.

So, you are in game, disabled the gibberish voicechat. (In case that the voicechat is still on, you will most certainly hear "i get shot for no reason" or "我喜欢鸡肉" or "number x is infected, i scanned him, trust me!!". All the damn time.)

The gameplay is a complete mess.

+ The concept of the game sounds really promising.
+ The game didn't crash

Resident Evil 5 is an action horror game which was released in 2009 by Capcom. In Resident Evil 5 you will play as a BSAA member: Chris Redfield along with his companion Shevo Alomor. In the co-op mode you can also play as Sheva or if you have completed the campaign. The BSAA (Bioterrorism Security Assessment Alliance) has been made by governments to infiltrate and neutralize the bioterrorist hotspots, to restore safety and stability to various regions around the globe.  You can choose about 3 different difficulties: Amateur, Normal and Veteran. Once you beat the veteran mode, the game gets a new difficulty: Professional. The game is located in Africa, at a non-real place called Kijuju. You can find guns somewhere around the map from different chapters or you can buy it at the shop. You can access the shop by dying, completing a chapter and when starting the game. In the shop you can organize, buy and sell your stuff. The most valuable of them are the (hidden) treasures.
In the beginning you start at Radcoon City, a place where the civilization hasn’t been affected by the bioterrorists. At least that was what it looked like… it turned out to be an infected zone by a mysterious masked woman. In the game you start without any weapons except a knife. Once you go to the objective you and your partner will receive a gun. After the end of the chapters, you will have to find against the bosses.
The genre of the game is marked as horror, but it isn’t scary at all. The game didn't even have any jump scares. If there was then it could be in the cut scenes. Which I watched. The cut scenes are somehow exciting to watch and when you skip one you will regret it and watch it on YouTube or by clicking cut scenes at the menu option. The graphics of the game isn’t really modern, it is bad if you compare it to the new games that released this year. The sound itself really improve the gameplay, it is well-made. The controls are easy to control, if you have played the game long enough. The controls can you find in the game at notes, but I would recommend you to go to the control settings at the menu. The gameplay itself is awesome, but it could be better if there were other endings that was decided by the way you play. The ending of this game is somehow sad/bad. It would be nice if there was a better ending.

Very nice addition to the Portal universe. The writing is great as well as the voice acting. Both don't reach the level of the original Portal 2 but it's still more to be expected from a free mod.
What actually does reach the level of Portal 2 are threefold: The art and level direction, the puzzles and the music.
The environments use many of the old assets and adds a few new ones. It seamlessly fits into the feel of Portal 2 and it just... clicks.
The puzzles are the biggest star here. They're smart, tough and they either made me feel very smart or very dumb for solving them 80% until I didn't figure out a very obvious last step. Top notch here! Also: No finger acrobatics needed to solve these. Very good stuff!
The music also fits the Portal universe extremely well, is nice to listen to... But manages to keep itself in the background. Exactly the way it should be when you're trying to solve these sweet puzzles!
Two final thoughts:
- It's a nice change to have an Aperture Science AI that's not a villain but just... A nice and helpful buddy.
- Love the paperclip on the portal gun!

Harry Potter is a series of fantasy novels written by British author J. K. Rowling. The novels chronicle the life of a young wizard, Harry Potter, and his friends Hermione Granger and Ron Weasley, all of whom are students at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry . The main story arc concerns Harry's struggle against Lord Voldemort, a dark wizard who intends to become immortal, overthrow the wizard governing body known as the Ministry of Magic, and subjugate all wizards and Muggles.
Since the release of the first novel, Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, on 26 June 1997, the books have found immense popularity, critical acclaim and commercial success worldwide. They have attracted a wide adult audience as well as younger readers, and are often considered cornerstones of modern young adult literature.[3] The series has also had its share of criticism, including concern about the increasingly dark tone as the series progressed, as well as the often gruesome and graphic violence it depicts. As of July 2013, the books have sold more than 450 million copies worldwide, making them the best-selling book series in history, and have been translated into seventy-three languages.[4][5] The last four books consecutively set records as the fastest-selling books in history, with the final instalment selling roughly eleven million copies in the United States within twenty-four hours of its release.
The series was originally published in English by two major publishers, Bloomsbury in the United Kingdom and Scholastic Press in the United States. A play, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, based on a story by Rowling, premiered in London on 30 July 2016 at the Palace Theatre, and its script was published by Little, Brown as the eighth book in the series.[6] The original seven books were adapted into an eight-part film series by Warner Bros. Pictures, which has become the second highest-grossing film series of all time as of August 2015. The franchise has also generated much tie-in merchandise, making the Harry Potter brand worth in excess of $15 billion.[7]
A series of many genres, including fantasy, drama, coming of age and the British school story (which includes elements of mystery, thriller, adventure, horror and romance), the world of Harry Potter explores numerous themes and includes many cultural meanings and references.[8] According to Rowling, the main theme is death.[9] Other major themes in the series include prejudice, corruption, and madness.[10]
The success of the books and films has ensured that the Harry Potter franchise continues to expand, with numerous derivative works, a travelling exhibition that premiered in Chicago in 2009, a studio tour in London that opened in 2012, a digital platform on which J.K. Rowling updates the series with new information and insight, and a trilogy of spin-off films premiering in November 2016, among many other developments. Most recently, themed attractions, collectively known as The Wizarding World of Harry Potter, have been built at several Universal Parks & Resorts amusement parks around the world.

Deceit is a game about 6 survivors who wake up. Two of them have contracted a disease that makes them thirsty for blood. The two infected have to work together to kill the other four innocent players. They can achieve this by drinking blood bags to fill their "blood meter". Once their blood meter is full, they can transform into a "terror" - a terrifying monster that can kill survivors in one hit if they don't have armor.
Every minute or so, a blackout will happen, when the infected can transform into their terrifying forms, and the most dreaded phase for the innocents. They can either survive for about a minute before the power comes back online anyway, or find 2-3 fuses to set the timer to ten seconds.
Deceit is a game about deceiving others if you are the infected, and knowing whether or not you can trust your "teammates" around you. In this game, you cannot trust anyone.
Sometimes the matches can become repetitive, though. But I guess that would apply to basically every single game with a multiplier mode.
Overall, great game, and would recommend it to everyone! :)

Still hold out hope they can get things back on track but with each update it seems less and less likely. Before update 0.3.0 back in March this was without a doubt my favorite game and I played it any time I had a bit of free time to do so.
After the update though the new fishing mechanics were/still are so unrealistic it’s more frustrating than it is fun. You’ll literally fight a fish for hours in game and hope that after all that work that this 5lb fish doesn’t completely spool your 30lb line in the end like it’s a shark or whale. I’d hoped they would fix this and kind of bring down to the level at which it was before the patch but so far we’ve still got these fish that are obviously on steroids.
Never in my life have I broke a rod or reel. While they have slightly fixed this issue they still break way too easy in the game, I think we may be using glass rods and reels. They also made all gear wear out so now you need to repair everything pretty much constantly, which eats a good chunk of the profit you earn.  The only logic I see here is they wanted people to have to purchase more in game currency as before you could play the game 100% free (buying a membership grants you 50% increased experience so I always had a membership for the boost and to help support the game) with no issues. You still can but the less experienced/new players really seem to struggle now.
Two good things that came in the patch were the gear matching (however the way it’s setup means that having max rod slots is all but mandatory to avoid constant gear swapping) and they fixed the right mouse button spam that plagued the game. To be completely honest I wish they would have just fixed the right mouse button spamming and left the reset of the fishing mechanics alone as they were fine.
In the end it’s probably still the best fishing game out there however the player base has really dropped off in a short amount of time. I’ll keep hoping they bring the game back to its former glory but as for now I’ve all but completely stopped and I wont recommend the game in it's current state as the fun factor just isn't there anymore like it was before the big update.

This game is absolutely phenomenal in every regard! Everything is reminiscent of retro-platformers (most likely from your childhood) but, in my opinion, done better! Now, I didn't grow up playing said platformers from a young age, but I have played enough to know that Shovel Knight could have been released back in the late 80s - early 90s and would have fitted in perfectly. It could have even been the most highly regarded platformer of that period!! That, ladies and gentlemen, is just how good Shovel Knight is.
The artstyle is very reminiscent of retro platforming games, and the music alone makes this game very much worth the full price! Let me repeat: this game's soundtrack is incredible! Then the gameplay, the main reason you would buy this game, just takes it up to level 11 on the awesome scale. You might at first think "a shovel for a weapon? Really?" (even the game points this out in NPCs dialogue in the main village and beyond!), but you will quickly learn to love this unfamiliar "weapon" and will gladly take it over a sword any day of the week.
Throughout the levels, you collect gold from enemies that can be put toward the purchase of upgrades to your weapons, armour, or even to purchase special abilities in the form of relics. In most of these levels, too, you will face bosses. Hard boss battles, yet fun! The variety of enemies in the game is exceptionally great too, and the scenes to back them up really add to the experience as you probably won't find yourself getting bored at the game. Every death may lead to frustration, but it is always going to be your fault - the game does not cheat you. The controls are tight, too. I'm not usually one to use a keyboard to play a platformer, but I tried it with Shovel Knight and had no issues at all!
For me, this has to be one of the best platforming games I have played in the past number of years. It only took me ~5hrs to beat, but I did not truly finish it, as there are plenty of hidden music sheets (which you can actually listen to in-game after collecting) that I missed as well as a New Game Plus mode which I have not touched (as of writing this review). If you too are a fan of platforming games or want to bring on some nostalgia in the best form possible, Shovel Knight is the game for you and you will NOT regret purchasing it.
Enjoy :D

The Assassin's Creed series just keeps getting better and better. The first game was a solid start, but the missions got repetitive after a while. AC II blew me away with the number of things they added; a compelling plot and characters that felt authentic, interesting platforming sequences, and a real sense of humor!
I just finished the story campaign of Assassin's Creed Brotherhood, and I can't decide whether I liked it better than Assassin's Creed II or not.
Graphically Brotherhood is obviously better, but it is not as big a difference as the change from AC to AC II. Also, 3D gaming is really useful while freerunning around Renaissance Italy because depth perception helps me to know whether I can make a jump or not.
I think I preferred the story of AC II because it was an epic narrative of Ezio's journey over several decades to train and grow from a rather self-centered lady-killer young adult to a mature assassin (still a lady-killer). AC Brotherhood was much more limited in scope, as it takes place over the course of a few years in the city of Rome. Don't get me wrong, it was epic, but I liked the tangible progression that Ezio went through in AC II.
However, I definitely preferred the gameplay of Brotherhood. They improved on a few of the things that had been iffy in the previous games (like horses!) and they added some really great things as well. The big one of course is recruiting assassins to help you out. I felt like a total badass whenever I walked by a group of guards, raised my hand and whistled, and a moment later they were dead. I also became rather attached to the recruits, and it made me very proud when they gained enough experience to become full-fledged assassins. Losing recruits didn't have quite as big an emotional impact as losing people in The Walking Dead did, but when I accidentally killed one it came pretty close.
The endings of these games keep getting more and more mind-blowing; I have heard that Revelations raises the bar once again, and I can't wait to get there. One thing that definitely gave me the chills was the date that the finale takes place on. Ubisoft has intentionally been converging all events on December 21, 2012 and the final scenes of Brotherhood take place 72 days before that.
So if you were to ask me which Assassin's Creed games you should play, I would say all of them. If you are short on time/money skipping the first one is excusable. AC II, Brotherhood, and Revelations make a nice little trilogy, so don't start after AC II.

Game: Most realistic fishing game I've ever played. Nice physics for the available lures, rods and reels. The water graphics are great. First game I've found that helps me scratch the fishing bug I get on days I can't actually go fishing. Friendly chat with helpful users makes the learning curve easier to handle. These are fishermen mostly, so they are mostly laid back people who aren't competing against you for anything, just enjoying their time fishing.
The controls feel a bit wacky at times, and the fish fight physics (that's a lot of "F" sounds) seems a bit off sometimes, with rod loading being more geared toward the apparence of a fight than being relative to the fish size/fight. (often a bigger fish will not bend the rod much, just pull drag, as if the rod/reel physics are set so that the drag is the difference in big fish/small fish fight vs the rod, which should take the majority of the load and be the first to max out at the proper angle).
Don't get frustrated because you start small with sunfish and work through bullhead catfish, bass and up through eventually larger species. It's a progression. Don't travel too much early on, it's not worth it and your money will go quickly. Just find a species you like to catch and have fun. Missouri, (maybe NY, but not sold on it being a decent lake yet), North Carolina, Florida (you'll level quickly here on peacock bass) and off to sunny California for monster stripers and chinook salmon/steelhead and if you're into the sucker lip bass, you can catch trophy carp over 30lbs there. You'll fil lyour bank account there (you'll need if it you go to Alberta). Then it's off to Michigan for trophy Muskie, Pike, freshwater Drum and other species. Many of these have unique fish that pay out gold and a lot of XP.
These days you get to walk around many of the lakes you coudln't walk around just a few months ago, and especially in Michigan that makes the lake feel larger, more balanced.
Have fun.

Following the footsteps of Resident Evil 4 this game is both a little better and a little worse. Still fun to play though annoying at times as it's predecessor.
The story happens five years after the events in Resident Evil 4 and you play as Chris Redfield. You with your partner are sent to Africa to track down some bio-terrorist and the story goes from there. You encounter Las Plagas or some kind of it's mutation (was not really paying that much attention) that again turns people into zombie like creatures. Those are not as previously as zombies but you wouldn't tell a difference. Though would a zombie ride a bike? I think not. The story is pretty nice and takes you through a lot of well designed zones.
On graphical side the game has much improved. From being dark and gray in previous title the pallet shifts to yellow and gray - thus quite nicely giving the African feel. The models are much better detailed and it's quite the step up comparing to the previous one.
Gameplay has not changed all that much though there are changes. First of - they've added strafing - that helps a lot! Secondly as this game is mostly designed for co-op play you are stuck with a partner which wastes ammo, though heals you a lot making it really hard to die. It's a shame you can't play without the partner. The game structure at first really reminds of the previous game. You are thrown into the most hard part of the game within the first half an hour. At least that was my feeling.
The weapon shops were removed in favour of what might be load-out menu that lets you store and buy items between levels - or when you die. The inventory system has been simplified a lot as well sadly. There are nine slots, no item stacking and arranging as previously. The weapons are pretty cool and feel nice. The electric rod however is so overpowered for regular zombies that it feels like game braking.
As with previous game I did enjoy fighting zombies and doing QTEs - not so much keen on the boss fights. Though those might be a bit easier than in RE4. Still played till the end and had enough fun to recommend.
I'd hardly even call it a mod - fantastic game and fantastic addition to the Portal series. It really feels like an official expansion.

A wonderfully, carefully, and lovingly done callback to games of time long gone. Unlike many pieces that attempt this kind of a deal, Shovel Knight is very convincing in that it could quite possibly run on one of the quite early gaming systems, with nothing really breaking the illusion (perhaps except the resolution of my screen). Yet still it manages to blend in relatively new and innovative machanics.
Very well polished combat and clever levels, paintlery and pleasant, yet still impressive graphics, well chosen and catchy music that makes good use of it's limited resources. Even a pinch of humor and cheek in the writing was quite well placed and attuned to rest of the deal.
Perhaps the only disappointment the game brought is that compared to the forefathers it manages to liken itself to so closely, it's quite short quite short. It's not quite all that rich on content by volume either. It's still definitely quite worth the price the developer is asking for. Perhaps the success of the game will prove the point of creating a bigger sequel of more respectable length and depth.

This review of Resident Evil 5 is based in part on my time playing this on the PC, originally via a physical copy, and also the many dozens of hours playing it on the PS3 over the years.
This may be a controversial opinion, but I feel like Resident Evil 5 is a refinement of many of the positive innovations of Resident Evil 4 - the AI partner (or co-op), Sheva, is now a full-time participant rather than part-time hero/part-time damsel in distress. Similarly, the over-the-shoulder shooting and signature tank control are more fluid than ever, always keeping you in the moment - Resident Evil 4 may always be remembered more fondly, and perhaps with good reason, but its gameplay is just not as seamless and solid as Resident Evil 5.
That said, where the gameplay succeeds, its story and atmosphere do not make a strong impression. Due in part to its refined shooting game and precise mouse and keyboard controls, Resident Evil 5 is undoubtedly an action game, and it makes only a minor effort to resurrect the atmosphere of terror and foreboding of the previous game. Yes, there is some sick, grotesque stuff in Resident Evil 5, but the characters always seem to be in control -Sheva and Chris are superheroes. Moreover, while there are some nods made towards the African setting, especially in the levels that take place in the swamps, a lot of the game's locations feel anonymous. In Resident Evil 4, the Spanish setting felt thoroughly imagined and unique - but Africa seems much more generic, and too brightly lit, to inspire a sense of horror.
All the same, it's a brilliant, polished shooting game.

EDF is a game with a lot to offer anyone willing to put a little time into it. You can play it on easier difficulties to just enjoy the bad voice acting and ridiculous spectacle of a plot (it even has splitscreen co-op). Or you can crank it up to where beating a mission eventually requires tremendous skill, coordination, and tactical evaluation of how to maximize your damage output in a variety of situations, with up to 4-players in online play.
No matter how you want to enjoy it, EDF offers a unique experience you won't find anywhere else. It's special blend of creative and explosive weaponry, hilariously carefree physics, and destructable environments has been winning over a small legion of hardcore fans for over a decade. And the most definitive entry in the series is now available on PC, running better than a console could ever hope to, without sacrificing any features or content (assuming we get the mission DLC later on).

Earth Defense Force is a very polarizing series. When people encounter it you usually get two types of reactions:
1. Bafflement that this game could be considered good, followed by rants about how bad the graphics, story, production values, and stuff of that ilk is. Optional rants about how boring it is.
2. People who profess their undying love for it.
Having put several hundred hours in the series over the years, I am firmly in category two. It's a gamers game for sure. If your are looking for a game with involved technical mechanics and high production values, look elsewhere. One obvious glance at the game will tell you that the devs didn't put much effort into AAA production values, but the beauty of it is that they just don't care. What this game prioritizes and excels in is being fun. You have one goal for each stage, kill all the enemies, and you have free reign over how you need to do it. No checkpoints. No objectives. This often means unrelenting chaos and destruction as building debris and bug carcasses fly around all over you over loud explosions. Single player is good enough, but co-op'ing with friends, when you pull off a crazy plan to beat a hard stage you were struggling with on Inferno difficulty and everyone is ecstatic and laughing, that's some of the best co-op I've ever experienced in a video game. There's nothing else like it.
If that sounds like the vibe you can get into. Instant purchase.

Let me start off by saying that this is a fun game. I am not going to deny that. But is it $50 worth of fun? HELL no. Not even close. I am not going to go along with the rank and file fan boys that are giving this game rave reviews.
As a Gaming Critic I have to ask and answer the same question every time I Review a game: "Is this good for the consumer?" And unfortunately the answer here is a resounding no.
The game is marred by it's being a shoddy port. Dated graphics, framerate drops, horrendous PhysX, glitches, multiplayer crashes, and reports of the game outright not working on AMD processors all bring down the game in a big way.
Here is an excerpt from my Review:
"this game’s title is about as long-winded as the gameplay itself. Now, before we get into things it’s worth noting that somehow these Earth Defense Force games seem to have a fairly large following of which I am not a member of. I have never played any of the previous titles nor do I expect to so please take that into consideration. I am no fan boy and I don’t expect to become an EDF Disciple. What I CAN do, though, is tell you about the game itself. It sucks. There’s no way around it. Looking at the mechanics of the game it fails on nearly every level, however like one of those B Movies that are pure horrendousness with campy lines, cheesy plot, and shallow characters. The graphics are dated, the port is riddled with flaws including poor optimization, framerate drops, horrendous keyboard/mouse support, lame samey horde mode levels, WAY too much screaming, broken multiplayer, and if you have an AMD Processor then forget about it. You will most likely not even be able to play it.
So, you’d think that would be the end of it. But no, it has some good things going for it too. And strangely enough, a lot of them are the same ones I’ve already listed. Pure horrendousness with campy lines, cheesy plot, shallow characters, and samey horde mode gameplay. This game has some odd mixture of badness that has actually somehow created an enjoyable game."

Game: Most realistic fishing game I've ever played. Nice physics for the available lures, rods and reels. The water graphics are great. First game I've found that helps me scratch the fishing bug I get on days I can't actually go fishing. Friendly chat with helpful users makes the learning curve easier to handle. These are fishermen mostly, so they are mostly laid back people who aren't competing against you for anything, just enjoying their time fishing.
The controls feel a bit wacky at times, and the fish fight physics (that's a lot of "F" sounds) seems a bit off sometimes, with rod loading being more geared toward the apparence of a fight than being relative to the fish size/fight. (often a bigger fish will not bend the rod much, just pull drag, as if the rod/reel physics are set so that the drag is the difference in big fish/small fish fight vs the rod, which should take the majority of the load and be the first to max out at the proper angle).
Don't get frustrated because you start small with sunfish and work through bullhead catfish, bass and up through eventually larger species. It's a progression. Don't travel too much early on, it's not worth it and your money will go quickly. Just find a species you like to catch and have fun. Missouri, (maybe NY, but not sold on it being a decent lake yet), North Carolina, Florida (you'll level quickly here on peacock bass) and off to sunny California for monster stripers and chinook salmon/steelhead and if you're into the sucker lip bass, you can catch trophy carp over 30lbs there. You'll fil lyour bank account there (you'll need if it you go to Alberta). Then it's off to Michigan for trophy Muskie, Pike, freshwater Drum and other species. Many of these have unique fish that pay out gold and a lot of XP.
These days you get to walk around many of the lakes you coudln't walk around just a few months ago, and especially in Michigan that makes the lake feel larger, more balanced.
Have fun.

This review of Resident Evil 5 is based in part on my time playing this on the PC, originally via a physical copy, and also the many dozens of hours playing it on the PS3 over the years.
This may be a controversial opinion, but I feel like Resident Evil 5 is a refinement of many of the positive innovations of Resident Evil 4 - the AI partner (or co-op), Sheva, is now a full-time participant rather than part-time hero/part-time damsel in distress. Similarly, the over-the-shoulder shooting and signature tank control are more fluid than ever, always keeping you in the moment - Resident Evil 4 may always be remembered more fondly, and perhaps with good reason, but its gameplay is just not as seamless and solid as Resident Evil 5.
That said, where the gameplay succeeds, its story and atmosphere do not make a strong impression. Due in part to its refined shooting game and precise mouse and keyboard controls, Resident Evil 5 is undoubtedly an action game, and it makes only a minor effort to resurrect the atmosphere of terror and foreboding of the previous game. Yes, there is some sick, grotesque stuff in Resident Evil 5, but the characters always seem to be in control -Sheva and Chris are superheroes. Moreover, while there are some nods made towards the African setting, especially in the levels that take place in the swamps, a lot of the game's locations feel anonymous. In Resident Evil 4, the Spanish setting felt thoroughly imagined and unique - but Africa seems much more generic, and too brightly lit, to inspire a sense of horror.
All the same, it's a brilliant, polished shooting game.

RESIDENT RAMBO 5
Actually this should really have been called RE4 Part II or perhaps another REVLATIONS title, nevertheless I am giving this a thumbs up because I bought it in the Summer Sale for Six Dollars, if I had paid full price then maybe I would have differen't opinions about it.
As others have mentioned  as far as gameplay and progression go this is almost a carbon copy of RE4, with a couple of really good (and sadly very short) "Operation Wolf" Type levels thrown in at the half way point, suffice it to say this was meand a big budget "Switch your Brain Off" shooter with the bizzare addition (experiment?) of an AI partner system for solo play which isn't too much of a problem for the First Half but then gets to be a BIG problem later on.  More on that later...
Everything about this game is BIG, Cinematic and Bombastic and for the most part it looks really good even though there is a distinct lack of variety in the Scenery.  With a few exceptions the graphics are all a mix of South African Shanty Towns with Mad Max that make up Roughly Two Thirds of the entire game.  The cutscenes are done in that dramatic Shaky-Cam style, which was very trendy when this was released, and on the whole it holds up very well for it's age.  Running on a NVIDIA GTX 870 this is smooth and flicker free although there are some serious bugs on the Tanker Level that make progression next to impossible depending on what Spawns and what does not.
So what of the actual Mechanics and playability?  Sadly this is a complete Train Wreck that is WAY too complicated to use and slowly gets worse as the game progresses making it virtually impossible without the use of a controller.
Actually things are pretty good until half way throuth the Third Stage and then, without warning.........It's "Goodbye Resident Evil" and HELLOOOOO QTE.......!!!!!
Yes Friends, when it comes to the Boss Fights and later the Maze and Corridor levels you will spend most of the time either looking at the keyboard or controler rather than enjoying the action on the screen. The Intrusive Quick Time sections that invade the levels and the Boss Fights without warning also change the keys each time causing the player to be looking perminently at the keyboard and missing the action.  It is also in these stages that the REALLY BAD AI of the partner becomes painfully apparent and it will then most of the time blocking you in corners and getting you killed from then on till the bitter end.  There really should have been an option to play without it and I am Amazed that this was not offered.
By this time CAPCOM had already gone too far away from what RE is meant to be and it is evident that they were listening to the "Suits" rather than the fans.  It is also evident that they were trying to be like the RE Films going so far as to transform Wesker from an interesting "Bond Villian" with character into an evil superhero part NEO Part Darth Vader.  The two versions of RE should have been allowed to exist as completely seperate entities.
What we have here is really a long version of MERCINARIES.
In conclusion I cannot really complain at Six Dollars, so it is for that reason I am giving it a thumbs up, but I would not have been so sympathetic if I had paid full price.
PS Trivia......did anyone else notice that the music between levels is a slowed down version of the Ocean Theme from Mario 64?

Do not buy Towns.  It has ripped off too many people.
Towns is a game about building a village for simulated RPG adventurers. Reading about all the features it had and all the downloads, I figured I would throw in my $5 and play. This is 2013 by the way. Unfortunately, the game was unplayable. With a glitchy interface and the inability to even pass the tutorial or even build one room.
A few months passed from August 2013 and Steam decides to release Green Light, I service indicating which games are incomplete but still up for purchase. To my surprise, Towns was lumped into the newly founded category. Basically, I bought a game I did not know was incomplete. The optimistic side of me thought that Towns would be complete some time in the future.
Fast forward a year to 2014 and I see news that Towns developers gave up on ever finishing the game. Meaning they simply took off with my money.
Upon hearing the news, I was again disappointed.
The following year, Steam released a refund policy. I was excited to read that they would allow refunds that were within 14 days with less than one hour of play time. Given that I have clocked a whopping, miserable 19 minutes on Towns, I figured I could do one last attempt.... DENIED.
So here I am, writing about how much I have been ripped off from buying the game Towns. It was $5 sure, but I didn't know it was incomplete at the time and Steam fails to acknowledge their mistake.
I hope this is the right forum to post to because quite frankly, I feel people should know the darker side that is Steam.
Moral of the story.
DO NOT BUY TOWNS

Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood suffers from a so-called 'intermediate chapter syndrome'. It's just as good as Assassin's Creed II with improvements in some areas. What it lacks though is surprise. Brotherhood continues the story of Ezio, becoming the second chapter in a sub-trilogy within Assassin's Creed tetralogy. As a result, few new characters are introduced, and the story progresses at a slow and steady pace. It's not any less interesting than in previous games, and its ending, again, is cool and unexpected, but while the second game was a major step forward compared to the first one, Brotherhood feels more like an expansion pack for the second game.
It introduces multiplayer which is surprisingly fun for something that shouldn't have existed in the first place. It has integration with Assassin's Creed: Project Legacy, a Facebook game that sheds some light on the series' mysteries.
That being said, AC: Brotherhood is still a must-play for everyone who enjoyed the first two games.

It's a tower defense game where you need to manage units and repeal invaders. You need to make it through a level and move on to the next one. Each time more units are introduced.
This time the invaders are zombies and your tower units are various plants and mushrooms. All the action taking place in your front garden. If the zombies manage to get into your house it's ZOMBIE ATE MY BRAINS!
I love it.
There is a humourous feel to the game that leads to genuine gufawing. The zombies are amazingly designed - some can pole vault, others can disco dance like John Travolta from the 70s with accompanying flared trousers. Others fly in from balloons and others carry ladders.
The plants you have at your disposal are also well designed and varied. Some throw huge melons onto the attacking hoard. Others are like gatlin guns. If you plant a jalapeno - it takes out the whole line.
With so many options to choose the game helps by providing an intial glimse of the zombie hoards and this will help you decide which plants and mushrooms to choose. Yep, at the beginning of each level you need to choose your weapons. It's a great feature as it allows for your own playstyle.
If you have not heard of PvZ or played an incarnation on the various platforms - get serious and enjoy one of the best games in this genre.

Hmm, this game is not bad, but I'm not going to lie, I feel it was a bit overrated. Kind of reminds me when Bioshock Infinite first came out and everyone freaked out saying it was the best game ever(it was good, just not that good). When this game came out, everyone kind of freaked out the same way. The game is good, just not that good. Shovel Knight is a lot like a medieval Megaman. Defeat the robot masters, then defeat the last boss. But that's the thing, this game just makes me want to play the old NES platforms more than Shovel Knight itself. I don't feel like it quite grasped the the same hook as the old games did. Maybe that's just me.
Pros:
+ Awesome controls
+ Cool soundtrack
+ Retro GFX bring back good memories and are very well done
+ Character sprites are awesome and variety of the types of creatures is very creative
+ Great level designs
+ Good flow of difficulty, things get harder as you progress but the game teaches you along the way so you are prepared
+ Defintiely captures the old school platformer rage, when you die, you get really annoyed
+ New Game Plus feature is always awesome
+ Fairly Priced
Cons(Most of these, I feel, are more personal than general):
- Game is too achievement based as far as unlockables, I would prefer more in game unlockables
- Though the soundtrack is great, having to find all the songs is not a really fun unlockable, would rather just buy the soundtrack or have a different type of collectable sidequest
- Story is lacking anything interesting, now, in games like this, that wouldn't normally be a big deal, but an effort is made to tell a story, therefore, I have to critique it. No story was really necessary.
- The last castle could have used more stages instead of just 2, the game seemed to end too quickly
- You purchase all upgrades too quickly, as well as relics, then you just have a bunch of money, should be more things to purchase
Overall, a good platformer but a little too overhyped in my opinion. It's fun but if I were to choose between, say, Megaman 2 and this game, I would rather play Megaman 2 or other NES platformers. Sweet game. 4 classes, each having a huge unique arsenal to choose from, and a variety of enemies to kill. You can go Starship Trooper mode and be a Ranger, blow insects up in a jet pack with the Wing Diver, call in chaotic airstrikes and even giant mechs or vehicles with the Air Raider, or become a Fencer and smash bugs in a power suit with some serious firepower. Not only is there a millions of bugs to kill but there is hundreds of buildings to destroy too, if you have the right firepower, everything you see is destructable, from highways to giant skyscrapers. EDF is 100% gameplay and if you hate this game you might actually hate video games. EDF knows what it wants to be and it achieves it with flying colors.
As for performance, I'm impressed. Most japanese ports suck, but EDF is good. There's only a few options like to change shadows, turn on AA and change the resolution, AND there's a 60 fps lock (which isn't that bad) but I was running this with a constant 60 frames even when there was hundreds of bugs on my screen and I was leveling entire city blocks. HOWEVER, I personally don't have AMD but as I'm writing this review apparently there's a lot of crashes with AMD users to the point the game isn't even playable, specfically the Phenom II line so if you have that line of processors I'd hold off until they fix it.

This is only the second review for a game i've ever felt inclined to give, and it comes from an experience within the game that I don't think many can compare with.
Let me explain. I am quite the noob when it comes to fishing in the real world, but I love it. It has quickly become something I prefer to spend my free time doing, but being as new to it as I am, I had absolutely no idea as to what I am doing, all I knew was I had a prime spot behind my house, (the stillwater river is literally behind my house) and I wanted to catch some fish.
Well, with the very little fishing experience I have, I was actually able to land a few fish out of my spot behind my house, but it was all blind luck, and a very riveting experience that I had a blast with, but learned nothing from. So one day while browsing through steam, this game pops up on my queue and it seems to look rather realistic and a fun game to play, so I download it thinking of it honestly nothing more that a throwaway game that I'll play for a few hours and then uninstall as it just doesn't have enough to keep me coming back. Well, Let me tell you about yesterday, the day that all changed...
Throughout my time playing the game, I'm still only level 7 and let me tell you, this level has tried my patience with this game as no other has, and it has honestly been the most difficult but most rewarding level I've had thus far, and this is why. The game relies on real world fishing applications, (to an extent, i've never caught fish as quick as you do in the game) but the idea behind what lure to use, and when to fish is all there, and it actually holds real world value. By using what I learned in-game, I was able to go down to my spot and apply these lessons, and have them actually work! Granted I didn't pull out a "trophy" or "unique" fish, but I was able to land several rainbow trout using the logic I used in the game. It was honestly the second time I've ever actually tried fishing with a spoon lure, ( i prefer the ease of float fishing) but by using the techniques I learned in the game, I had the best fishing day yet down there... I'm not gonna say this game taught me how to catch fish, but I can say that it taught me a thing or two to help me out in my real world fishing adventures, thanks to the devs and I hope they continue with it. I just would lke to know why level 7 has been such a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for me... ;)

The only cons I have with this game are solely host-based.
Sometimes the game netcoding can mean some really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t deaths, however I've seen alot less issues on that end than there were.
Casual Matchmaking pitches all the experienced players against the newbies. Sure, it's incentive to get better and play more of the game to improve, but I feel like matchmaking in general could use some huge improvements.
Also, word of warning when buying and redeeming through Steam: Even with a Steam copy, you still need a valid uPlay account. When you install the game, make sure and open uPlay in your Taskbar, sign into your uPlay account you want to redeem the game to, and relaunch. If you're not signed into your uPlay account when you launch, you'll show up as guest-xxxxxxxxx. Redeeming the game to a guest account may as well be throwing your license out the window, so do be VERY CAREFUL with your game redemption. After all the initial setup tirades though, shouldn't be any issues.

There is something fishy about this game ... Sorry, couldn't help myself. This game is unlike anything else I've ever played. And that is a good thing. I absolutely love this game. Who would have thought that fishing in your couch could be so fun?
I first downloaded this game because I was bored and I was looking for something to kill time. Then I found this. At first I thought that I'd just spend a couple of hours in it, and then leave it behind. How wrong I was! I played it almost non-stop for a full weekend ... I didn't have many hours of sleep those nights ... I can't explain it, but there's something about just watching that bobber and waiting for the fish to grab your bait or lure that is very captivating.
If you, like me, like fishing, then you should absolutely give this game a go. It is among the very best simulators out there, and with great developers who constantly work on improving it, I imagine things will only get better in the near future.
Pros: Great looking environments, pretty realistic fish looks and fights, good variety in gear available, devs constantly improving upon existing stuff as well as adding new stuff. And it's free to play!
This is both a pro and con - sometimes it does take ages for the fish to grab your hook, however that is a part of the realism in the game, though sometimes it can get frustrating.
Cons: Leveling up takes a bit too long in my opinion. After you get access to Colorado and North Carolina, it feels like the leveling progress slowed a lot. Also, the DLC pricing is just ridicolous. The high-end DLC's cost more than the full base-game of many other top-of-the-line simulator games out there. But the DLC's are not necessary to enjoy the lovely game that Fishing Planet is.

Sweet game. 4 classes, each having a huge unique arsenal to choose from, and a variety of enemies to kill. You can go Starship Trooper mode and be a Ranger, blow insects up in a jet pack with the Wing Diver, call in chaotic airstrikes and even giant mechs or vehicles with the Air Raider, or become a Fencer and smash bugs in a power suit with some serious firepower. Not only is there a millions of bugs to kill but there is hundreds of buildings to destroy too, if you have the right firepower, everything you see is destructable, from highways to giant skyscrapers. EDF is 100% gameplay and if you hate this game you might actually hate video games. EDF knows what it wants to be and it achieves it with flying colors.
As for performance, I'm impressed. Most japanese ports suck, but EDF is good. There's only a few options like to change shadows, turn on AA and change the resolution, AND there's a 60 fps lock (which isn't that bad) but I was running this with a constant 60 frames even when there was hundreds of bugs on my screen and I was leveling entire city blocks. HOWEVER, I personally don't have AMD but as I'm writing this review apparently there's a lot of crashes with AMD users to the point the game isn't even playable, specfically the Phenom II line so if you have that line of processors I'd hold off until they fix it.

Although this may lower your hopes, when you have sort of conquered the ability to drift in this game, it's really fun. The race courses are all there, with time trial mechanics. There are also courses where you have to get points in a certain amount of time by drifting, spinning donuts, etcetera. Next to that, there's a free roam mode where you can explore quite a big world, all minimalistic and good-looking with quests to advance to the next area of said world (FYI, it's one big world. no loading screens whatsoever). Now, I would recommend this game, but there are two problems I have with it: the quests you have to do to advance to the next part of the world are extremely repetitive, and there aren't that many race/trick courses. For its price being 11,99, this really isn't much of a game. I WOULD recommend it if it's either on sale or cheap to get through retail. But yeah, for its price, the game is really short. I completed the free roaming mode in around 1,5 hours, and, like I said, there aren't that many other things to do next to break your previous record on racing or trick courses.
TL;DR: Too expensive, recommended if cheaper.

Loading Screen Simulator exists at an intersection between design and artistry, a crossroad at which pure tactile joy meets refined, intelligent design to create a rare spark of magic.
A Loading Screen Simulator, it finds accessibility not by lowering the skill ceiling, but by broadening the definition of skill. The person with deadshot clicking is no more valuable than the person  with the decision-making money . While it didn't exactly drown me in options with sindows, it’s blessed with a multitude of tactical layers, and none of them ever came between me and my enjoyment of its intense, swirling clicking, and thrilling pong and cmd. Loading Screen Simulator does a great many things well, but above all else, its success is built on the backs of its many excellent in game buys. It’s fitting that the main menu is dominated by one of them at all times.
In terms of features, Loading Screen Simulator is just a bit thin, but it meets most of the basic expectations of a Simulator and in some ways, exceeds them. Its impressive placement of the loading bar and accessibility options stand out. It also does a great job of identifying and surfacing good play to yourself and the loading bar through a novel commendation system and a sweet Sindows Update. Clicking is swift and reliable, and the Sindows unlockables are surprisingly charming and come at a pretty decent pace without clicking for extra money.
Loading Screen Simulator is an incredible achievement in Simulator design. It bobs and weaves almost perfectly between being the quick-fix adrenaline hit you might want after a long day of work, and the thoughtful, strategic placement of the loading bar experience that becomes the center of evening-long binges with yourself. It might not have the most exhaustive list of items in the sindows store, but it provides nearly endless opportunities for exhilarating, coordinated clicks, and when you’re the one at the center of it, it feels like nothing else.

This is coming from a gamer who has dropped hundreds of dollars in this game (multiple FP accounts), who has all but one advanced licenses unlocked, and well over 2 million in game cash, and so much inventory that it takes literally up to 15 seconds to load some inventory slots. Almost all the inventory of mine was purchased with gold coins just before the BaitCoins went live.
The developers obviously don't get it, or we as the gaming community keep on spoon feeding them money for their re-skinned content. I will get in detail about the game content below;
They would not need to rely on sales of BaitCoin, or Premium memberships if they just had DLC that people actually wanted. Things that would make the game different, or a nice perks (but does not need to be game changing to the point where people who don’t have it are at a serious disadvantage, but would make the people who don’t have it want it even more.)
You can purchase a Premium Membership to speed up the game XP, or to speed up the fast forward timer. But at the end of the day you are going to get to level 40 and realize that you wasted your money. The game experience at level 40 is exactly the same at level 1. However, being level 1 (and being new) you have many things to look forward to. At level 40 there is nothing left, and it has been this way for as far as I can remember. I repeat, nothing to look forward to so don't rush it and enjoy the free ride. The leaderboards don’t even work for all the fish species… so you better make sure you caught the biggest one of that species or you are not going to see how you ranked.
Many Games offer DLC as something new; it’s usually in the form of new places to go, new content to see and it keeps the game fresh. This game offers you DLC in the form of a "re-skin" of items that are ALREADY in the game and has nothing, once again nothing unique about it at all, you are able to use these items earlier to speed up your gaming process. If you knew there was new DLC that you had to be level 40 for (or whatever level), then I’m sure people would purchase the Premium Content in order to speed up their leveling so that they would be able to experience this new content. (In this case the developers would not only make money from the DLC but also from Premium membership if someone wanted to rush level.)
The game already has currency for you, you receive it for catching fish. If you are patient the game provides everything for you. Once upon a time there was gold coins, and you would receive them for catching unique fish. That has now been replaced with BaitCoins which can only be purchased for real money, and let’s face it, the items you can purchase with it are nothing really special (besides advanced licenses, but if you are a good fisherman/woman you make enough money to continue on anyhow without these.)
If you look at the steam charts, this game has lost a lot of players... but then makes up for it now and again. As for the longevity of this game, I could not say because there has been nothing new for the longest time. I want to believe this game will be around for years to come, because it is enjoyable but at the same time dull with a lack of luster from content. We have been looking at the physics bug fix since the last major patch (many, many months ago) without making a whole lot of headroom/ improvement.
I’m not saying for you to not spend your money, I have. I am saying that we should be expecting more from the developers in order for them to earn our money, and we should hold them to a higher standard.

This is coming from a gamer who has dropped hundreds of dollars in this game (multiple FP accounts), who has all but one advanced licenses unlocked, and well over 2 million in game cash, and so much inventory that it takes literally up to 15 seconds to load some inventory slots. Almost all the inventory of mine was purchased with gold coins just before the BaitCoins went live.
The developers obviously don't get it, or we as the gaming community keep on spoon feeding them money for their re-skinned content. I will get in detail about the game content below;
They would not need to rely on sales of BaitCoin, or Premium memberships if they just had DLC that people actually wanted. Things that would make the game different, or a nice perks (but does not need to be game changing to the point where people who don’t have it are at a serious disadvantage, but would make the people who don’t have it want it even more.)
You can purchase a Premium Membership to speed up the game XP, or to speed up the fast forward timer. But at the end of the day you are going to get to level 40 and realize that you wasted your money. The game experience at level 40 is exactly the same at level 1. However, being level 1 (and being new) you have many things to look forward to. At level 40 there is nothing left, and it has been this way for as far as I can remember. I repeat, nothing to look forward to so don't rush it and enjoy the free ride. The leaderboards don’t even work for all the fish species… so you better make sure you caught the biggest one of that species or you are not going to see how you ranked.
Many Games offer DLC as something new; it’s usually in the form of new places to go, new content to see and it keeps the game fresh. This game offers you DLC in the form of a "re-skin" of items that are ALREADY in the game and has nothing, once again nothing unique about it at all, you are able to use these items earlier to speed up your gaming process. If you knew there was new DLC that you had to be level 40 for (or whatever level), then I’m sure people would purchase the Premium Content in order to speed up their leveling so that they would be able to experience this new content. (In this case the developers would not only make money from the DLC but also from Premium membership if someone wanted to rush level.)
The game already has currency for you, you receive it for catching fish. If you are patient the game provides everything for you. Once upon a time there was gold coins, and you would receive them for catching unique fish. That has now been replaced with BaitCoins which can only be purchased for real money, and let’s face it, the items you can purchase with it are nothing really special (besides advanced licenses, but if you are a good fisherman/woman you make enough money to continue on anyhow without these.)
If you look at the steam charts, this game has lost a lot of players... but then makes up for it now and again. As for the longevity of this game, I could not say because there has been nothing new for the longest time. I want to believe this game will be around for years to come, because it is enjoyable but at the same time dull with a lack of luster from content. We have been looking at the physics bug fix since the last major patch (many, many months ago) without making a whole lot of headroom/ improvement.
I’m not saying for you to not spend your money, I have. I am saying that we should be expecting more from the developers in order for them to earn our money, and we should hold them to a higher standard.

Updated as of 0.7.0. - One year after original review.
If you wish to see a before and after comparison, continue reading after this section to see my old review for version 0.3.8. Regardless, this review has gone from "Recommended" to "Not Recommended".
A rather lackluster fishing game that is focusing on microtransactions over actual gameplay content. While Fishing Planet is still being advertised as a realistic fishing sim, the developers are gradually moving further and further away from that claim. Below, I'm going to list many things that have changed, for good or bad, since my last review of the game.
The Good:
Above average graphical and audio quality.
More fish species have been added to the game. A larger assortment is always nice.
A couple of new waterways have been added. Alaska and Louisiana are two new states you can now go fishing in. Texas is the new starter lake. Costs nothing to go there so, if you go broke, you have at least one place to go to.
3D views of your trophy fish and 3D views of gear in the shop.
The Bad:
3D Avatars. Not many people were requesting this and, when they were released, you could not turn them off. So, you would see what I term "clown car fishing" regularly. Six or eight avatars jammed in a three foot space to EZ-Mode land fish by casting a couple feet out. Once hooked, they're landed instantly. Devs finally gave us the ability to disable them after a month or so.
Smaller lobbies. With the implementation of 3D avatars, all lobbies went from twenty people per lobby, down to five or ten people per lobby, depending on what waterway you were at.
Prices for gear and travel have skyrocketed. A trip that once cost 25 Credits now costs 1500 Credits. A rod that once cost 100 Credits now costs around 1000 Credits.
Gold (the currency used to purchase "premium" gear), which could be earned by catching unique fish, has been removed from the game and replaced with Bait Coins, which can only be gotten with real money unless you manage to place well in competitions.
Permanent licenses have been moved from Credit purchase to Bait Coin only purchase. This, inheritantly, screws over casual anglers as licenses are based on RL days. For the player that that can only play an hour a day, it's nearly impossible for that person break even on a trip, now that temporary licenses cost even more credits.
Catching fish is still done via spreadsheet. Cast here, with this lure/bait, at this time for guaranteed full nets.
Still no night fishing or topwater fishing.
Rod and line physics are still wonky, at best. As are fish fighting mechanics, from time to time.
Financially, only certain fish are worth catching. It's pointless to waste time catching Bluegill because they're worth little to no exp or credits.
The Ugly:
The devs stated, back in February when 0.7.0 went live, that Bait Coins would be earnabled from Unique fish soon. Three months later, they still haven't enabled the feature.
Developer commumincation with the userbase is pretty much non-existant. You hear little to nothing from them for a month or more, only for them to reappear briefly when a patch is released.
One dev has stated that they don't care about the opinions of players who haven't spent anything on their F2P game.
Moderation of the discussion forum has declined greatly. Users regularly flame other users, calling other people idiots for having a differing opinion and those comments are there days later. Moderators used to actually make the forum a tolerable place to be by getting rid of content like that.
On the other side of the spectrum, mentioning other games, such as the yet to be released Ultimate Fishing, that may be competition to Fishing Planet are removed almost immediately.

A wonderful fishing game thats a little rough around the edges.
This is an early access review of Fishing Planet. As of this writing, the game is currently on version 0.3.8 with an average update cyle of one every other week. I also have 400 hours in this title since August of 2015. I am a liesurely angler and have only recently reached level 21 in game.
Fishing Planet is what I would consider a pseudo-simulator. The primary goal of the game is to relax and fish, though tournament style fishing is planned. As anyone who has fished in real life would know, you're never guaranteed a catch. This is the main point where Fishing Planet leaves the "true" simulation. It must balance gameplay with realism, and as such, catch rates are generally higher than what you would find in real life. On the other hand, you are offered a wider variety of rods, reels, lines, tackle, bait and misc. equipment designed to target a range of fish in a range of situations. You then couple all those decisions with your retrieval style, such as straight retrieves, stop and go, lift and drop, among others.
That being said, what is planned and what we have currently are two different things. If you come into Fishing Planet at this time, expecting a perfect simulator, you will be disappointed. Fish currently have spawn boxes and set times when they spawn. Venture your lure outside this box or through this box at the wrong time of day and you won't find anything. Fish randomization is something the devs are working towards but, for the time being, the same general strategy is required. There are guides and spreadsheets detailing where to cast, when and with what lure/bait that will, hopefully, be rendered completely obsolete in the near future.
There is a leveling system in place to limit where you can fish and what fish you can realistically catch. You can't just hop into the game and expect to catch 20kg Muskie immediately. You'll first need to catch smaller fish worth experience and credits to level up and purchase new gear, as well as licenses to higher tier lakes. The devs have recently ended a test in regards to removed level locks on lakes, and as such, it may be removed on all lakes in the future. If that's the case, your only limiting factor will be gear. You will still have to earn your gear by leveling up or bypassing level locks by purchasing DLC packs focusing on certain gear types such as heavy float rods or ultralight tackle. These DLC are completely optional if you wish to take your time and fish.
Waterways are currently limited to North America, specifically, the United States. However, there are plans for European and Asian waterways in the future. Fish species are diverse and dependant on where you are. Current species include, but are not limited to Gar (Alligator, Florida and Longnose), Bass (Largemouth, Smallmouth, White, Peacock and Striped), Catfish (Channel, Blue, Flathead), Panfish (Bluegill, Crappie, etc.), Pike, Trout, Salmon and more.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. Water physics are a sight to see. Ambient noise is great though some lakes can be a tad bit annoying to listen to.
There are some rough spots though. They range from physics (fishing launching into the air) to fish AI bugs (fish don't even bother fighting on ocassion) to equipment bugs (drag exerting tension on the line even when not under any load). None of them are major or game breaking, in my opinion. Your mileage may vary. I currently would recommend this title to anyone who enjoys fishing as a leisure sport. Perhap, once tournaments are added, more competitive anglers will have something of interest. Arcade anglers, however, I fear would not find this fu. There are no easy-mode toggles such as underwater cam, reel assist, automatic tensioners or the like. If you don't know how to fish from real life experience and are unwilling to learn the basics of how fishing gear works, you may find this a difficult title to pick up.
