Portal Stories: Mel is in its own right a new Portal game. A great one at that.
As you can see I put over 7 hours into this game, and that was in a 24 hour period. As soon as I saw this in the store, I knew there had to be something to it. It turned out I was right. I'm just going to cut to the chase so you can play this game sooner.
Puzzels: Hard. There is no opportunity to learn how to play the game. At minimum, play Portal 2 first. that way you understand the mechanics of the game.
Story: Amazing. NO SPOILERS, the way the game ties in the new charactors to Portal 2's story is flawless. It feels as if the game was written by Valve themselves. It is very satisfiying to see it all the way through.
What's New: Red Emancipation grill that you can't walk through. Retro portal gun. There are plenty of other new ideas, but I don't want to say too much and spoil the surprise when you get to the puzzles.
Voice acting is good to. The actors did a superb job with the charactors.
The only question left when you finish; Is the game canon? That's really up to you. This is like fan fiction when it comes to games. It's great and the story is well written, but you are left hanging thinking "Does this really fit in the bigger narative? It feels like it does but I'm not sure."
In conclusion, get this game. It's free and it's great to experience more portal.

Think Castlevania meets Ducktales meets Mega Man.  It has a world map straight out of Mario 3 and 8 bosses with an intro stage along with a village where you can buy and sell things, and an airship with armor and shovel upgrades.
The bosses are creative, colorful in personality, and fun to fight. All the boss patterns are fun and interesting and with no order of each move it can be challenging. There are many secret areas in where you can get more loot, relics, or music sheets to certain songs that you can sell and then play in the village. The gameplay and design are fairly thought out. You stop in your place to slash with your shovel. You can use your shovel to use a pogostick-like attack. Later in the game you can get a charge slash that makes the movement really awkward when you charge it. The movement feels a little too slow in my opinion and the jumps feel too high in comparison.

You are never faced with too much at one time with no chance to get the pattern. It always feels a bit too safe. I never died to losing all my life or to a boss. I only died to bottomless pits and spikes that sometimes felt cheap. This game is built around a speedrun and to get full completion you will need to master that speedrun and that is only a sign of good design.

Absolute Drift has that borderline feeling between trying to be arcade and trying to be sim, and doing neither well. The camera angle says arcade, the fine control of steering says sim, the overall physics say they don't know what they are - and I don't know either.
With the minimalist single-angle isometric style, they should have gone towards a challenging arcade experience, instead I got a frustrating blend of sim/arcade controls that is derived from what feels like a lightly modified UnityCar 2.0 asset package, which uses Pacejka curves and isn't great for drifting without code voodoo.
The game still has potential to be fun, perhaps alternate camera angles providing a better perspective of what is going on would bring out the game's arcade/sim mixture better and make the controls more enjoyable. As it stands, it's a decent DnB playlist with a car game on top.

This game looks and sound amazing! It's essentialy a side scrolling, space shooter game, with a ship that can be upgraded based on how high a score you get. The score is not only dertermined on how far you get and how many enimies you kill, but also the number of starbits you collect from enimies. After an enemy is destroyed, they will drop some starbits, so be sure to collect them. The upgrades vary from shields and engine speed, to weapon recharge rate and random clamore deploy rate. Speaking of weapons, your main gun fires automaticaly but stops when the left mouse is held. Odd, I know. Additionally you have a drill you can switch to by clicking right mouse, which allows you to drill through planets and, if your quick enough. Really Big sky features several different unlockable game types like survival, pacifist(can't shoot), Bossism(all bosses), and Hell. The colors and explosions are just beautiful, however sometimes they take on a sort of psychodelic fell to them and can make enimies hard to see. The music is great, as long as your just playing classic, as some of the music for the other game types doesn't sound all that great. I kindof feel it could use a bigger selection of music.  Overall Really Big Sky is a great time-killing game, and I'd recommend it to anyone who side-scrolling arcade shooters.

Whereas AC 2 struck the right balance between varied main story line missions and more random openworld sidequests, AC:Bro drowns the player in pointless, repetitive, busywork. Upgrading stores, recruiting and managing assassins, destroying towers, thieves guild tasks, brothel tasks...and the list goes on and on. In fact, it seems like halfway through the game new stuff is still being introduced, to the point that I kept wondering "So when does the tutorial end and the game begin?"
None of this would be a problem if all of this inconsequential fluff was interesting, but most is simply repeating the same things over and over again. When they aren't acting as dry tutorials for all the busywork the main quest missions can be quite good, but unfortunately they tend to be drowned out by all the added nonsense. Ultimately there's a good game beneath all the bloat (if you look for it), but this is still a small step backwards for the series.

DISCLAIMER: My review will be slighty biased as I have played the GDF/EDF series for a long time.
SPECS:(No fps drops or crashes so far and little to no bugs (no pun intended))
OS: Windows 7 Premium
RAM: 32gb
GPU: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070
CPU: Intel i7-4790k @ 4.00 Ghz 4 cores
Oh boy, where do I begin? I guess I could start off with a little history before I get into the meat of the review. This series is what got me into gaming, so I guess you could say it was my childhood. You play as a soldier of the EDF or Earth Defense Force fighting an alien threat that came to Earth known as the Ravagers who are hell bent on wiping out humanity. I started playing at the time of Global/Earth Defense Force on the PS2 back in 2005. I had the time of my life and no game to this date has brought me as much mindless joy as this one has. This game is a Genocide Simulator in essence. Yes, it has a story but not one you would expect. Imagine how DOOM has a story, but they focus on the killing sprees of it. That same formula applies here but instead of an RPG-like world this is mission based. I sold my console a little after EDF 4 or EDF 2025 came out and am happy they brought it to PC! I have easily played 1000 hours on GDF 1, 2, and EDF 3 or EDF 2017 doing every difficulty and collecting every weapon.
This game here (EDF 4.1) is the definitive edition of EDF 4. It contains better fps, more missions, more content, and just overall smoother gameplay. The way you collect weaponry is by picking up weapon crates from enemies (same for armor/health). The higher the difficulty, the better the weapons you obtain to help you destroy the Ravagers. There are 5 difficulty levels and things can actually get intense. There are a total of 89 missions in Single Player and 98 in Multi-Player (EDF 3 only has 52 total). Even though the missions go by quickly sometimes, you would be surprised by how much time can fly when playing this. (At the time of typing I have 30hrs on record and have only gone through 33 missions, some are quick and others are long). There are a lot of people I have noticed that complain about the graphics and the reason it doesn't look as great as Star Wars Battlefront is because this series focuses on putting as many enemies against you as possible. That's their thing. Also, I for one think the art style is neat for the series. There are 4 classes total (see the branch/class trailer for that) and 800 weapons to collect (EDF 3 had 1 class and 171 weapons total), and so far it has been better than its precursor. This game is a little grindy but the amount of things and massive battles going on at once makes up for it, and to get the full experience you need to play with a full group in MP, it rocks, literally.
I am not seeing any fps issues nor in-game anomalies on my system. The PC port seems to be amazing in every major way. The only gripe I have with it is that in MP, there is no push to talk, so you hear others breathing through their mics, and if you turn off voice chat it turns text chat off too so it's kind of a downer. Hopefully it will get changed.
There is a LOT more coming to this game including new missions you can optionally purchase and before people say it never happened, one of the Sandloft guys on the forums said later on they would support mods sometime. For reference on that just go search up "mods" on the discussion tab. This is really cool considering how this will be the first time EDF gets mod support and WE will get to experience it. No one knows how that will work so far so don't worry about it yet.
All in all, I may be biased since this was a big thing for me back then, but it is easily worth the price if you can stand a little repetitive gameplay from time to time. I HIGHLY recommend grouping up with others to get a more awesome time. That concludes my Earth Defense Force 4.1 review. If there is anything important I missed let me know so I can edit it in!

What a fantastic game.  I'll admit, when I first saw this I was worried it would feel too dumbed down, more like a mobile game than a full PC game, I thought that it would perhaps be a bit of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ization of drift culture...but I have never been so wrong.
Absolute Drift does everything right for me, it has an amazing soundtrack which is suited perfectly to the atmosphere of the game, the driving feels intuitive and incredibly rewarding (I drift competitively in real life and the handling felt right at home for me), and the drift culture references are everywhere from the "missile" S13 with #NFG engraved on the bottom to the little chime it plays when you unlock a new world.  Fans of drifting will find a special place in their heart for this game, but it's something everyone can enjoy.
Some things worth noting...
There is a thin storyline and tutorial to get you started, then you're pushed out into the open world.  You start in a replica of the iconic AE86 in an airfield.  As you complete "missions" in the world, you unlock more zones which give you access to big new areas to play around and hone your skills in while also unlocking new cars, missions and "events" (which are sorted into driftkhana, tracks, or mountain passes).  Overall the game's "story" should take about 2-3 hours to finish, but the game is far from over at that point.
From the videos it looked like the control scheme might be a bit hard to grasp but I was able to pick it up pretty quickly with an xbox controller, and after an hour or two of play I felt like I had pretty good control over my car.  The use of steering input, gas, brake and handbrake all come together and really start to feel intuitive after only a short time playing.  After 5+ hours I felt like I had mastered the art of drifting, and then I realized there was a manual transmission option, and my steering assist was on.  Turn these to manual/off and you'll be in for a whole new challenge.  The cars all feel different and each have their own strengths and weaknesses in certain areas of the game making them all relevant, there is no "best car".  All in all, the game is easy to grasp but hard to master which in my opinion is the perfect formula.
(I'd strongly recommend using a controller for the game.)
I purchased the game for $12.00 and feel like I have definitely gotten my money's worth.  Although the main "story" of the game may only take 2-3 hours, the replay value is incredibly high.  There are ~25 ranked courses that you can get to from the open world or just hop into from the main menu and this is where most of the "endgame" lies.  You are scored based on speed, angle, proximity to cones and ability to keep a good line without hitting walls or slowing down too much.  Your highest score for each course gives you your leaderboard ranking and percentile within the playerbase.  Repeating a course multiple times in a row just to climb a few spots in the leaderboards is very addicting, you've been warned.  The open world is another place where the game really extends it's value, once you've unlocked all 6 zones you'll see just how massive and varied the world is - free for you to create your own tracks.  The fantastic soundtrack and rewarding car handling really let's you just zone out and drift around for hours without feeling bored.
No game is perfect, this is no exception.  After a while I've noticed a few minor audio and visual bugs, noticeable but nothing gamebreaking at all.  The unique art style definitely fits the feel of the game, however I do feel like more color wouldn't be a bad thing.  The art style doesn't really take anything away from the game, but it doesn't add much either.  I'd like to see more colors, assets and effects, something to please the eyes while I mindlessly drift about the open world, bobbing my head to the beat.  Multiplayer sadly doesn't make an appearance here and I'd really like it.  Being able to tandem drift in mountain passes with a few of my friends would bring the experience to a whole new level.  The ability to set up your own courses in the open world, or even perhaps build your own with a level design tool would also be a huge addition here.
If a sequel is in the works (which I hope for more than anything) I'd really like to see a more fleshed out environment with colors, lighting, etc etc.  Multiplayer and a track builder of some sort would be a big plus, but the only other thing I'd really like to see is MORE!  More cars, more customization, more open world, longer tracks, etc.
This game is easy to learn and hard to master.  The driving formula is just right and pulling off a hard drift just feels good.  There are a few minor bugs and the art style doesn't give your eyes much to look at but the sheer amount of content and enjoyment you get for the price tag is hard to beat.

In spite of the hours I've logged on AC:B and ACII, don't be fooled: only about half of those hours are worth the playing. Most of all the AC games involves running around and trying to avoid being attacked by guards, who seem to spawn just in time to complicate your escape. The storyline and actual missions are great, but they tend to be variations on the same basic types: tail someone. Assassinate someone without being detected. Hold down W + RMB + SHFT indefnitely (what the game calls "freerunning"). AC:B seems to be particularly annoying with regards to how the controls and freerunning works: sometimes Ezio will leap off a tall building even though you told him to walk cautiously in the opposite direction, and sometimes he will lock on to something you didn't even know was there and save your hide before you even realized it was in danger. There are also several annoying features of the game, like the camera switching perspective, which throws off the direction Ezio moves in.

So far I enjoy it.
Performance wise, it takes a bit of time investment to adjust the game's performance/graphics ratio; doing some tweaks not only via in-game settings but with other means - editing the .cfgs file, as an example - helps a lot in that regard.
After doing the above, the game runs truly well - tested with a GTX 950, i5-4460 3.2gHz); it maintains an average of 63 fps around cities, while 58 - with 53 spikes - inside the cities themselves.
The community made mods are well worth it the download investment - ten to twenty GB, IIRC - bringing back the old Chernarus made me smile. Even without Apex, the game demonstrates its potential, but Tanoa has its justice as a really polished map.

I've always thought that this game was perfect at understanding the operations of the human mind and creating a true horror environment from it. There are a lot of nuances in this particular game that allow it to get in your head to a remarkable extent. The lack of music, the environments, the story, the necessity of opening doors and moving switches manually instead of pressing a button; all of these things contribute to you being so creeped out and scared that you will even be frightened if playing this game in broad daylight sometimes. Even though it's tough, I do recommend playing the game in the lights out with headphones for the true experience.
I think that i felt very close with the character by the end of this game as well. You (Daniel) try to "defeat" the main antagonist (Alexander) to escape his castle, and you unconver the backstory while you do. The backstory itself is not super elaborate, but quite feasible. When you do (spoilers) escape the castle at the end of the game, you also feel a sense of relief (because you don't have to play the game any more, in a way!) similar to the one that you imagine occurs in Daniel.
The monsters in the game are pretty scary at first, but you eventually can get used to working around them and you will learn that dying is the best thing in the game because it means that you don't have to be scared any more.
In particular, this was the one title that put Frictional out on the map, and it is an absolute masterpiece. It is a truly unique experience that cannot be replicated and I would recommend it to everyone.

Once I realized that I could use points I got in-game to upgrade my ship so I didn't die from one shot I started having fun. I'm dumb.  This is pretty crazy bullet hell shooter. There's times when there's so much going on on the screen I have no ♥♥♥♥ing idea what's happening and then my ship materializes from a purple-blue blaze of laser fire still intact with all the enemies gone. It's those moments that make the game.  I have to say it's a rather confusing game, but not just because there's a lot going on.  Some of the mechanics aren't very intuitive. Same with the boss fights, or what even constitutes a boss.  I enjoy the fact that what the game throws at you each time is different; or, at least, the order in which the game throws fixed battles at you is random.  The drill-through-planets concept is pretty cool, too. It also has a bunch of game modes, which adds a good amount of replay value.
I think the weakest points are the voice acting (would've been better to have none...sorry) and the occasionally surreal enemies that seem way out of context, like those dinosaur heads that rotate and shoot lasers. Seriously, wtf is that about?  That just breaks immersion. The game also seems to be missing that final polish.  I can't really put my finger on it, and it's not an unpolished game, but something feels loose.
All in all, if you like bullet hell shooters, you'll probably like this. I did, and still do. It's great fun to jump in and see how long I can last against ridiculous odds. Pick it up.

The first area is fun. After that the games issues are glaringly obvious.
The level grind is pointless. You will be able to travel to new areas based on your level but, you won't be able to catch all the fish. This means if you manage to hook something larger, it will break your gear.
Even if you have the right gear, fish will still break your gear. A 4lb fish *should* never ever EVER break 10-15 or 20lb test. Most of the gear doesn't work correctly with each other and/or it's difficult to figure out. Nothing like putting 20lb test on a reel that has max drag of 19.58 and breaking your reel... wait what? Maybeeee the devs should worry less about getting a sponsorship from one of these manufaturers and just make it work. It's just a game.
Technique means nothing. The only thing that matters is the right lure or bait.
Broken random system. After 4,000+ fish and 500+ Trophies I still had never caught a Unique. I could be standing toe to toe with a friend (and did) doing the same technique with the same gear and same lure at the same time of day for days on end and he would catch them and I would not. *Whul ya must bae doon sumtin wong* Even a blind pig finds a truffle.
You'll end up with a lot of money with nothing to spend it on.
OR you'll encure a negative balance from releasing a fish and getting a fine anyway. No one will help you if this happens. So, If you want to just log in for a month for your daily log in bonus to try to clear the negative balance, have fun.
Not a sustainable game. If the level grind doesn't bore you to death, the bugs will drive you insane.

EDIT 2: Someone added me today and asked more about Resident Evil 5, so I'm going to post a little bit more here about co-op and the game's replayablity.
CO-OP
Co-op is very fun in this game. If you've played Resident Evil 6 it's almost like that but with one core difference. Trading. When playing co-op you take control of the second playable character and take on their role. During the game (either singleplayer or co-op), there are areas that require you to split up. For example, Sheva can access places that Chris cannot. Sometimes you'll both be separated and have to cover one another, which makes you depend on your co-op partner, so choose wisely with who you play with. Now, back to trading. In Resident Evil 5 in between chapters/parts, you gain access to your inventory, stash, and store screen. You can buy weapons or items, but not ammo. In this screen you can trade things from your inventory over to your co-op partner's inventory to share and help out. This is especially useful if you stock up on ammo and your friend ran out.
REPLAYABILITY
This game has emense replayability. If you're playing for the first time (seasoned or recruit), it's always a good idea to start on Amatuer or Normal just to build up your arsenal and upgrade your weapons a bit. There's no harm in that. When I play, I always start on Amatuer for the first playthrough to unlock everything and get started. By the end of the game if you've collected all the treasures and picked up lots of money, you should have a few weapons maxed out and able to be upgraded with unlimited ammo in the main menu. After this I skip the other difficulties and go straight to Veteran. This is good because it give even more challenge. By time you beat Veteran you might have another few weapons to max out, but maybe not enough points to purchase unlimited ammo. What do you have to do? You have to beat more chapters/parts!
I'd have to say that in order to fully unlock all the special content, upgrade all your weapons, and purchase infinite ammo for all of your guns, you might be looking at at least 3 or 4 full playthroughs. If I remember correctly, you get more points based on your rank at the end of a chapter/part depending on your difficulty.

"Let's take a look at the original Megaman and attempt to imitate it. Except, let's only look at it superficially without any attention to detail. This way we can make players feel nostalgic while at the same time keeping the worst design aspects of those games!"
Albeit the game does start off well with some decent levels, has a great soundtrack and a somewhat interesting story, Shovel Knight's decision to keep and use some of the same design choices as the games it was inspired by eventually makes the game experience fall flat.
The difficulty of some areas and bosses, combined with limited save options and an archaic system of checkpoints (or lack thereof) makes the game less of a challenge and more of a hassle. Things like the boss AI (for every boss) whose agency completely dictactes player agency makes for a poor experience as well, as it is hard to stay in control. Areas that connect vertically also allow players to fall through, meaning that you not only not get to restart, but that you have to backtrack to the original area/challenge room in order to complete it.
It's a real shame, as this game could have been a modern classic had the developers not had rose tinted glasses on while reviewing the design inspirations for the game and instead updated them to a modern standard.
There's also no Dash move, which degrades the grade of this game by 1 whole big mac.

This is a hard one to review. Really Big Sky is a twin stick shooter, a bit bullet-hell-ish at times with.
I really enjoyed the first couple of hours I played it, but it soon revealed itself. There are several thing I really like about this game, but their implementation leaves a lot to be desired, specially from a balance standpoint.
I'll start with the pros of Really Big Sky:
-It looks great! Even from the screenshots you can see that, but it looks much prettier in motion. There are a few resolution issues, but I was running it at 720p and it looked pretty good. I used this game has a pause between work, so playing in a smaller window didn't realy bother me.
-Several modes. There is a classic mode, which includes bosses, events, scores, and shop in which you buy upgrades. There are modes that focus on difficulty, not attacking, giving a retro feel to the game, for just relaxing without worrying about scores and dying etc. So, there is choice, that's a plus.
-Shop in the Classic mode let's you upgrade the parts you prefer and give you a sense of progression (which is also one of its faults)
-Very detailed information. Everytime you end a run you get a score screen with more entries than anyone needs, really. And also a comparation to your average run, having the player strive to get better. Besides, there's a library with information about modes, events, bosses, upgrades, and so on. That's good, although it's way too detailed, and I doubt that anyone would go out of their way to read it all. I think that showing the entries as tips throughout loading screens would be more useful.
-Bosses respect certain patterns, which change according to difficulty.
-Decent variety in enemies, events and locations.
-The music was pretty good. Not really my cup-of-tea, but I see some people really enjoying. Plus, it fit the context of the game.
Now, the problems I have with it, some of them inherent with the pros' bad implementation, in my opinion:
-The visuals are full of particle effects and filter changes, which can get a mess too often. Between those changes, you'll often lose track of what is on the screen, and what damages you or not. Most of the times, you'll die from something you didn't see. Also, it has performance issues later in the game, where particle effects are too many. I have a GTX660Ti and a 3.4GHz Quad Core... and it dropped to 5 fps at one time. That's pretty bad. But it ran mostly well on it. Still a reason to beware.
-Bugs. Well, everytime I quit the game it crashed. That's not a big deal. Everytime I tried to see the Scores (as this is mostly as arcade game), it crashed. That's a problem now. And highly diminished the game's value. If there is no one to beat, why would I play more of it, after a while? Score attack games are fueled by.. well, score. This game has it broken. There are also a lot of people who can't get the game to run.
-Dificulty Curve and balance. This is the worse part of the game. In the beginning, you're essentially running on trial and error, dying over and over until you learn how to get through certain things. But that's ok, learning the patterns and so on. But, as you progress through the game, it just gets a blurred mess in which there is no skill, and your score is mainly dependent on what you buy from the shop. And luck with the events you get. It's more of a grind-fest than struggling to get better at the game, since all you do after a while is to upgrade the ship and hope that the screen doesn't get too crumped with enemies and filters.
-All the modes are too similar to increase the game's longevity too much. There's no drive to really play them, since most don't change too much about the game. The big one being Pacifist, in which you can't shoot, only dodge.
=====================================================================
So, conclusion.
This is a game that is pretty, although relying entirely on particle effects and filter to achieve so, which often gets very messy.
Progression is through grind and trial and error rather than skill, which isn't very good either.
BUT, what I've played of it, was pretty enjoyable. The game feels good, for 3-3.5 hours. After that, with scores broken, it loses momentum and gets grindy and repetitive.
If you're looking for a shoot-em-up to play for a few hours, this will be fun. If you're looking for a game to last you, or just a very good game... pass this one up. It's full of flaws and bad implementation, despite being a fun and well thought game in its core.
I have to say, it feels satisfying whenever you score in the millions, but you also realize that it was more luck than skill. It is a fun game, sometimes, but I can't think of it as a good game.
It seems to follow Boss Baddie's games' trend. Really neat concept, nice art direction (although too many annyoing effects), but then those games try to be bigger than they are with too many badly implemented mechanics.
Please, keep it simpler. And polish them a bit more after release.
I understand that other projects and games are more important than old ones, but several things are simply broken, and there are people paying for it.
Cheers!

The new models and textures are very good and fit in seamlessly, and the levels and introduction give a wonderful sense that you are seeing more of the aperture facility and its vast depths, which Portal 2 left me wishing I could do. Everything is so well designed that it looks completely convincing.
The voice acting is excellent, and also adds to the superb atmosphere of the whole, as does the soundtrack, which is absolutely in keeping with the series and very well made.
As far as I'm concerned Valve should make this the official canon third game of the series. It really is that good.

Absolute Drift is butter on toast.. Smooth af
Driving is similar to the early top down GTA games, in that the camera doesn't sit behind the car so steering becomes inverted at times. The cars themselves, handle as if fine tuned to float like sand bags on an ice rink.
It's a little like the 'Skate' games in that you'll be finding areas of the free roam map and then sessioning that area, only instead of a curb or a rail it's a docking crane and a lamp post.
The "5 Worlds" are pretty big, each with a couple dozen drifting challanges (tricks highlighted in red) that need to be completed for the bridge to the next zone to drop. Once all zones are connected they form a rather epic playground, diverse and beautifuly crafted. There is no loading between zones so free roam is exactly that.
The "Events"  are Driftkhana, Drifting, & Mountain Drifting (foremost being a timed freestyle session, the others being un-timed single/3 lap trials respectively). All masterfully crafted, resonating a 'hitman GO' kind of ambience.
There are another two dozen of these, and I found everyone of them enjoyable.
The Events, were rather challanging while the free roam challanges known as "Missions", were far too forgiving. You could half complete a spin twice and it would register as succesfull, for example.
The Soundtrack is exceptional and worth the price of admission alone. I'm not being facetious, growing up in an era where albums sold for £15/$25 I would have happily dropped a tenner on this score. The music is perfect, sliding through a ceramic China town to C41 - On my way, everything just comes together.
Worth noting that while the game isn't in a pre release state the devs are still actively pushing out content and patches, the creator has said this game was a labor of love, and it shows.
9/10
Could use more content and maybe a way to save and share footage. But what is there is a masterpiece in top down drifting and game design.

Shovel Knight from Yacht Club Games is a love letter to games of old, the 8-bit era of video games on the original Nintendo Entertainment System. And boy does it deliver. Plenty of upgrades and items to collect, different armors, weapon upgrades; all these come together for a surprisingly deep platformer.
All this is added to by a killer soundtrack, awesome level design, a neat main character, and a not-so-unique but inspiring plot. I must also again emphasize the music. The music of Shovel Knight is leagues ahead of a lot of soundtracks today, even with its 8-bit roots. The variety in each stage's theme, the various boss themes, and even the overworld music are all phenomenal. It does not disappoint at any level.
My only gripe with the game is that its short - however, it does not overstay its welcome, so thats nice.
Overall, Shovel Knight is a wonderful 8-bit experience, and a welcome trip back to the days of retro gaming/platforming.

While the game is not as hard as it advertised, its multiple modes, killer soundtrack, and cheeky commentor will allow for hours of amusment. Personally, this game gives me nostalgia for Geometry Wars; while it doesn't match up completely to that comparison, it holds up well enough on its own.
Be advised though: the lighting and multiple enemies may cause your computer to chug quite frequently. (I play this game on an everyday laptop.) Sometimes, it's easy to get lost in the chaos and get shot down. Also, the advertised "Retro" mode is nothing more than a different control layout with some disorienting filter effects.
As for the multiplayer aspects, I cannot judge on how it plays with 2-4 players on the same screen (though with the aforementioned processor woes, I don't see it being a better experience.) But for a game where you pass the controller around, it's should offer plenty of living room/Steam Box entertainment.

This game is a steal for 15 bucks. Although the learning curve is high and some matches can be frustrating, Deceit offers serious entertainment value for people who are willing to accept some unpredictability.
Sometimes you will get screwed no matter what you do.
Maybe the russians online at 4 AM will shoot you for no reason.
Your infected partner might be a troll.
There are many many ways that the match could devolve into chaos. HOWEVER. The reason Deceit soars is because it's YOUR sole responsibility to keep all that from happening, and it's totally possible with the right mix of luck, strategy and communication. The unpredictability keeps it fresh. When you pull off something epic despite the odds, or trick the entire innocent team- that's a unique thrill.
On the technical side, the game runs fine for me, and I've only experienced one crash duing my 22 hours of play.
More people should try Deceit. I want to see it thrive!

Here is the best way I can explain this game. It is an Alpha fishing simulator that is pulling in people not only from the gaming community, but the fishing community too. It's the kind of game that if you take the time to learn, and level, you will be able to do pretty much whatever you do and have fun. It is definitely best played with friends, or members of the community. The thing is, like most alphas, you have to remember there will be bugs. No game breaking bugs are there right now, and they have been pretty good about addressing them. I even had a rare bug break a DLC reel, which was my fault too because I had too much line test. When I contacted support they immediately helped me out no questions asked.
The community of this game is better than any other I have been a part of by a landslide. Everyone is helpful, the streamers are all cool, and everyone is actively trying to improve the game. The developers do something amazing too. They listen to the community, and even work closely with them, like with the upcoming tournament they are putting on for real life prizes.
The game has a TON of cool things they are bringing in the future, and the beauty of it is, they aren't just blowing smoke. They are putting out legitimate dates they want to release additions, and they follow up. If every alpha game followed up like they do, they wouldn't stay alpha.
All in all, I absolutely love this game. I can just relax, put on some music, hang out with friends and catch fish. I look forward to what they are adding, and enjoy what they have already. I highly recommend at least trying the game, which can't hurt anything because it's free to play. There is another beauty, it's not P2W. This is a true F2P game that the only reason you would invest in is if you want some cool DLC they release, and want to support the game.

First off, if you're questioning the price of $50 ($35 at launch), let me tell you that this is well worth that price. Especially if you have a friend who can splitscreen with you. If you don't, then they'll have to cough up some money for it as well, but trust me, as far as co-op games go, this is one of the best. You'll lose hours and hours into it. I just played it 8 hours straight yesterday, and it only felt like maybe 2 hours. I'm sitting at mission 50 or 60 in singleplayer (out of 94 I believe), and I'm ready to go through it again with different classes and on higher difficulties.
Okay, so let's start this review proper. Earth Defense Force is a strange series. It looks pretty dated, controls a little stiff, doesn't have much else in the game aside from shooting hundreds of bugs and mechs, and screams 60s-70s sci-fi low budget flicks. From the outside looking in, it might seem like an extremely overpriced indie title. However, when you play the game, you'll soon wonder why most AAA games don't pack this much fun into one package.
Let's start with graphics. When this game first release (called 2025 I believe) on PS3 and XBOX 360, it could barely run on the hardware. The framerate dipped CONSTANTLY as the screen was filled with hundreds of insects. Textures were blurry, and the game wasn't a pretty sight. Fast forward a few years later, and we have an updated version, 4.1, which looks much, much better. For starters, it runs at a smoother framerate (though it still dips when the action gets insane). Second, the lighting and textures have been touched up and look pretty damn good. Again, looking at screenshots, it might seem like this game looks awful, but once you play it, you'll see why it doesn't have the best graphics ever. There are literally HUNDREDS of things moving on the screen. Explosions everywhere, debris flying, soldiers gunning down hundreds of insects...it's truly amazing. I stood in awe when an airstrikes pounded down on a large group of mechs, as balls of plasma came crashing down beside me, throwing a few of my allies a few feet into the air. During these moments, the game is pretty breathtaking. It has a sense of large scale battles unlike anything you've probably every played before.
As for gameplay, it's a fairly simple third person shooter. You don't have to worry about ammo, just pick two weapons and go guns blazing into the action. As you kill insects and alien mechs, they'll drop boxes that you can collect to upgrade your armor and obtain new weapons (which are randomized, and apparently locked to difficulty level). This is where the bulk of the replay value comes in. With 4 (5?) classes, you'll be spending a LOT of time killing and killing and killing to get more weapons to kill more efficiently so you can get even more weapons. However, in the 15 hours that I've put into the game, I'm always finding some fun new ways to kill things. From small scale explosions, to mini-nukes, to an EXTREMELY powerful sniper that kills everything in one shot but completely depletes the energy gauge, to guns that fire in all directions, and pretty much everything else, this game has it all, and it's a LOT of fun. There's a few weapons that seem useless, but most of them range from good to AMAZING.
Mission design is pretty much as basic as it gets. You go in, kill all of the enemies, and then the mission ends. Some missions will have you destroying certain objects (like giant holes in the earth that insects pour out of), but it still boils down to shooting every red dot on the map until they're gone. However, that's not exactly a bad thing. This game mixes a ton of enemy types to keep most encounters fresh and exciting. Out of the 50-60 missions that I've played so far, probably 10-15 felt absolutely useless, but the rest were good. The main problem with the mission design is that a lot of them are based in the exact same area, so destroying the same city over and over again can get a bit dull. Also, some missions are epic in length (requiring 20-25 minutes of nonstop action and maneuvering), but others are completely throwaway missions that take 4 minutes tops. However, the game usually finds a good balance in-between.
The music in EDF is nothing to really write about, but the game does have very good audio design. Soldiers have TONS of battlefield quotes that are amusing. It's so much fun running around with a squad, hearing them talk to eachother and comment on the situation at hand. If you find a group of soldiers without a squad leader, you can lead them yourself, complete with battle cries and song (EDF! EDF! EDF! EDF!). This is honestly one of the best parts of the game. The amount of detail that is put into these conversations and interactions is just amazing considering this is a budget title. There's even some mission specific dialogue that is hilarious. One of the most memorable so far is when you're going up against some kind of huge Godzilla monster. All of the soldiers start screaming as it rises from its sleep, and the battlefield turns into a huge wave of gunfire as they all start commenting on how it just won't die.
I could go on and on and on and on about this game, because it's just THAT much fun, but I think I've covered enough for you to see why I like it so much. At $50, this isn't a bad purchase. However, you might want some friends to play with if you decide to buy it at that price. You can play online with strangers, but there's nothing quite like going on a rampage with your friends, leveling an entire city block as you fight increasing waves of giant killer mechs and insects.

Super high-quality mod. The story was unique and inventive, the characters were pretty well done, and the tie-in to the main game was likewise creative and well done. I took my time to carefully evaulate this game, developers approach to the game and is it really Free2Play or is it Pay2Win. I will cover all aspects.
Lets cover them in short first:
1. If you are looking for a Fishing game (like I did for years) Fishing Planet is for you. While game is in early access and is not perfect it is BEST FISHING SIMULATOR in existence and it is only improving from Patch to patch.
2. Developers\Support are working really hard on the game and creating new content patches is making the game only better and better.
3. It is NOT IN ANY WAY Pay2Win. It is completely Free to Play and you can get EVERY item, EVERY lake, Everything of everything for Free by buying it with in game currency which is easily obtainable by just fishing ;)
You can buy DLC to support the developers and the game and get some gear but that gear is not exclusive. You can buy it with either Money or Gold in the game. DLC just helps developers and helps you by giving you a lot of the various items from the game shop.
Premium... Premium will only give you 50% more XP per Fish caught and Basic Fishing licenses for all lakes. NOTHING ELSE! It may have something different in the future but for now it just helps you to level a bit faster.
You can see a lot of bad reviews from people who played for like 1 hour and they complain about breaking their gear, going in debt and such. Do not listen to that.
While it can happen and you will probably break your gear if you hook a 10kg fish with a line that supports 2kg fish or such, if you play the game the way it is meant to be play it is almost impossible to break your gear. Granted, there are bugs and such and fish can escape and break your line but even that happens rarely and usually it is fixed fast.
If you read some guides about the tackle and get familliar with how the game works and really immerse yourself in the game you will play it 24\7. It is addictive as hell and with new updates recently fishing experience is much better.
There are currently 10 lakes in the game. 1 (Lone Star in Texas)is Your home lake where you can practice as much as you want since staying there is free and no license is required. You can also earn money and xp there and slowly move to the next lake which will mostly likely be Missouri. From there you go to New York... Colorado... North Carolina... Oregon... Florida... California and then finally at lvl20 Michigan and lvl22 Alberta Canada.
During your journey you will encouter beautiful lakes with ton of different fish variety. You can see a lot of details about the lakes, fish, tackle (rods, reels, lines, lures, bait, etc...) and info\help here:
To write a proper review it would take  me about 20 word pages. Game is completely Free to Play and you can buy everything in the game store without spending a penny on a DLC or Premium. If you wish to support the developers and the game you might get some DLC to get some gear to help you level and licenses to save a bit of money.
Experience is really great. When you start hooking bigger fishes for the first time you will feel your heart pumping and especially when you start to catch Trophy and Unique fish.
But also remember that this is a Early access game and that there are bugs. Sometimes patch breaks something and such but it is always fixed very fast and generally patches bring 85% improvement, 15% bugs.
On purpose I didnt write much on the game features because:
1. It has huge amount of features and as said it would take me like 20 or 30 pages.
2. Finding the stuff by yourself is much more rewarding.
Community is really great and if you need help catching certain fish or other info just ask in game Chat or on the forums.
I strongly suggest that you try the game. See some guides on the Forums or Youtube to help you and if you like fishing I am 100% sure you will love the game.
When you start catching beasts like:
You will see why it is best Fishing game currently available!

My original review is below - it was posted prior to the "bait"coin changes right after they released the realistic mechanics that make up the core of the gameplay today.
Anything you want to do in this game is going to cost money, or time.  This is how most games work, that is fine.  The problem with Fishing Planet is the AMOUNT of money and time it takes.
Don't have multiple hours a day to play?  You can't earn enough money to do what you want between traveling and licenses - namely licenses.  Want to buy what you need?  Go ahead, you're still time limited.  Unless, of course, you spend hundreds of dollars unlocking all the licenses in the game.  Any location in the upper levels is going to cost a minimum of $20 to unlock, stack that 5-6 or more times and you can  see the problem.  Want to get into tournaments so you don't have to spend that money?  Good luck, the people who win have the game down to a science, and will out fish you every time using lures they bought with real money - or baitcoins they have won from tournaments.  You see the cycle?
This isn't a free to play game, it's pay to play and pay to win.  I have no problem paying $50 outright for the game, or spending more than that due to the free to play model over time if I feel like I am getting my money's worth.  But that is not the case in this game.  There are single licenses for locations that cost ~$50.  If you don't spend that $50, you will never permanently be able to access that location without being time limited for x amount of days spending the cash you earned in game with, you guessed it, more time.
At least give a little bit of reward or feelings of accomplishment to your players.  What benefit is there to not charging money for the game, yet not appealing to a more traditional free to play model?  Money.  I'm all for business, and understand the motivation behind something, as much as you care about, has to be money.  But there is a fine line between income and greed.
This truly is an excellent game, and an excellent engine, with awesome mechanics, content, improvements, and even customer service the few times I have interacted with them.  But the insecurities projected into the game by the developers in the form of locking you into a stagnant playstyle akin to farming MMO's in the East is horrible.  Actually, scratch that, even those MMO's have a more understanding free to play style with more ethical income systems.
Despite dissent in the community and player concerns over long periods of time regarding this issue it remains a black hole.  Rarely, if ever, has the issue been addressed or even acknowledged.  If you want an example of this just check the Steam forums, specifically the ideas and suggestions section.
The problem isn't the cost of baitcoins - it is the cost of items or licenses you buy with baitcoins.  If this ever changes, I'll be first in line to start up the game again and play everyday like I used to.  It is such a glorious game, and they're ruining potential customers and their playerbase by limiting your gameplay opportunities.  Hell, if premium ($15 / month) gave all advanced licenses for the duration of the subscription I'd still pay for it and play.
The game goes through waves of interest on Steam, but the overall player numbers remain fixed - it is neither gaining nor losing players in the long run.  Over time these players will spend the money they need to spend to play on the broken system - the only explanation for why the system is still in place, it works.  Perhaps when they get everything they need, and income starts to decline, the devs will listen to the community to bring in more players.  Until then, adios.
Edit: Oops, one more thing I didn't touch on.  Forgot to include that despite all this, there is a way to earn more money - buying premium for $15 a month.  Granted, this still doesn't include advanced licenses - another quick fix which would get me, and I'm sure others playing more.  And my last issue: we were promised multiplayer and boats for years, literally.  I'm not even going to touch on the price of the boats, or the fact that there is a $35 DLC giving you 3 of them.  Damn, imagine how much trollers and fishing boats will be in the future.  I'd really love to play this game again, hopefully things change and I can catch you guys out on the water or the dock in the future.

A really good game that you can beat in two or three sessions. It's short but quality. I think the first playthrough is way too easy, though, and new game+ is barely a difficutly increase (mainly just makes checkpoints farther apart). There is self selected difficulty increases/push your luck elements where you can destroy a checkpoint for more money, but the game overflows with cash at every turn and you'll never find yourself lacking for it so there's little reason to actually destroy checkpoints. Once you reach New Game+ you'll have everything unlocked anyway, so money becomes literally pointless. Troupple King should charge gold for his amazingly strong potions instead of just giving them out for free because then there'd at least be a reason to try to keep hoarding gold. Instead, once you unlock everything (which takes very little time) you spend the last few dungeons not caring whatsoever about making mistakes - which makes the penalty for dying dissappear, and thus completely kills the game's difficutly since every room is just a fairly simple puzzle, some of which are directly ripped from classic old games (loved the Mario-esque tower climb towards the end though).
I'm really tired of games trying to get their replayability out of a "new game+" mode (that isn't really different at all or significantly more difficult) and out of possible achievements to hunt for. Huge dissapointment there. The first runthrough was so easy I had to intentionally not use armor upgrades because they made the game a faceroll. The game also feels way too short (barely 7 hours for a full runthrough), but I think part of the problem is the Mario 3 based map reminds me of that game, which was significantly longer and had far more little side missions to do (this game has like 4) and random map encounters (I saw I think 6 or 7 total, 4 of which were scripted battles).
Still, it's otherwise a very well designed game with amazing music. Most of my deaths made me laugh or applaud them for their clever design. Probably will finish my new game+ playthrough at some point just because the gameplay is so solid, but as someone whose favorite games of all time include Zelda 2 and Mega Man 2 - as someone who happily lives and breathes the mega challenging platformer, this is only a respectful nod to the historical greats with really tight, fun gameplay - but with all the teeth and bite removed.
I'd give it a very solid 8/10 and recommend it, but if you aren't into the idea of chasing achievements or playing through nearly the same content again but easier because you have all the upgrades, the hours per $ spent falls flat of my personal standards ($1/hour of gameplay).

Portal Stories: Mel is the unofficial, but most certainly considerable DLC of the Portal series. If you enjoyed the experience that Portal gave, and Portal 2 enhanced, then this mod is one to add a kind of flavor that you would find to charm the series as a whole.
This mod is at the top shelves of community work. The script, the voice acting, the pacing, and the lore are very much comparable to a stand alone indie game that you may find floating around the steam store. It's more than just a mod of the game really, it's another experience.
Of course, this "another experience" isn't something a player would find unfamiliar. The puzzles, along with the gun being the main feature of the franchise, and the AI voice that bugs the player are all there, along with a very hitting musical score that drives the whole atmosphere of the play along with the player in a way that makes you think Valve writers are handling the car. What's challenging of course, is that the puzzles here are made by the community. Even so, playing through them doesn't guarantee over-the-top frustration, and every solution is a solution that everyone can come up with, given their own patience and understanding of portals.
Speaking of understanding, playing all the way to the end of this more-than-a-mod mod all the way to the credits is a euphoric moment in reasons you'd understand if you ever were involved in the community. Everyone involved here did their best to give you the experience that Valve pitched and got right on the try. The result? They got it. The atmosphere, the feel, THE EXPERIENCE, of a Portal game, the modmakers got it. And all that effort to catch something so, SURREAL, was put in just for the player that is you.
Dear modmakers, we thank you by playing though your work.

First off, if you're questioning the price of $50 ($35 at launch), let me tell you that this is well worth that price. Especially if you have a friend who can splitscreen with you. If you don't, then they'll have to cough up some money for it as well, but trust me, as far as co-op games go, this is one of the best. You'll lose hours and hours into it. I just played it 8 hours straight yesterday, and it only felt like maybe 2 hours. I'm sitting at mission 50 or 60 in singleplayer (out of 94 I believe), and I'm ready to go through it again with different classes and on higher difficulties.
Okay, so let's start this review proper. Earth Defense Force is a strange series. It looks pretty dated, controls a little stiff, doesn't have much else in the game aside from shooting hundreds of bugs and mechs, and screams 60s-70s sci-fi low budget flicks. From the outside looking in, it might seem like an extremely overpriced indie title. However, when you play the game, you'll soon wonder why most AAA games don't pack this much fun into one package.
Let's start with graphics. When this game first release (called 2025 I believe) on PS3 and XBOX 360, it could barely run on the hardware. The framerate dipped CONSTANTLY as the screen was filled with hundreds of insects. Textures were blurry, and the game wasn't a pretty sight. Fast forward a few years later, and we have an updated version, 4.1, which looks much, much better. For starters, it runs at a smoother framerate (though it still dips when the action gets insane). Second, the lighting and textures have been touched up and look pretty damn good. Again, looking at screenshots, it might seem like this game looks awful, but once you play it, you'll see why it doesn't have the best graphics ever. There are literally HUNDREDS of things moving on the screen. Explosions everywhere, debris flying, soldiers gunning down hundreds of insects...it's truly amazing. I stood in awe when an airstrikes pounded down on a large group of mechs, as balls of plasma came crashing down beside me, throwing a few of my allies a few feet into the air. During these moments, the game is pretty breathtaking. It has a sense of large scale battles unlike anything you've probably every played before.
As for gameplay, it's a fairly simple third person shooter. You don't have to worry about ammo, just pick two weapons and go guns blazing into the action. As you kill insects and alien mechs, they'll drop boxes that you can collect to upgrade your armor and obtain new weapons (which are randomized, and apparently locked to difficulty level). This is where the bulk of the replay value comes in. With 4 (5?) classes, you'll be spending a LOT of time killing and killing and killing to get more weapons to kill more efficiently so you can get even more weapons. However, in the 15 hours that I've put into the game, I'm always finding some fun new ways to kill things. From small scale explosions, to mini-nukes, to an EXTREMELY powerful sniper that kills everything in one shot but completely depletes the energy gauge, to guns that fire in all directions, and pretty much everything else, this game has it all, and it's a LOT of fun. There's a few weapons that seem useless, but most of them range from good to AMAZING.
Mission design is pretty much as basic as it gets. You go in, kill all of the enemies, and then the mission ends. Some missions will have you destroying certain objects (like giant holes in the earth that insects pour out of), but it still boils down to shooting every red dot on the map until they're gone. However, that's not exactly a bad thing. This game mixes a ton of enemy types to keep most encounters fresh and exciting. Out of the 50-60 missions that I've played so far, probably 10-15 felt absolutely useless, but the rest were good. The main problem with the mission design is that a lot of them are based in the exact same area, so destroying the same city over and over again can get a bit dull. Also, some missions are epic in length (requiring 20-25 minutes of nonstop action and maneuvering), but others are completely throwaway missions that take 4 minutes tops. However, the game usually finds a good balance in-between.
The music in EDF is nothing to really write about, but the game does have very good audio design. Soldiers have TONS of battlefield quotes that are amusing. It's so much fun running around with a squad, hearing them talk to eachother and comment on the situation at hand. If you find a group of soldiers without a squad leader, you can lead them yourself, complete with battle cries and song (EDF! EDF! EDF! EDF!). This is honestly one of the best parts of the game. The amount of detail that is put into these conversations and interactions is just amazing considering this is a budget title. There's even some mission specific dialogue that is hilarious. One of the most memorable so far is when you're going up against some kind of huge Godzilla monster. All of the soldiers start screaming as it rises from its sleep, and the battlefield turns into a huge wave of gunfire as they all start commenting on how it just won't die.
I could go on and on and on and on about this game, because it's just THAT much fun, but I think I've covered enough for you to see why I like it so much. At $50, this isn't a bad purchase. However, you might want some friends to play with if you decide to buy it at that price. You can play online with strangers, but there's nothing quite like going on a rampage with your friends, leveling an entire city block as you fight increasing waves of giant killer mechs and insects.

This game plays out like a fast paced murder mystery.  You can’t trust anyone and have to use the information you gain during the game to determine who is innocent and who is infected.  This includes who picks up what items, who scans who with the scanner, and who just ran out of the room where you see missing blood packs….  I've already purchased this game for 4 of my friends, and will probably continue to buy it for people.
General thoughts - Shooting seems "off" to me.  Having played a ton of shooters in the past, I don't feel like the gun play is on the level of a Battlegrounds, a CS:GO, or even an H1Z1.  This recent patch seems to have tightened this up a bit though.  Also the new knife mechanics feel familiar and strong in game.
Pros - Matchmaking attempts to put you with similarly ranked players, but I feel like we don't have a large enough player base yet.  I'm hoping we can change that!  If you can get by the learning curve, this game has everything you could possibly want in a survival horror / whodunit.  The game shines even brighter with a group of friends.    Please feel free to contact me if you’d like to discuss the game in depth.  I’m a huge evangelist of this game, so reach out to me!
Cons - To me, the main downside right now is playing with people that haven't given the game enough of a chance.  This is reflected in a lot of the negative reviews.  If you check them, they’re typically from people with less than 50 hours played.  Everyone that has played 50+ hours has been through getting stomped by higher level ELO players, getting a partner as the infected that doesn’t know quite what to do yet, etc.  If you can get through that and embrace the game for what it is, you'll have a great time.

Portal Stories: Mel is the unofficial, but most certainly considerable DLC of the Portal series. If you enjoyed the experience that Portal gave, and Portal 2 enhanced, then this mod is one to add a kind of flavor that you would find to charm the series as a whole.
This mod is at the top shelves of community work. The script, the voice acting, the pacing, and the lore are very much comparable to a stand alone indie game that you may find floating around the steam store. It's more than just a mod of the game really, it's another experience.
Of course, this "another experience" isn't something a player would find unfamiliar. The puzzles, along with the gun being the main feature of the franchise, and the AI voice that bugs the player are all there, along with a very hitting musical score that drives the whole atmosphere of the play along with the player in a way that makes you think Valve writers are handling the car. What's challenging of course, is that the puzzles here are made by the community. Even so, playing through them doesn't guarantee over-the-top frustration, and every solution is a solution that everyone can come up with, given their own patience and understanding of portals.
Speaking of understanding, playing all the way to the end of this more-than-a-mod mod all the way to the credits is a euphoric moment in reasons you'd understand if you ever were involved in the community. Everyone involved here did their best to give you the experience that Valve pitched and got right on the try. The result? They got it. The atmosphere, the feel, THE EXPERIENCE, of a Portal game, the modmakers got it. And all that effort to catch something so, SURREAL, was put in just for the player that is you.
Dear modmakers, we thank you by playing though your work.

Shovel Knight is a love letter to classic 8-bit games. This action platformer takes cues from classics like Mega Man and Castlevania, but manages to blend it together and establishes its own feel.
The level design is outstanding and well thought out. It provides a modest but fair challenge that is reminiscent to its inspirations. It tests your platforming skills at times, which combined with its tight controls makes the experience a joy to play.
Rounding out each level are excellent bosses. Each member of the Order of No Quarter is unique in their design and fighting patterns. They are a tough bunch, but once you recognize their patterns taking each one down is ever so satisfying.
Capping the experience is an excellent soundtrack. The chiptunes are another loving touch to the 8-bit aestetic. Each track is head-thumpingly catchy.
Overall, Shovel Knight manages to envoke nostalgic feelings of classic games from 20 years ago, but yet feels fresh. It provides a challenge, but never feels unfair. If you're a gamer that grew up in the NES era, you really need to play Shovel Knight.

Absolute Drift is a *gasp* drifting game. Of course the most important part of a vehicle game of any sort are the controls. I will admit that the controls in Absolute Drift are quite tight while the driving itself does feel a bit too slippery, but as you might guess it’s not a big deal in a game where your only goal is to slide stylishly. Absolute Drift also boasts a unique Japanified minimalist aesthetic, paying homage to one of the origins of the drifting motorsport. It isn’t all roses but let’s not hesitate to pop the hood and see what we got, this is Absolute Drift.
Free Roam mode serves as the Story Mode, and will serve to introduce you to the controls as well as different challenges and events. After spinning out a few times and learning the art of counter-steering you will begin to grasp what the game is really all about and because there is very little hand-holding, conquering a world challenge or topping the global highscore for any track feels like a great accomplishment. Absolute Drift has a total of 23 tracks to enjoy; 10 circuit Drift tracks, 9 open-world Driftkhana courses, and 4 one-way Mountain Drift tracks, so you can find the event that suits you best.
While the world challenges and events have as much variety as can be expected, I find that it still isn’t quite enough. Drift around this, drift between that, it isn’t until the last stage that things start getting really interesting. All I’m saying is I wanted to jump on a few more roofs. Car customization is limited to 6 body-types, which all have a slightly different feel. You can also pick a color and a decal, but nothing beyond that. I would really like a chance to fine-tune my engine and shocks. Stripped-down customization and lack of real-time damage are gigantic missed opportunities.
I enjoyed my time with Absolute Drift, with its low-key dance music soundtrack, inoffensive looks, and high degree of mastery. Lack of customization and content hurts replayability, but the difficulty curve and global scoreboards means it still has quite a bit to offer. The story mode can be completed in around 2 hours, and if that’s all you’re buying this game for then $12 might be a bit overpriced. It is a bit of a one-trick pony, but it does that trick extremely well. If you’re in the mood for a score-attack drifting game, give Absolute Drift a try. Though it might be worth waiting for a sale. Big thanks to Funselektor Labs for the review copy! We at IGB hope to see more quite soon.

This all leads me to still recommend this game even if there is the dreaded "buy a licence" component. Frankly, I not done this yet anyway so that experience is for another update but I don't seem to feel nearly as much of a problem in this title's case compared other titles using the same model.
Original Review:  15 April 2016
This review is an initial reaction after 3 days.
I will need to come back and edit this review after I've spent more time in here.
I picked up this game in early April, just as 0.3.7 update (Texas) arrived.
Having read about 5 reviews and seeing a 'mostly positive' rating on STEAM, I downloaded.
Installation was easy during which I watched a few YouTube videos. By installation complete, I knew enough to get out and go fishing.  A few hand holds greet you as you first play and they're great. Within no time, I'd been fishing. I can easily stay out of the 'realistic discussions' as I'm no real life angler but I appreciate the degree to which this title has achieved certain aspects of the real world activity.
Any simulator is a compromise but if it's not fun, then it's no good. I can certainly see myself spending a while here and there going fishing between my other simulator gameplay activities.
So with 3 days under my belt, I've found the setup easy, got into fishing without problems, found it very relaxing and enjoyable and even experienced my first update which adds a huge attraction to the title.
I expect I will go ahead and purchase some items from the shop as I develop my experiences.
I tend to be wary of 'free to play' in a title but not against them or even spending some money on this as long as I can get value and the money I spend remains as purchased value.
One area I am slightly concerned about is the purchased license validity time. If they are in terms of 'Game time', then I will be happy. If they are real time however.... I will be quite disappointed.
I am totally happy I took the time to check this title out and immediately, I would encourage anyone wondering about it, to try it out.

Absolute Drift... Let's see; its like Micro Machines meets Mirrors Edge with a soundtrack that takes me back to the early Test Drive and NFS days. Dead simple to pick up and play, but incredibly challenging to master..
The areas in free-roam are large and diverse, flowing seamlessly from industrial districts to twisty mountain passes, which keeps things interesting throughout the map. Each car also has very different handling characteristics, which makes it possible for each person to find their perfect car for different events.
Visually the game is crisp and clean, dare I say almost elegant in it's minimalistic nature. Because 95% of it is white, it is tricky to see where the track is going uphill or downhill, but even that becomes a moot point once you get used to it.
The way each vehicle slides is surprisingly realistic, with all the usual drift ideas working as you could expect in first-person driving simulators; slamming anchors in the middle of a slide will allow the car to drift out wider, flooring the accelerator with a high angle drift will spin you out more often than not, even the steering feels like the vehicle weight actually transfers fore and aft, allowing for some pretty spectacular moves while flicking the car around tight bends...
All in all, this game is put together incredibly well. I do so hope we get some extra content for this in the future, I've run out of road and now I need more! (:

Well apparently I can't refund this game after 3.9 hours.
Let me start off by saying that this game is fun, I've had fun for the first 1-2 hours, but then problems starting popping up, and fairly serious problems for a game that is NOT in early access, so I unfortunately can't recommend this game.
***If you are the developer or a player considering buying this game, I highly suggest you read my bad section before you do.***
Good
------------
-Super fun werewolf kind of game, definitely a blast when playing with friends, or the right group of strangers
-Items found around the map are fun
-Character traits are pretty cool, the leveling curve seems just about right
-The 3 room mechanic flow feels very good, not too rushed, but not too easy either
-Meet people from all around the world (I had a girl from Korea, a girl from Denmark, a Russian guy, a Chinese guy, me (Canadian)
Bad
------------
-No solo queue/no report system
Meeting the right group of strangers is fun, but meet a 3-man premade that is farming points and it gets REALLY bad really quick. If you aren't aware, a game has 6 players, 4 innocents and 2 terrors, terrors must kill the innocents and innocents must escape the map/find the terrors and vote them out. To my knowledge you used to be able to queue as 4 and 5, but obviously this brings a lot of problems where people would just bully/kill the 1-2 pug players.
If I lost you, let me give you an in-game situation that happened to me while playing yesterday.
I was the terror with another guy, he told me he had 2 innocent friends with us in the same game, all I had to do was follow him and do as I was told. they shot one of the innocents (you need 4 votes to vote someone out in the first room) so even though I knew what they were doing, I also wanted to win, so I just voted the innocent guy out, we then voted the other innocent guy out, and then proceeded to farm point for the remaining of the game while the 2 other guys were watching us. At the end of the game they were pretty angry (I was too...), I wanted to report them but there are not report feature implemented.
Which brings me to my points: 3 man queue is just as bad as 4 and 5 if played right, and unfortunately makes the experience a lot less fun (even if I was on the winning side). You can't expect everyone to behave according to the game rules, which has to be expected when you are designing this kind of asymmetrical game. Solution? I think the best solution should be to have 3 different queues. Let me explain:
Competitive
1- Solo queue, you understand are aware that when you are queueing for solo queue, you will not be in discord with other players, and any unfair/farming behaviour is reportable.
2- Team queue, where teams of 2 can queue together, and are matched with other teams of 2, any unfair/farming behaviour is reportable
Public
3- Team queue, any number of players (1-2-3-4-5-6) can join, and no behaviour is enforced, you always risk running into people who will sandbag you/kill you, but at least you can still queue up with your friends if you want too. Although for obvious reasons you can't be allowed in the competitive mode.
I'm not sure if there is a big enough player pool to implement these queues, but the following solution fixes all bad reviews this game currently has (people complaining about premades, people complaining about not being able to queue with friends). For this to work as I mentioned, we need a report function and have the community/ops guy review the reports.
-Stability (crashes, freezes, lagouts)
I can't really provide any suggestions for this one, but I've had a lot of them in 4 hours of gameplay, way too many for a game that isn't in early access. To give you an idea, I've lagged out 5 times (the whole lobby lagged out, not just me, I didn't notice if my rank went down as I was just trying to have fun), crashed twice, and froze 3 times at random locations.
-Bugs
I'm pretty sure there are more, but I've come accross 2 game breaking bugs that can be extremely frustrating
1. There is an exit door on one of the maps, once your open the door, you get thrown out of the map,you can't do anything and must wait for the game to finish on its own (you still lose)
2. There is a floor on the second floor on one of the maps that has no collision, if you walk on it, you fall off the map, with the same consequences as bug #1.
Conclusion
------------
If you are a group of 6 players thinking about getting this game, do it, you'll have a blast! Otherwise, I think I would wait and see if these problems gets fixed.
Vote for developers: I will change my rating to positive if a competitive/solo queue mode and a report function gets implemented, I don't mind dealing with lagouts/crashes/freezes from time to time, but if I can't even have a fair gaming environment when the game actually works, I'd rather not recommend this game to potential customers.

An amazing game recreating the retro 2D platformers. If you love the retro and difficult 2D platformers then get this. The game is funny, challenging, inovative, creative, and overall great. Levels, bosses, upgrades, and gameplay is designed very well. The checkpoint system is creative because you can destroy a checkpoint for some gold or keep it so you don't have to backtrack when you inevitably fall into a bottomless pit. Roaming stages are awesome, but there's only like 4 to 5 of them. The levels are designed well but there are very few of them compaired to retro 2D platformers.
Although for $15 it does lack content (look at reviewer's play time it's around 8-20 hours). Also most of your deaths will come from falling into bottomless pits. No matter how much health upgrades you buy or relics you use, if you fall into a bottomless pit (or touch spikes but you can use a relic to avoid them), you die. This wouldn't be a problem exept sometimes the last checkpoint is far behind or a boss kicks you off. Nothing ruins a boss like an attack that one shot kills you (imo). Although I say it's challenging the penalty for death isn't restarting a level like some retro 2D platformers. You only lose some money and go back to the last checkpoint. Sometimes you might get stuck on certain parts for quite awhile and it can get frustrating, but with infinite lives the worst it gets is frustration.
I do recommend the game, but I personally think I shouldn't have bought it since I've never really enjoyed the retro 2D platformers as much as others. If you want to relive those game then get this. If you have never played those kinds of games and want to experience them then pick this up on sale.
EDIT: With the new expantions bringing in plague knight and spectre knight I can say this game definitly has the content to go with its price. Also plague knight and spectre knight have more forgiving platforming (atleast for me) so I now reccomend this game for anyone who would enjoy it unless you really don't like 2d platformers with challenging platforming.
