This is mostly a comment on the state of the port, though I have played EDF 2017 & 2025 on consoles for +120 hours each so I will say that the base game itself is very, very good as long as you know what you are getting yourself into. Please consider reading more reviews here and reviews elsewhere to consider if this game and it's gameplay is for you.
I have a fairly recent build (Intel i5, 16gb RAM, Geoforce 960) and for me the game runs at a solid 60fps even when there are literally hundreds of enemies and a lot of mayhem happening on the screen. The game runs solid, the load times are more than acceptable and the netcode seems very solid (when it doesn't disconnect which I'll get to in a bit) and all in all I feel that this is a port that is somewhat acceptable after a patch ironing out a few issues. However with that said it is because I am comparing it to it's source material - the EDF series, for as much love as it rightly deserves, has ALWAYS run like absolute s**t on consoles (we're talking that you are LUCKY to get ~20fps most of the time) and to actually get something that is this stable was way more than I'd ever hope for, and it brings me no small ammount of happiness to play EDF as it was rightfully intended. However, you have to consider that I consider this port a compromise compared to the originals:
There are no graphics options to speak of except for resolution options. The menus are not able to be navigated with the use of the mouse in a normal sense, instead movements of the mouse are used to "scroll" through menus as if it was a D-pad. The game has no option for adjusting it's FOV. These are serious flaws, and if I can consider a port to be "acceptable" despite all this you have to understand how bad the originals ran on consoles.
My main issues is that I have experienced several disconnects and crashes when playing online. My internet connection is not the fastest (~14mbit up/1mbit down) but I have talked to my friend who also bought the game who sits on a high speed line (100mbit up/100mbit down) and he has experienced both issues several times as well. When a disconnect happens it happens to all in the group that you are playing with. This is unacceptable, and I am unsure of it is due to busy servers due to the fact that from what I could tell there were not that many games going on at any time.
I believe that the disconnect and crashing issues can be fixed in due time, so I remain hopeful.
I lastly want to stress that this port is not optimal, but I want to mention once again that despite all of the issues this is most likely the most optimal version of EDF to date no matter the platform. It is a heavy compromise, but I'm willing to accept it. Frankly I'm just very, very happy of finally having a dream come true of getting a version of EDF without any heavy slowdowns. I'm going to have many, many hours of fun with this one both online and with a good pal next to me.
Thank you for reading.

First let me address everybody's biggest issue lately with the newest update and how much harder it is to reel in big fish, as well as the increased damage on rods/reels/lines.
This game is advertised as 'The Ultimate Fishing Simulator.' If you like simulators and you like fishing, you will probably really enjoy this game. After 2600 lbs of fish my rod and reel sit at 75% durability. The way you get paid for the fish you could have the most expensive gear available right now for the highest level and still have your gear paid for 100x over at least from those fish. If you use the same rod and reel for years irl that's cool, chances are you aren't pulling in 2600 lbs of fish in 10 days irl though, if you are then I need the gear you're using!
If you see this as a free game and figure, "Hey why not, I have never fished but it's a game right?" You're probably going to be one of the people coming back here giving a negative review about how hard it is to catch fish and how you're always breaking reels or rods. You have to have a basic idea of how rod/reel combos work and drag/tackle mechanics. This is very easily learned with about 20 minutes of youtube videos. So if you're one of those people who think they're going to log into a game and learn it without any research at all-you aren't meant to play simulators. There are other options for fishing games that are more arcade style and less simulation. None are as beautiful or advanced as Fishing Planet, but it's not a weakness to want to play something a little more basic.
"Fish are so hard to catch now." No... and yes. Compared to before the update people were putting on light lines on heavy rods/reels to be able to cast out 200+ feet, as the bigger diameter your line the less distance you can cast. So you had people pulling in 80+ lb trophy Aligator Gar on like 6lb test braid line. The max setups will let you pull in 50-60 lb fish fairly easily at higher levels, but people are still finding 80lb Gar to be pretty much impossible right now. The game is still being developed and changed. A lot of the gear available isn't capable of pulling in some bigger fish-like much of the match (float) gear is too light to pull in trophy flatheads and some other big fish. The devs have said they are working on new gear though and there is still a lot of content to do besides the few fish that are too hard to catch right now.
So what am I saying? If you use the right setups and know a little something about fishing you'll probably enjoy this game. If you just want something to play around in without giving it much thought then you shouldn't play a simulator. They are constantly making changes to the game and listening to feedback. The game has more support as a free game than most p2w or sub games have in my experience. I will admit that the lower levels are quite a bit harder now than when I first started, but it's still possible to do well and level fairly quickly. The game is still being balanced out and is ever changing though. I believe most of these negative reviews come from people who don't understand exactly what the word 'simulator' means and were spoiled by the more arcade-style aspects that the devs have begun to phase out for realism. Anyway, I hope to see you all in game!

Deceit is a game that is simple in concept, but somewhat brilliant in execution.
The premise is as follows: you and a group of five others (six in total) have been kidnapped by a mad scientist who has a strange liking for rabbits (come to think of it, I vaugely remember him bieng called Dr. Hare). The doctor has injected two of you with his serum, and then you all have to escape from the forest or asylum (it's updating as I write this, so there may be a new map, I'm not too sure).
So as afar as gameplay goes, you wake up in a random spot in the first section of the map, and you have about a minute until it goes dark. In this time, you can run aroundand activate levers which let you complete objectives. These range from simple 'stand in the circle for a few seconds' to the still simple 'shoot three spinning targets'. These grant you rewards, such as a camera, tracker, antidote, and a scanner. When night time hits, you huddle together, and wait for daytime. The length of the night, or blackout, is determined by how many items you got, as well as the length of the daytime. You keep doing this through three section: in the last section, one lever activates the escape hatch; you open it, then, as the name suggests, escape. Game over.
And yet that would be boring, so clearly some nasties were added in. Two players are infected: you don't know who, and you can't immediately tell, not unless they're foolish anyways. Terrors have the goal of stopping the innocent (non-terrors) from escaping. They can do this ina  number of ways, but the two obvious ones are taking/stealing good items, or killing players. The terrors have something called 'Terror Strength', which they can fill by downing an innocent, or drinking blood (those are the main ways anyway). However, if you want to stay alive, you can't just go around and drink the blood like it's water and down people like it's a sport (which, let's face it, it is). Instead, you have to be sneaky. You have to drink the blood on the sly, and blame it on someone else (preferably an innocent), or use items to your advantage. One item is the scanner: whne used it tells whoever is holding it if the scannee is infected or innocent (one time use though). It's up to the group to decide if they're lying, or telling the truth. The terrors have the real power during night time, when they can unleash their inner Freddy Krueger and execute the innocents, provided they have the strength to do so. Strength is depleted when you execute, so you have to be smart.
Anyways, that's the basics, there's a bit more too it, but you gotta play the game. The community is nice, apart from the odd idiot, and very dedicated. Don't let the low player count fool you. Anyways, I totally recommend this game: it's a little bit buggy sometimes, but the Dev's work hard, and it truly shows.
EDIT: The game has changed a bit since I wrote this, but about 3/4 months later, the above still applies. However, while this is what I would envision as a perfect game, the player count is rather low... while I have little to no issues finding match, finding a match with even one person who can speak English/is willing to speak can be a challenge. As for queuing for competetive? Not happening, it takes too long.

WOW.
First, the elephant in the room--I did in-fact grow up on 8 and 16-bit action-platformers like Super Mario Bros. 3, Zelda II, Castlevania prior to Symphony of the Night, Ducktales, and Mega Man which are such direct influences on Shovel Knight that I am not the most impartial judge. Now that I've explained my bias, I do think this game is genuinely appealing to just about anyone. It's tightly designed, seemingly effortlessly charming, and while it's most certainly a throwback-style game it shows zero hesitation to modernize and streamline old school design principles for 2014.
It is easy to think that this game is only retro-style because the designers couldn't make a more modern-looking game, but you'd be very very wrong to think that. While a deliberate NES style may seem easier due to the lack of pressure to look "real," and there's some truth to that, Shovel Knight features a staggering array of individual animations and aesthetic design choices that are anything but easy to pull off well.
If you're a kid who balks at how "ugly" pixel art is, but loves Dark Souls, you should give this game a shot too. It is a game that is punishing if you do not step up your game and figure out its various enemy and environment "puzzles", along with a surprisingly well-realized world that reveals itself slowly through gameplay and rewards for skilled play. It also directly rips off the "if you die your currency remains at the location of your death for you to retrieve... if you can..." mechanic from Dark Souls, which I think we can all agree is a good one.
Really I was planning to like Shovel Knight just because well-made throwbacks do appeal to me, but once I started playing I realized I was in the middle of something magical. The sense of true love and care that went into nearly every choice of the game's design is palpable, and that sense of love is infectious.
This gets my highest recommendations.

We are alone. The six of us, left in some kind of ♥♥♥♥ed up game of life and death, with a maestro on the loudspeaker, laughing at us as we fight and die. I don’t know who to trust anymore. This maniac told us that two of us are infected. Monsters, shapeshifters, hiding among us in human form. I’m scared. I didn’t know these people before I woke up here, but now I need to either trust them, or accuse them, because any one of us could be infected. Do I take another’s life based on mistrust alone, or should I have faith in them, risking my own survival? Maybe it’s all just a game to him, a game, of Deceit.
Hey Guys, Thomas, aka Weise here from
bringing you my review of Deceit, a game of mistrust and survival by the developers at Automation. In Deceit, a Game Master has taken six individuals and thrown them into a game of life and death, a game, of deception.
Two of the six are infected by a virus and can transform at nearly any moment, turning into a monster that will eat you alive. You need to survive through three zones as you travel to the exit and escape with your life.
Before I get into the gameplay or too far into this review, I want to say that the footage you are seeing in my video review is from my live stream with a group named House of Cards gaming that I belong too at
. I’ll have the link to my stream in the description below, make sure to follow me to chat with me while I play this and other games in the future. Oh, and at the end of my commentary on that video, I’ll have a full round of gameplay with audio from my perspective from start to finish so you can get an idea of how intense this game is. Sorry for any language you hear during the video. And now, to describe the gameplay.
You start each game with a lobby of 6 players. You can pick one of the various survivors, and as you wake up you pick up a pistol with one magazine. At this point, a graphic will appear on your screen letting you know if you are innocent, or infected.
The map you play on varies each time you play, both in the location and the layout of the location. Whether it’s a campground in the forest with cabins, an insane asylum, or one of the other areas the game has placed you in, each time you play the map little things change such as where items spawn, exits to the next zone appear, and the final escape hatch show up.
You want to work as a group, because if you are noticed being alone for too long the others in the game will think you are infected, collecting blood bags which will allow you to perform execution attacks and murder the innocent survivors. But if you stick around people too long as an infected, they may collect one time use items that can hurt you such as a lethal syringe that is a one hit knock out, or a scanner that can be used to see if someone is innocent or infected. Along with these, the maps are scattered with cameras that can stun the infected when the flash goes off, ammo for your pistol, shotguns, and a few other things to aid the survivors.
As you play, the title of this game comes out SO fast. Whether you’re in a full part of six like we were, which is what I recommend, or just a group of random players, you can use in game voice to communicate with the other players as long as you’re still alive. As a survivor, you need to make it through all three zones and then finally escape the exit hatch with as many people as you can. As an infected, you must not reveal your identity, and try to kill every survivor without anyone else knowing. Two of the six will be infected in each round, but the infected have no way to communicate since voice chat can be heard from anyone so you have to be creative in working together.
Some things we did included trying to get the scanner item first as an infected, then scanning the other infected person so you can say that they are clean. This way you gain trust in scanning someone, but also that team mate is now safe from being scanned in the future usually. There’s a lot of ways to lie and try to throw people off. I’ve seen people randomly scream they saw an infected, even when there was no one around, just so they could clear their name off the list. It’s a hell of a lot of fun and a lot to explain, but watching the gameplay at the end of this should help.
Visually this game is pretty amazing. It was built using CryEngine, and the environments are beautiful. There are a few issues where sometimes the randomly placed items appear in a rock or something like that, but it’s never broken the gameplay for us. The death animations are absolutely incredible and scary as hell. Before moving to the next zone, all the lights go out in a blackout. This allows the “terrors” as they are called, to transform and murder the innocent in the cover of darkness. The way the lighting plays in these moments causes so much tension and panic, my hands literally started shaking at times due to the anxiety.
With anything in the horror category, be it a movie, show, or video game, audio is absolutely key to the experience. Deceit did not let me down here. Between the effects of listening to footsteps around you to figure out where someone may be in the dark, hearing someone gulp down some blood, or hearing the screams of someone dying as a terror rips them apart, the game puts you so deep into the experience.
There’s some great voice acting over a loudspeaker of the game master egging you on, and when the characters pick up items they’ll make little comments about the items too, and while this doesn’t add a lot to the game necessarily, it just makes everything more real.
I can’t overstress enough how much this game got my anxiety and stress up, and a large part of that was the visuals and audio combined in the blackout periods mixed with people screaming back and forth, arguing about who the infected are.
Replay ability wise, for me this game without a question can only be played with friends for any length of time. There’s a fun element of playing with random people, in that you don’t know their tricks or how they act, but really the random lobbies I had just weren’t at all as fun as when I had a full lobby of five other friends, and we’re all trying to figure out who’s not telling the truth.
Because the game relies on chat so much, specifically voice chat, there is a downside of playing with random people because as we probably have learned by now, trolls are out there and sometimes you may not get the same experience when not everyone is invested.
In summary, your mileage may vary when it comes to how much replay ability you will get out of it, but for me, when I have a full party to play with, I enjoy the hell out of it.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. If this was a little too fast or confusing to get an idea of the gameplay, look up a let’s play or two on YouTube or check out the gameplay from
.

I'm not going to lie, looking around at all the negatrive reviews reminds me why CoD developers gave up on PC in general, you people are extremely hard to please. Trying to get you guys not to give a bad review simply because of a gun sound is hard enough. Overall I believe this game really did come back to the CoD roots. The way it feels, the controls, the classes, the playlists, almost all of it, I can say make it feel like a CoD game again. Some things still need tinkering, but it's the first month of release, almost every game has needed a balancing period in the first month (look at R6: Siege, a lot of people still think it needs balancing). Sledgehammer came out with a game that, personally, rekindled my love for CoD that I lost after MW2.
Campaign:
Well, the campaign could have been better, it was a little short, and seemed a bit rushed towards the end. However, if I were to say that during the campaign I wasn't on the edge of my seat, anticipating every cutscene, every wave of enemies, I would be lying. I got super into the campaign, I might of even thought it was very short because I sat down for a couple hours and just ran through it without batting an eye.
Multiplayer:
Yes, cheating is still a thing. It's very minimal compared to other CoDs, but it is there. I've noticed that these accounts (if you report them via. their steam profile) get banned very quickly. The MP feels very similar to other CoD games. It feels like, personally, this is the first game to not have stopping power and still feel like a good old CoD game. The MP flows well, every game type is a new experience and, of course, with the change to scorestreaks, they really do give the incentive to play to win the game, not frag out and be useless for your team (much needed in CoD since the old days, happy when they brought it in a couple years ago).
New Divisions/Customization:
These classes feel great, no more perks, just attachments and one "basic training" (essentially a perk). Essentially your entire class stems from your division (Airborne, Armored, Infantry, Mountain, Expeditionary). As you level them up, you'll gain more perks (kind-of) for the specific type of gun they are meant for. So for Airborne, they specialize in SMGs, they allow you to suppress your SMG and the perks involved including running faster and for longer periods of time (think Marathon/Lightweight, mainly used on SMG classes!!). Overall, all the thought put into the divisions, basic trainings and attachments blended well in the game, creating a great feeling MP. The customization they added is a pure bonus, being able to change my classes' uniforms and changing the skins on my weapons from crates, as well as earning camos and skins through challenges is quite fun.
Microtransactions:
The only thing you can spend CP on currently is crates and rare crates (as well as the starter bundle). These are purely aesthetic, they don't give you an advantage in the game (unlike Star Cards, if comparing to SW:BF II). This game does NOT promote microtransactions for gameplay, but much like CS:GO, promotes it for the aesthetic value of the skins/uniforms.
Challenges:
As well as the typical CoD challenges (typical Killer, Humiliation, Game Mode challenges, etc), we were introduced to something called "orders". This is probably one of the greatest thing a CoD game has had implemented in it (as well as contracts). Being able to work towards an objective for bonus exp, a supply drop, or more, starts really making you focus on the gameplay. I never find myself running around in games bored, as I'm always going for a challenge, whether it be a weekly challenge for 200 explosive kills, or it's a daily for 10 headshots with a rifle, you'll always be working towards something.

Hands down the best mod effort in Portal saga you'd find anywhere. Nothing comes even close.
Overall Rating: 9.5/10 - A must play for every fan of Portal universe and/or Portal puzzles.
Story: 10/10 - In my humble opinion Valve should accept it as the canon filler between Portal and Portal 2.
Level Design: 9.5/10 - Valve-quality level design, no bugs, glitches or shortcuts. I finished the game on default difficulty, before they introduced the easy level mode and I found the difficulty to be just perfect, actually. Still, people who want to experience story and spend very little time puzzle solving have that option so it's cool I guess.
Soundtrack: 8/10 - Yes, yes I know it's a free mod and all that but I found the track a bit repetitive and in some levels when you're redoing one part over and over it made me mute the music once in a while. If you play story mode I guess you won't have that problem.
Dialogues: 9.5/10 - Give the writer a medal from my side, seriously. It's as if Portal's original team wrote this stuff. Loved the writing and the sound acting execution too. Take a bow!
Effort: 11/10 - I have to give the creators my personal hat-tip for this gargantuan effort. Valve, please hire them! To create such a top class content, at par with a AAA game dev like Valve, and that too for free (so I presume almost everyone made it as a hobby "for fun") is just unbelievable. These guys are downright crazy and they deserve a 11/10.
Achievements: 9/10 - Not much to say, pretty well integrated with the apt dose of quirky achievements. Fun stuff.
Overall, I'd just say this: This free mod is worth buying Portal 2 base game (at least on sale) just to play this.

We are alone. The six of us, left in some kind of ♥♥♥♥ed up game of life and death, with a maestro on the loudspeaker, laughing at us as we fight and die. I don’t know who to trust anymore. This maniac told us that two of us are infected. Monsters, shapeshifters, hiding among us in human form. I’m scared. I didn’t know these people before I woke up here, but now I need to either trust them, or accuse them, because any one of us could be infected. Do I take another’s life based on mistrust alone, or should I have faith in them, risking my own survival? Maybe it’s all just a game to him, a game, of Deceit.
Hey Guys, Thomas, aka Weise here from
bringing you my review of Deceit, a game of mistrust and survival by the developers at Automation. In Deceit, a Game Master has taken six individuals and thrown them into a game of life and death, a game, of deception.
Two of the six are infected by a virus and can transform at nearly any moment, turning into a monster that will eat you alive. You need to survive through three zones as you travel to the exit and escape with your life.
Before I get into the gameplay or too far into this review, I want to say that the footage you are seeing in my video review is from my live stream with a group named House of Cards gaming that I belong too at
. I’ll have the link to my stream in the description below, make sure to follow me to chat with me while I play this and other games in the future. Oh, and at the end of my commentary on that video, I’ll have a full round of gameplay with audio from my perspective from start to finish so you can get an idea of how intense this game is. Sorry for any language you hear during the video. And now, to describe the gameplay.
You start each game with a lobby of 6 players. You can pick one of the various survivors, and as you wake up you pick up a pistol with one magazine. At this point, a graphic will appear on your screen letting you know if you are innocent, or infected.
The map you play on varies each time you play, both in the location and the layout of the location. Whether it’s a campground in the forest with cabins, an insane asylum, or one of the other areas the game has placed you in, each time you play the map little things change such as where items spawn, exits to the next zone appear, and the final escape hatch show up.
You want to work as a group, because if you are noticed being alone for too long the others in the game will think you are infected, collecting blood bags which will allow you to perform execution attacks and murder the innocent survivors. But if you stick around people too long as an infected, they may collect one time use items that can hurt you such as a lethal syringe that is a one hit knock out, or a scanner that can be used to see if someone is innocent or infected. Along with these, the maps are scattered with cameras that can stun the infected when the flash goes off, ammo for your pistol, shotguns, and a few other things to aid the survivors.
As you play, the title of this game comes out SO fast. Whether you’re in a full part of six like we were, which is what I recommend, or just a group of random players, you can use in game voice to communicate with the other players as long as you’re still alive. As a survivor, you need to make it through all three zones and then finally escape the exit hatch with as many people as you can. As an infected, you must not reveal your identity, and try to kill every survivor without anyone else knowing. Two of the six will be infected in each round, but the infected have no way to communicate since voice chat can be heard from anyone so you have to be creative in working together.
Some things we did included trying to get the scanner item first as an infected, then scanning the other infected person so you can say that they are clean. This way you gain trust in scanning someone, but also that team mate is now safe from being scanned in the future usually. There’s a lot of ways to lie and try to throw people off. I’ve seen people randomly scream they saw an infected, even when there was no one around, just so they could clear their name off the list. It’s a hell of a lot of fun and a lot to explain, but watching the gameplay at the end of this should help.
Visually this game is pretty amazing. It was built using CryEngine, and the environments are beautiful. There are a few issues where sometimes the randomly placed items appear in a rock or something like that, but it’s never broken the gameplay for us. The death animations are absolutely incredible and scary as hell. Before moving to the next zone, all the lights go out in a blackout. This allows the “terrors” as they are called, to transform and murder the innocent in the cover of darkness. The way the lighting plays in these moments causes so much tension and panic, my hands literally started shaking at times due to the anxiety.
With anything in the horror category, be it a movie, show, or video game, audio is absolutely key to the experience. Deceit did not let me down here. Between the effects of listening to footsteps around you to figure out where someone may be in the dark, hearing someone gulp down some blood, or hearing the screams of someone dying as a terror rips them apart, the game puts you so deep into the experience.
There’s some great voice acting over a loudspeaker of the game master egging you on, and when the characters pick up items they’ll make little comments about the items too, and while this doesn’t add a lot to the game necessarily, it just makes everything more real.
I can’t overstress enough how much this game got my anxiety and stress up, and a large part of that was the visuals and audio combined in the blackout periods mixed with people screaming back and forth, arguing about who the infected are.
Replay ability wise, for me this game without a question can only be played with friends for any length of time. There’s a fun element of playing with random people, in that you don’t know their tricks or how they act, but really the random lobbies I had just weren’t at all as fun as when I had a full lobby of five other friends, and we’re all trying to figure out who’s not telling the truth.
Because the game relies on chat so much, specifically voice chat, there is a downside of playing with random people because as we probably have learned by now, trolls are out there and sometimes you may not get the same experience when not everyone is invested.
In summary, your mileage may vary when it comes to how much replay ability you will get out of it, but for me, when I have a full party to play with, I enjoy the hell out of it.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. If this was a little too fast or confusing to get an idea of the gameplay, look up a let’s play or two on YouTube or check out the gameplay from

Tokyo Drift? Initial D? VDrift? If anything of this appeals to you, this might too.
In any case, this game's remarkable. It's challenging, exciting and unforgiving. But let me tell you, it's just as satisfying once you get a feel for it.
You start out in a minimalistic world, sitting in the infamous Toyota Trueno AE86. Your destiny? Drift. A brief tutorial follows, which will probably result in you crashing into walls a lot, but that's fine, as nothing else really is needed to understand how this game works! The game then releases you into a free-roaming environment with a few missions you have to do to unlock more stages. You can then also select stages, cars and tracks once in Free-roam mode, a bit like in NFS or other racing titles.
As you get more familiar with the controls, the stages get more exciting and challenging/longer. They also come in several formats: Lap-based drift-tracks, Driftkhana, which is a highscore time-attack inside an arena, or mountain sprint tracks. The goal is always the same, drift gracefully, score points, interact with objects such as poles to drift past or boxes to shatter, add that up to the final score and remain away from hitting walls or losing your combo. Sounds easier than it is, trust me, the Japanese themed tracks and names will kick into your curb at first.
That said, car handling is the key, each car has their own way of handling, so finding what suits you most will be the way to go. Ontop of that, drifting's the deal, so going fast won't always be the key to success either. Manual or automatic shifting? How high should be the turning sensitivity? Well, all these factors will help you optimize your driving style, making it possible to reach up to be the drift king.
I personally had, and will have a blast with this title in the future. It's been a while since I found an appealing drifting/racing experience and I can safely say this game has done it right. Now go... Go... and be the next Drift-King.

Fantastic little game. I had been following this for a couple months leading up to release anxiously awaiting. And it has not disappointed. First off; the drift physics are exactly what you'd want. Throttle is pressure sensitive, allowing you to be very precise with how hard/soft you push the car in a drift. Car sounds are crisp and vary from car-to-car. Handbrake is applied JUST right; some arcade driving games have handbrake engage WAY too strong and sling shot you around. I really dug the Mirror's Edge-like minimalist graphics theme, with red colored items being important against a white backdrop. The game is a bit short w/ 5 "worlds" each with 20 or so challenges to complete that don't take long at all to run through. I am hoping this will maybe receive Workshop support to add things like custom car skins & Events for extended replayability.
All in all, for ~$10 I highly recommend if you are a fan of drift car culture at all.

Whether you're familiar with old school platformers from the NES era or someone who wants to try one out, Shovel Knight will be money well spent. An amazing soundtrack, simple controls, tons of abilities and gear, and level design that challenges your skills and holds a plethora of secrets waiting to be discovered by keen-eyed players, Shovel Knight is one of the best games I've played. The main game may be about 5 hours, but the number of ways to use subweapons and the ability to visit previous stages for extra money (or just to experience the banter between knights) along with a more difficult New Game+ feature adds to the replayability of the game. With a story that manages to be simple but complex at the same time, Shovel Knight has the right things in all the right places. Overall, a fantastic game that's super fun to play, and will bring enjoyment for anyone willing to give it a shot!

Gameplay is fair, fun and balanced. It takes the time to introduce new gameplay mechanics before developing them into challenging platforming segments. Difficulty can be varied by the player through the destruction of checkpoints, and the NG+ mode builds upon what is - for an average platform gamer - a game of reasonable difficultly. Many of the items acquired throughout the game remain useful further on, especially as the final levels draws previous mechanics to a satisfying close.
Nods to the genre range in subtlety, but never felt ham-fisted. Humour is plentiful in this game, but its story, although meager, is very well told. Between Shovel Knight's conversations with The Order of No Quarter, and his recurring dreams of saving Shield Knight (whose value outside her draw as a plot hook is refreshing) I fell into a world that I couldn't stay away from, quitting only to reboot the game again and play just one more level.
I would recommend this game to anyone, platform-freak or no.
Hell, gamer or no. Shovel Knight has value in spades.

The most innovative multiplayer shooter I've played in years.
The game's pacing sits somewhere nicely between the arcadeiness of CSGO and the glacial waiting of ARMA, which is exactly what I was looking for. You will die in milliseconds and probably from where you weren't looking, so positioning, intel, and tactics are what matter here far more than mouse aim.
But the best feature by far is the destructability. Walls and "doors" (barricades) can be shot through or breached, as well as floorboards and hatches. You can poke out kill-holes to shoot from a hiding place, or toss a grenade to remove a wall for a quick flank. There are dozens of gadgets to trap your opponents, seek them out, or make them furious. Yes, you will die during a round, but then you can hop on the cameras and drones to find enemies for your team.
Teamwork wins games, but 1 player left standing can still clutch against 5. I still have love for CSGO and Overwatch, but at the moment this game has captured my attention.

Shovel Knight ranks among the top of the heap of platformers.
Any fan of retro titles like Megaman 2, Super Mario World, or DuckTales will absolutely love this game.
Unfortunately with any retro platformer you can expect some difficult levels and areas of the game.
The levels get progressively harder, but your skills will have improved enough to push through.
No matter how hard or frustrating it gets, Shovel Knight is definitely a loot quest.
What I mean is this: You will collect tons of cash throughout each level, and that cash can be used
to buy items, upgrade, and even more loot. The game does not use a lives system like most traditional 2D games,
but drops cash every time you die. This may sound easy, but reclaiming your ~$1000 every time you die makes things
much more serious. Many times have I gotten stuck on one screen of the game trying in vain to collect a bag of cash containing $600 and dying again.
Money may be the main focus of the game, but that doesn't mean it is essential. Upgrade-less runs are entirely possible, albeit difficult. Even if you aren't attempting to reclaim any cash, you will still get stuck on some setpiece screens, fights, or jumping puzzles of the game. Early in the game I found a level that was particularly dificult compared to the rest and, unaware of the game's shenanigans, proceeded to spend 15 minutes trying to pass 1 checkpoint.

Buildings crumble all around you as giant dragons walk right through them. Citizens running and screaming in terror everywhere. Somewhere there's another EDF soldier screaming that he's being eaten alive and on top of that you have an alien "expert" chiming in over the com, laying down the facts about this new type of enemy and how it should be named. And as if that's not enough, suddenly your squadmates start singing the EDF song.
EDF for you: a pure B-movie in videogame form. Both, thematically and gameplay wise.
And talking about gameplay, EDF is as straightforward as an arcade game gets. Run & gun, roll, dash, charge up etc. Everything is there, spread out over the four classes. The classes are:
It's kinda hard to describe how the game feels when playing, if you've never experienced it yourself. EDF has a mission based system, with varying objectives
but still has kind of an arena shooter feeling to it. Ever played Geometry Wars? EDF often feels exactly like that kind of game, only in third person, and with a bunch of guys singing and shouting...
Port wise, the settings are fairly basic. Resolution, AA, Anisotropic filtering and Shadows off/on, are all you get. And tbh, it doesn't feel like the game needs more, because it runs flawlessly. I was really concerned because we all know how Japanese ports can turn out, especially from devs new to the PC. But this port really is amazing.  Where it visibly dipped in frames on the console, it's pulling straight 60FPS across the board here.
The price point may be a bit of a dealbreaker for some, because on PC, we're used to getting older titles considerably cheaper, or at least bundled with all previously released DLC
But the content of EDF makes it worth the price in my opinion. Be it singleplayer, co-op with friends, or splitscreen with your buddy, EDF delivers pure and straightforward arcade fun, the way that only Japanese devs are able to deliver.
EDF is certainly a game you either love or hate. I for one, certainly love it. I mean how many other games let you sing the first line of a song, and your AI squadmates automatically sing the next line in turn?
One warning at the end: If you think about getting Insect Armageddon for its cheap price instead, to see if you actually like this kind of game -
While thematically similar, the games are worlds apart in terms of gameplay and content quality, and you'll get nothing out of it.

This is an excellent, laid back game about drifting through life with a chill soundtrack in the background and some really interesting physics-based gameplay in the foreground.
Keep in mind that mastering control of your car through a drift is the primary gameplay loop here, so if you simply can't stand ice levels this is probably not the game for you.
If you can get past that, though, there's a beautiful open-ish world (segmented off by challenges) with a wealth of things to drift around, through, in and over - as well as special levels that challenge you to drift through a course, or score as high as possible in an arena with a time limit. There's even a lighthouse named Donut!
At this point, the game's even taken its special anti-nausea edibles - so if you were put off by the camera in older Let's Plays (particularly during spins), give it another shot.
One thing I
like to see is a bit more interactivity throughout the open world - sure, there's challenges you can accomplish and ramps you can jump off of and stacks of blocks you can knock down, but there's not much you can do to change the layout of the levels; it would be neat if you could (for instance) trigger a crane to raise a wall by doing a donut around a lever, or create a ramp by knocking over some of its supports. That sort of thing would be really cool, but it would just be an enhancement on an already great game.

Shovel Knight ranks among the top of the heap of platformers.
Any fan of retro titles like Megaman 2, Super Mario World, or DuckTales will absolutely love this game.
Unfortunately with any retro platformer you can expect some difficult levels and areas of the game.
The levels get progressively harder, but your skills will have improved enough to push through.
No matter how hard or frustrating it gets, Shovel Knight is definitely a loot quest.
What I mean is this: You will collect tons of cash throughout each level, and that cash can be used
to buy items, upgrade, and even more loot. The game does not use a lives system like most traditional 2D games,
but drops cash every time you die. This may sound easy, but reclaiming your ~$1000 every time you die makes things
much more serious. Many times have I gotten stuck on one screen of the game trying in vain to collect a bag of cash containing $600 and dying again.
Money may be the main focus of the game, but that doesn't mean it is essential. Upgrade-less runs are entirely possible, albeit difficult. Even if you aren't attempting to reclaim any cash, you will still get stuck on some setpiece screens, fights, or jumping puzzles of the game. Early in the game I found a level that was particularly dificult compared to the rest and, unaware of the game's shenanigans, proceeded to spend 15 minutes trying to pass 1 checkpoint.
I think the game has potential. At the moment a bit short and to few game modes. overall okay game

This game is an extension to Portal 2 and is almost like a prequel with sequel elements added in. In this single player story, you tackle puzzles that are extremely difficult in hopes of shutting down an unknown power that is deteriorating the facility.
You could say this game's like Portal 2, but without the emotional bond. What replaces that bond is a drive to defeat malice instead. Considering how many puzzles there are and how extremely well-thought out each of them are, this game is most certainly worth money, but can be played for the wonderful price of free as long as you own Portal 2 already.
Some newer elements that are heavily relied upon in the puzzles include but aren't limited to
-Block destruction via buttons
-Block stacking
-Gravity (But not momentum)
-Emancipation barriers (discintigrates humans as well as objects)
I'm not a fan of the developers using block destruction via buttons as a requirement to solve puzzles, but it does open up several opportunities for puzzles that would otherwise be impossible.
All in all, definitely worth playing if you feel up for a Portal challenge that makes you think outside the box.

It's a perfect extension of the portal universe in a way that the paid mods can only hope to achieve. It's clever, complicated, sometimes hilarious, but more often than not very intense.
For one thing, the scenery, the music, all of it, bring together a feeling of utter desolation and loneliness in a way that Portal 2 could only hope to accomplish, and you know very well that you're in the bowels of a gigantic facility that's so large it has its own weather system inside. Most importantly, you can tell the development team has put amazing effort into it, from the difficult level design to the original soundtrack by Portal's most official unofficial musician, Harry101uk (Harry Callaghan)
The only issue that some players would encounter is probably the sheer difficulty of the levels. Playing through once takes about 10-15 hours for the average player, and you will find yourself almost ragequitting more than once, only to realize the ingenious timing, momentum, or precise portal placement that you needed to solve the level. I've played through 3 times now, and it's still harder than portal 2!
Overall though, I'd give the game a solid 9.5/10 for how vivid an experience it is, and I would definitely recommend any portal fan get it as soon as possible.
Whether you just got the game, or you're an experienced and dedicated player, this game will really teach you how to think with portals.

Crazy lighting effects, a bazillion enemies, meteors, asteroids, powerups, lasers, explosions,  all being thrown at you at once.  If you haven't bought it based on this alone, it's probably not your sort of game.
RBS is a twin-stick shooter that semi-randomly generates levels based on your kit, and likes to ramp up the difficulty to insane levels to test your wits and reaction time.    It's balls intense action that can cut you down to nothing in 20 seconds or less when you're first starting out, but once you make it past the first few minutes of a level, it's all greatness.
Bare in mind, at time of writing, there are some "issues".  Performance can dive into the 10's and 20's when lots of action is on-screen, higher resolutions are limited to 1280x720 and 1920x1080,  and you may have to tweak some Windows settings for your controller to be properly detected.
With any luck it will receive some patches to fix these issues later on; For now, issues aside, it's still great fun.

Buildings crumble all around you as giant dragons walk right through them. Citizens running and screaming in terror everywhere. Somewhere there's another EDF soldier screaming that he's being eaten alive and on top of that you have an alien "expert" chiming in over the com, laying down the facts about this new type of enemy and how it should be named. And as if that's not enough, suddenly your squadmates start singing the EDF song.
EDF for you: a pure B-movie in videogame form. Both, thematically and gameplay wise.
And talking about gameplay, EDF is as straightforward as an arcade game gets. Run & gun, roll, dash, charge up etc. Everything is there, spread out over the four classes. The classes are:
It's kinda hard to describe how the game feels when playing, if you've never experienced it yourself. EDF has a mission based system, with varying objectives
but still has kind of an arena shooter feeling to it. Ever played Geometry Wars? EDF often feels exactly like that kind of game, only in third person, and with a bunch of guys singing and shouting...
Port wise, the settings are fairly basic. Resolution, AA, Anisotropic filtering and Shadows off/on, are all you get. And tbh, it doesn't feel like the game needs more, because it runs flawlessly. I was really concerned because we all know how Japanese ports can turn out, especially from devs new to the PC. But this port really is amazing.  Where it visibly dipped in frames on the console, it's pulling straight 60FPS across the board here.
The price point may be a bit of a dealbreaker for some, because on PC, we're used to getting older titles considerably cheaper, or at least bundled with all previously released DLC
But the content of EDF makes it worth the price in my opinion. Be it singleplayer, co-op with friends, or splitscreen with your buddy, EDF delivers pure and straightforward arcade fun, the way that only Japanese devs are able to deliver.
EDF is certainly a game you either love or hate. I for one, certainly love it. I mean how many other games let you sing the first line of a song, and your AI squadmates automatically sing the next line in turn?
One warning at the end: If you think about getting Insect Armageddon for its cheap price instead, to see if you actually like this kind of game -
While thematically similar, the games are worlds apart in terms of gameplay and content quality, and you'll get nothing out of it.

A Isometric town management game where instead of you playing the RPG, you are the RPG. Instead of giving quests and farming and such, you are all of these things, commanding your heros where to go. It is a completely different experience than most other town simulators. Unfortunately, the developers have abandoned the game, thus it will not be developed further. It is a shame to see this happen, especially since the game's reputation took a big hit because of it, but that doesn't stop me from recommending it.
Bottom Line: This game is great fun if you want to be the one who gives out the quests and sends potential heros on adventures, instead of the one doing all of the work as one person! This is great fun if you also like managing cities. The music while repetitive suits the style of the game, the mechanics are serviceable, and the graphics pay homage to games like the Ceasar Series, which look great! I recommend this game to those who are interested!

Plants vs. Zombies is a fun, addictive, tower-defense game or all ages, even though it’s old. It’s an awesome game, with a fun, entertaining, simple story. It also never get repetitive. Crazy Dave is a very unique character, too.
The point of the game is that, zombie are trying to eat your brains. The only defense are the plants, that you place down to kill the zombies. Each level, you get a different unique plant like: potato mine, cherry bomb, and peashooter. Also each level, there is a different zombie like: cone head zombie, bucket head zombie, and football zombie.
If you find Crazy Dave's taco you will be allowed into: Crazy Dave' shop, where you can buy upgrades to help you in battle. Some of the upgrades are: the Winter Melon for the Melon-pult, Cattail for lily pad, Gatling-pea for the peashooter, and much more! You can also get special lawn mower to help kill zombies, and items for you zen garden.
The zen garden is a peaceful place where you can grow plants. You can get plants from two things, getting them from killing zombie or by buying them at Crazy Dave's shop. You have to meet your plant's needs by water, giving them fertilizer, spraying bug spray, placing music for them, and then you get a little reward. And also you can sell your plants for money, the bigger the more you will get.
You will be allowed to play the different modes when you beat the campaign mode. There are several modes including puzzles, mini-games, and survival. Vasebreaker is one of two of the puzzle modes, vasebreaker this where you break vases, you can get a plant or a zombies. Mini-games mode is where there is several mini-games you have to beat, and survival mode is where you have to survive the day, night, pool, fog, and roof for five flags. There are hard version of day, night, pool, fog, roof that have harder zombies, and you have to survive ten flags.
Plants vs. Zombie is a must get!

This game is an extension to Portal 2 and is almost like a prequel with sequel elements added in. In this single player story, you tackle puzzles that are extremely difficult in hopes of shutting down an unknown power that is deteriorating the facility.
You could say this game's like Portal 2, but without the emotional bond. What replaces that bond is a drive to defeat malice instead. Considering how many puzzles there are and how extremely well-thought out each of them are, this game is most certainly worth money, but can be played for the wonderful price of free as long as you own Portal 2 already.
Some newer elements that are heavily relied upon in the puzzles include but aren't limited to
-Block destruction via buttons
-Block stacking
-Gravity (But not momentum)
-Emancipation barriers (discintigrates humans as well as objects)
I'm not a fan of the developers using block destruction via buttons as a requirement to solve puzzles, but it does open up several opportunities for puzzles that would otherwise be impossible.
All in all, definitely worth playing if you feel up for a Portal challenge that makes you think outside the box.

It's a perfect extension of the portal universe in a way that the paid mods can only hope to achieve. It's clever, complicated, sometimes hilarious, but more often than not very intense.
For one thing, the scenery, the music, all of it, bring together a feeling of utter desolation and loneliness in a way that Portal 2 could only hope to accomplish, and you know very well that you're in the bowels of a gigantic facility that's so large it has its own weather system inside. Most importantly, you can tell the development team has put amazing effort into it, from the difficult level design to the original soundtrack by Portal's most official unofficial musician, Harry101uk (Harry Callaghan)
The only issue that some players would encounter is probably the sheer difficulty of the levels. Playing through once takes about 10-15 hours for the average player, and you will find yourself almost ragequitting more than once, only to realize the ingenious timing, momentum, or precise portal placement that you needed to solve the level. I've played through 3 times now, and it's still harder than portal 2!
Overall though, I'd give the game a solid 9.5/10 for how vivid an experience it is, and I would definitely recommend any portal fan get it as soon as possible.
Whether you just got the game, or you're an experienced and dedicated player, this game will really teach you how to think with portals.

Plants Vs. Zombies is a tower defense game by Popcap Games, notable for basically being the Jesus of casual PC games, bringing us such classic titles as Peggle, Insane Aquarium, Zuma, Bejewled, and Bookworm.

Tired of all the zombies? Why not hang out in your zen garden, picking up coins from happy plants?
All in all, I feel like Plants vs. Zombies is a great game that everyone should at least try once. One of my must plays!

I didn't know anything about Absolute Drift before buying it, but I knew I liked racing, drifting and that this game had a large portion of positive reviews. So I thought, "why not?". Here's what I think of this game after a few hours of play:
Graphics: I've always been a huge fan of minimalist/subtle designs, and Absolute Drift pretty much nails that. Everything has a low polygon count. The track is white, the important things are red and the death zone (water) is blue. This very small color palette is great because you can very quickly understand any situation you are in, but it also carries a message that, I think, translates the game well: "No BS, just drifting".
The black skidmarks felt kind of strange at first because they are here even when not drifting, but then I understood they were here to serve as a visualization of your driving, because they contrast the pure white track. By simply looking at the skidmarks, you can judge how well your took that last corner. More simply, it just looks nice.
On a more technical aspect, at the time I am writing this, the game is very poor. The graphical options are very limited: no custom resolutions, no V-Sync and the graphical quality is limited to a few presets, which means you can't set the anti-aliasing, texture filtering, etc. on your own. Then again, the game launched very recently, so I have faith the developer will add those options later.
Audio: The cars sound good, you can really feel how powerful they are when accelerating and the hissing sound of the tires when drifting is satisfying. The soundtrack blends in very well with the game. It's all electro music (like Drum & Bass), but all of the tracks are very calm. It was a good choice to make the soundtrack relaxing because the player will spend a lot of time failing and retrying, but the tranqulity of those tunes help remain calm.
Gameplay: Here comes the most important part, and fortunately, it's the best. The control scheme is pretty much what you'd expect in any driving game: Left-Right-Accelerate-Brake-Handrake-Gear up-Gear down. Learning how the game works takes two minutes at worst, but knowing how to handle the cars themselves is a harder task. You cannot make a normal turn in this game, you will always slide. On top of that, the cars feel very heavy: even when you think you're going pretty slow, drifting will barely make you deccelerate and you will very often end up in a wall because of that at the beginning. When you get the hang of this, however, driving becomes a very smooth experience. You can easily chain multiple drifts and properly gauge acceleration/decceleration.
The developper made the very interesting decision of only giving the player an isometric point of view instead of the good old 1st/3rd person cameras you can find in other racing games. It's quite useful because it allows the player to see further ahead than they normally could, and plan their drifts in consequence.
Content: The game is split in two modes: Free-roam, where you drive in open spaces completing missions (which usually are "drift near this", "donut around that", etc.) to open new worlds where you complete more missions, and Events where you can choose to play on either Tracks (with 3 laps), Driftkhanas (small, open spaces where you must score as many points as possible in 2 minutes) and Mountain Drifts (tracks where you drift downhill to the end). There is, at the time of writing, 5 worlds and 24 tracks. The 5 worlds can be completed in about an hour or two and each world also unlocks various Events and one car.
Something unfortunate is that all cars are, unless I have not played enough to realize the difference, model+sound swaps. It would have been nice to give all cars a different handling, but perhaps the dev will add this in the future.
The good thing about Events is their replayability and the presence of a Leaderboards system. If you want to climb that ladder you will have to master every corner of every track, which is not an issue given how good the cars feel. The large amount of hours sinkable justifies, I believe, the price tag.
One thing I would really love to see is the addition of a map maker (perhaps with Workshop integration) in order to enhance the lifespan of this game.
In conclusion, I would definitely recommend this little gem if you are the kind of person who likes spending a large amount of time on a single game in order to master it.

Saints Row 3 is , as the title implies - the Sequel to Saints Row 2. Unlike the first 2 titles, this one features a rebuilt engine along with a competent PC port developed in house by volition. This means DX11 level graphics that are a monumental step above anything featured in the second game. Even now, in 2016 , cranking the settings up on this and running at 1080P or all the way up to 4K creates a very clean good looking game. This isn't going to give either GTA4 or 5 a run for it's money when it comes to presentation obviously but then, it's not trying to do that either.
So, it looks great , what else ? Well from a mechanics perspective this game improves upon it's predecessor in every way imaginable , no longer are the controls for driving and walking kind of an oddball mishmash unfamiliar to other games of this type. Instead , the triggers act as gas and brake while driving , aiming is improved and even things like taking cover and weapon switching are handled better here. So , simply put - this game plays better than SR2.
What's left then ? Well it follows a similar structure to the previous game - you get access to a city that has 3 ruling gangs each with a half dozen or so missions culminating in their defeat. Of course , in this entry a specialized anti-gang task force also shows up to pad out the gang missions. These missions are generally pretty fun and much less frustrating then SR2's buggy story missions ... although there are still a few bugs that may occasionally lead to a restart or fail state. Really then, the only issue SR3 has versus the previous installment is that the side missions aren't quite as much fun , the septic avenger missions have been completely scrubbed for example. Trail blazing still exists but it's not quite as exciting. What remains are a number of trafficking and escort type missions that range from annoying to downright not fun. But, unlike SR2 , your respect level doesn't seem to have as much bearing on gaining access to new missions. If it does , I didn't notice , perhaps the requirements were lowered substantially ? This means that you aren't forced to experience as many side missions to advance your level forward to get on with the story. Both good and bad I suppose.
These days , the price of entry for SR3 also includes all 3 DLC mission packs as well as the DLC car pack. Each mission pack adds roughly an hour of gameplay although the Proffessor genki DLC adds a new side mission event that could last longer if you enjoy doing them.
Ultimatly - this is a far more polished product compared to the PC release of SR2 so I can't help but recommend it to fans of the series. You'll be treated to a much more playable game that looks a lot nicer at the expense of cutting some of the more enjoyable side missions present in 2. Despite the loss , I feel this is the better game which I realize is a less popular opinion but there it is.

Inspired by Ken Block’s Gymkhana series the best way to describe the game is the driving view point of micro machines, the score system of the trick sections in Project Gotham racing, the progression system of an N64 era platform game and a fantastic drift system that takes an age to master but always makes you feel it is your fault if you screw up.
The game sees you progress through a number of worlds that act as the hub to complete missions. These range from performing stunts around obstacles to performing on tracks to gain points and get a world ranking.
There are 3 types of events Driftkhana, Drifting, & Mountain Drifting but all are essentially a playground to gain as many points as possible. Controlled best with a gamepad the game takes about 5 minutes to understand, 10 minutes to become competent and even after several hours of game play I still did not feel I had truly mastered it.
Visually the game is minimalistic but lovely to look at and run at a solid 60fps. The music soundtrack is also filled with tranquil base numbers.
Now the game is not perfect. Relatively short I finished everything in a few hours and while trying to get higher up the league tables offers the game some replayability I feel that this will not be for everyone. I also felt that a more detailed tutorial to give tips on how to perfect drifting at the start as it took a lot of crashing into walls to really get the difference between how brake and handbrake acts.
I enjoyed the game a lot and for the low price of £9.99 of your regional equivalent it is hard to not recommend but this isn’t a game which you will be playing for ages unless you really are a score attack gamer.

A really nice nod to NES classics, Shovel Knight feels like one part Duck Tales, one part Mega Man, and one part Castlevania. The story is simple; rescue your friend and fellow warrior Shield Knight. She was taken by the Dark Enchantress and is being guarded by a team of evil knights, each with their own themes. In this way, the game feels like Mega Man. There is "King Knight", who's level is a giant castle filled with royal themed villains. Specter Knight inhabits a graveyard and has an army of ghosts and skeletons. The banter between your character and others is witty and made me chuckle from time to time.
The visuals look like the final generation of NES games. The pixel art is well done and feels authentic. I feel like its limited visuals never take away from the game, but do add character and flavor. Music and sound is good, but never had me really impressed. It just kinda does the job.
The difficulty in this game is tricky. Many of these games pride themselves on being difficult, and Shovel Knight would like to make you think it's challenging, but its not. Sure some of the jumps are tricky and you do instantly die when you come in contact with spikes, but the game is so amazingly forgiving in other areas. There are numerous checkpoints, infinite lives, and 2 items that refill all your life and mana. Anyone with basic platformer skills and the ability to learn from experience can beat this thing in under 6 hours.
Sadly, the replayability on this one is pretty minimal. Once beating it, there is a new game+ mode, but I found little interest in it. This game shines in its character and polish. Worth a play through for those wanting something nostalgic, charming, and somewhat challenging.

Edit review: game is fully playable and no longer crashes. This game has a small tight community but we are very fun to play with.

Resident Evil 5 is markedly different from all the previous games in the series in that the focus on the horror aspect is almost completely diminished. The creepy atmospheric terror of the past games is gone, but there is a different kind of violent apprehension present in this game which gives you the feeling that you definitely want to avoid dying if you can help it. Aint nobody want whatever the hell that monster is up in your junk!
I first played Resident Evil 5 many years ago now in a friend's house, sitting next to him on local co-op and the experience was fantastic. So it is a bit perturbing that the PC port has the local co-op stripped out, but online co-op seems to function fine.
Overall, if you are after a convincing horror game then you may want to look elsewhere but if high quality action is your thing then buying this is never going to be a bad choice. If you've got a buddy to play with then you're both in for a great time.

Well it took 13 years to bring the official EDF steam (excluding the Insect Armageddon version made by Viscious Cycle Software), and the wait is finally over.
For the overdue Steam release they made it count! Running at 1080p at 60FPS and instant loading times, it's almost like playing it for the first time. This truly brings all the fun of the classic arcade shooter with none of the non-since you see in a lot of modern day games. The game does not take it self seriously , and is not trying to be real world realistic in looks or psychics, but that is part of what makes this game different.
What you get.
1080P bug killing non-stop action.
60FPS for liquid smooth game play.
Over 800 weapons to use.
4 different characters with there own weapon load outs.
Randomized enemies spawn locations for even better replay value.
Over 80 missions to beat and some online only missions.
Destructible environment.
Online Co-op and vs.
What you don't get.
There are no unskippable cut scenes. (don't you just hate games with long drawn out cut scenes)
No fetch quest busy work(find a trinket across the map and then bring it to xyz)
Long loading times like on the Xbox 360 / PS3 2025 version.
(Seems to be issues for AMD users until a patch comes out,  but I'm a Intel owner so no issues for me at all)

I used to think I had a beast of a computer, until I started hitting long loading screen times.
As the march of technology moves forward our wallets and our time that we can waste on fun little things dwindles.
this might not LOOK like much now, but if you were to flip this out on a old classic nes system, the fact the sprites didn't look like garbage would have made this the best game money could buy graphics wise.
To call this a piece of art of the current medium would scarcely do something as nonsensical as this justice.
don't get me wrong, the content is lacking the coding seems like a kid made it and the music that plays when you get the loading audio is definitely ripped from somewhere else.
but therein lies the beauty of this tiny clicker app.
the bane of all our existence ... being made fun of. The grotesque simplicity of a loading screen mocked at because we otherwise don't believe our computers haven't frozen. All 90's kids can unite and autistically scream this was our lives when windows wasn't based on lies and NETSCAPE was the best internet thingy with the spinny orbital around a giant N
That THAT ICON WAS a loading screen.

So should you buy this game and support the developers? Definitely, yes!

Resident Evil 5 is markedly different from all the previous games in the series in that the focus on the horror aspect is almost completely diminished. The creepy atmospheric terror of the past games is gone, but there is a different kind of violent apprehension present in this game which gives you the feeling that you definitely want to avoid dying if you can help it. Aint nobody want whatever the hell that monster is up in your junk!
I first played Resident Evil 5 many years ago now in a friend's house, sitting next to him on local co-op and the experience was fantastic. So it is a bit perturbing that the PC port has the local co-op stripped out, but online co-op seems to function fine.
Overall, if you are after a convincing horror game then you may want to look elsewhere but if high quality action is your thing then buying this is never going to be a bad choice. If you've got a buddy to play with then you're both in for a great time.

This is a really cool game for racing fans, especially those that either, A: feel let down with the lack of drift events in newer games such as GRID Autosport, or B: just like going for high scores on leaderboards. Great presentation and audio mean that it's a pleasure to sit there for an hour or two, plugging away at the High Score on the Driftkhana boards. Take it from me, at the time of the review, I'm ranked anywhere from 2nd to 6th on all of them.
The cars handle nicely, and feel like they have a lot of weight to them. The drifting requires you to think ahead about where you want to end up, and requires minute adjustments as you fly around a corner in order to not crash. It requires a little bit of practice, and top down view can occasionally be disorienting, but overall the game controls well and it feels good. It feels good to slide around a corner at high speed, and consistently nail drifts in order to build up a multiplier and score high points. The games core mechanics are incredibly solid.
The Mirror's Edge style visuals are also a nice touch, and give a lot of flair and personality to the game. The music makes for good background noise, and there are a couple of pretty good tracks that I actually find myself enjoying a lot.
Really, my only complaint is the lack of custom maps. This sort of leaderboard-focused game seems designed to come with a map editor.

Arma 3 is what I’ve been looking for. Something with more realism than any other shooter on the market. I was tired of the whole “if I die I will respawn in 10 seconds” mentality. Arma gives gameplay a whole new sense of gravity. When you die instead of respawning in 10 seconds with full kit, your left with nothing. Now every engagement isn’t a suicide mission with the idea of getting as many kills as you can and then respawning, it’s almost “life or death”. Deciding if killing that person is worth YOUR life, or if you need to egress that situation. And about the engagements, they are few and far between, however, when you do find yourself in a conflict, it’s much more weighted and intense. The controls are a bit daunting at first however anyone willing to learn and have patience with them will find themselves easily performing actions which at first, they thought difficult. I’ve only played a few hours of Arma 3 so far; however, what I have played has been thoroughly enjoyable and well worth the $15. Coming from Arma 2, which was not the game I had been looking for, Arma 3 is miles ahead. If you’re on the edge about buying Arma 3, just do it and don’t look back. If you bought Arma 2 and didn’t enjoy it, or just found it kind of “meh” Arma 3 is a completely new game. So, if Arma 2 was holding you back, don’t let it, Arma 3 is a whole different ball game. From me, for what it’s worth, Arma 3 is 10/10.

This is a really cool game for racing fans, especially those that either, A: feel let down with the lack of drift events in newer games such as GRID Autosport, or B: just like going for high scores on leaderboards. Great presentation and audio mean that it's a pleasure to sit there for an hour or two, plugging away at the High Score on the Driftkhana boards. Take it from me, at the time of the review, I'm ranked anywhere from 2nd to 6th on all of them.
The cars handle nicely, and feel like they have a lot of weight to them. The drifting requires you to think ahead about where you want to end up, and requires minute adjustments as you fly around a corner in order to not crash. It requires a little bit of practice, and top down view can occasionally be disorienting, but overall the game controls well and it feels good. It feels good to slide around a corner at high speed, and consistently nail drifts in order to build up a multiplier and score high points. The games core mechanics are incredibly solid.
The Mirror's Edge style visuals are also a nice touch, and give a lot of flair and personality to the game. The music makes for good background noise, and there are a couple of pretty good tracks that I actually find myself enjoying a lot.
Really, my only complaint is the lack of custom maps. This sort of leaderboard-focused game seems designed to come with a map editor.
Getting all the achievements was pretty fun.

Chris Redfield and Sheva Alomar are investigating possible bioterrorism threats in Africa: as it befits the series these threats become real soon enough and their investigation'll turn into a fight for survival against infected locals and B.O.W.s.
Resident Evil 5 follows in the footsteps of its predecessor with an even more action-packed combat and fully fledged partner system: while those looking for a true survival horror will likely be disappointed the game is an excellent, if different, entry in the series.
-overall graphics and character/ enemy models and animations make this a good looking game
-nice soundtrack and sound design
-a pretty interesting and serious story with a few twists, gone is also most of the cheesy dialogue
-the action oriented combat is very enjoyable and fairly challenging
-boss fights are tough and tense affairs
-a considerable amount of weapons to find/ buy and upgrade
-good level variety
-story mode is quite lengthy, taking 12 to 15 hours to beat
-controls can feel a bit clunky at times, nothing too bad but some sections requiring quick movements/ fine aim might feel harder than they'd be due to it: cover system is very awkward
-there's still a few QTE cutscenes and, while I personally don't enjoy them, they're at least way easier than the RE4 ones
-inventory management can still feel fiddly at times due to the limited spaces
-the whole "having a partner" thing and the game being designed with co-op in mind can make single-player a bit annoying at times especially on boss fights
-gone are most of the atmosphere and survival horror elements
-a chapter (including its boss fight) is basically a lengthy turret section, it honestly was annoying to play and felt out of place
As said RE 5 leaves most of its survival horror roots behind in favor of fast-paced combat against a plethora of enemies: it's different but it works well and things can get pretty tense when you're facing a crowd of infected or a particularly strong foe/ boss. The story is also quite deep, interesting and tied to previous entries of the series: the fact most of the cheesy lines are gone is also something I truly appreciate. You'll meet both new and returning enemy types while exploring varied levels such as shanty towns, marshes, caves etc... this not only keeps things fresh but also requires you to change your tactics whenever a new foe comes up.
The co-op oriented game design is a mixed bag, while heaps of fun if played with someone the single player suffers from it at times. Sheva's AI is a very good shot but her reactions aren't always sensible and she'll sometimes waste ammo, not follow you fast enough or generally make a nuisance of herself: this isn't too bad overall but I can only imagine how terrible it'd get on the higher difficulty levels. Bosses can also become harder than they'd be if you're playing with an AI companion as they might find it hard to maneuver accordingly or use their weapons at their best.

Shovel Knight is basically the greatest NES platformer I never knew we needed.  It uses a classic retro 8-bit look but it doesn't limit itself to simple designs and sprites instead using all the know-how at hand to craft a beautiful and detailed game of yesteryear.  Aided by an incredible soundtrack, tight controls, inventive level design and well written dialogue, Shovel Knight is a case study in how to do everything right with crowd-funding.

There really is something to be said about this game's pitch-perfect machination. Resident Evil 4 revolutionized the series and, here it is, Resident Evil 5, perfecting every living fiber of its majestic predecessor.
Whatever positive thing I'm about to write in this review has probably been said numerous times by countless of others. Hear me out, though: I've been playing this miraculous concoction of a video game on a crappy Intel HD Graphics-powered Hewlett-Packard laptop since 2013. It's laggy as heck. But therein lies the beauty. If you've beaten the campaign many times already on every available difficulty setting and are bored by it, I suggest you to run it on a mediocre-to-crappy laptop. The lags create an unnerving sense of dread in that you're never quite sure where to aim and run to. Come the boss fights, the low frame-rate actually sets up a challenge on its own. Everything hurls before your eyes like hellish mayhem.
This might just be me overselling my soon-to-be-replaced school laptop, but really. I cannot imagine RE5 without the lags. Truly the ultimate Resident Evil experience.
PS: Actually, I played it on my friend's much more powerful PC. The buttery smooth performance renders shooting enemies an abysmal piece of cake. Lags are where it's at.
