This game got so hyped that I expected it to be good with its unique premise and all, even great perhaps but instantly began finding it annoying.
GAMEPLAY Very subpar
You get into the game and the game doesn't tell you how to play(which I found really annoying after people go on about how it tells you how to play as you go along). This seems to be a trend among modern games because they think its somehow clever, regardless of application. It works in some games, everyone knows to run around with arrows or look around with a mouse, or to attack the skeletons and dodge the lasers. Generally arrow keys are movement in arcade games with other keys like Z and X used for attacking, WASD usually for games that use a mouse. This game uses WASD default, which didn't take long to figure out but then how do you attack? oh you just use J, a button I don't think I have used in any game that isn't a text game. When you do attack holy crap do you attack slow, every time I press the attack button I have enough time to make a sandwich before the animation kicks in, this is particularly annoying when I got to the first boss. What a prick this fight was, he is basically you with 3x the health, an extra attack, and knows how to play.
By the way when you die you lose money, this is really rewarding because it makes you feel like you have wasted your time. Some would argue it forces you to get better, but again, this isn't true of every application, it's just a hindrance, especially if it makes my brain cloud with the thought of not dying every time I move. Rogue Legacy was great with this, and also executed the downstrikes better. I also keep finding some kind of potions that max out at 30 that I have no idea how to use, they kind of seem like mana potions but I have no spells so why give me them. Chests are filled with the same loot you get from creatures, as are sub-boss drops, and secrets(to a very close degree).
I talked to a fish at a lake for an item and I thought the game was broken, the animation went on FOREVER, possibly on of the longest 'in game' animations I have ever seen, and it didn't help that it was really not compelling, even if you could just walk away when it was happening. Some platforms are so skinny it's silly especially early in game. Hit box is tiny, but enemies seem to have good reach. Achievements are ludicrous. Checkpoints are uneventful, I didn't even know they were checkpoints until the boss killed me. No idea whats going on with the inventory. I actually spend a good portion of my money(and a lot of waiting time) getting a healing potion, I found out this is one use(or seems to be) until I go and refill it again, and that it can be used automatically if you accidentally hit  keys too fast. There's a really lame target hitting minigame hidden under the first town.
Stupidest shop ever, to upgrade you have to talk to either of 2 merchants, who require the EXACT same item, and you have to purchase this from a third character, why not just have 1 for all 3?. The rest of the shopping is needlessly downstairs, no items are of much interest, or seem more interesting than they actually are.
Bunch of buildings that you can't interact with. Levels are pretty samey all the way to the boss. Even the name enter screen doesn't automatically go to 'end' when you mash down, which by the way used the arrow controls even though the game is WASD. Everything moves faster than you. Monsters respawn but environment does not. Sometimes treasure just falls into pits, why would you want that, it's like you intentionally want to make people not feel rewarded. A sprint button could have been nice since he runs and jumps like Professor X.
The game was tagged as metroidvania but it doesn't feel like it qualifies at all. Exploration doesn't feel very free, you can choose which level to play but it's more like Mario than Castlevania, your weapon is barely used for exploration sans the hitting blocks done in every other game, there aren't multiple ways to get around like wall jumping, sequence beaking doesn't really exist even in level selection since you must beat particular bosses to progress, pits are bottomless, low ceiling, no clever ability foreshadowing, no maps. This game is not metroidvania.
CONCEPT Unrealized
I was so disapointed after what sounded like a good idea on paper was not executed very grandly. For someone with a shovel you do not dig very much. Digging in this game is basically either scrapping a pile of gems, or knocking a wall out of the way. With such a premise I would have thought it to be essential to gameplay, that you could dig up all kinds of exciting treasures, sure gems, but maybe new weapons or key items, maybe some blocks require a higher level shovel, maybe you have a garden to manage, maybe dig trenches to redirect water flow, maybe instead of hitting enemies you flick them up, maybe you need to bury treasures, maybe your enemies are earth elementals, nope none of this. Just a generic attack. This game should be called pogo knight.
As for the plot it's pretty standard, I was mildly intrigued by the Shield Knight who feels like they will be a penultimate boss of some kind, and the idea of knight who lives this way but everything is very bland. Some NPCs had potential to be interesting but it didn't seem to be going anywhere. There's a girl that asks you to play with her and you find you can hit the ring she is tossing around but it does nothing. You prove to one guy you are the shovel knight he gets excited ooh what is he going to give me??? nothing, no item, no info, nothing. Hey theres some animal people I bet they have something interesting to say about how they- nope. Woah a gold knight he be really important to- nope.
VISUALS More dated than emulated games
This game is really tough to look at full screen, if it were static maybe it wouldn't be so bad but it's a game, things move. I understand pixel graphics are cheaper and that give a surprising amount of people a heart beat in their trousers, but it really does strain the eyes, more so the more active it gets. It's kind of like watching a TV show and deciding to put your nose against the glass. Menus are exceedingly plain even for an older styled game. The intro cinematic was oddly slow, I feel like it was done for nostalgia but was still annoying(old =/= good).
MUSIC Muted
Seems kind of cool for about a minute but then gets old REALLY fast, like someone playing a toy keyboard through the amplifiers in the opening sequence of Back To The Future. I actually adjusted my speakers several times, not just once, several times, even quiet wasn't quiet enough. And it just loops forever, never changing dynamics or doing anything musically interesting, thematic or otherwise. New songs can be unlocked  and only listened to in one spot, a spot with nothing else of interest happening, couldn't get into any of them. Within 20 minutes I muted the game. The song collecting could have at least been an interesting idea had ACIV and MSG4 having already done it(and doing it a lot better).
Waste of $20 for a clunky infuriating game that doesn't know what it wants to be or accomplish. Every game I have gotten for under $10 have been far better and I would rather play a Kongregate game or Freecell. I feel like a lot of people pretend to like this game because other Youtube gamers have commented on it positively. Your money is better used if you lay it out flat on the ground and unleashing your bladder over it, then leaving it to fester into a nice butter, though the odour be powerful, it will be no match for how much this game stinks. Not only can I not think of anything it done even slightly better than any other game in any regard, I can't think of anything it didn't do worse than most games. Shovel it into the recycle bin.

So, I'd backed Shovel Knight on Kickstarter, but while everybody was ♥♥♥♥ing in their pants over how great it was, I was still waiting for it to be released on Mac. Then, it finally came out, and it's great, but…I couldn't get past the 3rd stage (stupid moving platforms plus death spikes!), so I put it down for a couple of weeks (months?)…until now, and I was able to get through the troublesome stage without too much difficulty (a half-dozen attempts and I was past my prior roadblock).
So yay!
Anyway, this is a really great game. With art that styles itself in the limitations of the 8-bit NES era (but without the true hardware limitations that would lead to sprites flickering, slowdown, or music channels cutting out to make room for sound effects), Shovel Knight is both grounded in and reminiscent of the platformers of that era, but simultaneously much more advanced in its design.
And the music is really, really great. Like, whistling-it-while-I-wash-the-dishes great. It's probably the most authentically 8-bit part of the game, although the music could never run on the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) hardware, because it uses the Konami VRC6 cartridge chip that was used with the Japanese Famicom (the difference between the NES and Famicom music for the game Castlevania III is a frequently noted example of the regional differences in soundtracks for the same game due to the NES's incompatibility with the VRC6 chip).

Portal Stories: Mel, a journey I set out on to regain my initial thoughts towards Portal when I first played it years ago: to provide me with a one-of-a-kind puzzle experience, with a story so good the puzzles seem annoying sometimes. Some have probably quoted me saying 'The Talos Principle' is like Portal on steroids; well it’s safe to say 'Portal Stories: Mel' pushed the limits of portal with most of its tests and far exceeded my previous thoughts towards it's difficulty. I had to work on some of these for hours on end, only to find I was either overthinking it or had done something in the completely wrong order. As it stated within the game's page 'Portal Stories: Mel focuses more on sequencing and execution, it does not require ninja-like reflexes to complete'. I must say this description is quite accurate (however I may have bent the rules on a few levels using precision and a lucky portal placement or two) but in all honesty some of the tests within this game take 15-45 minutes, if you do decide to download the game be prepared to get stuck on levels larger than anything you have ever previously experienced. I (honestly) never cheated by looking any of the levels up and vowed to before playing to maximize my experience (this however, made the time at which I finished the game largely fluid unfortunately). It felt as though I was still playing 'Portal 2', it executed all the duties of a 'Portal 2' mod by tying in, but not so much that it became all speculation and game theory. One of the only things that ruined my immersion was the excess of empty, useless space, rooms and passages in between levels. I'm a thorough gamer; if you give me space to explore chances are I will go through every last area looking for something of substance. Within this game, (outside of the occasional vitrified test chamber) most of the extra offices and rooms provided me only with repeating textures of posters that I had otherwise seen in 'Portal 2'. Despite repeating loads of textures within the game, the voice acting was impeccable; even within the unoriginal introduction it seemed as though they had created a new sequence in which the character spoke or as if they had totally rerecorded it. I highly advise this for gamers who played portal 2, but don't remember it so much that it would cause you to become picky over the details within this game (I'll be totally honest I remember almost nothing from 'Portal 2', this gave me an excellent refresher) not to mention you can pick it up absolutely free on the steam market.

A very strange game.
I'm not sure exactly how Resident Evil went from a survival horror game to a bad imitation of Gears of War, but... it happened.
The game starts off in a good space and actually stays very entertaining for a significant chunk of time, but around the time the zombies start riding motorcycles (?) and you defeat a giant by sitting still on a turret and shooting at his feet (??) the game takes a rather weird turn for the worse. Enemies suddenly become bullet sponges and you spend massive amounts of ammo either locking an enemy in an animation until it dies, or hoping to hit the tiny weak spot that will eventually kill it.
I would not put a vote of confidence for single player, but if you're going to play with a friend through the cooperative mode, you'll probably have a good time and share a mutual feeling of "What the hell is going on?" when you realize you're playing a really crappy cover shooter instead of a Resident Evil game.
I mean, I get it, I played RE4, and it was not quite a survival horror game either. However, this is just weird and I'm not sure what I really think about it. I totally understand why longtime Resident Evil fans despise this game to the core.
All that being said, I still had a decent time with this game, but it was quite the downward spiral from fun to what-the-hell?

One of my favorite games to date, and it runs fantastic on DX10. Its frantic real-time item management and tank controls offer a learning curve for the typical third-person shooter player, while leaving a wide enough gap for brand new players to learn and adapt through the campaign. Co-op is rewarding, with an inventory sharing-system, occasional branching paths and even voice commands for gamers who don't want to use a mic. Mercenaries is extremely addicting, and with the formerly console-exclusive DLC finally available, I highly recommend this game for anyone.
Some will give the game a negative review because it's so unlike the earlier games in the series with its OTS camera and emphasis on shooting action, which is a fair assessment, but if you come into RE5 without a predetermined expectation of what a "Resident Evil" title is supposed to be, I'd say it's one of the best of its generation of AAA titles. Clean, beautiful, optimized and just plain fun to play. Plus the combination of top-tier voice actors and bottom-tier writing makes the cutscenes worth watching again on every playthrough.
Note: I have far more hours on record  than my Steam account shows, as I originally played the game since 2009 on my GFWL account. Between GFWL and Xbox, I've likely logged about 900+ hrs. Like I said, love this game.

I've been a long time player of ArmA 2 and now 3, (even if my steam profile says otherwise) and I have to say this game is awesome. The only down sides I can find to ArmA 3 is as follows: 1) Poor optimization (or lack there of). The engine ArmA was built on is great at running single player, scripted missions. It's weakness is optimized multiplayer. Even on my respectable rig (8gb DDR3, FX-6300 4.2 and GTX 1060 6gb) suffers in a decently populated server using the same video settings that I use for single player. 2) Controller Support. I know it does support a controller and it does function as it should, but at best I feel it is sluggish. Personally I was on console for years before hopping on the PC train, so I feel I know how the analogs should feel, and for lack of better wording, the ArmA controller support definitely lacks. 3) Lastly, the steep learning curve. There are so many things to learn in ArmA in order to get "good". For instance, each weapon has a different velocity and bullet drop rate. Each weapon deals different amounts of damage to enemies due to caliber of bullet, the wearing of armor or not for the enemy, the aforementioned distance, etc.
As for the up sides, here is a list just to name a few:
Open World/Sandbox gameplay
Military Simulation
Huge Community
Very Active Servers
More interactivity than "Press E to..."
Etc.
My overall opinion of this game: Worth it? Yes. Absolutely. Would I recommend it to a "meets minimum spec" gamer, probably not seeing as how this game is notoriously hard to run at 60+ fps.

On paper, it had everything going for it: resource gathering, micro management, needs of villagers, crafting, construction and combat. Instead, everything is implemented in a basic way that for some reason just doesn't work, and ends up being a cluster♥♥♥♥, to put bluntly. The screenshots showcasing busy townfolk running around a bustling city look amazing, but don't be fooled: whilst it's true a picture says a thousand words, gameplay says a thousand words + 1.
there were a few games using similar painted-art style, but I can't remember their names. The interface is ugly and obstructive, thankfully though the buttons can be minimised. The entire game looks like a free game you play on those Flash sites. Not necessarily bad I must add, but surely if they took a backseat towards the visual department, then they could have pumped more beans into the gameplay side of things? Apparently not.
They'll randomly dart across the landscape for no apparent reason, and the way they slide across the place looks freaky. They have no goals and just stand there doing nothing, permanently frozen in an upright stance for eternity (except when they die they rotate 90 degrees). Order them to chop down a forest, and they'll just fly towards the area en mass, stand completely motionless in front of the tree and it magically dissapears, through use of sound effects. Couldn't they at least have the sprite of an axe in their hand?

Granted, they actually do a very good job of following orders: ask them to hack down some trees, mine some rock and what not, and they'll literally drop everything, rush towards the area like a bunch of gophers and gleefully carry out said task until it's done. If only public service workers in real life were as committed as these folk are.

They'll often, for no reason at all, decide to wonder to the complete opposite end of the map and get killed (or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥rather, due to the bad animations) by some high level monsters. Then again for some unknown reason, another villager will decide it's their turn to dash to the other end of the map and repeat this morbid process. It's extremely frustrating as there is no explanation nor solution to this phenomenon, I've actually lost an entire village due to this sick process. If it's not a bug and actually some invisible monster using mind control on my villagers to turn them into suicidal lemmings, than I do apologise.
Well here's an example. I tell a villager to go bake some bread, he does so without delay. Next to the bakery is a designated area for storing bread. Said villager then bakes the bread, and takes the finish products to the store room. Simple right? What actually happens is SOME bread gets put in the store room, whilst the rest is just littering the floor of the bakery, for no explained reason. And now the villagers are eating the bread off the dirty floor INSTEAD of the stockpile, despite the stockpile being closer to them. And again for some unknown reason, some of the villagers decide to find food in the dangerous jungles be yonder, rather than pluck it from the safety of their own town. Maybe they suffer from wheat and gluten allergy?
a problem with other city building games is that sometimes buildings weren't been built because the villagers were too busy with other trivial tasks or "idleing", so props to Towns for fixing this common issue (even if it's due to bad AI). You can custom build your houses block by block, choosing a variety of different colours, furniture, etc, and decorate the surrounding area with plants and other decorations. So in essence, Towns does actually deliver what the name implies, assuming you can get past the bugs and terrible AI, and the fact is you need the AI to get the most out of Towns.
Do yourself a favour, switch that damn thing off and play something in the background of Youtube, as this single endless loop will drive you absolutely insane.
It actually got abandoned after it was pushed out of beta and into its final, albeit broken release state. I guess they jumped onto the city building craze every other indie game was doing, but didn't have the know-how on how to actually make a game properly. It's a colossus shame as Towns could have very well become a massive hit and a new standard for village building games. If the original developers were to release the game engine/source code for open modification, that could potentially completely turn this game into a success as I bet there's many talented people out there just hoping to get their hands on this and fix all the problems.
There's tons of other similar games that does everything way better. And for the record, to end the Towns vs Gnomoria debate, Gnomoria wins tenfold. At the time of writing, I've only spent 3 hours in Towns, as opposed to 65 hours in Gnomoria. Don't need to say more.

This is the infamous game that has gave a bad name to steam's early release program.
This was one of the first games to be available to purchase from a new (at the time) steam division which was intended to give funding to games which were partially developed and showed a lot of promise.  Back in 2011ish, this game was seen as having amazing potential. Lots of people bought the game, and we thought the money we gave would be used so that the programmer would work full time on the game.  (There is a big write up on exactly how much money was generated from game sales, I can't remember if it was in the hundreds of thousands of dollars or more).
What happenned instead, was that the developer took the money and stopped working on this game.  Disbelief, outrage, and anger from the community ensued.  No refunds were issued. Steam didn't withhold any of the cash.
So many people feel they were burned by this affair, that they swore off purchasing pre-release games ever again. And that's the real loss here.

After a day of strressful work (or stressful gaming) this an incredibly satisfying, yet relaxing casual fishing simulator.  I have not played too many fishing sims but I have played enough to find this one far more enjoyable.
If you are highly competitive even in your casual gaming you will probably not find this appealing at the moment.  Multiplayer exists and the community is really great -- but there are no tournaments and you're left with a leader board for each fishing location but nothing super special.
And of course if you are super competitive you will be frustrated by the DLC and micro transactions.  When approached from the perspective of a casual game, I find the micro transactions to be distateful but much less bothersome.
As with most fishing sims, you are of course rewarded more for catching the "popular kids" of the sport fishing world (Bass, Salmon, Pike ect ect) but you are still able to progress/level with trout, catfish and panfish.  They are actually how I grabbed some decent ingame cash early on though they fade in importance over time.
The graphics are enjoyable but at the moment the software is certainly not optimized.  I regularly have minor (read: non-game breaking) graphical errors.
The sound track is peaceful and enjoyable as well.
In short, if you want to actually feel like you're really fishing with complicated sporting gear in the actual environment...you need to purchase a fishing license and go out side.
But if you're interested in casually gaming and like fishing this is not a bad option and honestly one of the best currently availabe (though that says so little).

I've been a long time player of ArmA 2 and now 3, (even if my steam profile says otherwise) and I have to say this game is awesome. The only down sides I can find to ArmA 3 is as follows: 1) Poor optimization (or lack there of). The engine ArmA was built on is great at running single player, scripted missions. It's weakness is optimized multiplayer. Even on my respectable rig (8gb DDR3, FX-6300 4.2 and GTX 1060 6gb) suffers in a decently populated server using the same video settings that I use for single player. 2) Controller Support. I know it does support a controller and it does function as it should, but at best I feel it is sluggish. Personally I was on console for years before hopping on the PC train, so I feel I know how the analogs should feel, and for lack of better wording, the ArmA controller support definitely lacks. 3) Lastly, the steep learning curve. There are so many things to learn in ArmA in order to get "good". For instance, each weapon has a different velocity and bullet drop rate. Each weapon deals different amounts of damage to enemies due to caliber of bullet, the wearing of armor or not for the enemy, the aforementioned distance, etc.
As for the up sides, here is a list just to name a few:
Open World/Sandbox gameplay
Military Simulation
Huge Community
Very Active Servers
More interactivity than "Press E to..."
Etc.
My overall opinion of this game: Worth it? Yes. Absolutely. Would I recommend it to a "meets minimum spec" gamer, probably not seeing as how this game is notoriously hard to run at 60+ fps.

When I first saw the trailer for this game it was promising with an outwardly quality experience with a unique story and new content. However, when I started playing I was reserved just in case the game proved bad and forgoing the bitterness that would have come from high expectations. As I played, I saw the effort that went into the game, and for a free mod I was impressed. The level design is original and spacious, but I often found that I would be sidetracked by portions of the maps that seemed like they were going somewhere but would ultimately be deadends. This being a pretty linear game, I feel that it had too much room to explore without anything to reward you for taking time out of playing the campaign to go and visit. The tests are challenging but I felt there really wasn't a learning curve, some tests at the beginning were complex and when I solved them I felt satisfied with my solution but there was other tests towards the end that were so painfully simple that I overcomplicated it thinking the test was building upon my previous experiences but when the test seemed to magically solve itself after me shooting into the dark I was completely underwhelmed. Thankfully there was a sense of progression as there would be themes of game mechanics that would flow one into another. Throughout the game I would have a hard time trying to distinguish which surfaces were portal-able and what things I could jump or walk on, especially later on when there are electrofied portions that you need to platform through. Finally, I also had difficulty figuring out how I was supposed to advance to the next part of levels, it helps to know that they use lighting like they do in Left 4 Dead to show where you need to go next but it's not always the case.
Next, the story isn't bad, it was fresh to see them open an area of the Portal universe that has creative legroom. Pacing was good, really only hindered by complicated room layouts. There is a good mixture of humor and seriousness and there are a lot of logical points that help advance the story but they can be questionable. One thing that really helps is the music, all done by Harry Callaghan he does an excellent job with the score that matches the universe. The music matches the environment and really sets the atmosphere, it is one of the selling points.
In conclustion, it was a good game! For a free mod for Portal 2 it held under the pressure and I would recommend it to anyone that already owns Portal 2! Additionally, when you get this game you can get its soundtrack for free as well, a sweet bonus. Just give it a try and form your own opinion from there!

This is the best Megaman game that's been made in nearly 2 decades.
This game is a very very high-quality tribute to the games were popular during the late 80's/early 90's. The influences are obvious - The character itself, the level design, boss fights, graphical style and music are very reminiscent of the early Megaman games. The level selection pays tribute to the slightly-less-than-linear level select screen of Super Mario Bros. 3, where there is a general direction of progression, but you may be given the opportunity to stray from the path at times. The shovel jump mechanics are a less-than-subtle throwback to the pogo stick in Ducktales. Most importantly, however, is that the controls are both simple and responsive. If you miss a jump, it'll always because
missed the jump, rather than the game itself boning you. As with most 2D platformers on PC, I would strongly recommend a controller (with the Xbox 360 controller being the standard).
The difficulty of this game is often spoken about. The game is
, but I do have to stress that this game is NOT
. The difference is mainly that although Shovel Knight does have challenging sections, there is rarely a point in the game that is strictly unfair. Most of the time when you die, it'll be more of a "dammit, I messed up" than a "this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" type of thing. Furthermore, unlike many NES games of old, there is no limit to the number of lives you have. Instead, dying causes you to lose a portion of the gold you've collected, which gets left at the point at which you died. You then spawn at the latest checkpoint and have an opportunity to obtain the money that you dropped. This means that there are rarely any parts of the game that require extensive replaying of the same areas over and over again. Seasoned platform gamers (for which this game is most likely targeted at) will probably get through this game without too much of a struggle. Newer gamers however are likely to get stuck and potentially frustrated at various segments of the game. With that said, regardless of how difficult you may find the game, each level you complete will feel like an accomplishment.
As previously mentioned, both the graphics and the music in the game are very much influenced by game such as Megaman. The graphics are, in a sense, "beautifully ugly", in that it is an 8-bit style game done in high resolution. The music is more or less the type of chiptune that you'd expect from a game like this. It's catchy, yes, although I found the music less memorable than the NES titles that inspired this game.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a good NES-style 2D platformer. Yes, the price of this is currently relatively steep for an indie game (as it has never been bundled or, to my knowledge, gone on special for any significant amount to this date). With that said, as PC gamers, we are spoilt for choice. We live in an age where, on Steam, and with the overabundance of bundled games, we are able to get decent-quality games for very cheap. From a value-for-money point of view, I would recommend getting much cheaper-but-high-quality 2D platformers such as Super Meat Boy, Limbo, Braid, Spelunky and a host of other games well before you got this one. However, if you're like me and
is a considerably more limiting factor than money, then Shovel Knight is the best value.
In other words, I strongly believe that Shovel Knight is the best 2D platformer currently on Steam, bar none.

So, Towns. Oh boy, where to begin...
This game is not a game for casual play. It's not a traditional game (although I will always believe it helped pave the way for an emerging genre) like most people will expect, and it's not most peoples' defenition of "easy".
It's a game where you get out what you put in, and then some. But the catch is, the "and then some" is an exponential value. After a while, you realise that you've gone from mildly interested, to challenged, to excited, to inspired, to totally hooked.
Now, in all fairness, the initial challenge is steep. Like I said, it's not an easy game, it's not pick-up-and-play-and-eventually-win.  In fact, Towns is designed to encourage experimentation and multiple approaches. There are no unlocks, it's quite possible to take your first town through the whole game and reach the "end"... but to get there, you'll need to unlock your own creativity and disaster management skills. That takes practice, plain and simple. But like any hobby, after that initial investment the first wave of reward convinces you to keep going, and after that it just gets better and better.
Towns gets a lot of flak. Partly that's because it is genuinely lacking in content - at least, compared to what the content was obviously intended to be. However, I'm convinced that the flak is only spat so vigorously because Towns forces players to take a look at themselves and their own play style. In my view, a lot of the complaints are based off of the horrible realisation that some people just can't get their heads around the new strategies required to do well at this game. Because Towns is a game of strategy. It takes a keen perception and a lot of understanding to see the strategy in all its layers, but there is an underlying logic that is oh so satisfying to crack.
That's not to say this is a game only for super-nerds. Rather, it requires a bit of patience and a bit of humour, plus a healthy curiosity. The patterns are simple enough once you spot them, and infinitely scaleable - that's the beauty of this game. Once you crack one challenge, you can expand and expand that solution and take the same basic logic into other challenges. That's not attractive to some players, but for others it's an absolute joy.
Fortunately, there's a free demo - so you can see for yourself whether you enjoy that challenge or not.
I wholeheartedly reccomend this game to anyone who is prepared to invest the time and open themselves to the experience. It's not what everyone will enjoy, but those who enjoy it will enjoy it a lot. If you're sick of the instant-gratification games, the ones with no substance or originality; if you just want to deeply engage with a challenge and figure it out; if you're the kind of person who thinks "gah, this is so complex... I love it, how do I solve this?", then Towns may well be one of the games you never entirely forget.

This is the best Megaman game that's been made in nearly 2 decades.
This game is a very very high-quality tribute to the games were popular during the late 80's/early 90's. The influences are obvious - The character itself, the level design, boss fights, graphical style and music are very reminiscent of the early Megaman games. The level selection pays tribute to the slightly-less-than-linear level select screen of Super Mario Bros. 3, where there is a general direction of progression, but you may be given the opportunity to stray from the path at times. The shovel jump mechanics are a less-than-subtle throwback to the pogo stick in Ducktales. Most importantly, however, is that the controls are both simple and responsive. If you miss a jump, it'll always because
missed the jump, rather than the game itself boning you. As with most 2D platformers on PC, I would strongly recommend a controller (with the Xbox 360 controller being the standard).
The difficulty of this game is often spoken about. The game is
, but I do have to stress that this game is NOT
. The difference is mainly that although Shovel Knight does have challenging sections, there is rarely a point in the game that is strictly unfair. Most of the time when you die, it'll be more of a "dammit, I messed up" than a "this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t" type of thing. Furthermore, unlike many NES games of old, there is no limit to the number of lives you have. Instead, dying causes you to lose a portion of the gold you've collected, which gets left at the point at which you died. You then spawn at the latest checkpoint and have an opportunity to obtain the money that you dropped. This means that there are rarely any parts of the game that require extensive replaying of the same areas over and over again. Seasoned platform gamers (for which this game is most likely targeted at) will probably get through this game without too much of a struggle. Newer gamers however are likely to get stuck and potentially frustrated at various segments of the game. With that said, regardless of how difficult you may find the game, each level you complete will feel like an accomplishment.
As previously mentioned, both the graphics and the music in the game are very much influenced by game such as Megaman. The graphics are, in a sense, "beautifully ugly", in that it is an 8-bit style game done in high resolution. The music is more or less the type of chiptune that you'd expect from a game like this. It's catchy, yes, although I found the music less memorable than the NES titles that inspired this game.
Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a good NES-style 2D platformer. Yes, the price of this is currently relatively steep for an indie game (as it has never been bundled or, to my knowledge, gone on special for any significant amount to this date). With that said, as PC gamers, we are spoilt for choice. We live in an age where, on Steam, and with the overabundance of bundled games, we are able to get decent-quality games for very cheap. From a value-for-money point of view, I would recommend getting much cheaper-but-high-quality 2D platformers such as Super Meat Boy, Limbo, Braid, Spelunky and a host of other games well before you got this one. However, if you're like me and
is a considerably more limiting factor than money, then Shovel Knight is the best value.
In other words, I strongly believe that Shovel Knight is the best 2D platformer currently on Steam, bar none.

I've been a long time player of ArmA 2 and now 3, (even if my steam profile says otherwise) and I have to say this game is awesome. The only down sides I can find to ArmA 3 is as follows: 1) Poor optimization (or lack there of). The engine ArmA was built on is great at running single player, scripted missions. It's weakness is optimized multiplayer. Even on my respectable rig (8gb DDR3, FX-6300 4.2 and GTX 1060 6gb) suffers in a decently populated server using the same video settings that I use for single player. 2) Controller Support. I know it does support a controller and it does function as it should, but at best I feel it is sluggish. Personally I was on console for years before hopping on the PC train, so I feel I know how the analogs should feel, and for lack of better wording, the ArmA controller support definitely lacks. 3) Lastly, the steep learning curve. There are so many things to learn in ArmA in order to get "good". For instance, each weapon has a different velocity and bullet drop rate. Each weapon deals different amounts of damage to enemies due to caliber of bullet, the wearing of armor or not for the enemy, the aforementioned distance, etc.
As for the up sides, here is a list just to name a few:
Open World/Sandbox gameplay
Military Simulation
Huge Community
Very Active Servers
More interactivity than "Press E to..."
Etc.
My overall opinion of this game: Worth it? Yes. Absolutely. Would I recommend it to a "meets minimum spec" gamer, probably not seeing as how this game is notoriously hard to run at 60+ fps.

Summary: Towns is a good game, in a beta-like state. The devs have not continued the game, if you purchase this game (at a price far too high for what it should be), then you are supporting developers who have inethically abandoned a game. Do not buy this. If you have a friend who has this game, it's better to just download it from them and play it from that. The best thing about this game is that it's DRM free.
Full Review:
Towns is a game that is well known for being abandoned by the developers. It was created and sold many copies, and then later abandoned.
So the game is given all these bad reviews for being abandoned, however the content itself isn't bad. It has a few glitches, none of which I've experienced being game breaking, mostly just visual. The game is small in size, and runs well. It's graphically not the best, but it's not terrible either. The music is basic, and there isn't much of it. The actual town building aspect has a good amount of stuff to it. It has good management tabs, but ordering your townies is slightly strange. There is a fair amount of content and as a town builder you can do quite a lot with it. The content of the game is actually pretty good.
So should you buy this game? No. If the game sold for less than $3, then it would be better. However for $15 you could much better games that are much more worth it. If this game got continued, then perhaps it could be better too. However, right now, it has been abandoned and is not worth it for the price of the game.

I'm actually doing this review just to get some badge, but after about 5176 hours in this game, I have to post a review about this one day, right?
So, Team Fortress 2, or also known as TF2, is a game that I could explain like about everyone else. Its about wearing hats and shooting everything down. But lets be real, the game can be pretty dang fun, even after you've played this game for 5000 hours, there are a lot of things you could do, but also a lot of ways to destroy your enemies. So I'm going to be making a hopefully small list and maybe it could at least help you know the Pros, Cons, and the Middle.
The Pros!
-The Battles:
They're always filled with some suprise, rather it can be 3 rocket jumper soldiers shooting you down with shotguns, or the usual team of 9+ pyros, or maybe 5 engieers, or maybe a team with at least 1 of each class, there can be a lot of other things, some will also be based on the map which is interesting but I'll be talking about that on a other side of the list.
-Weapons:
Some might be trash and others may be overpowered, but with the amount of weapons in this game, you could change your playstyle in plenty of ways. I won't give out too many examples, but some would be a Heavy that is into tanking lots of damage, or a Battle Medic (Just a reminder, don't try this out.)!
-The "Economy"
If you have no clue what I mean by this, I'm talking about those people who trade or buy/sell stuff for TF2 items. I won't go deep, but trading is a much better way of getting some cheap hats. If you want to get a Unusual for whatever reason, good luck because that can take a lot of time (And yet I never got more than 1 legit Unusual!). Theres also the market if you want to grab some things with money you can't make much of a use with, but be warned that the market doesnt include everything!
-Health
Just a quick Pro, some people say this is dead yet after 10 years there are still around 60,000-80,000 people on whenever I check the TF2 community hub, so don't worry about the player count, you should be finding servers filled with people (yet its still possible to come upon a empty Valve server in matchmaking.).
Now with that nice stuff out the way, lets disappoint you with:
The Cons!
-Team Balance:
Are you depressed after going down 3 ranks in CS:GO (I didn't play long enough to get into those ranks yet.) because of your teammates getting stomped by the other team? No? Is it not enough? Then this game will change your good times with its balance issue. As of right now (From what I've known) the matchmaking have ranks that are pointless, which means that you will likely be going against a team of experienced players while being in a team of people who started their first game. You can be one of them, and I'm sure you'll try to get better, but don't let your possibly good or horrible skills reflect back to your face because if that team is running your team over, it might not be you, but it could be that horrifying balance that Valve didn't yet take care of (or probably never will.) while creating this game.
-Updates:
Don't let this con bother you much because there isn't much to do about it. The TF2 team is really small compared to the other popular titles, and the reason why I complain about the updates is that the recent ones aren't that good (except the   Jungle Inferno Update in my opinion, yet some things still need to be fixed.) and the recent update (Jungle Inferno) took more than a year to be developed.
-Mann co. store:
Also not much, yet its the only reason Unusuals exist, if you aren't buying a key, buying a campaign, or trying to change your account from F2P to P2P, the prices here aren't worth it, even if a key is worth its price and I occaisionally use them on crates, don't use them on crates, they're a currency for the TF2 economy and are actually quite a bit of value.

The zombies in this game are like your regular everyday dead guys, similar in a way to Left 4 Dead's, only that they don't sprint that much, and they can shoot arrows and throw grenades (smart guys!). There are a few exceptions which may throw you off the first time yoy play, but nothing too hard really.
Second of all, it has great replayablity, especially if you play with a friend. There are many QTE moments that will either hurt your hand or make you feel a sense of accomplishment when completed (again, this is on the first playthrough).
The biggest con for this game is the AI partner. End of story. It's so bad, so don't ever give it a gun, unless you played the game a couple of times and can afford infinite ammo for it, then it gets better.

PvZ is one of the cutest games I have ever played.  My son and I each beat it years ago on Steam.  My younger daughters have enjoyed it on iOS and the Nintendo DS.  This game regularly goes on sale and should net dozens and dozens of hours of fun.  The core mechanics are interesting enough, but it's the extras that kept us coming back and encouraged us to complete the game.
New unit types are received as rewards for progression and are used to offset the more difficult locals (3 locations with night/day playing differently) and enemy types that appear throughout the game.  There is a fair amount of skill involved when deciding which units to take into battle and where to place those units during frantic moments.  Mini games and the zen garden spice things up a bit.  The zombie encyclopedia is a good way to research how to beat a level if a new enemy type appears too difficult.
Beating the game rewards the player with the cutest and funniest music video ever, which features some of the most memorable plants and zombies in the game. Feel free to YouTube it.  Whatever you do, just don't let the zombies eat your brains!

Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
Is there really much more one can add to this game's reputation other than to reiterate "It's scary!"? For me, Amnesia carries a bit of personal significance - it was my first real attempt at playing a survival horror game. To say that I was scared wouldn't be doing this game justice - the experience of playing Amnesia for the first time left me physically shaken and disturbed on a level few games have done even since.
Atmosphere matters in horror, and The Dark Descent doesn't pull any punches in this regard. There are very few moments in this game where you can feel truly at ease - even the calmer areas have an air of uneasiness as you prepare yourself for moving deeper into the gothic Victorian castle. Amnesia could almost said to have reminded developers at the time about the importance of anticipation - there are few actual monster encounters throughout the story, but the downtime in between oozes with such relentless paranoia and sound tricks that it feels as if these encounter pervade the entire experience.
Unfortunately, I found the impact from the monsters in Amnesia to be relatively short-lived. Although the story isn’t exceptionally long (about 8-10 hours, depending on your nerve), the final act struggles to maintain that same tension that’s delivered in spades during the game’s first half - a common problem in this genre, as the player learns the method behind the game’s madness. It also marks the weakest point in the story. The ideas for the story are solid enough - I’ve always admired Frictional for their audacity in storytelling, even if the execution leaves a lot to be desired. Amnesia is no exception - the setup spins a potentially haunting yarn of insanity and the dark depths of the human soul, but becomes increasingly silly and convoluted as the game progresses. This isn’t helped by a somewhat abrupt conclusion which offers the player three potential endings, none of which are particularly satisfying or revelatory.
I could ramble on further about Amnesia’s other strengths: the immersive and visceral physics interaction system Frictional is known for; the symbolism hidden within the castle’s murky passages; the water part. At the end of the day though, there are plenty other reviews that go into those better than I could ever hope. I simply wanted to add my thumbs-up to the review section and perhaps offer a bit of insight into what made Amnesia The Dark Descent a significant experience for me personally.
If you want a coherent story that combines thought-provoking ideas with a strong conclusion, then I’d say you’re better off with SOMA (in which the moral quandaries do amount to something), Frictional’s more recent title. If you’re looking for a dynamic monster-evading experience that doesn’t lose its sting later on, then Alien Isolation is a better game in that regard (where the monster feels like a living part of the world rather than part of haunted house ride).
When it comes to sheer unadulterated nerve-shredding tension though, it’s no surprise that people still hold Amnesia The Dark Descent as being one of the scariest games ever created.
Side Note: This release of Amnesia also contains two interesting tidbits: developer commentary and the Justine expansion. It really is a shame developers don’t put commentary into games more often, since the one included here provides a fascinating insight into the minds of the developers. Justine is an intriguing experiment that really should be experienced knowing as little as possible.

An excellent platformer in every right with throwbacks to the 8-bit games of old. Shovel Knight's gameplay, and fighting mechanics, go back to old, classic games such as the Legend of Zelda 2's forward slash, and Duck Tales' Pogo jump (with a shovel instead.) Fighting most enemies is truly fun, especially with the small arsenal of relics you gather to help you through the levels. The bosses are all in my opinion, pretty damn difficult, but when you beat them, it's so satisfying.
The actual platforming is mostly really great. Occasionally, there's an obstacle which you might think is really cheap, like an enemy hitting you from a distance when you jump over a small gap, or you are pogo jumping on top of an enemy, and as it dies you fall into a pit... but it's still great, as those moments are uncommon. As you progress through the game, the platforming becomes rather difficult, with precarious enemies placed on ladders, icy floors, or the wind trying ever so hard to kill you in a section with little land. It's difficult, and if you die, you are obviously sent back to a checkpoint (which interestingly enough, can be destroyed for money, but you won't be able to return there on death anymore.) But it is not unforgiving, as you can retrieve your money bags (usually) as long as it's not in a bad spot, and in a zone with a moving screen simultaneously.
The story and characters are unexpectedly great. The storyline is a bit cliche perhaps, but especially the boss enemies have great personalities, and aren't just unexplained bad guys that you give no second thought to after defeating them.
Overall, this game is unexpectedly and absolutely amazing. I would recommend it to about anybody. 14/15 stars.

An absolute classic game that is well worth the purchase.
Great tower defence game where you need to use your arsenal of plants to stop the zombies raiding your house to eat your brains!  A simple gird system dictates where you can place your plants.  To be successful you need to have a balance between economy (sunshine), offence (pea shooters and watermelon launchers) and defence (walnuts) when choosing your plants.
The adventure mode has a fantastic sense of progression whereby in every level your explosed to a new plant or a new enemy.  As the adventure mode progresses you will be defending your hosue in the sun, rain, night, by the pool and on the roof - with each environment throwing up new challenges.
The game of the year edition includes all the puzzle, mini-games, survival and zen garden modes - for those who played this on iOS many years ago like myself it was a nice surprise to have all these additional modes in one package.
The graphics and design of the plants and zombies are cute and humorous, the level of humour throughout the game keeps it lighthearted and entertaining (special mention to Crazy Dave).
Overall, strongly recommended for anyone who hasnt yet played it as well as for those who played it years ago.

I spent countless hours on RE5 on xbox 360. The PC version has great graphics and still delivers dynamic game play, however it does lack local co-op :(. All in all, definitely worth a purchase on sale.
RE5 takes place in Africa with Chris and Sheva, agents of the BSAA group which contains bio-virus weapons. You are basically fighting zombies with some cognition about what's going on, they aren't blindly stupid walking around like most zombie games. Rather, these "infected" come at you from all sorts of angles and drop down from all sorts of heights to greet you with a chainsaw, machete, crossbow or just a good old fashioned hammer. Characters vary from simple opponents which can be taken down with a few shots, to heavier opponents that may charge or swing obscenely heavy weapons at you.
What makes this game so good though? At first, I hated the game layout as it was tough to access my equipment menu or to pull out my gun. I should say that you CANNOT fire from the hip. You have to aim down your sights first in order to get a shot off. These two reasons sort of put me off but as I got deeper into the story, I got pulled in and liked how they intermingled melee with the ability to shoot opponents. You CANNOT simply press a button and start hitting someone. Just like pressing two buttons to get a shot off, you need to hold LB (to pull your machete out) then hit RT to get a hit off. This is one melee mode, the other involves "stunning" the opponents (boss's and regular opponents are susceptible to this) and then running up to them and pressing X which usually knocks them on their bum. Additionally, when the opponents are on the ground the player has a moment to curb stomp them (as seen in Gears of War). This melee mode is very particular, just as the entire game is made this way. You do not feel in complete control of the game until you've familiarized yourself with the game mechanics. Either you'll hate what Capcom did or you'll like it, simple as that. When you recognize when an opponent is stunned it makes a world of difference. I should also add when your partner is being held down by a zombie, the other partner can run up and press B to free the partner. I'm going to say it again even though I already said it, you'll either get along with this sort of game mechanic or you'll find it annoying you can't simply fire from the hip or melee at will. The movement controls over all feel smooth while the camera cannot be moved from an over the shoulder position. I have to give them credit for trying to include a wide variety of weapons from rifles, shotguns, automatics and pistols. On top of that, incendiary grenades, regular grenades are also included with a compliment of herbs that you can mix to heal yourself (or your partner on the fly). There is a slight RPG element to the game where you can upgrade weapons for better impact and a quicker reloading scheme. I would highly suggest spending your money wisely and choosing a weapon you know you'll be using a lot.
The graphics as I've mentioned are a lot better than xbox 360's version, everything feels smooth and the cinematics are pretty tight. The sounds are decent and do not really sound different from shot to shot, or when you break a barrel. The opponents also sound generically the same (unless you're facing a unique boss).
Overall, if this version had local co-op it would get a higher rating. Since it's a PC version and apparently we don't play local, it's going to hurt it's score a bit. None the less, a great game and would highly recommend it on sale.

Shovel Knight feels like the culmination of every single great idea that has been introduced in platformers since the late eighties. With perfectly precise gameplay and incredibly clever level design, Shovel Knight proves that "retro platformers" do not have to be uninventive under the guise of "homage". The whole game feels fresh and exciting, presenting already existing gameplay elements in new and original ways. The difficulty is perfectly balanced, with a well thought-out learning curve : new obstacles are introduced one at a time, giving the player time to adapt and thus making him feel like he is getting better almost effortlessly. The game is also jam-packed with things to do, from music sheets to collect to optional levels, a higher difficulty setting, and many achivements (with none of them feeling tedious). Add to that really good visuals and a very enjoyable soundtrack, and you get one of the most beautifully crafted games in recent years.
Shovel Knight is not just a fantastic indie video game, it is a fantastic video game by any standards, and one of the definitive experiences of 2014. Its price is entirely justified and I cannot recommend this title enough. Buy Shovel Knight : you will fall in love with it.

It is fun micromanaging your town, trying to get immigrants to come to it and attract heroes to it as well, but the food system seriously needs to be reworked. My villagers can go all the way down to the bottom of my mine before needing to come back up again to eat, and since your town can experience hunger lock (Where you don't have any food at all and all villagers can't do anything due to starvation), expect a massive kill off if your food supply ever dwindles to an incredibly low number.
There was a lot of potential behind this game, enough potential that I threw my money behind it back in 2011. This mod has such a fantastic high production value and it's clear the people behind it are pro's at environment design.
It's the level design that lets this great mod down. It's hard to explain what they've missed but the layouts of areas don't feel very organic. For example, the Apature science town has a layout that just feels wrong. the building entrance is at the exact centre of the courtyard. Buildings are mirrored on either side in a way that normal buildings are not. All the detailing is fantastic but they don't have an eye for real world design unfortunately.
Gameplay wise this mod is also a let down. With Portal and Portal 2 and in Half Life 2, puzzles have a sweet spot where the point clicks and the player yells AHA as they figure it out. Too often here there are useless portal surfaces that aren't part of a puzzle or other distracting functional elements that fool you into thinking they're important.
As in Chekov's gun theory, if there is a cannon on stage, the audience will expect it to be fired at some point in the play. A careful level designer ensures that the player is aware of what is actually important in a level and what is not.
This lack of understanding leads to the puzzles being frustrating rather than fun and many players have rage quit far to early in this mod unfortunately.
It's a shame because it really is so well presented....

Plants vs. zombies is a great game if you can look past the fact that any decent modern resolutions are missing, and a PC port that has received little love from the devs.
Pros:
+ The gameplay is fun and varied, while being incredibly simple to pick up and play.
+ The artstyle is beautiful, and everything, from the enviroments, to the different designs of the plants, shines with charm and creativity.
+ Tons of optional content, like the zen garden, where you can take care of plants you pick up in the game for cash, survival modes etc.
+ Great soundtrack. It dynamically changes based on the state of the level, and never gets old.
+ Cheap as all hell. For around 2 bucks on a steam sale, you're getting alot of value for your money. Just look at my playtime.
Cons:
- This PC port is tolerable for this kind of game, but very dissapointing. Many extremely basic resolutions are just flat out missing (even 1080p, and other 16:9 resolutions mind you), the game is locked at 100fps for some reason (??), and options are barebones. It's absolutely playable, since this is a very slow and casual game, but is definitely something to consider.
Conclusion:
A fantastic game bogged down by a really half-hearted port, but is still a good time if you can look past these technical shortcomings.

RE5 is RE4's basic gameplay and setpieces set in Africa with a slapped on co-op. It only ends up working because RE4 is such a masterpiece of a game. Now about the 'racism'. Feel free to skip on if you'd like. A little history lesson. After RE4, the development of the fifth game was handed off to a team of "Capcom yes men" who couldn't come up with anything new for a sequel that could top the last game so instead they were just going to do RE4 again but set it in Africa. And honestly I would've been fine with it personally. You can see from the very first trailer for this game that it was going to be singleplayer.
That was until the whiny people at the time complained how there was indeed black people in a game set in Africa. Nobody still doesn't care about the Spanish in RE4. Double standards much? A trailer showing black people as scary infected is not the same as showing scary black people as infected, which is what some people thought was happening. The first trailer isn't scary because of black people. It's because you're alone and outgunned in a foreign country against an even greater number of foes than in RE4. I know I'm years late on this but the people who cried racism should do a bit more soul searching and ask themselves if they're just seeing what they want to see. By the way the answer is yes.
It's so dumb for people to complain about this when it makes absolute sense for this game to be set in Africa. And that is that Umbrella Corp. is ♥♥♥♥ing evil. Why wouldn't they conduct virus research in a developing nation where people lack basic rights and nobody is there to see all the illegal thing's they're doing.
Anyway after the backlash the 'Capcom yes men' added Sheva Alomar in to the game. And while I don't hate Sheva, I think she's a good character, it's clear that the singleplayer spooks of RE were lost in favour of action co-op. And sadly they had to make a lot of compromises to make that gameplay style work. It's funny how an internet ♥♥♥♥♥torm can influence the entire course of a series in such a way. Either way RE5 was and maybe still is the best selling game in the franchise so maybe I'm the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Even if a lot of those sales were riding of the hype of how acclaimed RE4 was and still is. But I suppose that's enough about that.
The game uses Capcom's own MT Framework which graphics wise is my favourite engine. This game still looks good today (on a side note the Panta Rhei looks to be a great replacement). The gameplay is great. There's just really good craftsmanship at work with all the sounds, animations and feedback. The soundtrack is pretty great too. Especially Wesker's theme. Despite the faults with it's AI, I've played this game hundreds of hours on two different systems.
RE5 is a great co-op game that could've been much different if the devs had a backbone.

I love fishing, I live in FL and fish all the time.  I've been dying for a fishing game that's worth anything since sega dreamcast was around.   I want this title to do well, this game has all the right ideas, all the things I would want in a fishing game.   Since it is early access I won't harp on game mechanics and physics as I know they will improve.  My biggest problem with the game is its just not fun.  Let me explain, in Fl in real life I go to a lake I can catch many species using the same bait by adjusting I how I present it to the fish, where I'm from bass,bluegill,catfish,etc,etc will eat a nightcrawler.  It may not be optimal but it happens.  In this game its not like that at all, I find myself searching guides after frustration sets in.  You then find to catch this species you cast in this exact spot, during this time period, with exact leader setting at this amount, using this exact lure or bait and then grind for hours using that exact setup.  There isn't really any rng.  Once you get the xp needed to reach next lake you then go to guides find exact spot and grind for hours on the next fish.  To me thats not fun.
If you don't like grinding you can spend 150$+ of real money to get the better lures, and xp boosts.   I probably don't play this game mostly because of the costly dlc that comes out that you need to buy if you don't want to play for 12 hours a day to compete with others.   The very first day this game came to steam I spent 20$ for a weekly boost of some sort and it does not go by game time it goes by real time so it forces you to play alot to make it feel its worth it purchase.   I would rather this game be 40$ and come with all content then claim to be free to play.   Its free to play to get you in the door then when you feel the grind you pay out the A##.

I'm a RE fan, sometimes despite myself. The games aren't scary, but they are enjoyable. RE4 was, perhaps, the high mark of Capcom's decision to go in an action-oriented direction. The gameplay was fresh, the story was enjoyable, and the setting they chose was remarkably well done. I'll go so far as to say that they hit the 'rural horror where something is terribly wrong with the locals' vibe better than most proper horror titles do.
RE5 came fast on the heels of 4, and basically has the same kind of gameplay with a reduced emphasis on exploring the environment and a focus on violence. The choice to move to Africa for the setting wasn't a bad one - colonial issues aside, there's plenty of things to be scared of out there. It provides a great excuse to combine dilapidated equipment and urban environments with a vast selection of rural locales. Nothing wrong with that at all.
The Good:
Chris and Sheva are both fairly fun to play, with a handful of distinct weapons to each one. They also have distinct combat styles, with Chris being a 'roid-pumped bruiser and Sheva being more of a finesse fighter. The enemies are more dangerous than RE4 - the humanoid enemies are better armed, and the non-human ones are tougher than their counterparts in RE4. There are new ones running around which are almost too tough (those damned mantis-ants, for instance), but you'll find a decent challenge throughout.
There's a large supply of weapon and costume unlocks as well. The costumes are a bit of a wash (the club gear ones are especially terrible), but the weapons are solid. The minigun in particular is great to play with - it chews enemies to pieces, but you'll need time to let it rev up.
The Bad:
The inventory system is crap. There's no other way to describe it. The elegant attache case from RE4 was far better, but they swapped it out for a more traditional limited slot system. You'll find yourself swapping ammo and the like with your partner more often then you should need to.
The partner AI is...okay, for the most part. Okay, but not great. They'll still waste healing items on you when you don't need them, and they do tend to get mauled if you leave them off by themselves.
Wesker, your main opponent, has crossed over into Mary Sue territory by this point. He's your typical modern body horror anime villain cranked up to 11, bouncing RPGs and heavy caliber weapons like he was half Kryptonian. It's only his over-the-top voice acting and performance that saves him as a villain.
And, of course...the race issues. Really, this isn't too bad for the first and later acts of the game. Most of your enemies are a variety of ethnic types, not out of line for the right parts of Africa. In the late stages, the Manjini you're facing are in advanced stages of infection, so most of those are a necrotic blue with obvious decay creeping in around the edges. Again, not a problem.
The middle acts of the game, which take place in a tribal reserve and underground city...there's the problem locale. You're up against tribesmen who wouldn't be out of place in a mid-quality pulp novel, attacking you with spears. The game tries to hand wave this by stating the locals went crazy, and reverted to the 'old ways', but it's a bit crass and kind of silly at best. I don't think there was an intentional bid to be offensive, this is pulp story/action-adventure cliche territory, but it's definitely not a comfortable thing and I don't fault people who find it offensive.
Would I recommend?
Absolutely. This is a fun game, and issues aside you'll have a good time shooting monsters and running for your life when you're not shooting monsters. The voice acting is cheesy, the story is pulp silliness, the setting is great, and the action delivers more often than it stumbles. If the second act of the game doesn't put you off, you'll have a blast.

As a patron of Minecraft, I very much enjoyed musing the idea of having multiple people placing the blocks, especially in the form of a functioning town rather than a purely aesthetic one. Towns has the potential to be that awesome crossover, but it is not.
Although listed as a finished game it feels very much as an Alpha. The control over the "Townies" is extremely limtied, and each map begins the same way : a horrible struggle.
The question is why is it a horrible struggle? Right off the bat there are a number of monsters covering the surface of the map, many are able to kill a townie 1 versus 1. The townies will engage anything they encoutner and unlike the "Heroes" do not ever disengage until one of them is dead. So very early on your main task is gathering resources but in very controlled ways to avoid your townies by chance encounter a monster.
So you lost some townies, how does one get them back? Well you will need to have rooms built individually for each town plus any extras you want, they must be well furnished and food must flow in abundance, this together allows them to maintain their happiness which will entice others to join. Here is the kicker: work quickly saps happiness, so when you lose a townie or two the others must work twice as hard to provide happiness. I am sure you can see the paradox happenning.
Ofcourse many other small time problems persist throughout the game which make building anything close to the promos provided to be a long, long way away. Sure this sounds like the right approach, you cannot build a city over night, but the truth is you will spend many weeks before seeing anything resembling a couple huts.
In conclusion this game was greenlit with the hopes of it being grown, expanded and ultiamtely polished. Here is how it looks.
Greenlit - September 11th, 2012
Last Monthly Update - September 21th, 2013
Date of Review - June 24th, 2014
It has been nearly a year to the date of this review since anything signficant was changed and it will be a surprise to see another.

Team Fortress 2.
This is more of my personal experience with TF2, but there are reasons for why I recommend this game near the bottom.
Four years ago, some way through 2013, my friend brought over his laptop, cracked it open, and told me "You've gotta check out these games."
He showed me a couple, Super Meat Boy, Overgrowth, The Binding Of Isaac- All of which I was sort of blow away by since I had really only ever
played console games before then. But before we settled down to play a multiplayer game since all he had was singleplayer at the time, he
wanted to show me just one more game, TF2. I had seen it once before as a hard copy that my brother owned, but I never gave it a thought until
now since I figured the game must have been ancient or obscure. But after watching my friend play a couple sessions against bots, I was
mesmerized. The ubercharges, the sentries, the stick traps, the rocket jumping- and the spy was one of our favorites to mess around with since
the bots interacted strangely. So after he was done, I had my fun with a few rounds and proceeded to fail terribly since I hadn't played a
first person shooter on PC before, save for being able to play World at War a couple times. Even with my terrible ignorance for controls and
lack of ability to do anything past move and look around, I was honestly having a blast.
Fall and winter of 2013-2014 was so much TF2. My internet could barely handle it and I ran risk of going over the usage limit every month, but
I was getting better, getting unlocks. Eventually, I started getting acheivements, earned my iconic gibus and pyrovision goggles, and I even
found some friends that I could join up with basically anytime.
Time went on, thousands of hours later on 2fort, orangex3, minecart_jail(whatever version), and I had come to be a decent player. Got some
stranges through trading away my slowly earned scrap, got a couple cosmetics from generous friends or lucky drops, and understood most
mechanics of the game. But, after a while I took a break for one reason or another, and I figured my TF2 days were done, and that there was
nothing left to get from it.
Half a year since then, summer came around and I didn't have much to do, though I had a shiny, brand new computer to play things on above 30
FPS. First thing I thought of getting back to, was Team Fortess 2. I waited out the download, hopped on some old servers I used to go to, and
got to see old friends that were still around. The game's fun hadn't changed one bit, and by now it was 2015. TF2 wasn't just a fun game
anymore, it actually had some meaning behind it. Something to pass the time, a place to hang out with friends, a way to hone my skills and do
silly or serious things.
But... Something was different about TF2 at that point. None of my friends in real life played anymore, and a lot of my old TF2 friends had
either gotten too busy, stopped playing, or in one way or another, we stopped talking. Yet it didn't stop me from coming home and logging in
another couple hours each day, playing on valve servers, community servers, and sometimes when the internet was down I'd even practice on
rocket jump maps or tr_walkway, or hell, sometimes I'd even go back to the roots of the game and play bots. I'd say I was around 2000 hours at
somepoint in 2015, and though I was no professional, I had those shining moments of 10 or 15 kills in one life, or mroe often, having a really
good life as a medic. Medic is my most played class, but I won't bother getting into that yet.
So I kept playing. Gun Mettle update came along, matchmaking was changed and some things were wonky, but it was still TF2, and I loved it. The
long awaited pyro update, or now called "Jungle Inferno" certainly was a long one, but I was able to play during the wait, and I had fun. It
really was a lot of the same things through 2016 into 2017. Pubbing, going to some comminuty servers for a little more skilled gameplay,
occasional mvm, and still sometimes playing offline when I really had nothing better to do. By now I was becoming a seasoned player, if I dare
to call myself that. I understood more hidden mechanics of the game, such as crit heals, trimping, surfing, crit chance, c-tapping (alright
c-tapping I never quite mastered), pogo jumping, and whatever else you can think of, there's a good chance I know about it to some extent, and
I've had the most ridiculous things happen to me that I couldn't even begin to write down.
So, now we're nearing the end of 2017. Nearly 3000 hours according to steam, 1900 according to the in game stats, 800 of those playing medic
alone. (It's worth noting that at some point I reset my in game stats, which I regret even now, so potentially more hours as medic.) I've
gotten 50+ killstreaks as medic, soldier and heavy, at least 20+ killstreaks on scout, 27 on demo(knight. Once.), and on other classes...
well, there's always room for improvement, but at least I'm not absolutely horrid at them. I've completed a few rocket jump maps (with many
tears and cramped hands), completed ghost wave on mvm (with so many soldiers and so much laughing),  played god knows how many games, and
earned 483 achievements out of the 520. Sure, I probably wouldn't get last if I tried competitive 6v6, and I might not even be second last.
But I'd need work for it. And if I ever get the chance, I probably will.
But enough about what I've done, it's time I answered the big question:
Why am I still playing this game after 3000 hours?
It's... Fun. Satisfying. Challenging, rewarding, hilarious, visually appealing and uncluttered, easy to get into and easy to keep playing, and
how can you go without mentioning the community.
Now I've already used up all my space and can't cover everything as much as I would like to, so I'll settle with what I think is one of the
most important things of TF2, right alongside the community.
Team Fortress 2 is challenging, and rewarding. When you first load up the game, you have absolutely no idea what is going on. And you die. A
lot. But you swing your bone saw around as a confused battle medic a few times, and eventually you land that random crit on the the lime scout
with the australium scattergun and two unusuals that was dominating you, and part of you just explodes with joy. It might not have been a lot
of effort and more a stroke of luck, but it was still a challenge, and hell is it ever satisfying to see his ragdoll flop down for your team
to do the schadenfreude taunt at. But it doesn't just stop there. When you've mastered the basics and want to learn more, there's most
certainly more. What's the most effective way to move as scout against such and such class? What's the best time to deploy an uber? Would I be
more helpful if I stayed with my team and pushed together, or tried to flank as this-or-that class? Which unlockable weapon is best, or maybe
even stock? These things are eventually learned, and then they become second nature. So you move to the next step by learning more hidden
things about the game, such as just how long it takes to recharge a sandwich, or how heavy does more damage the longer he's spun up, or how a
spy can peform a trickstab. Did you know that the crusader's crossbow ignores the healing debuff on pyro's back scratcher, but does not ignore
the healing debuff on soldier's escape plan and equalizer? And even when you're done there, you can go further, into even more specific
things. And when you've truly mastered a class, if you really can, there's all other classes to learn. And on each map. With each weapon. On
defense, and offense. It goes on, and on.
There's so many more reasons to play. I've only covered why its fun skill wise, and how you can become a better player no matter how good you
think you are. But hell, it's free! Play it for 10 hours, and if you don't like it, you can forget about it without a dent in your
