it's so difficult to produce something genuinely scary.  Amnesia is.
It tells a very tragic story of revenge and redemption, gradually revealed as you progress through the game.  The story itself is not scary though.  What makes this game truly different and completely engrossing is that you, the player, are defenseless.
There are things all around you that will kill you, but you can't fight them.  You can't fight at all.  That's refreshing and makes for a very suspenseful experience because all you can do is run and hide.
Other horror games give you weapons and explosives and plenty of tools to help you survive.  The enemies become less fearsome because you can take them down, and eventually they won't be a threat at all.
Not in Amnesia.  You walk down dark halls with no means to defend yourself.  So when you hear a monster around the corner, it's scary because you know you can't fight it.  Just hide... don't look at it... hope it goes away...

You play as Shovel Knight, a knight equipped with a Shovelblade that must take back the kingdom from Enchantress and her Order of No Quarter. Along the journey you gather gems and crystals and use them to purchase additional relics and weapon and armor upgrades. The overworld map is setup nearly identical to the layout that overworld maps are set in Super Mario Bros. 3. Players can choose which order they want to do levels, but all levels on a map must be cleared before moving onto the next map. Just like the annoying Hammer Brothers, random enemies can appear on the map, blocking the player from accessing certain parts of the map until they are defeated.
In spirit of the Mega Man series, each level has it’s own unique look, feel, and music. The platforming parts of the game are well done, and bring a much needed challenge to newbies and veterans of platforming games. The controls are tight and responsive, just what you need to make pixel perfect jumps and attacks. In addition to unique enemies to each level, each end boss is very different. While their mechanics can range from stupid easy to borderline range inducing, it’s satisfying when you deliver the final blow to end the level.
When I mentioned that Rex Rocket lacking identity, I meant that the game lacked these elements. The levels in Rex Rocket all looked the same and while bosses has originality, the ordinary mobs lacked variety. The backdrop from level to level doesn’t offer enough differentiation from section to section to break up the monotony. In Shovel Knight it’s blatantly obvious what the tone of the level is. The art and music direction work in perfect tandem in the same way early Mega Man games did. Just hearing a few notes from any stage song immediately conjure up images of the backdrop, level enemies and the precarious platforming that entailed getting to the stage boss.
Despite how near perfect the combat, art and music direction, and everything else about the game may be, there is one annoying addition to the game that I feel is unnecessary: the addition of a death penalty.
Other than this blemish on the the game, Shovel Knight is a well executed retro-game. I would highly suggest playing it. The controls are tight, the art is fantastic, the music is well done, and the gameplay is solid. If you can ignore an unnecessary death penalty mechanic then you’ll have a wonderful time playing this game.

I recommend this game to everyone, those who likes FPS games, and those...who don't. It's really fun if you want it to be. Can be a casual shooter game or a competitive one depending on how you wanna play it and who you play it with. Some may say it's not fun because it gets too hard for them, or just that they play with guys who are new to it or with those who just wants to fool around. Don't just assume it is not a fun game just after a few hours of playing it. It can take time for you to get used to.
And even though T.I. is made by the same guys who made C.S., don't compare the two games. Just take it as a whole different game, or at least that's what I suggest.
I like this game a lot. It allows you to get guns permanently, there are achievements that may take you a long time to get, a number of maps and modes to play (after the latest update), driving maps which quite a number of FPSs do not have, and also several skins you can purchase to have a different and a more badass look for your own character. To be honest, I got hooked on this game for months and I still like this game a lot more than other FPSs I have played before. T.I. is also not so much of a 'pay to win' game compared to some of those I have played. Yes it is true you can purchase stronger guns when you are only a level 1 with real cash, but even so, everything can be bought with in game money other than skins. So I personally wouldn't call that pay to win, since you are just buying things to have it faster. It's not like you bought a gun that's only purchaseable with real cash. But well, I respect the opinions of others if they do disagree with me.
But of course, there is also the downside of this game.
1. Little laggy.
There are quite a number of players in this game that face lag. Even though there are players from all over the world, it is still kinda bad. But even so, if you are able to deal with a little lag, it shouldn't affect you that bad. And for those of who you gets really bad lag, like maybe around 20 FPS or lower, if you are using a laptop, try keeping it charged. That's what I do and the lag is gone. May only be for me. I don't know..
Ohh. And if you are playing with lag, I suggest you to not play at driving maps that often. Can be chaotic..
2. T.I. community
Well, just like in most games, there will be people you will meet who are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. There will be ragers, whiners,  trolls, etc. Just ignore them if you can't take this kinda crap. And if they annoy you over the microphone, just mute them in-game. Good thing they have that option.. If you are able to deal with them, good for you. If you can't, well....try harder..
3. Hitmarks
After the latest update in July 2014, the hit registers have been screwed up. It's harder to land hits on target now that the hitmarks aren't as accurate compared to before. Not sure if this applies to all guns, but I notice this problem mainly for the assault rifles. Would appreciate it if this issue gets fixed quick, like say..to how it was before the update on April 2014? Then, the hitmarks were dead on.
4. Game development
Sadly, there are only 4-5 developers working on this game at the moment. So, updates can take awhile. But when updates do come, it may not necessarily make the game a 100% better. Like from the latest update in July, it's good they brought in new maps and new game modes. But the hit registers also got messed with. It can take awhile for problems to be fixed and all, but it would be nice if there were more people helping out on the game development. More people to get things done, and more people to get to understand what people actually want to see in T.I and implement them. If things go well with the development of the game, and when more people start playing and supporting this game, the developers would get more income which would keep them motivated. Would be nice for both sides don'tcha think?
Well, to sum it up, I recommend Tactical Intervention to gamers out there from all over the world. Yeah, there are problems here and there, but it's still pretty fun. And hey, it's FREE! Would call it a poor man's C.S, but it is better than it sounds, in my opinion at least. It would be nice to have some of you guys to volunteer to help out developing this game too. Also, from what I mentioned about the issues after some updates, don't be too disappointed from what you get as of now. It will be fixed and it will get better....hopefully..

In 2011, THQ and Volition positioned Saint's Row: The Third as the wacky alternative to the Grand Theft Auto franchise. Melee kills are over the top, weapon variety stretches from pistols to a giant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat, and the missions and story just get more and more insane as time goes on. Unfortunately, Saint's Row: The Third ultimately drops the ball. Much of the story missions in the first act and the beginning of the second act are just used to introduce the player to the various side missions in the game. While some of these missions are really fun, it feels like filler content with story bits tacked on. The story missions don't become interesting until the second half of the game, where Volition really turns up the sheer level of crazy.
The story is nothing to write home about. It's pretty disjointed, with multiple plot threads being introduced and only a handful getting any meaningful closure. The characters are fun to interact with though. The core gameplay mechanics are solid, allowing much more maneuverability than other open world games. Combat encounters become quite repetitive by the end of the game though, which drags down the experience a bit.
Will you get some enjoyment out of Saint's Row: The Third? Probably, it's just that what fun there is buried under a tedious first half, poor writing and uneven pacing.

You play as Shovel Knight, a knight equipped with a Shovelblade that must take back the kingdom from Enchantress and her Order of No Quarter. Along the journey you gather gems and crystals and use them to purchase additional relics and weapon and armor upgrades. The overworld map is setup nearly identical to the layout that overworld maps are set in Super Mario Bros. 3. Players can choose which order they want to do levels, but all levels on a map must be cleared before moving onto the next map. Just like the annoying Hammer Brothers, random enemies can appear on the map, blocking the player from accessing certain parts of the map until they are defeated.
In spirit of the Mega Man series, each level has it’s own unique look, feel, and music. The platforming parts of the game are well done, and bring a much needed challenge to newbies and veterans of platforming games. The controls are tight and responsive, just what you need to make pixel perfect jumps and attacks. In addition to unique enemies to each level, each end boss is very different. While their mechanics can range from stupid easy to borderline range inducing, it’s satisfying when you deliver the final blow to end the level.
When I mentioned that Rex Rocket lacking identity, I meant that the game lacked these elements. The levels in Rex Rocket all looked the same and while bosses has originality, the ordinary mobs lacked variety. The backdrop from level to level doesn’t offer enough differentiation from section to section to break up the monotony. In Shovel Knight it’s blatantly obvious what the tone of the level is. The art and music direction work in perfect tandem in the same way early Mega Man games did. Just hearing a few notes from any stage song immediately conjure up images of the backdrop, level enemies and the precarious platforming that entailed getting to the stage boss.
Despite how near perfect the combat, art and music direction, and everything else about the game may be, there is one annoying addition to the game that I feel is unnecessary: the addition of a death penalty.
Other than this blemish on the the game, Shovel Knight is a well executed retro-game. I would highly suggest playing it. The controls are tight, the art is fantastic, the music is well done, and the gameplay is solid. If you can ignore an unnecessary death penalty mechanic then you’ll have a wonderful time playing this game.

I didn't play Resident Evil 5 much at the moment the game came out, although I've bought it and then somehow lost it. Recently I've bought Resident Evil 6 to play with and was more than pleased with the game mechanics, cutscenes, voice acting and more action-orentied gameplay (with both tight and fluid keyboard and mouse controls) than classic chapters of Resident Evil. I played all the classic chapters on PC and PSX and always loved the franchise, either it was a horror-survival or action-survival game. After beating Resident Evil 6, getting all the achievements, all skills and all of other stuff, I wanted to try the preceding chapter, so I bought Resident Evil 5 second time, now both the main game and the gold edition add-on to have this game with Steamworks support. Turned out that the game is actually better than sequel and more fun too, I've beaten the game on all four difficulties with S-rank, I bought and upgraded almost all weapons, now heading to get all those achivements. Back to the game - the camera is under your full control, no annoying "director" in your way like in RE6, way less QTE moments but they look awkward on keyboard. You cannot walk while shoot (remember - I've already played Dead Space and Resident Evil 6 at this moment) but the devs were taking it into account so it works really well. The only drawback is your AI partner, which can be pretty annoying on Professional difficulty - you'll be hearing "Shevaaa!" a lot as she will die from the sunbeam in 4th chapter most of the time. Damn, it pisses me off, believe me. Oh, and it consumes my ammo - shame on you, Capcom, it's mine - get your dirty hands off it! And QTE moments - while RE6 has a ton of it, they feels ok - good luck becaming a pro in pressing F+V in RE5. All of this cons were addressed and corrected in RE6 but still RE5 is better game almost in any way. Maybe the multiplayer section and the mercenaries is better in RE6. The major difference is that the RE5 is more a game rather than "playable movie" style of RE6. I suggest you to buy both games and play RE6 first. The game is more than good. It's not the best way to follow the games' storylines but I played this way and after completing both games it doesn't really matter which one came first. And then play RE5, which is awesome. If you tend to play with the gamepad I suggest you to play Resident Evil 4 which is also a very good game and, as they say, better than both RE5 and RE6, but suffering from bad keyboard and mouse controls support, even in HD re-release, and I don't possess the Xbox controller. Yet. Oh, and I hate to save on typewriters, don't know why though, as it doesn't require the precious ink ribbon in RE4.

While the lights are on, I can race around for the same objectives as everyone else, and I know I have one loyal team mate. As a fisherman myself, I can highly reccomend this game.  It is still early in development, but the work they are doing is great.  The amount of rods, reels, tackle etc is already a lot and ever increasing with almost each patch.  The future plans for the game is also exciting.
As for realism - The fish seem to fight like they do irl.  You can feel the different fighting styles and strengths of different fish species.  You can't simply cast any bait anywhere at any time and catch something, you will need to have some understanding of where the species you are looking for will feed, at what times and what bait they go for.
There are also a lot of places you can travel to catch the fish you desire and this is also increasing after almost every patch.
One of the top things about this game is the service they offer to players, which other games lack.  The devs listen to players when we feel something should be added etc.  Yesterday I had an in-game issue, I emailed the support and was helped withing 2 hours.
All in all, for a free to play game you really can't ask for more - Tight lines! :)

So, I have over 2000 hours in this game. I'm nominating it for The No Apologies Award because, despite its flaws, it is still my favorite video game. When I first brought it as part of the Orange Box, I didn't really give it much thought. I wanted to play Portal really badly because it was the late 2000's and gamer culture had been drenched in "the cake is a lie" memes. Also, I had seen a playthrough of it and it seemed really fun. Anyway, I brought the Orange Box and eventually tried everything it had to offer. Team Fortress 2 has stuck with me, most of all. Even as Half-Life 3 has seemingly died, maybe taking the Portal series with it. We still have Team Fortress 2, a lasting beacon of hope from a Valve that I can no longer see. One without inspired writers, incredible gameplay or originality. To me, it has become like every other major video game developer, one void of originality or semblance of its previously amazing track record.
I do think that everyone should at least try it. But don't invest thousands of hours of your life into it.

Do you like megaman? Do you like knights? Then enjoy this game, which is essentially knight megaman! While many games will throw in some pixellated graphics and say "there it's retro", Shovel Knight seems to have been made by people who actually get what made these retro games fun.
The controls feel solid, yet I do find it easy to sometimes accidentally use an item when I didn't want to. That could just be me however. The soundtrack is done true to style and incredibly well, you'll most likely be looking up the songs pretty quickly after hearing them.
The story is basically any NES game's story, a simple tale of saving the kingdom from an evil force. Nothing much, but then again, that's intentional! Not every game needs a sweeping plot full of twists and turns, after all. The dialogue is full of humor, whether intentional or not.
The game may be a little too difficult for some, full of moments in which you'll be thrown into bottomless pits by knockback. The difficulty is just as retro as the rest of the game, which isn't always something people go for.
All in all, if you enjoyed the platformers of the NES days or are just looking for a difficult yet fair platforming game for the PC, get Shovel Knight.
P.S.: Use a gamepad.

Resident Evil 4 remains my favorite game of the series. I realize that this is blasphemy to the original fans of the franchise, but I simply prefer the over the shoulder camera to the original. Don't get me wrong, I certainly don't dislike the earlier iterations, and the camera system in those games did provide a certain unique element that I respect and enjoy.
That being said Resident Evil 5 had the oportunity to build upon the successes of RE4, but I feel it missed the mark. I enjoy the game and have played through it several times. Some of the boss battles are very memorable, as are many of the other enemies encountered, yet at times the boss battles are difficult, not just because they demand effort, but because it can be really unclear if what you are doing is having any effect at all. I also think there are too many quick-time events, which is something I hoped they would go away from after RE4. My understanding is that it only gets worse in RE6. I frankly enjoyed RE;Revelations a bit more. Overall it is a fun game, and I give it a favorable review, if only just.

it's important to bare this in mind, as many of the 8-bit style nostalgiafest indie games out there really don't do it for me, due to the fact that they cater exclusively to nostalgia.

On October 10th of this year, the Orange Box and Team Fortress 2 turned 10. It is a 10-year-old game that has claimed so many hours of my attention and produced so many thrilling, absurd moments.
Simply put, the game is an amazing shooter. Without that, it wouldn't have lasted the 10 years that it has. TF2 features rewarding, varied weaponry and incredibly deep movement mechanics that form the core of its FPS DNA. There is very little more fun or chaotic than a full match of 24 players, more Snipers or Spies than anyone would deem sensible and a distinct lack of team coordination. In such an environment you could pause to observe the beautiful craziness of a Heavy dispensing sandwiches to both teams, a circle of Engineers in a banjo contest or the antics of confused new players. If you want to get more serious, the game offers complex mechanics and strategy beneath its cartoony exterior with community competitive leagues to test your mettle. Then, you could just queue up with a friend to play Medic and together go beat the enemy to death with a limp fish rolled in newspaper. It is all oldschool FPS gameplay, but gameplay that hasn’t lessened at all with age and is still a wild good time.
All this said, there are a few issues with the current state of TF2. The competitive mode available within the game is flawed and all but abandoned while there is minimal support of community made competitive leagues by Valve. While there is an in-game tutorial, it is woefully inadequate to prepare an entirely new player for the pandemonium in games ahead. Nor does the wall of settings presented in the option menu make it easy to optimize your game for how you want to play. Being a 10-year-old piece of software, it is a patchwork behemoth of code, prone to a host of minor bugs. Finally, TF2 is only being worked upon right now by a small, passionate cadre of developers at Valve. The waits for updates are the stuff of legends and memes.
But, the remedy to all these flaws, is the sterling community that has grown around this game. They have maintained completive TF2 despite little outside support and are always open to new player entering the comp fray. They have made a legion of videos and guides to help you learn the ins and outs of every aspect of TF2. They have created and compiled configurations for settings that you can download, install and enjoy. They have modeled and textured hats, weapons and maps in the TF2 workshop to fill the game with community created content. They have produced crazy, enthusiastic entertainment in the same spirit as the game they all love. This community is amazing, and will welcome you with open arms.
So, in short, get TF2. Maybe spend $2.50 on a key, trade it for a pile of Ref and get an entire hat-stand worth of cosmetics to play dress up with your mercs.  Look at some community guides, download a config and throw yourself into battle. Push through chokepoints with your team, fight tooth and nail for control of a barn and tremble at the fashion sense of some people. Jump into the best multiplayer FPS experience ever put together.

Honestly, I wasn't surprised when I loaded the game to see a loading screen. That voracious bar of suffering, taunting me with its very existence. "It won't take long," I thought. I decided to be patient and just wait it out, but the loading still hadn't finished. "Alright," I said to my self, idly tapping my fingers on the desk. I really wished the game would just load already. But still, that loading screen persisted. I decided I needed a cup of coffee, because I might be waiting for a while.
I made the arduous treck from my mancave, haphazardly knocking over stacks of cola cans and action figures as I scuffed my way to the door. I turned the sticky knob and pushed the door open, letting the wafting scent of wasted ambitions and post masturbation seep into my mother's home.
"MUM!" I screeched with a raspy voice. "COFFEE!"
"Yes, dear, I'll start you a pot." My mother replied with a hint of sadness.
The idea that the coffee was not already prepared was more than infuriating. I stomped my way to the kitchen with the fury of a righteous warrior, but my mother was already gone, and the teapot was already on the burner. Since she was not there for me to cry to, I had no recourse but to stand and wait for the telltale whistling of the pot to signal that the water was ready.
It felt like an age, but I was finally able to make the trek back to my sanctuary with a stained cup of coffee in hand, ready to tackle this game. I decided to grab a box of twinkies as well, they're my favorite.
As I sat back down, I witness a true horror: The loading screen was still there. Laughing at me. I lost control as my anger and sadness took over me. I screeched a mighty "RRREEEEEEE" as I slammed my fists on the desk and keyboard, breaking a few of the keys off and spilling the coffee I had just suffered through so much to obtain.
It was at that moment that I realized I was playing Loading Screen Simulator, and not Grand Theft Auto Online.

First, if you love portal, you will love this, even though it’s a brilliant game in its own right.
- It's free (even though it feels like a payed experience)
- The voice acting is superb. I love Virgil's voice and accent.
- The gameplay and puzzles are fantastic. Not too difficult as to ward off players and also not too simple as a lot of the previous Portal puzzles were.
- The graphics are great, the same as Portal and Portal 2.
- The amount of detail is extraordinary. I sometimes just walked around for the sake of exploring, knowing there are no collectables to justify my curiosity of the world.
- The levels are designed perfectly. Even though it is a puzzle game, I never once thought that the strings of puzzles thrown in front of me were tedious or boring. They were cleverly put together by entertaining events.
- I was surprised as to how perfectly this game's story fits in with the rest of the Portal games’ stories.
Finally, I applaud and thank Prism Studios for this game. It was an absolute delight to play!

Ah. Resident Evil 5. A game that to this date seems to suffer from the love-it-or-hate-it syndrome.
Too bad for it, RE5 was a follow up to Capcom's most excellent (and to this day one of the best games ever made) Resident Evil 4. Let's start with a simple question: Is it as good as RE4? Hell no. But that poses another, possibly more important inquiry: Is it a good game? Hell yes.
RE5 on its own is a solid, pretty (despite the gray-ish color palette) and fun experience. For its age it still holds up surprisingly well, it runs at constant 60fps even during cutscenes (which sometimes seems not to be intended causing some graphical issues) and its replay value is actually quite high. Even more so than RE4's.
As far as gameplay goes it's more of the same if you played RE4. Run around, aim, shoot, explore, hit some bad guys, solve some incredibly simple puzzles (except for one particular one that actually makes you think a little bit), break boxes with your knife, get hit by a snake and run some more. Oh, and the ocassional boss fight here and there. It even adds up to the already solid gameplay with more contect-sensitive actions, like melee strings with your partner (Oh yeah, this game has an active partner) which can be very useful.
Its main attractive of course is co-op, which drastically improves both the experience and replay value. Online co-op works well but as always playing with people you know is the best choice, as items, ammo and weapons are shared and that can get a bit complex when playing with randoms.
Speaking of weapons and replay value, another great point for the game is its upgrading system. After you -or your partner- get a weapon you can buy it from the store, so no worries if  you missed it. Upgrading your weapons is a very effective tool to survive longer, though it costs money. You can then use those weapons on previous episodes and make your life easier, or your partner's if you are playing with a newcomer or wanna get stuff you missed. Let me tell you, replaying the first chapter is a whole different experience with an upgraded arsenal and some serious firepower.
Overall this game benefits greatly from co-op and I'd dare say it makes it an actually unique experience, at least for its time. If you're one of those who skipped it because it wasn't RE4-2 or forced the co-op on you, give it a chance, I know I did and I don't regret it.

Shovel Knight deserves some major praise. Something about it didn't let me stop playing. I sat down and beat it start to finish, non-stop. (Okay I had to pee once) I'd like to blame it on nostalgia, but the only thing truly unoriginal oldschool thing about Shovel knight is the 8-16 bit style. I suppose you could say the boss fights remind you of Megaman. The overworld reminds you of Mario. But there's relics, secrets and technical combat you don't really get from those games.
Shovel your way to riches and hoard it until you can afford the ever increasingly expensive upgrades. Search for the relics, which will not only give you combat advantages or movement boosts, but provide useful for future secrets and challenges. The gameplay is just different - and in a good way. You wield a freakin' shovel!
GUESS WHAT, THOUGH. There's a
to Shovel Knight and it's awesome. You lose you beloved Shield Knight (f) and have nightmares about saving her. You battle your way to the Evil Enchantress who has either captured or killed Shield Knight. Black Knight, your rival, runs into you often along the way. You must defeat the Order of No Quarter in order to proceed to the Evil Enchantress, which consists of different modded Knights with interesting and often humorous characteristics.
I started Shovel Knight expecting to screw around. Decided to do some playful voices and be dorky with it. Maybe rush through it, being all tryhard. But I ended up falling in love. At some point I forgot I was doing voices and really got engrossed in the entire situation. I'm glad I was streaming because this is a game I want to remember. It's on
as a playlist now, for those interested. It took me about 4:45 to beat the game fully.
My favorite part is how well Shovel Knight teaches you how to play without directly telling you. Every level introduces a new mechanic, and there's always a part on each level (especially the tutorial) that teaches you new things. And you'll have to reapply the things you learned at a moment's notice.
As far as challenging yourself... When you die, you release what seemed like 1/3 or 1/4 of your gold. Think of it as a more forgiving Dark Souls. You can go back to where you died and pick up that gold. Alternatively, there are checkpoints on each level. If you feel like the level is easy, you can actually
the checkpoint crystal for gold. If you do well on the level (I'm uncertain on the specifics, could be not dying or taking damage) the crystal changes color and holds more gold the more you pass without defeat. So you can also get accumulative growth in gold for taking the risk of removing the checkpoints.
Shovel Knight has great functionality IN SPADES....... Just play it.

I don't know what to say about this game, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings. We love cheese and Marmite for an extra British twist! Delicious!!

I reviewed this title a while back, and while I didn't recommend it then I was too leniant on its cons as I really wanted the title to succeed, and I believed in the developers.
It is also a good looking title, and feels good in many ways.
I dont believe anymore, the developers are frustratingly similiar to politicians, they react to positive posts that are 'harmless' but completely ignore any serious questions, like ...
- Why is the drag setting so limited ? 7 Settings only (0 - 6) ?
- Why does heavier tackle struggle to cope with small fish ? A 0.7 kg smallmouth redlining a 9.1k line on a 10.5 kg reel on a heavy rod ? At half drag setting ?
- What EXACTLY does the message 'Fish tried to bite and escaped'  ? Specualtion is , hook size is wrong but that doesnt make sense as the same hook can catch a 5.1 kg striper and a 0.9 kg smallmouth , so what fish is struggling to take that hook ?
These questions could be easily answered and the whole debacle put away for good, but no answer.
There is also the unrealistic mechanics in place, like...
- Catching 'uniques' , you dont just fish away and have a 'whopper' take your bait... nope you check online videos or lists, or your own excel spreadsheets for 'proper timing and rigs' and fast forward time to the 'correct window' and for an in game hour or two you try catch 'uniques'. You cant be patiant as the time is ticking away, the window is small and the in game time is accellerated.
- The game gives you charts that show when the fish activity is at its highest, but that doesnt include 'uniques' , outside that particular window they are close for business utterly.
- The game has 2 types of in game stores to buy tackle and baits, the megastore that has everything but you cant use it when at a fishing location, you have to leave the location and then access the megastore, and the pay travel to return to your fishing location. There are store local to the fishing location but they make no sense, more often than not they will not stock the bait you need for that location (Wax Worms for Sunfish in Cali - not in the Cali shop).
- Hope you dont like catfish or panfish, they aint worth a damn according to this game, nope you need to catch bass, pike and Salmon for any decent exp and rewards.
- Physics are mess, the fish will be staring at the sky with thier tails facing the bottom yet pulling on your line while being dragged sideways while the fish is in a vertical posture. You will often need to drag fish through the ground, your rod will attempt to use ninja clone techniques while fishing (double rods) and your fisherman will often reveal that they are blue aliens when the skin colour 'washes' off.
Defenders of the title will pull out the old Early Access defence, yet  the title has 4 current DLC packs and has had 2 event DLC packs, 6 DLC packs since August, yet the title has numerous mechanical faults which have been brought up pre-early access during its close beta period, and not addressed.

Out of all the scary games I've played, this one is the best. Story wise, the plot is incredibly intricate and unique. The player himself has a really long backstory that just makes you want to learn all about him. The other characters mentioned throughout the game are also very relevant to the game and really bring it all together.
As for gameplay, it is very smooth and encourages you do a lot of thinking before your next move. In order to avoid the monsters, you will need to think on the fly and be ready to run if necessary. In my opinion, the atmosphere of the game is what makes it really scary. The monsters are what add in the danger element.
The soundtrack is fantastic and is arguably the best I've ever heard. The music is what adds to the levels and really builds up the suspense. If the environment is safe, the music is calming and adds a sense of safety to an otherwise dangerous situation. The composer for the game, Mikko Tarmia, is also the same composer who worked on Frictional Games' previous series Penumbra.
Overall, this is a brilliant game and I highly recommend it to anyone who likes adventure and story.

This game is like the culmination of ALL the classic, best NES games you had in your library during the late 80's to mid 90's. It got the art style down perfectly (though the color range is not as limited as the NES, thank the gods), the music is authentic and absolutely amazing, and the controls are tight and satisfying as all hell. It's a perfect platformer, action game that also makes any 90's Kid nostalgic deep inside.
But here's the ingenious, oh so beautiful thing about the game: It never needed the nostalgia novelty, the NES 8-bit grahpics, the chiptunes, or even the limited NES controls, to actually be so amazing. It's a damn fantastic game, long enough to not overstay its welcome, and every level is designed perfectly for forcing you to master said controls, and new elements.
So it may be a tired notion of Indie games using pixel art to pitch itself, but this is a case where the developers had a great game as a foundation, and then made it look and sound like a great NES game... not the other way around. Substance over style here, and damn is the style awesome!

Somewhere between fearfully sprinting blindly down a dark corridor and hiding in a bureau with your heart pumping, it hits you: Amnesia is genuinely terrifying. This is a game that all horror fans should experience.

Shovel Knight is an exceptional game. Every aspect of the game, from its design, story, music, and NES artstyle is nearly flawless and I have to recommend it to everyone.
Designed to resemble an NES game, Shovel Knight delivers on every aspect of this aesthetic. The controls are simple, you have four directions and two buttons (not including start/select). The core gamplay elements are simple, jump and attack; the rest of the game is it teaching you new and interesting ways to combine these and then testing you with challenges.
The story is excellent as well. At first it seems simple, but you dig deeper as the game continues and it fleshes out the relationship of these characters.
I really cannot recommend Shovel Knight enough. Taking so many elements from so many popular NES games and mixing them with just the right amount of absurdity, Shovel Knight is a love letter to games in general, especially for those with an NES history.

This game is like the culmination of ALL the classic, best NES games you had in your library during the late 80's to mid 90's. It got the art style down perfectly (though the color range is not as limited as the NES, thank the gods), the music is authentic and absolutely amazing, and the controls are tight and satisfying as all hell. It's a perfect platformer, action game that also makes any 90's Kid nostalgic deep inside.
But here's the ingenious, oh so beautiful thing about the game: It never needed the nostalgia novelty, the NES 8-bit grahpics, the chiptunes, or even the limited NES controls, to actually be so amazing. It's a damn fantastic game, long enough to not overstay its welcome, and every level is designed perfectly for forcing you to master said controls, and new elements.
So it may be a tired notion of Indie games using pixel art to pitch itself, but this is a case where the developers had a great game as a foundation, and then made it look and sound like a great NES game... not the other way around. Substance over style here, and damn is the style awesome!

Having played hundreds of hours, I have to say that this is one of my favorites of all time. Sure its got glitches here and there, but in the end who really cares? Where else can you drive around blasting each other on your way to hand off or intercept a package?
So the graphics aren't as slick as COD, but you know what? The game play is a million times better. If you only play games for the most up to date cpu intensive graphics, then go away.
Many decry "pay to win". The game works by accepting cash, or in game points to get better equipment or weapons. You start the game with 50K game points, enough to rent out some serious kit, or permanently buy a decent weapon and some extra equipment. You get more GP by doing well in the game. You can get all the equipment you need by playing for a while and saving up points. The only folks who complain are those who want instant gratification. I got everyhting I ever needed not spending a penny, but have supported the developers by buying some DLC items now and then. Believe me, there are folks who spend a bundle on the best weapons, and they aren't winning.
Maybe there are beter games out there for deathmatch, but thats not what makes this game shine. It's the mission mode folks, where you and your team must complete missions, or thwart others from completing their misions. Team play is encouraged, by requiring members to heal each other rather thrn thmselves. And sticking in a group is a force multiplier by increasing the teams accuracy.
Don't listen to the whiners, read a guide and get in the game. Don't be a tool, help your team and behave likea human. If you get pwned a bunch early on, so what? You gonna rage quit because someone shot you in a FPS game? Go play something else, like jewel quest.

This game is pretty much a DF extra-lite. Legos with monsters. It's not difficult, but there are city building and management aspects. You need to establish a food and resource hub so you can build a bigger city and get more "Townies" as they're called, then dig underground, build a tavern, attract some heroes, and dig deeper for better resources.
The goal of the game isn't to reach some unknown boss. I'm not even sure there is an endgame with Towns. I never reached the maximum depth because I never held it as a main objective. I played this game because I have a god complex and want to create a thriving city and watch my citizens thrive by my grace and strategic expertise.
The sieges are kind of a joke, but they're a good source of spiderite and goo. My only wish is that the devs went more in depth with the town defense aspect of this game, but it's no big deal. I have ~100hrs in this game, so I think I got my money's worth.
Personally, I don't understand all the backlash this game got. I got this game on sale roughly a year and a half ago for ~2.50(?). Worth every penny, given my playtime. I'm pretty sure if I knew how much time I'd spend playing it, I'd drop 10 bucks on it in a heartbeat.
I think a lot of the anger has to do with entitlement. Games in this genre now adays (legos with monsters: DF, Minecraft, Terraria) are being released as full games, and the devs are devoted enough to the games to continue to release content. I don't think Towns needs to release more content. I think it's fine how it is. Some people may not think it's worth 10 bucks. To me, it is, but I'm 100% certain it's worth at least 5. Then again, I didn't enter this expecting updates. They appear more as a pleasant surprise for me.

Back in 2008, a popular mod known as Portal: Prelude was released, detailing a fan-interpretation of the events leading up to the original game. The modders felt that the original Portal was far too easy, and wanted to add extra difficulty to their own game, adding difficult and obtuse action sequences far too unfair to be enjoyable.
Portal Stories: Mel seems to have designed with a similar idea in mind. A backstory for Portal 2, with far more difficult level design. To be perfectly honest, the level design in PS:M can hardly be compared to the brutish and mean gauntlet that was "Prelude" - The focus of the puzzles is definitely more cerebral than anything else, using clever tricks never intentionally used in the base game. The game is even advertised with "Logic based puzzles, not execution based puzzles".
This is its biggest problem. Portal is filled with a variety of interesting concepts and puzzle elements that could stand to be elaborated on (such as the woefully unloved Conversion Gel) but the main focus relies primarily on Fizzler Grids, and tricking cubes past them using overcomplex underhanded methods that feel like cheating. They might have felt less crappy if the designers had decided to introduce these as concepts, but instead the player is expected to have prior understanding of these complicated maneuvers and is left feeling bamboozled and stuck. This is not conducive to the fast-paced crisis scenario of the plot.
This feels like a game that was meant to be more fun for the modders to design and think up, than to be actually played by the average human being. Some introductory chambers. Some explanation. Some level of understanding that not every player knows the entirety of the game's mechanics. But PS:M's Chambers are designed with a single solution in mind, meaning the player has no room for experimentation, or the ability to predict the endgame of any given chamber  based on a theme.
Pros of the game:
- The Deja Vu level was very good, and escalated its difficulty at a reasonable pace.
- The story was okay. It was a bit 2-Dimensional, and was a bit detached from the levels itself, but I could see myself enjoying something of a similar caliber again.

First off, I'm not like The Completionist. I haven't and won't be 100% this game, but to me this game is very important to notice, especially in our time where a lot of indie developers go for a retro aspect in their games. Shovel Knight gets it right. He hits just the right spot and digs deep... Come on, you can't talk about this game without including a pun!
In all seriousness though, Shovel Knight is retro in all the good ways, it has well composed chiptune soundtrack, is hard in the way that old games like the megaman games were and does the 8-bit look right. Everything looks like what it's supposed to be.
It has cheesy humour, bright colours, funny characters and a cute (and a bit cheesy) story but the absolute most important aspect of the game, is it's tight mechanics. There were few times in my playthrough when I felt like the game was screwing me over and that felt fantastic.
So... Did you like games like the old Mario, Megaman and Sonic games? Then this might be just your thing. My only complaint is that it's a bit short, but it's still longer than most AAA-games.

Not being able to run and gun is one, as is the limited inventory space, having to combine things.

is a game that was made to mock Greenlight and to remind you of days of horrible internet speeds coupled with loading bars.  You start off with a loading bar that seems like it'll take a lifetime to complete.  You click a button to earn money and you spend that money on the in-game store to either speed up the loading bar, by throwing all the money you earn at the internet.  Of course, to take your mind off of the objective, you can do a quiz in command prompt, play a one-player pong game...kinda' like racquetball, and waiting for your browser to load...
PROS:
+ Achievements
+ Easy/short (with autoclicker)
+ Mostly cat/dog videos at the end
CONS:
- Bland
- Boring
- You've gotten to the point of wanting to watch paint dry rather than complete other tasks in life

This game calls itself a Loading Screen Simulator yet the key aspect is not waiting for it to load but it is a simple clicker game variation. Instead of clicking to get money upgrade your clicks to get more money to upgrade your moneygain further you click to buy upgrades to decrease your loading time (the other upgrades are pretty useless).
Does that simulate a loading screen?
At least for me it does not.
What I thought this game would be was a never ending succession of creatively designed loading screens (or just ripped of from other games, like the beautiful GMod loading screen).
What you get is a flashgame with  no attention to detail. There was no effort made to make the game look appealing. And all the dropshadows are really annoying. Sometimes the Game has a Pixelated 8bit retroish look... would be great if it would not have that only partially.
In the end I can not not recommend the game as it is free.. but I can not recommend the game either

I'll explain my experience playing Loading Screen Simulator the only way I know how: Cuils
One Cuil = One level of abstraction away from the reality of a situation.
Example: You ask how much time is remaining.
1 Cuil: If you asked me how much time is remaining, and I gave you a loading screen.
2 Cuils: If you asked me how much time is remaining, but it turns out I don't really exist. Where I was originally standing, a picture of a loading screen rests on the ground.
3 Cuils: You awake as a loading screen. You start screaming only to have fragmented data fly from your lips. The world is in sepia.
4 Cuils: Why are we speaking German? A mime cries softly as he cradles a young loading bar. Your grandfather stares at you as the bar falls apart into binary code. You look down only to see me with pixels for eyes, I am singing the song that gives birth to the universe.
5 Cuils: You ask how much time is remaining, I give you a loading screen. You guide your cursor to the earn money button and click. Your eye twitches involuntarily. Across the street a father of three falls down the stairs. You click and look down at the loading screen in your hands. I give you a loading screen. You click and look down at the loading screen in your hands. You cannot click. There are children at the top of the stairs. A pixel shifts uneasily under the compression of an LCD display up against a plastic bezzle. I give you a loading screen. You look at my face, and I am pleading with you. The children are crying now. You raise the loading screen to your lips, tears stream down your face as you take a bite. I give you a loading screen. You are on your knees. You plead with me to go across the street. I hear only children's laughter. I give you a loading screen. You are screaming as you fall down the stairs. I am your child. You cannot see anything. You click on the loading screen. The concrete rushes up to meet you. You awake with a start in your own bed. Your pixelated eye twitches involuntarily. I give you a loading screen. As you k*ll me, I do not make a sound. I give you a loading screen.
6 Cuils: You ask how much time is remaining. My attempt to reciprocate is cut brutally short as my body experiences a sudden lack of electrons. Across a variety of hidden dimensions you are dismayed. John Lennon hands me the mp3 to a song that may or may not be his own work which plays on an endless loop, but it slips through my fingers. I am reborn as an Pong clone. You disapprove. A crack echoes through the universe in defiance of conventional physics as cosmological background noise shifts from randomness to a perfect A Flat. Children everywhere stop what they are doing and hum along in perfect pitch with the background radiation. Money falls from the sky as the OS engulfs all of the wallets, all of the banks, and all of the vaults and safes on the earth. You hesitate momentarily before allowing yourself to assume the locus of all knowledge. Entropy crumbles as you peruse the information contained within the universe. A small library in Phoenix ceases to exist. You stumble under the weight of everythingness, Your mouth opens up to cry out, and collapses around your body before blinking you out of the spatial plane. You exist only within the fourth dimension. The fountainhead of all knowledge rolls along the ground and collides with two adult cats. My head tastes sideways as load-time is reestablished, you blink back into the corporeal world disoriented, only for me to hand you a loading screen as my body collapses under the strain of reconstitution. The universe has reasserted itself. A particular pair of cats is fed steak for the rest of their natural lives. You die in a freak accident moments later, and you soul works at the returns desk for the Phoenix library. You disapprove. Your disapproval sends ripples through the inter-dimensional void between life and death. A small child begins to cry as he walks toward the stairway where his father stands.
7 Cuils: I give you a loading screen. The universe is engulfed within itself. A bus advertising bandwidth drives by a papillon. It disapproves. An unnatural force reverses Earth's gravity. You ask how much time is remaining. I reciprocate with a mildly convulsing potato. You disapprove. Your disapproval releases a cosmic shift in the void between birth and life. You ask how much time is remaining. A certain feline and his paramour feast on bandwidth for the rest of their unnatural, eternal endurance. Your constant disapproval sends silence through everything. A contrived beast becomes omnipotent. You ask how much time is remaining. I give you a loading screen. Your body becomes an unsettled pile of 0's and 1's, then divides by three. The papillon barks. The universe realigns itself. You, the papillon, and the loading screen disapprove. This condemnation stops the realignment. Hades freezes over. A single pixel is launched into the unoccupied existence between space and time with a specific loading scteen. You ask how much time is remaining. I give you a loading screen. It screams as you lift your hand to your mouse. You laugh maniacally as I plead with you. You X-out of the loading screen as it pleads for mercy. I disapprove and condemn you to an eternity in a certain void where a certain pixel and its specific loading screen are located. The Universal Space-time Continuum Committee disapproves of my irrational decision. You are locked away and are fed loading screens for the rest of your natural existence. A pixel dies during the process of digestion. You die in a freak accident. A certain pixel lives the rest of its life in a comatose state where it dreams of playing Pong. Your soul disapproves. Besides that, the game is basically perfect in my point of view, and the fact that the devs are always working hard to make the game even better just makes the whole experience a lot more enjoyable.
My final grade is a strong 9/10 and a weak 10/10

During the new "Operation Health" a season designed to literally FIX BUGS AND ISSUES has made the hit reg worse than it has been in the past.  Example: you drone out a room and find the enemy.  You know where the enemy is and shoot at them hitting the head.  In the kill cam, you see that their head is tilted back clipping into their body and a cloud of blood is covering their face. Rainbow Six: Siege teaches us one thing very quickly: Nowhere is safe. My only hope---our only hope---is coordination. Even then, the best laid plans of mice and terrorists often go awry.
Players have also been experiencing quite a few bugs, from little graphical glitches to more serious problems. One time my keyboard just wouldn't work anymore, but only for Siege. Other games were working just fine. I could hide but I couldn't run. Bugs and graphics aside, this is a tight, strategic shooter with great maps, destructible environments, and fast, fun matches. The core is PvP, but co-op is also available in the players-vs-bots mode Terrorist Hunt. That's a fun objective-based mode you can play with teammates or as a "lone wolf."
The smooth blend of stealth tactics and furious firefights keeps players on their toes, with the various operators offering unique ways to experience each map and game-mode. Different options for Attackers and Defenders helps keep Siege's playability levels high, and I personally can't wait to see what plans Ubisoft has for this game in the future.
I bought the game only. No dlc. I do not regret a thing. It takes a bit of grinding to unlock the year 2 characters, but it saves money. There are a few things that I would love to see change in the game.
Spawn peeking is frustrating.
Peekers advantage is annoying.
Combine both of them and it is horrible.
Glaz's buff is overkill. He was strong enough as he was.
Fuze's projectiles bounce too far, and they do too much damage.
Castle and IQ are basically useless in mid level games, beginners don't know how to deal with them and pros know how to use them.
Bartlett U Terrorist Hunt Bomb Defusal with the yellow gas is near impossible. Rainbow Six Siege is a solid FPS. The community is better than most and the developers listen to feedback, which is sorely needed and a breath of fresh air in the PC gaming world.
Of course there are some balancing, network latency, and team system problems, but Siege still has a framework that works and is constantly being improved upon. Every map has complexity that can be learned through experience, but is frustrating for beginners. Even the game system itself has so many mechanics to learn that it can be very frustrating at the start. This also gives the game great variety and replay value, however, and still retains its value well beyond a year after release. Just embrace that Siege isn't quite like the other shooter games that you play.

To put yourself in the minds of Shovel Knight’s creators, imagine you found a Craigslist ad that said, "DeLorean Time Machine: Free." You showed up at a designated parking lot to make the "trade." The Craigslister hands you the keys, says "good riddance." Before you can think about it, you're up to 88 mph and suddenly back in 1985. You ask yourself one simple question: how do I use my future-knowledge to improve the trajectory of videogames? Eventually you realize that none of your money works in 1985, videogames are actually much harder to make with an internet that doesn't run any faster than 9.6kbps, and everything smells like Tom Selleck. Quickly realizing that 1985 sucks, you decide to take your Nintendo game idea back to our present day and get your funds from Kickstarter. And it works.
New Game Plus kinda sucked all the meaning out of monetary gain. And though knights talk all about chivalry, everybody knows what knights really want. The pursuit of loot had been driving my enjoyment of Shovel Knight more than I realized. And it's precisely at the discontinuation of personal gain that I lost interest. Still, if a game only stops being fun after beating it the first time, it's hard to hold that against it too much.

There's something grudgingly admirable about Capcom's determination to make Resident Evil games feel like no other. And yet - even as a long-term fan - when you first pick up Resident Evil 5 it's almost impossible not to find yourself ♥♥♥♥♥ing about the way you can't move and fire. Or the glacial turning speed. Or the unwieldy inventory system. Just like you did with Resident Evil 4, in fact - and Resident Evil Zero before it, and all the others. It comes with the territory. These fundamental design decisions are illogical in a modern context, and part of me wishes Capcom would wake up to the present.
But the tradition of survival horror games has its place too. Make it tense. Place just enough ammo and health. Make it a struggle to get by. To enjoy them, you have to be prepared to put to one side the default annoyances. Once you adapt to the way this game plays compared to all the other third-person action-adventures out there, it all rather clicks into place. Perhaps the question to consider from the outset is whether you really want Resident Evil to feel like every other action game or not? Because if the answer's no, then you're halfway to getting the most out of it.
In many respects, Resident Evil 5 is content to follow the path of its much-loved predecessor and tweak a few things along the way. It's still very much a series of abrasive set-pieces strung together by camp hilarity. The main addition is the presence of a fully-controllable camera for the first time. Assigned to the right stick, you finally have the option to sweep the viewpoint around as you wish, and as a result the game is more fluid. Although four control configurations are available, the default works just fine, with a squeeze of the left trigger zooming the camera to the trademark over-the-shoulder view (which so many games aped in the wake of Resi 4, remember). The laser pointer remains, and a customisable level of sensitivity allows you to tweak to your own satisfaction.
Possibly the most jarring initial impression is how little has changed in the core game mechanics. While the prospect of split-screen or co-op online play tantalises, there's an inescapable feeling of deja vu and frustration as you play with an AI partner. To all intents and purposes, this looks and feels like a reskinned, high-def Resi 4, and what was hugely impressive back then often struggles to repeat the trick this far down the line.
Capcom does love a bit of tentacle action.
As you'll probably know from the numerous previews, the game kicks off with returning former STARS hero Chris Redfield (from the original 1996 Resident Evil) meeting up with local BSAA operative Sheva Alomar in a dusty African shantytown. Tipped off about a bioterrorist named Irving, it quickly becomes apparent that the hostile natives' attitude problem has more to do with viral shenanigans than a distaste for foreigners. As they are called to arms by a megaphone-wielding leader, Chris and Sheva find themselves running the gauntlet from a feral mob, forced to scale buildings, hop between rooftops and shoot fuel barrels in a desperate fight for survival, occasionally splitting up using co-op moves like the assist jump and then covering one another.
The setting might have changed a little, but everything else is inescapably reminiscent of the village sequence of the previous game, right down to the chainsaw-wielding giant, and the need to scale buildings to get some distance from the onslaught. Even the lurching enemies with their side-stepping attack evasion are the same. The weapons they wield are largely identical, as is their physics-defying animation, where foes reel back in familiar exaggerated fashion. From sound effects to graphical style to core gameplay and AI, there has been little or no change apart from an admittedly arresting visual upgrade. It's a different setting, with different character models, but the game you're playing has, for the most part, essentially the exact same template repeated in a different setting. Interesting that his axe doubles up as a storage device. Do you think he's going on holiday?
And if that doesn't strike you as mildly disappointing, then the almost complete absence of puzzles and exploration may come as a hammer blow. Where puzzles do exist, they're so crushingly basic as to be insulting, rarely amounting to more than simple, pointless object hunts that take place right next to their intended target. Far from the promised return to the adventurous exploration of old, you simply work your way through six extremely linear chapters where straying off the obvious beaten track is not an option. In addition, the presence of a new mini-map allows you to see exactly where you should be heading if there's any lingering doubt. The dumbing-down of almost every aspect of the gameplay is depressing, if not unexpected. There are even turret gun sections.
With so much of the gameplay distilled to a sequence of set-pieces, a significant part of what made Resident Evil appealing has been removed, and what remains is the shooting portion. Pushed front and centre, it morphs what was a survival horror adventure into a survival horror shooter, and many will find Capcom's transparent desire to appeal to the action gaming audience a little troubling. Whereas Resi 4 skillfully straddled a happy middle ground between old and new, Resi 5 embraces the action element without concession. Whether it goes too far, of course, will be a matter of serious discourse.

I played through the game wth a friend of mine (so there won't be much comment about the single player experience), as our lovely friend Chris, and was attacked by every living thing in Africa, including Wesker. Enemies would completely ignore Sheva's exsistence to go after Chris, as if it wasn't bad enough that Jill had fallen off-screen during a flashback. Thus, masterfully the atmosphere of the game: The lone American male, partnered up with an African lady in a business suit with the power to make herself invisible to all enemies, going through the adventure of a lifetime. This is his story...
See, Chris is in Africa following a lead on a very hazardous weapon... a biohazardous weapon! As well as looking for the reasons of his existence. But, because he's American, the African natives don't like him very much, so the B.S.A.A. sent Sheva to help him out, and protect him from the spookies. Wesker has made his base of opperations here, to unleash Uroborous, the biohazard that will spread across the world, but not if our hero Chris has anything to say about it!
There were so many wonderful enemies that Chris has to take on! Giant flying caterpillars with a soft heart, grasshoppers that force themselves on him (and give him the ride of his life), tribals with bathrobes on their faces, black blobs that inhale gas tanks, the giants from Skyrim with textures exclusive to RE5, and many more, including my personal favourite, boulders!
Chris is built like a tank, so it only makes sense that he plays like a tank, right? Well, that's why the tank controls have returned, yet again! If you've lived through the Ashley Experience back in 2005, you will feel right at home, because Chris, being bigger, tank-ier, and wanted by every living thing in Africa, plays just like Leon! Sheva is a lefty, so the targeting is on the opposite side, but not that it matters because if you play as Sheva, enemies will ignore you! And, true to the original Biohazard, Chris' inventory is incredibly tiny, just like the good ol' days~! You have 9 slots, and have to make the best of it, because ammo and weapons are abundant, and you will have to make the heartbreaking decision of whether or not Chris will carry the team, and hold the line from every beast, critter, native, and Wesker, or if you want Sheva to work her business outfit.
On a slightly more serious note, the game flows, dare I say, perfectly, as Sheva takes all of Chris' demands with little to no delay, at least, when you're playing with a friend. This adventure is very clearly meant for two people to go through it together, and it's a seamless experience. That being said, playing by myself felt like, every time you had to tell Sheva to do something, the pace would slow down to a crawl, until it was finished. I've only played by myself once, so I don't have too much experience on that, but it's evident to me that it's very clearly meant to be played with two real, thinking people. Y'know, like Chris.
So, what if you don't want to fight boulders? Well, that's fine, because there are also extra scenarios like The Mercenaries, where you play as Chris, and kill things, or you play as Wesker and kill things, or you play as everyone else, and kill things, on numerous stages, and you can use fire grenades! Big advocate of fire. There's also a scenario where you can play as Chris (and Jill) and play through the flashback explaining what happened to Jill and Chris. There are weapons to unlock, costumes, and you can even toggle infinite ammo, and use that in the story mode. But, play it with a friend, make sure you play as Chris.

It is nothing like the first 4 REs & gets a lot of hate as a result. Inability to run & gun adds to the atmosphere. The inventory space means you can't tomb raider it & must choose which weapons you want to bring into the level. This also means if you bring more than 4 weapons you wont be able to carry all the ammo types for them (once armor, heals etc are carried). This ammo management replaces the scarceness of ammo in the early games. The laser sight works better than a crosshair for 3rd person accuracy.

I'll start with the cons of this simulator, and follow up with the pros.  This is my opinion based on years of playing fishing games and spending countless hours fishing in real life.  (Note: I've read the most recent dev blog post, and it appears that the developers are hard at work already on some of this.  Good stuff!)
=== Cons ===
Physics - line slack in water doesn't correlate with how much line is released; confusing fish catches (the fish seem to 'fly' or teleport out of the water upon catching).
Xbox 360 controller - doesn't feel right with the controls of this game.  No game controller configuration options.
Controls - out of sync with fish bites; casting is a pain (no level of casting power?  simply click and hope for the best?); hooking/reeling fish is a confusing ordeal (fish on?  tension?  visual/audio feedback?  doesn't seem the game adds excitement to fish retrieval).
XP/currency - too much emphasis on points and currency rather than skills; microtransactions - a nice option, but seems to be designed as a cash grab.  Please - DO make money on this - development costs money.  But don't sacrifice fun and realism by making it pay-to-win.
Fish AI - unrealistic expectations (i.e. 'use a 16 inch leader with a size 6 hook').  Following guidelines to increase the odds of catching a fish is good - but forcing players to stick to a formula and grind away is just not fun.
Music - need more of it.
Interface - a bit confusing; example: ESC key does different things or nothing at all; GUI needs to be consistent amongst the different screens.
=== Pros ===
Graphics - WOW - spot on!  They are truly amazing.  3D texturing, beautiful ambience, plenty of attention to detail with the tackle/baits/etc.
Music - I've only heard a single track so far, but it's good.  That is the style that is fitting for a fishing simulation, and I'd love to hear more others like it!
Fish species - It's nice to see no limitation imposed; carp, bass, catfish, sunfish, etc. - they all matter.
Realism - FINALLY, no forced underwater view!  No annoying announcers.  No arcade elements.  A simulation :-)
Tutorials - A nice touch.
Support / dev feedback / wiki - Some of the best I've seen anywhere.  Listening to your user base and keeping them 'in the loop' will help keep this game thriving for years to come.

Shovel Knight is a retro 2D platformer game deeply devoted to its aesthetic and its puns. Designed as a pseudo-NES game, it harkens back to a long-ago era in gaming, and the game itself feels as if it fits into the era of Megaman. You are the Shovel Knight, a knight armed with a shovel who must beat his way past 12 stages to confront the Sorceress and rescue Shield Knight.
Story
For being such a simplistic game, there is a clear story to the game – Shovel Knight feels guilty because he could not save Shield Knight, and has recurring dreams of catching her while she is falling. Black Knight stands in between Shovel Knight and his goal, not out of loyalty to the Sorceress, but out of loyalty to Shield Knight. The Knights of No Order stand in the way for their own reasons.
Is there much story here? No. But there is enough of a story – and enough reinforcement of the central theme of the game – that it works, and is a bit more than an excuse plot due to the recurring dream of saving Shield Knight.
The game is also wonderfully full of terrible puns, and there are various townsfolk in a couple towns who can be spoken to and who often have silly dialogue.
Gameplay
The gameplay is very straightforward – Shovel Knight can hit things with his shovel, or use relics (of which there are 10), each of which has some special ability. Later on, Shovel Knight also gains the ability to charge up his shovel attacks to make them more powerful, and to switch which armor he is wearing for some minor bonus, frequently counteracted by some minor penalty.
The game is very much classic platforming, with the ability for shovel knight to attack enemies from the side with his shovel or spring up and down on top of them using his shovel like a pogo stick, occasionally necessary for navigating the levels or accessing secrets. The levels often make use of the fact that the protagonist wields a shovel, forcing them to dig through obstacles, sometimes taking advantage of the fact that the pogo sticking has to be stopped manually, and sometimes making use of the shovel otherwise by having Shovel Knight dig stuff out or dig through walls. There is a surprisingly decent variety of enemies, harkening back to Megaman type games, though some of them are repeated with only minor variations between them.
The relics add an additional complication to gameplay; however, I found that I didn’t end up using most of the relics very often, while the basic fireball attack relic, which granted a cheap ranged attack, and the temporary invincibility relic, were very versatile and useful. The rest were all very situational or just less cost efficient, though there were areas which specifically relied on the special properties of specific relics to navigate, which were interesting.
The levels themselves were reasonably varied, in a way somewhat reminiscent of the Megaman games, where each of the 8 major bosses had a specific world, and there was a prologue stage and 3 end-game stages which combined elements from all the previous stages. In addition to the main stages, there were a number of additional mini-stages which often focused on some specific aspect of the game; the overworld map even had Super Mario Brothers 3-esque enemies pop up and walk around on the world map, encouraging you to go fight them.
The levels also had various secrets hidden around them, and in hiding its secrets the game did quite well – the secrets are not immediately obvious, but if the player knows how to look, they stand out, and again remind me of secrets from the era. In addition to the relics, there are also musical tracks which serve as collectibles in the game, with one hidden in every level.
The bosses themselves were reasonably varied and had a decent variety of abilities, but unfortunately suffered from being rather too easy; only two bosses ever killed me, and both of those were because of environmental hazards in the stage which spelled instant death, rather than the actual boss whittling away my health. They were reasonably interesting to fight, but unfortunately the ease of beating them combined with ready access to relics and a couple items reminiscent of E-Tanks from Megaman (fully restoring both magic and health – you could refill them before every stage, too, and could carry two of them) meant that losing to them was extremely unlikely, making them a bit disappointing in terms of difficulty level.
On the whole, the game does a good job of recalling the 8-bit era, and it feels like a very solid game from that era. It is worth noting that the game also recalls the 8-bit era in terms of length as well – the game is pretty short, likely clocking in at 6-8 hours to complete, if not less, depending on how good you are at it and how much time you spend trying to collect achievements and gather money and search for every secret in the game.
Graphics
The game uses relatively simple pixel graphics, but they are not too simple; the game actually looks reasonably appealing, and looks like very high-end graphics from the NES era, though I’m not sure that the NES could actually support this game as it is. Even still, it does a very good job of executing on making the game feel like it could be from that era, and unlike many such retro games, it doesn’t feel cheap.
Final Summary
Shovel Knight feels like a game from the NES era, and is very heavily reminiscent of the later NES Megaman games in style, if not in actual gameplay. The platforming and controls are quite solid on the whole, and the game is overall quite decent. However, it really does feel like a game from that era, and while it is a very solid example of such a game, it still is such a game. It is fairly short and the bosses aren’t very difficult, which brings it down a bit. It is not a bad deal for a reasonably low price, but know what you’re getting.

Retro-stylizied action platformer where you play as a blue knight called Shovel Knight. The point of the game is to rescue your friend, Shield Knight, from the evil Enchantress and her Order of No Quarter. This game has a lotta references to other media, but not in a way that detracts from the atmosphere like Borderlands 2. The dialogue is well written and a kind of silly-funny. The bard has a little joke for each page you give them. Townsfolk say a select phrase from a list, some of them funny, others helpful hints on how to get around town and where to go.
Each member of the Order of No Quarter has a level dedicated to them that fits their theme. It's kinda like Mega Man; a knight that uses ice has an ice level with slippery platforms, a flying knight has a level on an airship that uses wind in different ways to help you move around. The game never really feels cheap, when it introduces a new mechanic or enemy it gives you ample time and space to review the surroundings and assess what's going on. When you die, it tends to be your fault. It's similar to Dark Souls in that you have to put some thought into when to attack and how you'll attack, since your attack animation is just long enough to expose yourself to an attack.
There are (at least as far as I've gotten in the game as of writing this) two towns you can visit to get upgrades and items. Here's where the personality of the game has a chance to shine, since the townsfolk are varied and interesting. There's kids in little ninja outfits that run around, there's old goat men with canes dressed like a LoZ2 villager, there's horsemen wearing fancy hats. The world feels varied and more mystical when you're buying meal tickets from a goat that continuously eats pages from a book they are carrying.
Speaking of which, the upgrade system is a bit odd. For health, you buy meal tickets from a villager in the town, then jump on a platform and hand the ticket to a chef, who prepares you food (which is a 10 or so second long animation) that increases your health. But to upgrade your magic, you just have to go a little bit to the right and talk to a sorcerer. This extra step that's added for the health upgrades could be because the meal tickets are limited in number, and if you wish to upgrade your health even further beyond what the meal tickets can give you, you have to get better at the actual levels of the game. This is a great way to encourage players to practice and hone their skills to prepare them for the later levels of the game, while at the same time rewarding players for doing well and completeing small challenges that give helpful rewards.
After you beat a level, Shovel Knight rests for the night by a campfire, and you have a chance of entering one of his dreams. The dreams are typically about Shield Knight falling as you control Shovel Knight, who has to survive the countless enemies that show up and catch her. A nice way to show his close connection to Shield Knight through gameplay since you, the player, are just as concerned as Shovel is about her well-being in the dream, since it rewards you with some gold. You can also get some money by putting out the fire after you wake up, a nice touch to add more character to Shovel Knight, a man so chivalrous and kind he wouldn't dare start a forest fire.
All in all this game is brilliant. From soundtrack to gameplay to design, this game really shines. If you pass this game up for any reason other than you get incredibly ill whenever you play games centered around knights, then you are missing out on an indie gem. Probably one of my favorite games I've played all year. Buy it, whether it's on sale or not.
