Yacht Club has done something amazing here. They've actually managed to capture the soul of what made classic NES platformers work. Literally thousands of others have tried and failed, but Yacht Club figured it out. They split the atom here.
So how do you give feedback to a minor masterpiece? Do you tell Da Vinci to put something behind the Mona Lisa? Do you ask Homer to tighten up the pacing of The Odyssey? I'll just be honest, if a bit rambly.
I can't tell you what it felt like when I automatically Pogo Caned (edit: Pogo Shoveled) my first enemy. It was automatic, totally out of my control. It just happened, and all my years spent stomping Goombahs and collecting diamonds came rushing back. The sound, the controls, the graphics, the gameplay... You get a tremendous sense of place and time. Shovel Knight is like visiting a theme park celebrating all the high points of 80s and very early 90s game design, but having full control over the ride. You reach for your tropical skittles, you adjust your day-glo painter's cap, you crank up your Vanilla Ice tape. You can't help it, it's automatic.
It could be said that Yacht Club cheated and weren't truly original with their design, cribbing heavily from Super Mario Bros. 3, Mega Man, Ducktales, and Castlevania... but to me such things are unavoidable. It's like complaining how much something sounds like Shakespeare- once the very DNA of a thing (theater, gaming) gets changed by a cultural landmark (Shakespeare, Mario), all works thereon are considered derivative (Ran, Rayman).
In some places the derivation is obvious- Plague Knight's lair (set to the catchy "Halls of Antimony") evokes the neon rainbow effect of Dr. Wily's lair from Mega Man 3. The towns are modeled after Zelda II. The overworld is Mario 3 through and through. Hell, they even got Mega Man composer Manami Matsumae to throw in a few tracks. And maybe it's just me, but  the Troupple King (which is the exact kind of oddball weirdness the Japanese loved to insert) reminded me of Capcom's Little Nemo.
Yet somehow the game is wholly original. Despite appearances, the story is hardly straightforward- you will be rewarded for completing the game and paying attention to the subtle clues regarding Shield Knight's fall. Each level and its boss are uniquely themed and clever, with lots of small details easily overlooked that add to the experience. Polar Knight's stage is especially interesting.
If Yacht Club had dumped this into an NES development cartridge and left it in an attic to be found, we'd make apt comparisons to Nintendo, Capcom, and Konami games of the same era, all the while asking ourselves how something of this quality could possibly have gone unknown for so long.
While I have come to praise Shovel Knight, I must still partially bury it- there are some problems, most of which are a side effect of so faithfully recreating vintage game experiences.
The game suffers in places from Mega Man syndrome. Later levels ramp up the difficulty mostly by increasing the frequency of the "knock-back" gimmick- trying to cross a death pit while under threat of being stunned mid-air and falling to your death. Few enemies pose a challenge past the halfway mark of the game. If you are wise enough to buy the Ichor chalices at the start of the game, you will likely never fail to beat a boss on your first try.
The lack of lives makes you much bolder in your decisions and risky jumps, even with the threat of losing large wads of your hard-earned cash. I never realized how much of a nail-biter getting to a boss on your last life was until I experienced the luxury of unlimited lives and ample checkpoints. It's not a bad decision, but an optional lives system might have been a fun addition.
I wish the game was the size of, say, Mario 3, but that's a tall order from such a small team. Maybe our next outing will be more substantial? I'd love to see where the Order of No Quarter has gone after a few years.
A must-do is to set the relic activation to a button and not the default up+attack. On modern analog joysticks (and D-pads which easily register diagonal movement) you will often find yourself either one degree too far to a side or one degree too close to up, activating a relic at an inopportune time or failing to activate one when you need it. I wish the developers had made the relics a button by default, since the vast majority of gamepads in use today would suffer from the above problem and increase player frustration. I only discovered this option on playthrough two and it reduced my frustration level immensely.
The short version? Shovel knight is good. Really good. Worth the price of admission and then some. With the promise of more free content, you'll find yourself coming back to the game again in the near future. I wish the game was longer not because I felt it lacked content for the price, but because I wanted more of it. Yacht Club has done some amazing work, and they deserve to be compared favorably to the other masters of their craft.

From developer Yacht Club Games comes Shovel Knight, a celebration and revival of the aesthetic and gameplay sensibilities of the NES library of the late 1980s. It's a game strongly reminiscent of the NES Mega Man games, from it's masterfully crafted boss fights to it's charged musical scores, but with a stronger emphasis on melee combat, including a downward attack similar to that employed in NES games like Duck Tales and Zelda II: The Adventure of Link. Set in a fantasy world of swords and sorcery, the game pokes fun at fantasy cliches and offers the player a world that is charming, silly and humorous. Visually and audio-wise, Shovel Knight automatically recalls NES games, but it offers a more diverse range of colors and more impressive visual segments than would have been possible on the NES. Perhaps most importantly, Shovel Knight emphasizes the same level of precision and focus in gameplay that NES games are notorious for, while also providing a checkpoint and saving system that is far more forgiving to offset player frustration.
While Shovel Knight is perhaps not startingly original, it deftly combines and refines what was great in NES games, while avoiding all of their flaws. The result is a true masterpiece, a game that feels like it should stand among other classics of the NES library, like Super Mario Bros. 3 or Mega Man 2. Anyone longing for a return to this type of aesthetic or gameplay style will find Shovel Knight a wonder to behold. But Shovel Knight is not just a nostaligia-driven experience. This game will satisfy anyone with a thirst for demanding sidescrolling platforming and combat, and will delight with it's diverse environments and sophisticated boss encounters. Highly recommended.

As someone who is a longtime Resident Evil fan, I have to say this. It’s definitely nothing like the previous games were. In fact, if you changed the name, and the characters, you would be forgiven to feel as if this was a new franchise. Doesn't mean it isn't a good game though. This game is based on Resident Evil 4 gameplay, but with an added co-op character to play as. I have to say that though this isn't the Resident Evil I know (Well...maybe outside the campy writing), I definitely had a blast playing the game with my brother. The final boss must also must be seen to believe. Definitely one of the best boss fights I've seen in a while.
This was one of the first games I tried out on my new PC, and I have to say, 1440P makes this game truly shine, especially when fighting the Uroboros monsters. The port of the game was also exceptional. I didn’t notice any FPS drops during gameplay, and usually I’m a stickler for that sort of thing. I used a Dualshock 4 controller via DS4Windows, and everything went off without a hitch. The added No Mercy Mercenary campaign also definitely took advantage of my powerful PC.
If I had to find some flaws, I would have to say it could use a little more length. I completed the game around the 12 hour mark, which is definitely a step down from Resident Evil 4’s length. I would also say it doesn’t feel as repayable as Resident Evil 4, which I probably replayed over and over, even when I had just completed it. Did I mention how much I like Resident Evil 4?
Actually, in fact, Resident Evil 5 seems more like a rehash of Resident Evil 4, at least in terms of enemies. You got your Spanish villager zombies just turned Black, your Chainsaw maniac now African, and the guerilla esque enemies also make a return from the later parts of Resident Evil 4. There are new enemies (Sort of), like the Lickers, and Reapers, which are definitely interesting enemies. The Uroboros bosses were also very unique to the game, and were a welcome touch.
Another complaint, inventory system can really screw you over sometimes. Apparently, a grenade or egg takes up exactly as much place as a Rocket Launcher. I’m not trying to apply realism to something like Resident Evil, but it definitely should have had something like Resident Evil 4’s inventory system or at least a way to increase your inventory size. Not too much of a problem though, since this was present in the other games.
All in all, I enjoyed this game, and wants I get my hands on the new DLC, I’ll be sure to give it a replay.

I've been playing FPS since Wolfenstein 3D...yes the original.  I'm old.  That said, when I beat FEAR 2 on my CPU while on a "business trip" I was looking for an online FPS to fill my time.  I tried CS and a few other Free To Play games.  I even tried TI and decided at first that I didn't care for it.  However, I realized that TI offered the ability to advance through earning levels and GP to purchase better equipment.  I began to play it more and more.  Once I picked up a few guns early on for cash, I improved a bit.  Then a bit more.  Then I earned enough GP in game to buy all the guns permanent.
My advice for new players.  If you like the game, drop $14 or so on it (1/3 of the cost of a game like CoD) and get a solid starter pack.  Then use your GP to buy all the rest of the guns.  Don't forget to outfit yourself with gloves, shoes and other gear to start too (much of which is in starter packs).  It's NOT a pay to win game, but paying a bit up front helps you get a better start.
I love TI.  It's the only game I play regularly any more.  It's a growing entity with so much to offer.  The community is pretty cool.  The developers are very involved.  It's just a ton of fun.

Retro-stylizied action platformer where you play as a blue knight called Shovel Knight. The point of the game is to rescue your friend, Shield Knight, from the evil Enchantress and her Order of No Quarter. This game has a lotta references to other media, but not in a way that detracts from the atmosphere like Borderlands 2. The dialogue is well written and a kind of silly-funny. The bard has a little joke for each page you give them. Townsfolk say a select phrase from a list, some of them funny, others helpful hints on how to get around town and where to go.
Each member of the Order of No Quarter has a level dedicated to them that fits their theme. It's kinda like Mega Man; a knight that uses ice has an ice level with slippery platforms, a flying knight has a level on an airship that uses wind in different ways to help you move around. The game never really feels cheap, when it introduces a new mechanic or enemy it gives you ample time and space to review the surroundings and assess what's going on. When you die, it tends to be your fault. It's similar to Dark Souls in that you have to put some thought into when to attack and how you'll attack, since your attack animation is just long enough to expose yourself to an attack.
There are (at least as far as I've gotten in the game as of writing this) two towns you can visit to get upgrades and items. Here's where the personality of the game has a chance to shine, since the townsfolk are varied and interesting. There's kids in little ninja outfits that run around, there's old goat men with canes dressed like a LoZ2 villager, there's horsemen wearing fancy hats. The world feels varied and more mystical when you're buying meal tickets from a goat that continuously eats pages from a book they are carrying.
Speaking of which, the upgrade system is a bit odd. For health, you buy meal tickets from a villager in the town, then jump on a platform and hand the ticket to a chef, who prepares you food (which is a 10 or so second long animation) that increases your health. But to upgrade your magic, you just have to go a little bit to the right and talk to a sorcerer. This extra step that's added for the health upgrades could be because the meal tickets are limited in number, and if you wish to upgrade your health even further beyond what the meal tickets can give you, you have to get better at the actual levels of the game. This is a great way to encourage players to practice and hone their skills to prepare them for the later levels of the game, while at the same time rewarding players for doing well and completeing small challenges that give helpful rewards.
After you beat a level, Shovel Knight rests for the night by a campfire, and you have a chance of entering one of his dreams. The dreams are typically about Shield Knight falling as you control Shovel Knight, who has to survive the countless enemies that show up and catch her. A nice way to show his close connection to Shield Knight through gameplay since you, the player, are just as concerned as Shovel is about her well-being in the dream, since it rewards you with some gold. You can also get some money by putting out the fire after you wake up, a nice touch to add more character to Shovel Knight, a man so chivalrous and kind he wouldn't dare start a forest fire.
All in all this game is brilliant. From soundtrack to gameplay to design, this game really shines. If you pass this game up for any reason other than you get incredibly ill whenever you play games centered around knights, then you are missing out on an indie gem. Probably one of my favorite games I've played all year. Buy it, whether it's on sale or not.

Yacht Club has done something amazing here. They've actually managed to capture the soul of what made classic NES platformers work. Literally thousands of others have tried and failed, but Yacht Club figured it out. They split the atom here.
So how do you give feedback to a minor masterpiece? Do you tell Da Vinci to put something behind the Mona Lisa? Do you ask Homer to tighten up the pacing of The Odyssey? I'll just be honest, if a bit rambly.
I can't tell you what it felt like when I automatically Pogo Caned (edit: Pogo Shoveled) my first enemy. It was automatic, totally out of my control. It just happened, and all my years spent stomping Goombahs and collecting diamonds came rushing back. The sound, the controls, the graphics, the gameplay... You get a tremendous sense of place and time. Shovel Knight is like visiting a theme park celebrating all the high points of 80s and very early 90s game design, but having full control over the ride. You reach for your tropical skittles, you adjust your day-glo painter's cap, you crank up your Vanilla Ice tape. You can't help it, it's automatic.
It could be said that Yacht Club cheated and weren't truly original with their design, cribbing heavily from Super Mario Bros. 3, Mega Man, Ducktales, and Castlevania... but to me such things are unavoidable. It's like complaining how much something sounds like Shakespeare- once the very DNA of a thing (theater, gaming) gets changed by a cultural landmark (Shakespeare, Mario), all works thereon are considered derivative (Ran, Rayman).
In some places the derivation is obvious- Plague Knight's lair (set to the catchy "Halls of Antimony") evokes the neon rainbow effect of Dr. Wily's lair from Mega Man 3. The towns are modeled after Zelda II. The overworld is Mario 3 through and through. Hell, they even got Mega Man composer Manami Matsumae to throw in a few tracks. And maybe it's just me, but  the Troupple King (which is the exact kind of oddball weirdness the Japanese loved to insert) reminded me of Capcom's Little Nemo.
Yet somehow the game is wholly original. Despite appearances, the story is hardly straightforward- you will be rewarded for completing the game and paying attention to the subtle clues regarding Shield Knight's fall. Each level and its boss are uniquely themed and clever, with lots of small details easily overlooked that add to the experience. Polar Knight's stage is especially interesting.
If Yacht Club had dumped this into an NES development cartridge and left it in an attic to be found, we'd make apt comparisons to Nintendo, Capcom, and Konami games of the same era, all the while asking ourselves how something of this quality could possibly have gone unknown for so long.
While I have come to praise Shovel Knight, I must still partially bury it- there are some problems, most of which are a side effect of so faithfully recreating vintage game experiences.
The game suffers in places from Mega Man syndrome. Later levels ramp up the difficulty mostly by increasing the frequency of the "knock-back" gimmick- trying to cross a death pit while under threat of being stunned mid-air and falling to your death. Few enemies pose a challenge past the halfway mark of the game. If you are wise enough to buy the Ichor chalices at the start of the game, you will likely never fail to beat a boss on your first try.
The lack of lives makes you much bolder in your decisions and risky jumps, even with the threat of losing large wads of your hard-earned cash. I never realized how much of a nail-biter getting to a boss on your last life was until I experienced the luxury of unlimited lives and ample checkpoints. It's not a bad decision, but an optional lives system might have been a fun addition.
I wish the game was the size of, say, Mario 3, but that's a tall order from such a small team. Maybe our next outing will be more substantial? I'd love to see where the Order of No Quarter has gone after a few years.
A must-do is to set the relic activation to a button and not the default up+attack. On modern analog joysticks (and D-pads which easily register diagonal movement) you will often find yourself either one degree too far to a side or one degree too close to up, activating a relic at an inopportune time or failing to activate one when you need it. I wish the developers had made the relics a button by default, since the vast majority of gamepads in use today would suffer from the above problem and increase player frustration. I only discovered this option on playthrough two and it reduced my frustration level immensely.
The short version? Shovel knight is good. Really good. Worth the price of admission and then some. With the promise of more free content, you'll find yourself coming back to the game again in the near future. I wish the game was longer not because I felt it lacked content for the price, but because I wanted more of it. Yacht Club has done some amazing work, and they deserve to be compared favorably to the other masters of their craft.

From developer Yacht Club Games comes Shovel Knight, a celebration and revival of the aesthetic and gameplay sensibilities of the NES library of the late 1980s. It's a game strongly reminiscent of the NES Mega Man games, from it's masterfully crafted boss fights to it's charged musical scores, but with a stronger emphasis on melee combat, including a downward attack similar to that employed in NES games like Duck Tales and Zelda II: The Adventure of Link. Set in a fantasy world of swords and sorcery, the game pokes fun at fantasy cliches and offers the player a world that is charming, silly and humorous. Visually and audio-wise, Shovel Knight automatically recalls NES games, but it offers a more diverse range of colors and more impressive visual segments than would have been possible on the NES. Perhaps most importantly, Shovel Knight emphasizes the same level of precision and focus in gameplay that NES games are notorious for, while also providing a checkpoint and saving system that is far more forgiving to offset player frustration.
While Shovel Knight is perhaps not startingly original, it deftly combines and refines what was great in NES games, while avoiding all of their flaws. The result is a true masterpiece, a game that feels like it should stand among other classics of the NES library, like Super Mario Bros. 3 or Mega Man 2. Anyone longing for a return to this type of aesthetic or gameplay style will find Shovel Knight a wonder to behold. But Shovel Knight is not just a nostaligia-driven experience. This game will satisfy anyone with a thirst for demanding sidescrolling platforming and combat, and will delight with it's diverse environments and sophisticated boss encounters. Highly recommended.

So, here is the successor to Counter-Strike: Global Offensive from the developers of the CS series themselves. In short, I don't think so and here's why:
- the quality of the game feels a bit underwhelming like it was given a low budget to work with ranging from animation, sound, voice acting, and graphics (don't really mind the graphics that much)
- controls feel a little bit clunky, but I usually get used to games with clunky controls for some random reason (unless it's at the point where the game is considered to be unplayable)
- in addition to clunky controls, the recoil of the guns are pretty strong to the point where it gives me a headache when I hold down the trigger of an assault rifle
So, those are the main reasons why it feels like a Half-Life 2 mod to me, but here is why I think the game is still fun regardless of how bad it is:
- the stupidity: what I mean is that on how bad it feels, especially the voices coming out of their mouths is pretty funny for me if not annoying for most people
- the VIP Escort mode: arguably the best game mode in the game because of how ridiculous the driving is
- they did add in a couple of mechanics like leaning and combat rolling for your pleasure, even though I forget it exists for some odd reason
All I can say now is that this game is not the true successor to CS: GO, but it's still fun regardless of the negativity people say.

Original review: "I wish I could recommend this game, but unfortunately the Devs have neglected the most important part of it: Anti-cheat.
In a pay to win game like this, you can't allow hacking or cheating of any type. Omega has consistently failed to address this issue. For years. I love this game, but I wouldn't recommend it to any new players."
Addendum:
I wrote this review late at night when I was crabby after running into a couple speed "hacks" (ping discrepency?) and I failed to mention any of the things that I love about this game. Thank you for Bilbur and Plat for checking me on that.
I'm leaving the original review, partly to explain and partly to encourage me not to write a review like this again.
I don't have evidence for my complaint about cheating, just my game-play experience. It's unfair of me to call out Omega for this one issue when he has been working to improve the game and release content since I first started playing. There are a few issues (such as the water lag in Office and the positioning of hit boxes) that have persisted through several updates. It seems to me that Omega and Fix Games have prioritized new content over these other issues. I would say that the new content improves the game and adds strategic depth, but these issues still need to be addressed.
I DO love this game and play a lot, and I do not plan to stop playing it or to stop supporting the game financially.
I want VAC because I think the community suffers without it. Because I'm an established player with gear and the experience to use it, I can usually hold my own against any opponent, even one using injectors or other exploits. It's hard enough to play against experienced players as a newb without adding the frustration of dealing with cheaters and trolls/griefers.
If you do put the time and effort in, this game is very rewarding. I love the community and the game is just FUN once you learn it. If you are not willing to learn to play and meet the other players, don't bother.

Every once in a great while, a game will come along that redefines the genre.
Since the first game was invented in the depths of history (Q*BERT), games have been defined by gameplay, by their mechanics, by how the player interacts with the medium.
Loading Screen Simulator turns all of that on its head. By removing the elements of play that normally "engage" or "entertain" a player, the creator distills down the very essence of a game into its most pure form: not really doing much.
Clearly, we are on the precipice of an entirely new genre: meta-idling. Before, someone who wanted this experience would have to leave the comfort of their computer screen to do things like watch paint dry, or grass grow. Now, though, for the first time we can have the same experience in a virtual environment.
As the experience is impossible to define, the only appropriate score for this game is 0/0. Transcendent.

I don't know much about fishing or fishing simulators, but I think this game captures it best. Variety of lures, hooks, rods, and fish probably make for an in-depth experience for someone who knows what they're doing. Perfect for those rainy days or when you're too sick to go out for real fishing. Maybe put on a podcast or some chill tunes while you play. Read a book perhaps. I don't see the appeal of playing the game on its own, but it is fairly relaxing,
A couple things I feel the game is lacking in are location variety and fish occurences. Maybe I'm playing wrong or maybe its meant to simulate the doing nothing aspect of fishing, but I find it a bit annoying when I'm sat for five minutes with no bites. Though I think that's more personal preference, as again, I'm not the person to go to for fishing related things. I did like the inclusion of the real time log of how other players are doing.
Compared to other games I don't think there's much to it, though its aimed at a fairly specific niche. As a simulator though, it seems to be really well made, and for free I can absolutely recommend it if you were already interested.

Buyers Beware - This game has long been on life support (I'd consider it to be effectively abandoned.) The creators seem unwilling to invest what it takes to actually make this game succeed long term, and the developer that was hired to continue the project has just quit:
As someone who liked the game and very much wanted to see it continue to expand, I am very, very disappointed with how this has turned out.  I've been watching things go sour for quite a while now, and in light of these events I think I have reserved judgement for long enough.  Perhaps even too long.
The developers released a good product, and sold hundreds of thousands of copies.  They actually grabbed the golden ring of indie game development.  Then they took that golden ring and chucked it in the swamp.
It was rather obvious months ago that they were not serious about continuing to support the product that was released, especially as they repeatedly failed to deliver on expectations and sales declined.
I hope they enjoy their money, it's obvious now that it is not going back into Towns development as was implied when I bought the game on Steam Early Access. I also hope they didn't spend it all, because I will never buy another game from these jokers after watching them get handed bags of cash during Steam Early Access only to have them fail to reinvest those funds to improve the product.
I'm usually not this harsh, but watching developers squander success like this really pushes my buttons.
I think it is time for me to abandon Towns, too.

Ah Shovel Knight, what a wonderful tale of Shovelry, Loot and many, many, pointless and stupid deaths. But don’t worry, it’s not the ‘stupid’ as in “This game is buggy and I died, stupid” but the “I may or may not have mental issues to not jump this stupid gap, stupid.” I’ll tell you this beforehand, I’m not exactly the master side-scroller, so for me, this was a test of my patience, but in a good way!
Shovel Knight plays perfectly with easy to learn controls and gameplay that really makes you think you somehow went back in time and stole it out of a NES. You don’t just get that feeling mechanically though, you also get that sort of cheesiness thematically as well. Whereas most games aim for some sort of metaphysical meaning or blow your mind with a cinematic storyline, Shovel Knight follows a simply formula that everyone can understand and get behind. The Enchantress wants to take over the world, she has a group of evil knights called the Order of No Quarter, you’ve gotta stop them. Simple right?
Gameplay wise, the controls are simple and can be easily ported to some NES controller if you’re a techno-wizard. This sort of game design also aids in the fact that the game is rather linear and simple, with small level specific quirks to make things interesting. There was no point where I blamed the game for me not making a jump or dying from a boss, but rather I blamed myself for being incompetent. This sort of feeling is perfect for a game like this because you want to feel like your mastering the game and battling the monsters, rather than battling the game itself for being so buggy.
On the design field, Yacht Club has done a fantastic job to emulate that classic sidescroller feeling. Each of the levels are strung together by a Super Mario World-esque overworld where you need to beat certain levels in order to progress, while the levels themselves are gorgeous and intriguing with certain themes to match their corresponding bosses. NPC’s are a bit dull, with only a few being memorable, but in a game like this it doesn’t matter as much. Monsters stick in my mind a bit more though because of some of their interesting designs, while some of them make me feel a bit mean for beating up something so cute. One aspect I absolutely loved though were the designs for both the
Bosses and the Mini Bosses. Each one felt unique and special and their designs added to that. My favorites in no particular order are Plague Knight, Specter Knight and Reize. I would hope that if they were to do a sequel, that they would expand on their storylines or at least give them a bigger appearance.
Individual level design was a bit lacking though. It was simply Mario-esque with the same ‘go right’ formula and of course in the end you’d have to defeat the corresponding boss. There were would some small hidden spots to get more treasure, but you would still have to travel the main path to get to the ending. Now I understand that not many 16 bit games had branching paths, or detours, but next time I hope they would add more variety to each level rather than just making it too linear. It’s a small gripe, but one I had to make nonetheless.
Another area I felt lacking was in the customization aspect of the game. There are only a handful of armors and literally only three moves you can buy. Not only that, but I feel like there are maybe one or two armors that are actually useful while the others just can’t compete. Now that’s not to say they should convolute the sequel with some sort of skill tree or anything, but I feel if you’re gonna have a Weaponsmith in the game, have more than three upgrades.
The in-game items also felt a bit on the useless side as well, with possibly only one item that could be used the entire game to win. The Phase Locket item, literally makes you invulnerable for a few seconds, and even though you can still die by falling off the platforms, it makes bosses and defeating monsters oh so easy. Hell, if I put my mind to it, I could probably make it through the entire game, only using that one item and that’s saying something.
Now despite this I still say the game is worth your money. Don’t let my ramblings of OP items and little customization get to you if you’re a big 16-bit side-scroller fan, because this is the game for you. All in all, Shovel Knight is a wonderful game that harkens back to a simpler era where kids could plop down in front of their TV and play to their hearts content without people yelling in their ears for KSing, high ping, being a noob etc etc. And if that doesn’t help, then just wait, Yacht Club are hard at work coming up with updates to the game like the much anticpated mode where you can play as some of the bosses! That should be loads of fun!

I feel this FTP Fishing Simulator has alot going for it, but most of all I think it's fun to play and the microtransactions don't interfere with my enjoyment of the game. As I understand it everything in the game you can unlock without spending real money which I like. The only thing you really need to invest is time at this point.
As far as Fishing Simulators go there isn't much to choose from but I feel this is one of the best. You can buy gear from a very imaginative "online store front" type menu which I got a big kick out of. It's easy to load an area get your rod out and fish. You have to experiment to learn all the different fishes habits, where they like to go, what they eat, what depth to fish at, weather, and time of day. The descriptions of the various baits, rods, lines, and hooks give you clues as to what fish they will catch.
Now the bad, there's a risk of running out of money farely early if you make some bad trips or don't bring the correct bait/rod, OR forget to buy the correct liscence. If you don't have the correct liscence for your target species and you catch a trophie you're forced to throw it back or face a hefty fine. You also need to make sure your stringer or keep net has the capacity to hold a large fish. If you run out of cash you have to either buy more with real money or stop playing and wait till the next real life day where the game gives you some in game cash. It's not a big deal if you know what you're doing and don't make some bad purchases, I however didn't realize this.
Overall I'm enjoying the game, the visuals are good and I hope they add more content as time goes on. A 2 player coop where you can actually fish next to your friends on a trip would be great.

This fan mod is so well crafted, it might as well be official. The story is excellent, managing to be entirely new while still capturing the feel of the Portal universe. The puzzles are more difficult that Portal 2's puzzles in a good way. The developers have come up with some creative ways to abuse the game mechanics that result in some very interesting challenges. The environments are amazing, with incredibly detailed new areas and many custom models that fit perfectly into the Portal world at Valve quality levels. The music is well made and contains several remixes of familiar tracks. Finally, the voice acting, which is often the weak point of many mods, was very well done here. I will admit that I didn't feel that the voice of Virgil fit perfectly in the world, but the voice actor did a great job regardless. The lines didn't feel cheesy or forced. I really hope to see more work from this studio in the future.
Overall, if you like Portal, try this game out.

This is hands-down the best fan-game I've ever played.
they recently added an additional "story mode" route with much easier versions of the original puzzles, so you don't even have to worry about the difficulty anymore if you're not up to the challenge. Either way, I'd say there's about as much content in here as in the original portal.
The voice acting is above average for what you'd expect out of a mod, and they certainly do a pretty good cave johnson impersonation. The original characters feel like they fit in well with the tone and writing style of the original game, and I was impressed at how much they drew from cut characters and concept art when crafting their setting, instead of trying to make up something completely original that might not have meshed with the portal universe so well.
What I liked most of all, however, was the dedication to detail and the amount of easter eggs and secrets hidden throughout the levels. And not just "hidden" things that are super obviously pointed out because the designers don't want you to miss their hard work, these are things that you genuinely might not find and really feel rewarding when you do. I personally love getting achievements for stupid little things like dying in ridiculous ways or finding certain puzzle exploits, so I'm thrilled that there's so many of those in this game.
Overall, 8/10 as a game, but 2056/10 as a free mod.

The game itself seems just like a standard multiplayer FPS. You get a gun wich you then run around and shoot people in the head with and eventually get shot in the head yourself. This review is a "compare & contrast" with another popular fishing title released around the same time, Dovetail Games' Euro Fishing. I like both and think they're both quality titles, but they do different things well and will satisfy different tastes. This review is meant to help you decide which one you might prefer. I wrote a similar review for Euro Fishing, and will update both when Fishing Planet comes out of early access.

Fishing Planet's FTP model is described on the wiki as "free to win", and while that sounds contrived it really is pretty accurate. Fishing Planet is very generous with what is available to non-paying players, and the devs have stated that they want people to pay to support the game, not because they were forced to in order to progress. Be forewarned that the mid-game can get grindy, but overall I think that Fishing Planet is living up to its FTP intentions.

Even in early access, Fishing Planet has a great variety of angling styles, and it even recognizes different lure presentation techniques within spin fishing. The devs have promised even more styles in the future (including boat and kayak fishing), but Fishing Planet is already a fairly comprehensive US fishing game, with potential to be even greater.

Fishing Planet has locations all over the US, and will include different water types in each (rivers, lakes, marshes, reservoirs etc). The devs have said that an eventual goal is to have locations outside the USA as well.

Panfish. Crappie. Catfish. Bass. Pike. Trout. Salmon. Gar. Lots of different kinds of fish, and more might be on the way. Such a diverse group of target fish requires lots of different angling methods, giving Fishing Planet a ton of longevity. This variety of angling methods, locations and fish is Fishing Planet's greatest strength against the rather one-dimensional Euro Fishing.

The water in Fishing Planet is beautiful, which means a lot when you'll spend most of your time in-game staring at it. Personally I love how well it reflects the surrounding environment, and reacts to your line. This is another area where one of FP's strengths aligns against a particular weakness of DTG's Euro Fishing, which struggles a bit with its water.

Geeking out over gear is part of the fun of the hobby, and Fishing Planet really delivers with a large store of real-world fishing toys. One nice nod to immersion is that while you're out fishing, the local shops will have different gear on hand.

Although you can fish all over the US in different kinds of water, each area only gives you a few cramped spots to fish from. There is little room for the exploration found in DTG's Euro Fishing, and each location does feel more like a videogame set piece than a real place. It doesn't take long for each area to feel a little stale.

Click LMB to fill the power bar. Easy, but honestly it's a letdown in comparison to the casting in DTG's Euro Fishing. This is where Fishing Planet falls short against a strength of its European counterpart.

Fishing Planet is in early access, so hopefully the audio will see some TLC before release. However, at this point it's noticeably incomplete, and hampers the immersive aspects of FP's strong points.

Currently you just reel the fish in, and there is no mechanic for netting or handling them. One could argue this is better than the pretty rough netting mechanic of Euro Fishing, but hopefully something is added at release.

Fishing Planet's presentation of your catch is disappointing. Your character just hangs them in front of your screen by your line, and they flop around until you click through the stats box. DTG's photo-op finish to each catch does a great job of showing off the fish, and helps give them a sense of personality. FP's fish (even the unique ones) end up feeling a bit cookie-cutter and bland.

As a game that bills itself as an MMO, I really expected more than this. The devs have more multiplayer features on the way, but at the moment Fishing Planet is basically a single-player game with a chatroom. DTG's Euro Fishing actually lets you fish with other players in the same location.

Fishing Planet's tutorials are cursory at best, nothing more than a few click-through menus. Hopefully a more comprehensive tutorial is added at launch. However, the wiki is, despite being a work-in-progress, quite good.

This is a unique one. I am NOT a PvP guy, but I can't get enough of Siege, and I'm hardly the best player.
The intelligence and destruction aspects of the game are unique and unmatched, the fast-paced shooting and objective modes... this game really stands out because of how ridiculously unique it is. There ARE a number of balance and server issues, and the learning curve is a plateau, but if you stick with the game enough to get the hang of it, find the operators you like, and start working with teammates, you'll find nothing like it, and you'll keep coming back for more and more.
Also worth noting is that this game has a MARVELOUSLY non-greedy asset system. The only things that require cash money [R6 Credits] are certain unique skins and appearances. Everything else, including a large portion of the skins, can be purchased with the earned in-game currency [Renown].
All in all, if you're interested in fast-paced quick kill shooters, and willing to work with a team, you'll find nothing else on the market that plays even remotely like this experience.

Be forewarned that the mid-game can get grindy, but overall I think that Fishing Planet is living up to its FTP intentions.

Even in early access, Fishing Planet has a great variety of angling styles, and it even recognizes different lure presentation techniques within spin fishing. The devs have promised even more styles in the future (including boat and kayak fishing), but Fishing Planet is already a fairly comprehensive US fishing game, with potential to be even greater.

Fishing Planet has locations all over the US, and will include different water types in each (rivers, lakes, marshes, reservoirs etc). The devs have said that an eventual goal is to have locations outside the USA as well.

Panfish. Crappie. Catfish. Bass. Pike. Trout. Salmon. Gar. Lots of different kinds of fish, and more might be on the way. Such a diverse group of target fish requires lots of different angling methods, giving Fishing Planet a ton of longevity. This variety of angling methods, locations and fish is Fishing Planet's greatest strength against the rather one-dimensional Euro Fishing.

The water in Fishing Planet is beautiful, which means a lot when you'll spend most of your time in-game staring at it. Personally I love how well it reflects the surrounding environment, and reacts to your line. This is another area where one of FP's strengths aligns against a particular weakness of DTG's Euro Fishing, which struggles a bit with its water.

Geeking out over gear is part of the fun of the hobby, and Fishing Planet really delivers with a large store of real-world fishing toys. One nice nod to immersion is that while you're out fishing, the local shops will have different gear on hand.

Although you can fish all over the US in different kinds of water, each area only gives you a few cramped spots to fish from. There is little room for the exploration found in DTG's Euro Fishing, and each location does feel more like a videogame set piece than a real place. It doesn't take long for each area to feel a little stale.

Click LMB to fill the power bar. Easy, but honestly it's a letdown in comparison to the casting in DTG's Euro Fishing. This is where Fishing Planet falls short against a strength of its European counterpart.

Fishing Planet is in early access, so hopefully the audio will see some TLC before release. However, at this point it's noticeably incomplete, and hampers the immersive aspects of FP's strong points.

Currently you just reel the fish in, and there is no mechanic for netting or handling them. One could argue this is better than the pretty rough netting mechanic of Euro Fishing, but hopefully something is added at release.

Fishing Planet's presentation of your catch is disappointing. Your character just hangs them in front of your screen by your line, and they flop around until you click through the stats box. DTG's photo-op finish to each catch does a great job of showing off the fish, and helps give them a sense of personality. FP's fish (even the unique ones) end up feeling a bit cookie-cutter and bland.

As a game that bills itself as an MMO, I really expected more than this. The devs have more multiplayer features on the way, but at the moment Fishing Planet is basically a single-player game with a chatroom. DTG's Euro Fishing actually lets you fish with other players in the same location.

Fishing Planet's tutorials are cursory at best, nothing more than a few click-through menus. Hopefully a more comprehensive tutorial is added at launch. However, the wiki is, despite being a work-in-progress, quite good.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege is a first-person multiplayer shooter that borrows from Counter Strike and hero shooters, mixing it together into a tactical, objective-based shootout where movement is slow and combat is fast. The game features asymmetrical gameplay where the teams are not always balanced in their abilities. Heavy emphasis is put on procedural environmental destruction allowing players to break certain structures by planting explosives, or shooting walls to make bullet holes or even larger ones to climb through.

+ Over 30 operators to choose from, based on real life counter terrorism units, each with their own unique weapons and gadgets.
+ No match will be the same thanks to the diverse cast of characters which is still getting expanded by Ubisoft, even 1.5 years after the game’s release.
+ Precise procedural destruction of most of the games floors and walls resulting in a tactical shooter like no other; simply running and gunning will only get you so far
+ Customization options for guns which also impact the way they operate. From a simple silencer to four different sights and weapon grips or fore grips, everything will change weapon behavior.
+ Pleasing graphics that look great and don’t require a monster PC to push 60 FPS or higher.
+ A fair use of micro-transactions where you can only buy skins and operators with real money but you can also unlock them through in-game currency.
+ You just can’t buy anything that gives you an advantage over other players.
+ Season pass owners get 1 week early access to new operators and all new operators in that year for free along with other skins and small benefits.
+ Maps are free for everyone, it doesn’t matter if you bought the season pass or not, everyone can play together.
+ Incredible sound engine that lets you hear precise enemy movement, like them walking into glass on the floor and other surfaces, or the exact direction where the steps are coming from. This is making good use of 5.1 surround sound or just good stereo headphones.
+ Music is fitting the game’s tone very well you just don’t hear much of it since it is only playing at the beginning and at the end of rounds which in turn is making you not really care for it all.
- Lag compensation, netcode and tickrate is still broken and you sometimes die out of nowhere while your enemy could clearly see you. (This is being worked on and hopefully fixed in the near future)
- Multiplayer against other players or against AI are the only two modes, there is no campaign which I think is a missed opportunity.
- Steep learning curve that can be very frustrating for beginners since regular players of the game will know exactly what walls can be shot through, what angles work best and how to quickly peek corners to make the best use of the sometimes broken netcode.
- Unlocking operators with in-game currency can take a long time based on your willingness to spend time with the game and how good you are. Just stay away from the starter edition or the game will be even more grindy since each base operators cost much much more than they normally would and you will be unable to upgrade to the standard edition once you bought the starter.

While this iteration of the series is vastly different than it’s predecessors, I think it’s a solid addition to the series. Rainbow Six Siege is very unique in what it does and we have yet to see a game like it. I recommend it to fans of SWAT 4, Insurgency, and generally anyone who enjoys or is interested in tactical first person games where you have to be cautious of your surroundings, be aware of your enemies abilities, and a strong emphasis on teamwork.

Shovel Knight is incredibly well designed.
At first inspection, it may appear to be just a derivative 8-bit platformer that just borrows elements from Ducktales and Megaman, but not only does it share its ancestors' best traits, it also throws in a lot of its own gameplay mechanics that makes for an interesting and well fleshed out experience.
There are no lives in this game, so you can infinitely respawn at checkpoints. Where Shovel Knight diverges from the drivel of most game's checkpoints systems is that it has an attached risk-reward system. You can bust the checkpoints and receive more gold, but when you die, you lose gold and have to return to that part of the stage to collect it... and if you busted the checkpoint, returning to that part of the level just becomes much more difficult. It's a means to the same ends as the traditional lives/game over system, but comes with the benefits of being more dynamic and player-controlled, and hence makes replaying stages more interesting.
The game is quick to get you right in on the action, but it also successfully manages to get the player to care about the story. You can talk to characters, there's an intro cutscene, and several quips of dialogues between Shovel Knight and the boss characters (all of which can be skipped), but what really sets Shovel Knight's story apart is how it melds it into the gameplay, with my favorite design trick being the dream sequence. After the first level, Shovel Knight dreams that Shield Knight is falling, and the player is told to catch her. There is no punishment for failing this. You can just let her fall, wake up and go the next level. But the player WANTS to catch her, he WANTS to succeed in this dream. And when you get out of your dream, you have to wake up yourself, then you can choose how to exit the cutscene. This cutscene is repeated and expanded upon into bonus minigames ("Save her from the monsters!") and the whole thing is completely optional.
This is damn good story design. Giving the player these moments where they are given direct control over story events creates an emotional attachment to the characters. It establishes a motivating drive for the player which intrinsically ties gameplay to story. And it's all designed in a way that is nonobstructive to gameplay, but rather benefits it by creating clear motivations and expectations for the player. Ever seen Egoraptor's rants on Ocarina of Time in his Sequelitis episode? This is the exact opposite of that. The plot is clear cut. There's no convoluted JRPG story arc ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It's just a gameplay-driven story, where the story serves the gameplay instead of the other way around -- a design type I would like to see a lot more of.
The lore is quite well-fleshed out and enjoyable to explore, but the game's other artistic aspects do not falter behind. The pixel art in this game is gorgeous, enemies are charismatic, well-animated, and diverse in theme and design, and the music... well, the music is created by Jake Kaufman; I think that speaks for itself.
The game is kinda short but has a lot of replay value. All of the items are unique and fun to use, New Game+ and the achievements (which, by the way, actually all feel really fun and skillful to pursue, unlike a lot of other games' achievement systems) offer lots of ways to amp up the difficulty and explore different aspects of the gameplay, and the stages themselves are well laid out and filled to the brim with secrets.
I will nitpick on what I think are some of the game's design flaws though:
* There is a disparity in the difficulty of platforming compared to the difficulty of combat. Shovel Knight doesn't throw any cheap shots at you, but it does punish you with instant death whenever you miss your jump on certain areas. This is fine of course, games as old as Super Mario Bros. do this; but you can take up to twenty hits from the enemies themselves, and the stages are full of instant health refill items. I'm personally far less afraid of the bosses than I am of certain platforming segments, and it's of no fault of either element; it's just how the game's punishment system works. If it were me, I would have toned down the player's health a little bit, but I also would have integrated some sort of Dynamite Headdy-style or Zelda-style death pit system, where the player doesn't instantly die and has a chance to recover after falling.
* Phase Locket is easy mode. Doesn't seem like a problem in a non-competitive non-multiplayer game, but it kind of is because it detracts from the player's incentive to experiment with other items. I have to deliberately avoid this item in order to feel like I'm playing the game correctly. This is something I can forgive if the item took a lot of skill to overpower the rest of the selection, but it's pretty disappointing when you realize its power on your first or second playthrough.
* This is kind of personal preference more than anything, but I kinda do like the old lives system better at times. Finite retries creates a tension where the risk of having to start all over heavily incentivizes the player to rethink his plan of action.... Losing money works to the same end while also having a more dynamic checkpoint system attached to it, but because it's just money, it's not always as effective of a motivation as the traditional lives system was.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who is interested in platformers, but I'd also recommend this to anyone who's not interested in platformers and just wants a jump-start into the genre. It's easy to get into, has a lot of gameplay depth, and is very immersive for its genre. I can think of very few platformers that would rank as high as this in terms of gameplay quality. At $15, it is easily worth your money; I already have this game for both the WiiU and PC, and I don't regret either purchase.

Shovel Knight is incredibly well designed.
At first inspection, it may appear to be just a derivative 8-bit platformer that just borrows elements from Ducktales and Megaman, but not only does it share its ancestors' best traits, it also throws in a lot of its own gameplay mechanics that makes for an interesting and well fleshed out experience.
There are no lives in this game, so you can infinitely respawn at checkpoints. Where Shovel Knight diverges from the drivel of most game's checkpoints systems is that it has an attached risk-reward system. You can bust the checkpoints and receive more gold, but when you die, you lose gold and have to return to that part of the stage to collect it... and if you busted the checkpoint, returning to that part of the level just becomes much more difficult. It's a means to the same ends as the traditional lives/game over system, but comes with the benefits of being more dynamic and player-controlled, and hence makes replaying stages more interesting.
The game is quick to get you right in on the action, but it also successfully manages to get the player to care about the story. You can talk to characters, there's an intro cutscene, and several quips of dialogues between Shovel Knight and the boss characters (all of which can be skipped), but what really sets Shovel Knight's story apart is how it melds it into the gameplay, with my favorite design trick being the dream sequence. After the first level, Shovel Knight dreams that Shield Knight is falling, and the player is told to catch her. There is no punishment for failing this. You can just let her fall, wake up and go the next level. But the player WANTS to catch her, he WANTS to succeed in this dream. And when you get out of your dream, you have to wake up yourself, then you can choose how to exit the cutscene. This cutscene is repeated and expanded upon into bonus minigames ("Save her from the monsters!") and the whole thing is completely optional.
This is damn good story design. Giving the player these moments where they are given direct control over story events creates an emotional attachment to the characters. It establishes a motivating drive for the player which intrinsically ties gameplay to story. And it's all designed in a way that is nonobstructive to gameplay, but rather benefits it by creating clear motivations and expectations for the player. Ever seen Egoraptor's rants on Ocarina of Time in his Sequelitis episode? This is the exact opposite of that. The plot is clear cut. There's no convoluted JRPG story arc ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. It's just a gameplay-driven story, where the story serves the gameplay instead of the other way around -- a design type I would like to see a lot more of.
The lore is quite well-fleshed out and enjoyable to explore, but the game's other artistic aspects do not falter behind. The pixel art in this game is gorgeous, enemies are charismatic, well-animated, and diverse in theme and design, and the music... well, the music is created by Jake Kaufman; I think that speaks for itself.
The game is kinda short but has a lot of replay value. All of the items are unique and fun to use, New Game+ and the achievements (which, by the way, actually all feel really fun and skillful to pursue, unlike a lot of other games' achievement systems) offer lots of ways to amp up the difficulty and explore different aspects of the gameplay, and the stages themselves are well laid out and filled to the brim with secrets.
I will nitpick on what I think are some of the game's design flaws though:
* There is a disparity in the difficulty of platforming compared to the difficulty of combat. Shovel Knight doesn't throw any cheap shots at you, but it does punish you with instant death whenever you miss your jump on certain areas. This is fine of course, games as old as Super Mario Bros. do this; but you can take up to twenty hits from the enemies themselves, and the stages are full of instant health refill items. I'm personally far less afraid of the bosses than I am of certain platforming segments, and it's of no fault of either element; it's just how the game's punishment system works. If it were me, I would have toned down the player's health a little bit, but I also would have integrated some sort of Dynamite Headdy-style or Zelda-style death pit system, where the player doesn't instantly die and has a chance to recover after falling.
* Phase Locket is easy mode. Doesn't seem like a problem in a non-competitive non-multiplayer game, but it kind of is because it detracts from the player's incentive to experiment with other items. I have to deliberately avoid this item in order to feel like I'm playing the game correctly. This is something I can forgive if the item took a lot of skill to overpower the rest of the selection, but it's pretty disappointing when you realize its power on your first or second playthrough.
* This is kind of personal preference more than anything, but I kinda do like the old lives system better at times. Finite retries creates a tension where the risk of having to start all over heavily incentivizes the player to rethink his plan of action.... Losing money works to the same end while also having a more dynamic checkpoint system attached to it, but because it's just money, it's not always as effective of a motivation as the traditional lives system was.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who is interested in platformers, but I'd also recommend this to anyone who's not interested in platformers and just wants a jump-start into the genre. It's easy to get into, has a lot of gameplay depth, and is very immersive for its genre. I can think of very few platformers that would rank as high as this in terms of gameplay quality. At $15, it is easily worth your money; I already have this game for both the WiiU and PC, and I don't regret either purchase.

I haven't played a huge amount of Tactical Intervention, but I now have a general picture of what the game is like. I got Tactical Intervention becuase of two reasons. Number One: There was a car pursuit gamemode, like something out of GTA. Number Two: It was Free to play.
Besides the pursuit gamemode, theres also bomb defusal, hostage rescue (both from Counter-Strike) and Deathmatches. Like Counter-Strike (Because the creator took part in making this game) you can't aim down the sights of the guns, except the sniper rifles, and that's where the similarities pretty much end. There are a bunch of "unique mechanics" that are either useful, or weird, such as tactical rolling, wall rappeling, taking a hostage as a shield, leaning, and healing other teamates. These mechanics are generally pretty good, except for the rolling, which is nearly useless except for very specific situations. You can earn gold by playing, which allows for better weapons and unlocks, but to really win the game, you're going to want to spend a fortune on limited-time weapons and unlocks. That is probably the worst aspect of the game. DON'T SPEND A PENNY ON IT.
Now I'm not a graphics snob that needs every game to look like Crysis 3 or else I'll go ballistic, so I don't mind graphics almost at all. But taking a closer look, I notice wonky animations for the playermodels, low resolution textures, and blocky models, but like I said, I don't really mind them, while some other people may.
I think the audio in general for the game is OK, except the laughably bad voice acting. I've especially noticed this when every five seconds my character says "I'm Dyain!"
Overall, the game seems to present itself as mod to counter strike, and should still be thought of that. The game also has many glitches, such as commonly getting stuck in the car's geomerty. I know many people will strongly disagree with me, but I STILL recommend this game, becuase I honestly have fun with the game, and more importantly, It's free to play, so there's no point in NOT giving it a try.
Buy it, Love it, Enjoy it, Beat it, Love it, Beat it, and have fun.(I refuse to make shovel puns)

The first Saints Row game I've played, and all I knew getting into it was that it was "Grand Theft Auto with no idea of being taken seriously." An accurate description.
PROS:
+Driving, gunplay, and fighting mechanics are all pretty solid. Nothing amazing, and nothing as great as GTA V, but still solid.
+Weapons all have a line of customization and upgrading which works pretty well.
+One of the most customizable character creators I've ever seen, and I've seen quite a few.
+An immature (similar to Archer) sense of humor.
+A wide variety of musical selections for radio, from death metal to gangsta rap to classical music to techno.
+Unlike GTA, any car put into the garage is yours (and often customizable). This includes SWAT vans, tanks, and VTOL Gunships.
+You take control of a city by a combination of buying properties, killing rival gang members, and minigames. The more control of the city you have, the more money you make per hour.
+Customizable gang members, from G's with bulletproof vests to women ready to hit the clubs to pink ninjas.
+You can call up your fellow gang members (including the story-based characters) and go on a rampage with them.
+Outstanding soundtrack, with one of/the best Main Menu theme I've ever heard.
+Decent enough storyline with memorable characters.
+BURT REYNOLDS!
+Zombie Island!
+Cooperative campaign and free-roam!
+Survival mode!
CONS:
-Compared to other open-world games (even of its time) Steelwater is small.
-Despite me liking its humor, I have to admit that it is stupid, and not everyone is going to like it.
-Some of the minigames are boring as hell, and I found myself dreading having to do them to get control of islands.
-It's possible to make yourself impossible to kill (unless the vehicle you're in is destroyed). I reached that point and became quickly bored. Be careful not to give yourself full immunity.
-I've heard that people who liked Saints Row 1 and 2 have been hugely disappointed in this game, especially the switch from GTA-ripoff to comedic parody. Be aware that this isn't the Saints Row you played on the PS2, this is a change as big as from Call of Duty 3 to Modern Warfare 1.
I had a blast with Saints Row: The Third, and so have many. It's not for everyone, though, and I don't blame you if you don't like it. The opening missions (up to when you take over a penthouse) are pretty representative of the rest of the game. If you don't like that, stop playing and get a refund. You won't like the rest. If you had a blast with those missions, though, you're in for one helluva ride!

Saints Row: The Third is a 2011 third-person, “open-world” shooter where you play as the Boss (your customized character) who takes on a revenge quest against a rival gang leader who tries to destroy your gang and your reputation in Steelport. Saints Row: The Third is the third title of the Saints Row franchise as this game takes a radical change away from the first two games. The game has plenty of action with massive explosions and shootouts, alongside with humorous jokes and strange acts that might make you cringe (in a good way…or bad). The game has aged and probably “forgotten” by many gamers, but does this game attracts your attention in the present time?
Admittedly, I never played the first two games so I do not know or understand the lore in the franchise. Most importantly, do not take this game seriously. I mean it. Saints Row: The Third has plenty of hilarious moments and does not have a serious crime genre like the Grand Theft Auto franchise. Go naked and shoot at random things or spamming grenades and rockets at objects and rival gang members that would make Michael Bay overly excited. There are a variety of missions in the game, such as driving the vehicle with a tiger in the passenger seat or participate in a game show with Genki the Pink Cat (something like that). Most importantly, the customization for your character, vehicles, and your gang members are astounding with large varieties. With all the good factors listed for single player, co-op mode is, probably, one of the most chaotic and fun experience I ever have. Lastly, the chemistry among your character and your fellow gang members is pretty impressive.
While the game is good, there are some negative attributes that has to be considered. The graphics is pretty mediocre with facial animations looks like melted clay figures. It’s not too distracting, but this should be mentioned since the textures and graphical fidelity is low resolution, even with all settings maximized in modern PC architectures. Some missions can be mundane, even painful for the eyes (specifically on the virtual reality mission in the main campaign). The story is not too bad, but tends to get sidetracked a lot and doesn’t really focus on the main plot (but the plot is good and competent). Probably the most criticized attribute for Saints Row: The Third is the collectables. There are a lot of collectables and some of them are not even worth getting, unless you are achievement hunting. It is a bit “stressful” on doing the challenges and getting the collectables, but this is up to the person’s personal preference.
Regardless on the game’s radical change of direction and “minor” criticisms, the game is fun. I did not have a good, initial impression on the game, but as I play longer, the game is very entertaining, really hilarious, and most importantly, an enjoyable experience. With video games developers and some gamers focusing too much on graphical fidelity (which I initially fell for it when I played this game), the actual gameplay tends to be “downplayed” by some gamers and we forget what fun really is. You can take part of the “tank mission”, where you blow up anything like cars, pedestrians, military vehicles, and all of alike or you can do anything you want (sort of) in this “open-world” game. Saints Row: The Third can be compared to the Just Cause franchise, but funnier and a little less explosive game (if you know what I mean).
The game is usually on sale for a good discount, roughly around -66% to -80% off and I strongly suggest you get the game during the Steam Sale. If you never play the Saints Row franchise before, like me, it is best to get the game and the other titles from the Saints Row Franchise sale (roughly -75% off). The game has my recommendation and probably brings people back on what makes video games more fun than graphics.

So, Shovel Knight.  This game is ment to be a nice throwback to the NES era of gaming.  The fuel for this game is nostalgia, through and though.  Also much like the NES era of gaming, you could have games about, roughly any sort of weird nonsense you can throw together and alot of it would stick because it was origonal.
Shovel Knight plays like alot of your favriote games if you are old enough to have been raised by Nintendo.   You play as the title character, Shovel Kight, who is an honorable knight who weilds a fearsome shovel to vanquish his foes!  Shovel Knight himself is likeable, though his backstory cliche' he really is the honrable type, and trys to talk his way out of a situation before being accosted.
The Level designs are great, unqiue, and each one offers a diffrent experience (Personal favriote and most hated is the graveyard level.), there are two towns, a host of bizzare characters within, and all of the bosses have just about as much personallity as you do.  The other knights are also based on simmiler gimmicks, like Plague Knight, King Knight, Specter Knight, and each boss battle is rather enjoyable.
The game does take a measure of skill, it starts off nice and easy and has a gentle learning curve to never make it frustrating.  There are also plenty of hidden easter eggs and secrets strewn across the levels for you to find, from music notes, to more gems, to strange fish-fruit people.  Shovel Knight himself has a large arsonal of relics to use, each also new and unique with that perfect edge of fun and nothing feels worthless.
So, overall if you crave the olden days and tripple A hasn't been scratching your itch for awesome RPG like settings, or if you permanatly wear your nostalgia goggles I can recomend Shovel Knight to you.

Finally, a game developer who understands how horror actually works.
This is not a "monsters jump out of closets and yell boo" experience, and it's about as far as you can get from the typical "gross-looking monsters that you shoot with lots of big guns" games that somehow get labeled as "Survival Horror".
The folks at Frictional Games are huge fans of H.P. Lovecraft, and their games draw heavily from his works. They refined the true Horror game formula through the Penumbra series. Amnesia pulls together everything they did right, trims out the fat, and makes for a terrifying experience of nightmarish psychological horror. If you consider yourself a fan of Horror games, you must play this game and see how it redefines the genre.
And be sure to play it the right way: with headphones, in a dark room. You may never sleep again, but it will have been worth it.

Fun, atmospheric horror game.
Audio in the game is great with creepy noises and grunts constantly barraging the player. Graphics are a bit dated now, but they were never cutting-edge, even at the time of release. But that isn't the reason to play this game: it's easily one of, if not the scariest game to come out in a long while. There's not much to say about this game that hasn't been said a hundred times already, but I'll add my own thoughts on what makes this game scarier than something like Outlast (another great game in its own right) or Alien: Isolation (yet another stellar game [no pun intended]).
The reason why Amnesia is so terrifying is that you can never know what it is you're hiding or running from. Staring at the creatures in this game will result in your character either going insane or being detected. You can only catch quick glimpses now and then before you need to hide in a corner and avoid looking at the location you saw the monster. All you can do is wait and hope it goes away. This fear of the unknown is what sets Amnesia apart from games like the aforementioned where you are free to look at and examine the enemies to your heart's content.
In terms of storyline, Amnesia is intriguing and you'll want to continue on to uncover the past. The protagonist is someone suffering from memory loss and only told that he needs to descend into the castle and kill the owner.
There's nothing much to say about the controls. Everything works as it should, and using the mouse to manipulate objects in real time is a fun mechanic.

A buddy of mine gifted me the Starter Edition, and it was a really good choice. I love the old SWAT games, and i love CSGO. Siege brings the best of both worlds together. Well, almost. Ubisoft has made a big mistake in the netcode, servers, hitboxes and pings. They are trying to repair it with Operation Health, but none of the major changes has been implented at the time of reviewing, so keep that in mind.
Graphically, the game is stunning. Ubisoft has a great design team when it comes to location, level design and atmosphere, i cannot fault the game in any way possible when it comes to those aspects. It looks great, and runs great on a medium rig.
The operators are well balanced, tho some of them are under powered, leaving them less desired to play with.
The game modes are lacking, i would love to see more choices of game modes, as well as map choices. I could see a pure DM setting be quite fun for casual.
As for casual vs competetive, they both serve their purpose fine. Apart from casual can be a bit unbalanced, and can sometimes be a bit boring if you have a slow team and you die first.
The competetive option is quite a better challenge, as people tend to try to play the game as its meant, and they fool around less. The ranking system is however flawed, as there is no personal gain from being bad, or good. A win gives you the same amount of ranking points as every other team mate, no matter how good or bad you are, as long as you win the match. A system like the ELO in CSGO would be a better approach.
Game mechanics are pretty good, but it takes a bit of getting used to, as some actions require more mobility and fast movement than others. But nothing can beat the feeling of hot breaching into a room and wipe out a couple of bad guys before they even realize what hit them...
All in all, i rate the INTENTIONS of this game a solid 10/10.
As it stands today, with netcode and tickrate issues, i have to lower it to a 6/10, as its really detrimental to the total experience.

LSS is a unique gaming experience that is a throwback to windows 98 and windows XP. It combines a clicker with a simulator and brings a new style of ironic simulator to the table.
Whether using LSS as a game, or using it as a past time for when something actually is loading, you can be assured that LSS will deliver a (somewhat) enjoyable few minutes.
And with such a short download time, why wouldn't you give it a try. There a no microtransactions or 'pay to win' features. In fact, LSS even makes fun of that attitude (there is a buying option for 'Give us money' that does nothing and takes your in game money and never goes away...).

This game is a charming little breath of a game with retro charm.
This game sorta spins together classic mega man games as well as Zelda II: The Adventure of Link with the side scrolling combat style. Shovel knight has a downward stab and a regular shovel swing. Once he progresses far enough he can upgrade his equipment and forge new armors that give him special abilities or make his shovel able to perform new tricks.
Every level has a special item that if you find it in the dungeon, you can get it right then and there- the only issue is you need to purchase it. If you do not find the item in the level, don't fret! You can buy it in town from the underground salesman. The bosses are unique and provide an interesting spin on each fight that requires for you to play a different way each time.
Perhaps the best part of the game is the replay value. In most games released today there isn't much replay value. The game is typically too long to enjoy a second playthrough in most games and there aren't many reasons to do so. In Shovel Knight if you beat the game you have the classic new game + but considering how short the game is, it's easy to pick up again and play a different way. The steam achievements also help push for this game to have multiple play throughs (A no death run, no money run, no item run, etc etc) which goes back to the roots of achievements: Awarding the player for achomplishing something that would be worth a reward.
If I was to give one specific reason to buy this game: It is because the game is easy to pick back up when you take a break from it, each level is short enough to finish within 10-15 minutes and if you want to take a break the game auto-saves. It's easy to pick up and put back down and helps a ton when you're trying to take a break from other things.

Although it may not have the super-stellar visual effects of some other games (the 'you're-going-crazy' effect can be a little cheesy and let's be honest, no one has furniture that matches that perfectly!) and it's about as single-player as you can get, this game is fantastically fun to play. The puzzles have the right amount of 'challenging' to be fun, but not so much that it's too frustrating. The game provides you with limited resources that you're required to use, and plays on less-used aspects of 'survival horror.' You don't WANT to use the items you've got (no player does, you're saving them after all!) where they'll be wasted, but you're going to HAVE to use them, and that makes you anxious and worried. ("What if I needed that more later?)
Still images don't do it justice. You really have to see it in action and be behind the controls to get the full experience- on a dark night, with all the lights off, this game can be incredibly immersive.
