Sadistically frustrating, not a fun game.
First, the postives:
This game has a ton of visual charm. The enemies, the bosses, and the NPCs in towns between levels are both adorable and interesting. The game's quirky mythology, pitting Shovel Knight against the Order of No Quarter, meshes perfectly with the visuals to create a lovely little game world. A lot of love and a lot of polish went into the way the game looks and the way the game's world feels. And while the story is engrossing enough, the game never takes itself too seriously. The gentle, self-deprecating humor that permeates the entire game gave me a lot of smiles, though no outright laughs.
Shovel Knight's big problem is its gameplay. Each level is structured as an increasingly difficult gauntlet of instant-death traps. In a game where your character has a health bar!  Pits, spikes, fields of lava, and more pits. Now, Super Mario World had lots of instant-death pits too, and that's a nearly flawless platformer, but Shovel Knight doesn't pull it off gracefully.
For one thing, you don't feel as if you have much control over where your character lands when you jump. Your character feels weighty when he walks and jumps, which isn't bad in itself, but it makes each jump feel needlessly perilous. Furthermore, he slips around a little when he lands, which makes all the really precise jumps and sequences that much more difficult. Also, enemies knock you back when they hit you or--and I will never understand this--whenever you land a hit on them. So, you jump from one narrow platform to another, nearly slide into an enemy, strike it with your shovel, and then fall to your death because--game design. And while the levels have a decent degree of variety, and some are a little more forgiving than others, they are all built around the central design concept of instant death.
And dying a lot is counterintertuitive to the game's other gameplay elements. A major part of the game revolves around collecting gold, which you lose every time you die. The game gives you a chance to retrieve the gold when you die, but if you die again before you get back there, you lose it forever. So to recap, the game gives you RPG-style meta-objectives--collect gold, preserve your health--but then requires you to navigate ruthless platforming levels that make those objectives either maddeningly difficult or essentially pointless.
Seriously, you don't need a health bar in this game except for the boss fights. And the boss fights themselves are pretty anticlimactic since it's actually really easy to retrieve lost gold in most boss chambers--so losing isn't a big deal--and you can beat nearly every boss in the game just by mashing buttons.
And that's another problem: the game's combat. Hit boxes on your character and on some enemies are hard to figure out precisely, and the game doesn't give you a clear sense of when your strikes will damage an enemy and when the enemy will hurt you instead.
So basically, I had a lot of fun in this game whenever I wasn't actually playing one of the levels. But visual charms and a nicely fashioned world can't conceal the fact that this is essentially a mediocre game built around repetitive, flawed, and ceaselessly frustrating platforming.

For a game with only 4 gamemodes in single player and practically half that in multiplayer, this is a really good CQ strategy game.  In single player (Terrorist Hunt), you play against AI either by yourself or with friends in a co-op (so its 50% singleplayer) and you must either defend a HVT from varying waves of assaults (depending on difficulty), diffuse two bombs and defend the diffuser, kill every terrorist on the map, or extract an HVT and lead them to safety.  In multiplayer, you either attack or defend an HVT, bombs, or biohazards.  You can unlock different operators to play as and each has their own unique abilities.  Multiplayer is pretty difficult since most of the people online are pretty good and when you die, its usually because they were waiting for you so you never really had a chance.  I would recommend starting in singleplayer or co-op to get a feel for the game and then move on to multiplayer.  The AI aren't as fun to play against, but they will build up your skills before you go all in.

Saint's Row: The Third is unlike any game I have ever played. It's similar to Grand Theft Auto, and even then, it rivals it quite a bit, but in a very great, fun, and silly way. It's a third person and the fighting in it is awesome. Yeah, let's start with the fighting: You can use human-shields (And trust me, you'll need to use them every now and again) which needless to say, reduces the damage you take. You can pick from many different guns in specific "weapon type" slots. The weapons range from heavy-calibre pistols to machineguns to rocket launchers, to ridiculous (But very effective) sonic boom guns.
How well you fight, headshots in a row, nut/vag shots etc will give bonuses like cash & respect. The fighting in this game is really awesome and is one of my favourite things about it. Vehicular combat is... ok enough, but needs some serious grooming, what with the annoying camera snap while you're trying to line up a headshot.
Let's move onto character customisation & clothing. The latter suits everyone from the casual, to the leather-clad road warrior, to the insane bunny-suit wearing chainsaw murderer, and even more insane: The streaker. And much more. The former is... really, I've never seen such a powerful character creator system. You can make your character made of gold, literally; Literally made of shining gold. Make him/her a fatty, or turn him/her into the Hulk. All without losing you the ability to create a normal but epic looking character. Even better? You can do this in-game, even when you've already made your character.
Now, how about... storyline? Story's one of the best I've ever played. Never get bored of it. It's comedic, it's dramatic, it's grand. I won't spoil it for you, but trust me, you'll love it. It's fairly long, which is a good thing. Now normally I'm not a big fan of DLC for obvious reasons, but for Saint's Row 3, the DLC is worth the extra money. Adds way more fun & silly things into the game, including new missions and activities to keep you occupied.
Ah, let's move onto side-missions, activities and other things that are available to you. There are many side-missions or "activities" that you may play in. Take for example: Tank Mayhem, where you go around the city in a tank and cause a target amount of damage, $450,000 etc, under a fair amount of time. Or Insurance Fraud, where you must intentionally run into cars, and the logic is basically the same as Tank Mayhem: Rack up a target amount of money before the timer runs out, and you'll have done it. There are many instances of these activities, and much more different types of activities to be unlocked the farther you get through the game.
There's also a two-player co-op mode so you can play this great game with a friend as well. I must also say, this game is GRAND for rampages if you're into that sort of thing. Start a fight with a gang or the cops, and off you go, run across the entire city, guns blazing. They'll keep coming until you go to a safehouse. So you certainly won't run out of people to shoot!
Get this game, it's an 11/10.

This is a unique one. I am NOT a PvP guy, but I can't get enough of Siege, and I'm hardly the best player.
The intelligence and destruction aspects of the game are unique and unmatched, the fast-paced shooting and objective modes... this game really stands out because of how ridiculously unique it is. I don't mean to talk this game's quality up when I say this, but it really has no competitor, just because no other game even half matches all those aspects of the game.
There ARE a number of balance and server issues, and the learning curve is a plateau, but if you stick with the game enough to get the hang of it, find the operators you like, and start working with teammates, you'll find nothing like it, and you'll keep coming back for more and more.
Also worth noting is that this game has a MARVELOUSLY non-greedy asset system. The only things that require cash money [R6 Credits] are certain unique skins and appearances. Everything else, including a large portion of the skins, can be purchased with the earned in-game currency [Renown].
All in all, if you're interested in fast-paced quick kill shooters, and willing to work with a team, you'll find nothing else on the market that plays even remotely like this experience.

I personally like ArmA 3. The game has a large and multicultural community, who are generally mature-acting and rather kind. The former is still such in spite of the fact that ArmA 3 is a very intense and sometimes competitive game.
The computer needed to run this game "smoothly" is very high-end, and would require minimum a GTX 900series, 8 GB RAM, and a a current gen i3 overclocked. Even then, you will likely get some frame drops due to how many things the game renders at once. I have a GTX 1060 (Founder's Edition), Quad i7 and more than enough RAM, and I still get frame drops with and without VSYNC. Optimization doesn't work either, as this game is hardly optimized at all. Don't bother trying to run with with an AMD Graphics Processor, because you will regret it.
I would not reccomend this game to people who are biased towards faster or arcade style games, as this game can make most hardcore RTS games seem slow. After 2000+ hours I have still not discoevered all the quirks and little things to do in game, so the amount of gameplay time is defined almost solely by the player.

At first Arma 3 seemed very impressive to me; A military simulation type of game, with great graphics. I've kept the game installed for now, but this game always gets on my nerves so I might uninstall it soon. (See below).
Good things:
- The amount of detail in the game is awesome.
- You can move your player in so many different shooting stances for different situations.
- When you're in battle the depth and intensity of shooting is really awesome.
- The levels and terrain are well designed and massive and the vehicles are great.
- The Eden Editor is also built in so you can easily build your own maps/missions.
Bad things:
-  I find the Arma 3 community really weird. It seems to attract a bunch of strange military wannabe's that just stand around in servers planning who's going to do what. The problem is it's like that kid that is a wanna be hot shot football/soccer player... they always hog the ball and don't actually know what they are doing. The end result is everyone on the team gets♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off and leaves.
- Another downside is that most of the online game servers are all just mod servers, with mods like Exile, Wasteland, and RPG.  If I wanted to play a survival game, or RPG I would purchase Rust or a game that is actually good for that. This is probably the most mind boggling thing for me with this game. I don't get the weird mod community.
- That brings me to the point that the PVP (Player VS Player) battles online suck. The official servers host decent co-op missions but playing against bots gets boring quick. They have the "Unit" feature where you can join a clan/unit, but I had a really hard time finding any that actually did regular PVP.  If you are into playing against real people like I am, then this game's community isn't for you.
-  Another related thing is the performance on a lot of mod or custom missions is just horrible. Take KOTH for example, while it only uses stock game components and has promise for fun PVP, it is so bulky that when you get into battle the game frame rates go horribly bad making it almost unplayable. There is a mission EUTW European Tactical Warfare which also shows great promise for PVP type gameplay, but they only have servers in Europe.

There are some very rare games which are just so good that it is hard to find anything bad about them. Shovel Knight is one of those games and it's just the first game from Indie developer Yacht Club Games. The game is a brilliant "modern oldschool" Action-Platformer that draws inspiration from many classic NES games like Castlevania, Duck Tales and mostly MegaMan but still feels very unique in its own way: Here you have 8 Boss Knights from the Order of No Quarter instead of 8 Robot Masters like you would have in  MegaMan including themed stages that look awesome and are bursting with collectibles, personality ( the character design is simply flawless) and innovative gameplay elements. And there are even more optional stages, towns to explore and enemy encounters on the map that looks a lot like the one from Super Mario Bros. 3. And that's just the tip of the iceberg: Nice Soundtrack, a whole lot more bosses than just the knights, armor and weapon upgrades, magic relics, dialogues and although there is a heavy focus on gameplay here as you might expect, a story that is at first very shallow, but gets unexpectedly touching for an 8-bit-game in the final stages . And fear not: The difficulty in the main game is really not that high, everybody should be able to complete normal mode. To those who seek a challenge, there is a much harder New Game + and some difficult achievements (Speedruns, No-Death-Runs etc.). I completed my first playthrough in about 8 hours and even if you just play through the game once, it's worth the fifteen bucks. So I totally recommend this game to anyone that doesn't hate the platforming genre, in fact I think that this game is the best release in 2014 till now.

After much consideration, I've decided to reverse my recommendation.
Amnesia suffers from an over-reliance upon the helplessness gimmick to a degree that renders the game less fun to play. The story might be good, but the game has repeatedly failed to keep me interested long enough to find out. It's more fun to watch Let's Plays of people ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ themselves playing it than it is to actually play. I like horror games that give you a motivation and a tool set to solve your problems, rather than a game that appears to be engineered to crush your soul like Amnesia.
The uninteresting gameplay is the mortar, and the soul-destroyingly bleak and terrifying atmosphere is the pestle. No thank you, Amnesia, I'm not that masochistic.
I want to enjoy it, because it's a cult classic, and not liking it feels like betraying the cult-classic Indie Game spirit. But I like plenty of cult classic indie games, and I'm under no obligation to like all of them.
I think part of the question of "will I like it" can be answered if you contemplate the reason you want to play a scary game. If you want to be scared just for the sake of being scared, this might itch that scratch. I like scary games that feel like they exist for something a little bit more noble than just to scare players. When a game like Amnesia rolls along that's scary, but can't really be described with other terms, it feels one dimensional and uninteresting.
It's not enough to JUST be scary. Not for me.

I don't think I need to go into a great deal of detail and praise for Shovel Knight. It's in no need of any more of that.
I will say that Shovel Knight is a pleasant surprise compared to most indie games. It actually tries to improve upon a formula to a degree as opposed to forcing many design flaws from old games just because "that made the experience more difficult and more rewarding in those old games" according every retro loving geek ever. It's important to me that the game is difficult enough to be a challenge without being so difficult that I just refuse to pick it up again for weeks, but then I'm terrible at games (I'm not a filthy casual, I'm just bad) and I always have trouble with platformers especially (finish Cave Story for god's sake) but Shovel Knight is a game that I think any person could easily jump into, so long as they don't have a problem with the retro graphics.
The gameplay is solid, even though it's really just Jump & Shoot Man without the shooting. Plenty of jumping though. If I can knock the game for anything it would probably be that every boss is designed to be dispatched in the exact same manner, which isn't entirely a bad thing, but it makes the relics seem a tad useless outside of a few points where they are almost required. The Phase Locket is the most useful relic in the game, a little too useful though, as it is easy to abuse.
The soundtrack is pretty good. I mean it's chiptune but I've never had a problem with that. I don't make a fuss about most music that does not have lyrics. It's memorable and that's all that matters. You can get the soundtrack up on Jake Kaufman's bandcamp for name your own price, as well as an arranged version of the soundtrack.
Overall I'd say this game is worth a try if you're looking for a little nostalgia trip, or even just a game that's easy to just sit down and play.
The mechanics are quite superficial for a game in this genre, and it seems like the devs have more or less lost interest in ever taking this game to full release.

Shovel Knight is a game that brings back the good old NES days. Truth is, Shovel Knight fails to do one thing: Disappointing me. Shovel Knight is not only easily the best game of 2014 so far, but it's one of the best I've played in recent memory. It's greatness can be rivaled with others like Mass Effect and Minecraft. Shovel Knight is easily one of the best platformers of recent memory, too. The Rayman games, for example, were highly praised with their cute visuals and awesome soundtrack, but Shovel Knight takes these visuals and makes it hardcore nostalgic and the soundtrack into an 8-bit unforgettable masterpiece, thus making it far superior to that series to me. They say that "Nothing is perfect," however they also said, "Nothing is impossible." Where am I going with this? This might just be one of the few perfect games that I could've ever encountered.
The graphics take you back to the time when realistic graphics weren't the big thing. Shovel Knight successfully recreates the graphics from an NES game like this and also modernizes it with some new colors and also the amazing animated backgrounds. The characters, and more specifically, the Order of No Quarter, look outstanding. They're all knights, yet the creators were able to make each one unique. To me, King Knight was the best looking of all of them and really went well with his theme. However, they all look nice. Well, besides the Black Knight, who looks pretty ugly. However, you only encounter him less than 5 times in the game, so that isn't much of a flaw.
The gameplay, again, recreates what the NES games, and even games from that time and older did. They had the simplistic controls with no holding hands. Sure, it took a while due to how many last gen games I played since they all hold your hand, but it was easy to get adjusted to them. It also mixes some of the greats, like Mega Man, Zelda, even a hint of Mario. At first, the levels appear to be repetitive, but then you realize that they become more and more unique as they go on, and the bosses were amazing. No one was too difficult at all. There was the occasional rage, but I expect that from a game that wants to recreate the NES era. Speaking of difficulty, this game has been talked about because of its easy difficulty compared to the real NES games. This is true, but like I explained earlier, Shovel Knight does not hold your hand and also the bosses can make you rage when you go against the more notorious bosses like Plague Knight, Frost Knight, and Spectre Knight. In the end, you realize that the difficulty is easier compared to Mega Man and Zelda, however it's harder than the modern games like Call of Duty. It's a perfect balance and I see nothing wrong with it.
The story is straightforward. Shovel Knight had a companion named Shield Knight, who tagged along with him on his journey. However, one day, Shield Knight sacrificed herself to stay in the tower while Shovel Knight could get out alive before the tower seals. Shovel Knight, mourning the loss of his comrade, becomes a farmer and does cheap work. However, one day, the Enchantress, who is the main antagonist of the game, opens up the tower again and the Order of No Quarter, consisting of King Knight, Spectre Knight, Tinker Knight, Mole Knight, Plague Knight, Frost Knight, Propeller Knight, and Treasure Knight, begin to spread their evil throughout the land. Shovel Knight realizes that Shield Knight could be alive in there still, and he also wants to get rid of the evil knights who spread their terror. Overall, I enjoyed the plot and loved the last few minutes of the game. The ending was wrapped up effectively and told a great, yet simple tale that I saw no problems with.
The audio also highly impressed me with the good old chiptune soundtrack, and even had a few contributions from one of the all-time greats known as Manami Matsamune, who made the Mega Man soundtrack. The music is cheery, fast paced, and also unforgettable. The boss themes especially peeked my interest and made the bosses even more terrifying. Tinker Knight's theme 'The Schemer' also made you think that
The sound effects are simplistic and hardcore nostalgic. You will not be disappointed.
The replayability is very strong in this game. You can play different playstyles with the armor selection towards the middle of the game, beat Shovel Knight on New Game+, defeat the bosses without dying, and go achievement hunting. The achievements can keep you busy and the New Game+ makes it even more rage-inducing. You will get quite a bit out of this game unless you're a one-and-done kind of guy. In fact, if you are one of those kinds of people, why are you reading this paragraph?
Shovel Knight stands out among the crowd as one of the best games I've played in such a long time. Platformer fan, nostalgia fan, medieval fan, whatever you are, this is a must-buy for anyone on Steam and is one of the games you NEED in your Steam library, along with Garry's Mod and a few others. This game does something few games have ever done, and that, my friends, is have no significant flaws that ruin the experience. You NEED this game. You will not be disappointed.

It's a Resident Evil reviewing marathon!
tl;dr at the bottom
Having originally played this on Xbox 360, I have fond memories of RESIDENT EVIL 5. Seeing as it was on sale, my friend and I picked it up and played it all the way through twice, once on Veteran, once on Professional.
I can honestly say that anyone who dares try to play through on Professional is insane, myself included; you die in one hit, from almost everything, and QTE's are even harder than before. It's enough to pull your hair out!
But anyway.
RESIDENT EVIL 5, taking place several years after Resident Evil 4, follows BSAA members Chris Redfield and Sheve Alomar as they investigate a report on a black market deal set to go down somewhere in Africa, a deal that may involve bio-organic weapons. The duo will have to fight against obscene abominations and waves of infected locals, trying to shoot their way to the truth.
Contrary to other Resident Evil titles, RESIDENT EVIL 5 is certainly lacking in scares, which the root of the series is known for. However, it makes up for this with impressive production values and thoroughly enjoyable cooperative play. Having a friend by your side, covering you as you fend off waves and waves of monsters is a thrill. With the Outbreak games, Capcom had tried to make Resident Evil a fun cooperative venture, but wasn't really successful until this entry. RESIDENT EVIL 5 nails it in spades.
A lot of people hate on the tank controls the series is based on, but at least in the PC port there is an option to change the controls so you can strafe. Your feet are still rooted to the ground when you aim a gun, but dodging a charge is much easier now.
It must be said that this is far from the strongest game in the Resident Evil series, however. RESIDENT EVIL 5 gets compared to its predecessor, Resident Evil 4, quite often, and for good reason; in a series that was starting to grow stagnant, Resident Evil 4 was a minty breath of fresh air that revitalized not only a franchise, but a genre. It's evident that the developers wanted to ride this new train as far as they could, as the gameplay mechanics and style in this game are lifted straight from Resident Evil 4. This isn't 100% a bad thing, as RE4 was a terrific game, but it takes creativity away from RESIDENT EVIL 5. It also lacks its predecessor's oppressive tone and horror.
Some may say that positive reviews only stem from a comparison to its sequel, Resident Evil 6, and I suppose that it's true in some cases. But like I said, I had very fond memories of this game when it first came out; my best friend and I are huge fans of the Resident Evil series, and thought at the time this was a worthy title.
I still stand by that opinion today. It's not the best Resident Evil game in the series, but it's worthy of holding the RE title.
If you and a friend, online or offline, are interested in giving this game a try, I'm sure you two won't be disappointed.

Shovel Knight is one of the finest and most polished platformers I've played in years. Even if you can't relate to the whole nostalgic NES/Famicom gaming scene, you SHOULD still give this game a try. Belonging to the platformer genre, Shovel Knight has lots of jumping; fortunately, the jumping mechanics are smooth and easy to plan, so leaping over the many pits of death shouldn't be too stressful. Ninety-nine percent of my deaths were entirely my fault, which is good! The visuals are colorful and very distinguishable, so things that LOOK like they're in the background will NEVER turn out to be weird platforms or obstacles. You'd be surprised by how important this small detail can be in old platformers.
The plot is a simple "Defeat the eight big bosses and save the girl!" affair, the relatively short length of the game is remedied by the addicting allure of a more challenging "New Game+ Mode", and the soundtrack... Lordy, the SOUNDTRACK! I actually listen to quite a few of the standout tracks on their own, when I'm not playing the game. For $15 (that's like, what, a couple coffees at Starbucks?), Shovel Knight is practically a steal. Quite frankly, I dig this game.

Controls are tight and very responsive, the chiptune music excellently catchy and the graphics set a wonderfully diverse 8-bit atmosphere while subtly surpassing the actual limitations of classic 8-bit systems.

This is the best port of a game since Resident Evil 4. It's also on the same way length as the original retail GFWL version because none of the old glitches were fixed.
There were obviously many things they could've tried working on, the lag glitches in co-op (shooting an enemy takes no effect for a good three seconds, in mercs that can be a massive problem), the fact versus has many crash problems, likewise with merceneries (and reunion), the save file tool not being avalible is also a really bad thing to do if you're releasing a game that has been around for this long. I've dedicated hours to replaying chapters and trying to work through stuff I've had done for years. It's annoying.
We've waited so long for this DLC, but I could've waited a bit longer for a game that worked and wasn't repackaged cola.
If you ever played the original retail GFWL Mercs, you probably know what I'm talking about; the amount of people running around with trainers, cheats and the amazing fact you can glitch having more than two people in a session. However I'd rather be in a game with four Midnight Weskers trying to figure out who I was meant to be teamed up with than this. We were all the same Wesker, someone died during the game and of course it was a terrible session, but it was playable. So far I've spent close to an hour trying to sort out a Versus game that never ended up happening and Mercs games that drop for no reason.
By all means, it's great finally having the full DLC, I've been a longtime fan of Resident Evil despite the usual bad treatment you get as a PC gamer. It's nice finally getting to go through the full stories, but that doesn't exclude the negative, gaping problems they just overlooked with this release.

It's been a while since I enjoyed a single player game this much. Providing an interesting blend of classics like Megaman II, Super Mario Bros. 3, Ducktales (three of my all-time favorites) and Castlevania, it doesn't get bogged down by mimicking them too much.
While gameplay can get quite tough sometimes, it never feels impossible to progress, and the unique sense of humor featured in cutscenes and NPC conversations maintain a light atmosphere.
Controls are tight and very responsive, the chiptune music excellently catchy and the graphics set a wonderfully diverse 8-bit atmosphere while subtly surpassing the actual limitations of classic 8-bit systems.
If you enjoy 2-D platformers, classic NES games or a good challenge, this is an absolute must-buy. With same-screen multiplayer, a gender-switching feature and (more) playable campaigns recently added, it's guaranteed to have a lot of replay value. I can't wait for the still upcoming battle mode.

I am old now, old enough that people younger than me can poke fun about my age without it seeming ironic.  I remember the heyday of the NES, the days of four-color sprites and thumb-crushing difficulty, of four sound channels and obtuse, half-translated secrets.  That's all gone now, a relic of days gone by, replaced and paved over by everything that's come after it.  Flashy SNES sidescrollers gave way to primitive PlayStation 3D, which was in turn replaced by the sprawling epics of the XBox, and all that's now hidden behind mud-colored, multi-platform shooters where military personnel shout for you to move to the next waypoint in gritty, four-pack-a-day voices.  Sometime along the way, games stopped being about fun the way I understood it -- go back to the basement, geezer, you just can't handle a *real* game like Battlefield 4 -- and I started to lose interest.  I still played new games, still enjoyed them for what they were, but that sense of immersive, immediate fun, the kind of feeling that let me get completely sucked into a game when I was just a kid, that was missing.
Until I found Shovel Knight.
This is a great game, and I say that without reservation.  There is no "...for a retro game," or "...for an indie game".  This is a fantastically well-built game.  It is exactly what it needs to be and no more.  The play control is tight and intuitive, the graphics are lovably rendered with nearly all of the limitations of the original NES (save for a tiny handful of extra colors), and the soundtrack is mind-bogglingly good.  The characters and enemies are full of expression and life, animations carefully constructed to convey personalities and traits in a few scant frames.  The level design is intuitive, challenging, and well-thought-out.  At no point in the game did I ever feel cheated into death -- each time my spade-toting knight fell, I knew exactly what I had done to cause it, and I knew not to do it again the next time.
And yet, this is not just a slavish retro-clone, warts and all.  The developers have provided the player with a free set of rose-tinted glasses for the 8-bit era.  Gone are arcade concessions such as limited lives and continues.  In its place is a wonderfully well-designed checkpoint system whereby you have a chance to recover everything you've lost if you can overcome the challenge that killed you last.  Some of the limitations of the NES have, thankfully, also been set aside.  Sprite flickering, limited sound channels, and the like are nowhere to be found.  In short, there is nothing getting in the way of you immersing yourself completely in the game.  It doesn't play like the old 8-bit consoles did, it plays the way you remember them.
I have not played another game in the last five years that put as big a smile on my face as this one.  It is short -- but then, it is as long as it needs to be -- and it is not cutting-edge -- but then, it would lose all of its charm if it was.  I remember reading something somewhere which compared the advances in modern gaming technology to art.  We began, thousands of years ago, with primitive carvings and cave pictures.  We continued to advance, through the flattened but more realistic depictions of people in the dark ages to the rise of perspective and a mastery of light and shadow in the Rennaisance.  Eventually, we came to the point where we could create art almost indistinguishable from a photograph.  And from there, where did we go?  The artists of the world looked back on the years and years of tools that they had been given, and they chose not what was needed to make the most "realistic" art, but whatever was needed to best express their idea.  In a way, video games have seen a hyper-accelerated version of this trend.  We have our dirt-brown, ultra-realistic, dark and gritty modern games.  In fact, we have an abundance of them.  But is this something ever game should aspire to?
Shovel Knight is proof that it is not.  The game uses only the vocabulary it needs to express its statement.  I admit a certain degree of bias, given my obvious preference for older games, but I stand by the statement that if you cannot have fun playing Shovel Knight, then I pity you more than you will ever know.
Buy this game.  Have some fun.

This mod was an amazing play through from start to finish and well deserves the recent nominations and awards. There is a lot to praise, but today I would like to join the discussion specifically to lend those who worked on (or participated with) the level design my sincere appreciation.
Much more than simply "hard", these levels were challenging, well-presented, well-crafted and thought provoking. We all know the tools - blue portals, orange portals, blue gel, orange gel, bridges and others. But to design levels that truly challenge how you perceive each tool's interaction in complex, fun and engaging environments is a treat.
Not to mention, the integration that each puzzle's theme had with the story made for a very authentic experience. There was always a clear reason, related to the story, why Mel was participating in each puzzle.
The feelings of frustration when stuck on a puzzle, then the delight when finally overcoming the challenges, were amplified over any other Portal experience I have encountered.
The second section of st_a4_destroyed comprises all of these elements beautifully.
Thank you to the entire development and testing team, and hats off to the level designers.

This game, one of the best Zombie Tower Defense game to-date came out in 2009

anyway, onto the details
The Fun part of this game
Some gameplay and game aesthetic that I think is really fun to interact with and play.
- 5 Level in Adventure mode is absolutely fun, with variation not only of the enemies, but also the stage itself.
- You plant Sunflowers, that spew Sun rays, that is used to plant more Sunflowers and other plants
- Finished the Adventure mode ? Indulge into the fun Mini-Games + Puzzles + The Challenging endless mode.
- Variety of plants in this game, also includes variety of strategy you can use against the Zombies
- Tired from playing against the Zombies ? why not try out the Zen Garden, to Zen your stress....
- When you finished the Adventure mode, you can try again in Adventure Mode+ (so I called it), and after that, you can go ahead and play it until +++++++ somethin'
- Crazy Dave, he's crazy, but he's your only companion in this god-awful-forsaken world filled with zombies
The Not-so Fun part of this game
Basically, the opposite of the fun part, ofc. I Personally think there is not much of a Not-so Fun part in this game. But there are some that I do not like about it.
- only 5 Levels in Adventure Mode, in which I assume they can at least slip in 1 More level variety
- The Endless-mode level is non-Interchangeable, which kinda suck since there is 5 level in the game
- Zen Garden has some missing or I would say, lack of controls for either helping the plants or moving them
But nonetheless, there is a reason this game is Called a GOTY for 2009, and it is because this game is truly ahead of the time back then for a small game like this, that no one knew, would generate millions of dollars and a franchise deal to boot.
I Highly recommend this game for everyone, there is no reason to hate this one, but you can hate the mobile sequel.

Let me preface this review by saying that I would purchase this game again without hesitation.  For those of us old enough to have played them originally and for those who have played via emulator, this title is reminiscent of the NES platforming days.  Great 8-bit graphics and chiptunes accompany you throughout gameplay.  Difficulty isn't as staggering and frustrating as say, Mega Man (NES) but it provides enough of a challenge for the player to be satisfied when completing levels.

Don't let the nit-picking drive you away -- this game is worth a purchase.  10/10, would blow $15 again.

I didn't intend to cover this game originally, but then I figured it was certainly a big enough name to justify, and also a good enough game to talk about. Before Plants VS Zombies was following in the footsteps of Team Fortress 2 and interrupting an indie developer with mood-destroying music at every E3, it started here, as a simple tower defense. This is a kind that's a bit less common on Steam, where you're defending rows rather than winding path. As the title implies, you do this using militaristic plants to combat a bunch of eccentric zombies.
Compared to a lot of the games I've talked about, Plants VS Zombies is a pretty casual one. Experience in many of the above titles would make the campaign fairly easy to get through, and even when I played it years ago without any TD experience I don't remember having much trouble. Of course, not every game needs to be hard, far from it, and there's something relaxing about watching your garden take on all comers. Both your plants and the zombies are also both appealing enough to look at without trying too hard, and there's a good amount of enemy variety.
You start with a simple Peashooter for damage and a Sunflower for harvesting resources (you do need to manually click on them like Beware Earth, but that's the only thing like it in the game and it's not generally very hectic), and across the course of the campaign get access to forty-seven others that all have some different use, depending on what zombies you're up against or the level. The game mixes things up often enough to keep things from getting too repetitive, and aside from the normal sunny day you'll also have to defend at night, where you get less resources, or at the backyard pool, where you have to build terrain for most of your plants to stand on. You'll also get levels within those that operate on different rules, such as using the Wallnut to bowl down zombies or having to pick your defenses from a sort of conveyor belt.
Aside from the campaign there are a bunch of minigames and alternate modes you can unlock, including survival and a role reversal where you pick zombies to go after the plants' defenses. Quite a lot considering the game's only five dollars, the cheapest of any game mentioned so far. If you're looking for a more low-key entry into tower defenses, it would be a good one to pick up, as long as you remember most other ones aren't exactly like this. Even if you're not new to them though, if you somehow haven't played this I can't think of any reason to dissuade you.

Plants vs. Zombies is a tower defence game with a simple concept, yet highly addicting gameplay.
In the game; you're supposed to keep zombies away from your house so they don't eat your brains. Your best defence system are fruits and vegetables.
There are a wide variety of plants throughout the game, some being as simple as just shooting at the zombies, while some can do other tasks, such as hypnotising them.
Plants vs. Zombies also finds different ways to be funny, while still keeping you on your toes, the many zombies are very goofy, and you can read their bios, all of which are hilarious.
One of my only complaints I can think of is how slow the game can sometimes be. There are 50 stages in the game, and not all of them are a winner in my opinion. If you are playing a very easy stage, it is going to be very boring, considering the fact that each stage can sometimes be as long as 10 to 15 minutes, and there are 50 stages in the game, Plants vs Zombies can get really slow paced at times. Other than that; I had a lot of fun with it.
The game has a lot to offer: like the different plants, zombies, stages, and there are even some mini-games to go along with it. I think this is a great game ESPECIALLY for the asking price of $5! I recommend this game to anyone; even those who aren't really into tower defence games in the first place.

What can be said about Shovel Knight that hasn't already been said by countless fans and reviewers?
Shovel Knight is a retro action-platformer with RPG elements and an excellent soundtrack - as well as a great sense of humor. The game features classic elements, borrowing from games like Legend of Zelda: The Adventure of Link. Mega Man, Super Mario Brothers, and Castlevania.
The game is difficult. But in all the proper ways that make retro games good. Never did I feel the game was unfair or trying to hard to be difficult for the sake of being difficult. Where most "Retro Style" games these days aim for a ridiculous level of frustration and difficulty, Shovel Knight focuses on making a good, challenging, and entertaining game that's fun to play.
Plenty of replay value thanks to achievements being present that actually have some challenge to them (Don't get hit for a whole level, don't die for the entire game. Beat the game without buying any special weapons or items...etc.) So there's many ways to play, as well as the ability to choose what direction you want to go in on the world map. (Bosses and levels come in sets but the order you take them in is entirely up to you.)
The game is designed well and the visuals and sound are fantastic. I recommend turning up the excellent soundtrack and enjoying what is destined to be considered a modern classic.

No it's not as "good" as RE4 but that should not deter you from playing it. It had a hefty development process dating all the way back to that concept trailer shown back in 2005 and it didn't even release until March 2009. Yes, originally it was just Chris but Capcom cashed in on how easy "co-op" appeal is and with the whole racist backlash (That would be 10x worse in 2015, thanks tumblr) they threw in Sheva. It's still one of the best looking games of last gen even compared to RE6 although that's not much of an achievement when you look at RE6. Good music, good atmospheric design - By this I mean it's got a really nice murky urban feeling in the early levels of the game as opposed to being scary, sure it's daylight but it's Africa what do you expect? Story/Scenario is really stupid though, you're following up on things we know nothing about and we never really see most characters outside of cutscenes also for some reason despite being veterans Chris and Jill are both low ranking officers in an organization they started.
Playing solo is a miserable experience having to babysit the AI and feed it your ammo and use your money to upgrade its weapons if you want it to keep up, the real experience in the game is the co-op. Having a responsive partner to use the voice commands given in the game adds to the whole co-operative nature of the game. Getting grabbed and being helped out then to quickly press a button to say "Thanks for the help" really makes it more satisfying that you have someone to assist you. The core gameplay itself hasn't changed too much from the series it's essentially "RE4 with co-op" having no typewriters anymore, no merchant what little remained of the core RE series to begin with is the tank controls. The controls themself take some getting used to and having being spoilt by RE6's masterful character control (The only good thing about the game) I had some difficulty playing it a while back but now it's out of my system I can easily manage playing it again.
The post-game content is serviceable, as you go through the game you're to acquire hidden emblems that unlock content for you with the more you amass. Be they files on all creatures and people in the game, filters for the game itself, small statues that detail the models of the game or even unlockable costumes to which both Sheva and Chris have 2 each of. The game also contains the series staple Mercenaries which started in RE3 and carried over to RE4 and now RE5. The DLC content is also largely worth it having two scenarios that fill in the missing pieces of the story a lot easier granted you even care about it, two more costumes for Chris and Sheva (Well, technically only 1 each on PC since you get the other set you got on consoles PC had already) and a remixed Mercenaries mode featuring two characters from RE5 and two old returning characters from the first game in the series.
With a fair amount of replay value and the likes or Mercs (provided the community is still alive) it's a game definitely worth your time even with all the flaws present the amount of time put into it is staggering compared to some of Capcom's later efforts.

Having played Arma 3 since its early stages in 2014, and clocking over 500 hours I think i'm qualified to give a thorough review of the game. Let's start off with some pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Incredibly versatile mission editor and creator
+ DLC items still usable with base game
+ Thousands of content creations on the steam workshop and armaholic and other sites, in other words endless entertainment
+ Good introduction campaign
+ Very customizable controls which use your entire keyboard ( both a pro and a con )
+ Incredibly realistic when paired with realism mods and even realism units for multiplayer OPs
+ Great community
+ Many online gamemodes including KOTH, Battle Royale, DayZ, and realism OPs
+ A great representation of real life firearms
Cons:
- AI is pretty dumb with the base game, but an be fixed with mods such as ASR AI or VCOM or bCombat
- Base sounds are pretty wimpy, again can be fixed with mods
- DLC is very overpriced, especially Apex only offering some assets, a map and a coop campaign
- Combat and movement in general is very finicky and blocky
- Base medical system is garbage, fixed with Ace 3
- The game is horribly optimized, expect to be playing in 30fps on Ultra, even with a high end pc, but this is because the amount of things the game has to render at any given time
- Commanding AI is atrocious without a voice command program
- The game uses almost every key shortcut on your keyboard, aka very hard to memorize key strokes for different things
Throughout the years, Arma has been a great series, and a fun game to either mess around in the editor with, or go serious mode with an online realism unit. I would recommend this game to people who like tactical and realistic gameplay that you can enjoy by yourself or with friends online, in a wide range of game modes.

So much fun to play. If you enjoy the Portal world and the puzzles, then this game is a "must have". The puzzles are enjoyable and difficult, but I also found myself just getting caught up in the expansive world and the story. The voice-over work is great and the Core character who serves as the narrator is wonderful and hilarious; very well written and executed. The original music created for the game is fantastic; I enjoyed listening to it as I solved the puzzles and explored the world. It feels like Portal while creating it's own identity. Again, very well done.
The puzzles require (at least in my experience) a lot of non-linear thinking, but that's what made it so much fun for me. Every time I thought the solution was obvious, only to realize that I had to go about executing the problem solving much differently that I normally would have. It was and is a great brain exercise. The puzzles have the right blend of "Argh, this is impossible!!" and "How did I miss that?!". I had a blast solving the puzzles.
My only critique, and this is a small one, is that there were times in the game where I was going through tests without a clear understanding of why Mel was supposed to continue testing. I completely understood why in the first three chapters, but by chapter 4, I was wondering why Mel had to complete some of the tests. The Core would just say, "I'll do this thing and you go in that room and test". I enjoyed the puzzles immensely, I just feel like an explanation could have been given (maybe I missed it entirely and if so, then I recant my critique).
However, that critique does not diminish the immense amount of fun I had playing this game. Again, the story was great and well written, the voice over work was fantastic, the music is enjoyable (listening to the OST now), and the puzzles were wonderfully inventive. I wholeheartedly recommend this Mod to anyone who is a fan of Portal or a fan of puzzle games. Great job to all who worked on this Mod. :D

A lovely game for those that enjoy platformers. Built to look like games near the end of the 8-bit days, Shovel Knight plays like a mash-up of several games. Fighting is similar to Zelda 2 and Castlevania, and platforming is very tight, so controlling the titular Knight is very easy. There are a couple of frustrating moments that can end up getting catching you out, but a removal of a life system means the only things you lose are distance and money. The boss fights you encounter are simple at first, but slowly become more complicated and require deft gameplay to conquer. Coupled with fast-paced arranges of the stage themes, you'll soon find the one boss that stands out to you, either out of a sense of amazement or a sense of "JUST ONE MORE STRIKE"
The story is nice enough - it starts out a little cliché, and if you're sharp you'll spot the story's end-game quite quick. The characters are enjoyable (both with personalities and fights) and the world you explore is colourful and interesting (even if there's a bit of cliché here and there)
The sub-weapons (relics) in the game can allow people still learning how to play platformers expertly to get through tougher parts of the game (eg health potions, anchors that fly in an arc), but don't have to be purchased in order to complete the game. You even get achievements for beating the game in this wa, suggesting to folks that yes, it CAN be done!
The strongest part of the game, I feel, is the music - so many memorable melodies, from "Plains of Passage" to "The Vital Vitriol", there are very few tracks in the game that won't leave an impression on you. Unsurprisingly, everything is pure chip-tune to match the style of the game - the sort of stuff that you wouldn't be surprised to hear coming from an old NES.
Overall, it has a bit of cliché to it, but Shovel Knight is still very refreshing to play after a host of pure-platformer games. Whilst the developers are still working on additional game modes that range from mainly visual changing modes (similar to Butt Mode, something that changes a few words around) to playing as boss characters in their own stories, as it is right now the game is amazing in its own rights. And at £10.99, you can't go wrong!

Why am I even here reviewing Resident Evil 4?
Everyone already knows this game is totally awesome and...oh wait.
This review is supposed to be for RE5.
Hmm...
Depending on who you talk to, RE5 is either a respectable entry in the franchise, just another bro-op shooter, or the beginning of the end. I belong to the "I think RE5 is simply a great game" camp. It's entertaining, has a lot of good ideas, and how can anyone not love Mercenaries? With the recent transition to Steam I had to give the game another (3-4) playthroughs and tell you all about it.
"Uroborus will be released into the atmosphere ensuring complete global saturation."
This memetic line -- spoken by a man with evil eyes -- from one of the few unskippable scenes in the entirety of RE5 explains the plot. I can't recall any of the rest. Capcom used to develop arcade games, so every now and then these storylines seep into their console titles. While it's easy to write this game off as dumb action movie shlock, I think we have to look deeper. After all, dumb action movies are released every day, yet hardly any of them are on the level of Die Hard.
Let's start with the most important aspect: the mechanics. Yep, it's that word again. Everytime I review a crappy beatemup on Steam I have to mention the mechanics. Capcom has made some of the best beatemups ever: Aliens Vs Predator, Cadillacs & Dinosaurs, Final Fight, Dungeons & Dragons, and so on. They've attained mastery of mechanics as far as I'm concerned. With this knowledge, they can do everything from fighting games to third-person shooters. When somebody puts out a crappy beatemup, I know that they have no business making a game in any other genre (except for maybe a turn-based RPG).
But what is mechanics? Everyone has their own definition, but I look at it as the player's relationship with the world. This covers every action, no matter how subtle. This can be everything from the height and arc of Mario's jump, to what happens when a flying axe is shot, or how much space is necessary for a mayor to dodge a punch. Great mechanics work when you never notice them. It's supposed to be seamless, so when you dodge a thousand bullets in a 2D shooter, you feel like you've been doing it since birth.
The most prominent aspect of these great mechanics is in how the weapons feel. Each gun has its own characteristics, and using them properly is exciting and rewarding. Majini also respond appropriately depending on where you shoot them and what they're doing. This goes beyond shooting them in the head or in the knees to setup a melee attack. There's other tricks like clipping a shoulder, which causes their arm to fly back. This can be useful if an enemy is carrying dynamite, and it's just out of the player's sights.
It also can't be stressed enough how effective unrealistic or overly "gamey" mechanics can be. When you're surrounded by monsters in any other game, your first instinct isn't to punch the one that's staggering. In RE5 however, that maneuver can buy you precious invulnerability. All too often, videogames give you these cool techniques you can perform, but they leave you open to attack, so they're never used. Providing an incentive is key, it empowers the player, makes them more willing to take risks, and thus have more fun. In the interest of balance, not every game should function in this manner, but it suits the later RE games extremely well.
In keeping with the arcade game theme, RE5 is best-described as a compatibility shooter. Cooperative? That's the term I'd use to describe Borderlands or something. Sometime in the late 90s/ early 00s, Arcade light-gun developers like Sega & Namco started pushing the compatibility aspect. When you played a light-gun shooter like Let's Go! Jungle or Deadstorm Pirates, end-of-level ratings weren't given just to you. When you played with a friend, a loved-one, or even a complete stranger, it was the relationship that was rated. This meant that if you were doing stuff like hogging all of the enemies or allowing your partner to take damage, you and your partner would get punished with a lower rating. In a way, two people that performed admirably in a light-gun game could be considered lifetime best-friends, lovers, etc.
RE5 is designed along those same lines, that's what makes it a compatibility shooter. The next time you play RE5, keep an eye on your partner. Sure there are plenty of moments that force the co-op angle, like the shared QTEs, or those times where you have to cover your partner while they do something, but I'm talking about all of the subtle aspects. For example, note the laser-sights. This isn't just a holdover from RE4. You can see where your partner is aiming, so you know when to cover their back. Enemies tend to come from multiple directions, so situations where you do the lion's share of the work are few and far between. Over time you develop a sense of what your partner is thinking. You know when they have a situation handled, or when they need to be bailed out.
There's also the context-sensitive B button. When you give someone a herb, pressing the B button will say "Thank you", and you'll hear some variant of "Nice!" when your partner nails a sweet headshot. Typically, when you perform some action in spectacular fashion, you'll see "Great!" pop up on-screen or hear it spoken (My personal favorite is "Nice Driving" in Daytona USA. This is a holdover from the arcade days. Arcade games are short, and your actions have immediate consequences. When you do something right, the game pats you on the head. RE5 is designed so that you and your partner are expected to pat each other on the head, thus we have the B button.
RE5's campaign is altogether solid, but it has some definite mis-steps. Boss-fights in RE games tend to be generally hit or miss. More often than not they're about taking advantage of clumsy AI path-finding or shooting large glowing targets with the magnum. RE5 has all this, and a bullet-sponge turret boss to boot. There's also the 5-2 boss, which screams "Use a rocket launcher on me". Also, while not-zombies with guns aren't a huge deal to me, they're a massive pain in Professional mode. This, combined with the ridiculous short revival time (you have to be right on top of your partner to save them), is just annoying. For the most part though I think RE5 is solidly put-together. It pushes the compatibility elements quite well.
Mercenaries is absolutely perfect. There's no need for a wall of text to explain why.
Altogether, RE5 is a very satisfying game. Give it another go if you haven't already.

The year was...well, I don't exactly remember what year this game came out, actually, but it was a long time ago. I picked it up back in 2011 when I, as yet, didn't have internet access, and it was my first major experience with GFWL. Honestly, I have to say the service was my only favorable memory of this horrible game, since unlike Valve's Steam service, it didn't require an internet connection to do everything. I never even had to register the used copy of the game I bought (try doing that now, I dare you).
Still, we're here to discuss
not bash Steam (and trust me, this is a topic I can discuss at length).
The good:
Voice acting: Like in the previous title, Re5's voice acting is incredibly solid. This has been on an upward trend since
, despite the slight detour they took with
, and I'm honestly happy with it.
Music: Say what you will about the game, but Re5 has some of the best musical cues in the series. The themes during most of the boss fights are especially memorable; Wesker's is probably the best.
Graphics: Even five years later,
is still a great
game...and therein lies the problem.
The Bad:
Controls: The PC controls are simply unusable, except for the standard grapple break prompt, which is broken in the other direction (the average AD prompt takes about three seconds to break out of). The inventory is completely unusable (and doesn't even
correctly in Mercenaries Reunion, or so I've heard). This remains the only game I own I've never played start to finish with a mouse and keyboard. Buy yourself a gamepad if you intend to play this; you'll need it.
Mechanics: Probably my "favorite" two are the idiotic real-time inventory and Dying Status.
The
in
was perfect, so naturally Capcom went and broke it in the sequel. You can't move and shoot, or even move and heal, and enemies have absolutely no compunctions against beating you to death while trying to mix herbs or reload your guns. You've also got maybe a third as much space to play with, which cannot be upgraded, and half your inventory can walk away, in the form of your AI partner, who has to be next to you in order to trade items. While this makes logical sense, I still found myself missing the system from the last game.
is probably the game's most frustrating addition. Whenever your character absorbs enough punishment, they'll enter a state wherein they can no longer fight back and must be rescued by your partner. While its concept is similar to Last Stand from
, Dying manages to be about a million times more frustrating. You can barely move and can't fight back, but enemies can still attack you, and you can even be grappled into Dying by some enemies, which is almost always fatal. In Mercenaries, you have the option to revive yourself by spamming the B button, but again the same camping comes into play; I was once put into Dying three times within a minute by the same enemy hovering behind me and smacking me with his axe before I got frustrated and rage quit.
This brings me to my third complaint,
. Despite what people say, these have always been present to some degree in every
game to date, though they first became more obvious in the more action centric Re4. The dodge sequences from that game were probably my least favorite, so naturally Capcom adds even more in, and then some. We still have a boss fight consisting entirely of QTEs, though this time it's closer to the end of the game, which isn't as bad. However, fighting Wesker in both the main game and "Lost in Nightmares" is almost exclusively a QTE fest, which is compounded further by the game's irritating habit of not registering your button presses or simply not giving you the prompt. Another especially notorious sequence involves Chris punching a boulder; despite hitting every single prompt correctly, Chris still gave up on this
during one playthrough.
Of course, being a failure as a game wouldn't be so bad if Re5 at least had an enjoyable
, but sadly this isn't the case either. Since I'm not worried about spoiling a five year old game, I'll go ahead and lay things out for you:
Jill has apparently been killed at some point earlier on, except Chris doesn't seem to attach any significance to her death, since prior to the game actually starting he apparently learned she was still alive. Considering losing his best friend the way he apparently did should be the defining character moment for him, it seems odd that just about everything Chris went through is offscreen, compounded further by his lack of development. It's hard to become invested in Chris, since he doesn't seem to have much of a personality.
Sheva Alomar gets a lot of hate, but honestly I didn't mind her. Her AI is only as dumb as the human player alongside her; if you're lazy and expect her to play the game for you, you'll be disappointed, but if you take into account her limitations, she's a quantom leap ahead of your last partner, Bill "Can't Reload His Own Guns" Coen. Still, while Sheva is never
she never has the breakthrough characterization Helena Harper got in the sequel, so she's also kind of dull. All the mildly racist fan service she's put through doesn't help matters, either.
There are other problems, too. It's heavily implied by the events at the beginning of the game the BSAA are somehow in league with Tricell, but this subplot falls off the boat and is never fished back out. For that matter, Chris doesn't seem to much care for the organization he canonically
and no one really seems to respect him; Jill Valentine, meanwhile, is treated like a rock star by every operator
meets, and no one once expresses shock that she's not dead.
Tricell, a company similar to Umbrella but not actually them at all (in the sense they seem to have done sod-all before this point in the series) is the main antagonist of the game...we're led to believe. Their president, Excella Gione, has apparently been bribing Ricardo Irving (the game's one memorable villain) to release bioweapons in Africa. Why she's doing this is never explained, anymore than the presence of the
from the previous game, since both ensure the BSAA get involved and ultimately ruin everything, but hey, if not for this we wouldn't have a game, right?
It's not especially clear how giving Irving money was enough for him to willingly transform into a sea monster, either, since there's now no way for him to spend this money. Granted, when you consider this is a game which ends with Chris punching a boulder during the final confrontation with Wesker
I suppose logic is something in short supply.
Since this is now a pure shooter, I guess we can't
mention the guns. Re5 does have a pleasing assortment...except they're pretty much identical to the ones from Re4. The Beretta 92FS (called the M92F for some idiotic reason) is roughly comprable to the Silver Ghost, the P8 is the FiveseveN, the Sako 75 is the Springfield, the PSG-1 is the SL8...This is, of course, without the four guns which are carried over from the previous game and fill the exact same roles (the M3 is the best shotgun in the game, the RPG is the "Screw this boss fight" weapon). The handguns feel the most useless, since you're only given one (well, one for each of you) for free, and there's no reason to buy more. Equally worthless are the "machine gun" (read: automatic weapons) class, which are hilariously inaccurate and underpowered to a fault (shot for shot, the Beretta does something like five times the damage of the AK-74, and by the end of the game has a higher capacity to boot!).
Also, Steam will delete all your achievements if you import your save.

For the 2 hours I have on record there isn't much I can say...but I'm still reviewing it anyways.
FIRST THOUGHTS
First and foremost I think this game shouldn't be a Free to Play but I don't think the devs should charge a full $60.00 for this game. I think this game should incorporate what Treyarch used with Call of Duty: Black Ops by keeping the whole ingame currency part but I think the devs should get rid of the renting system and just force (yes force) the player to spend more of their ingame currency for the weapons and armor rather than renting. This wouldn't just be for fan service either this would make it so that instead of playing one game and than renting a weapon the player would need to invest time into the game and play more games thus getting them hooked. Not hooked in the way mobile games do it, but more like they love the game so much that they're willing to invest time into it.
GAMEPLAY
I think this game is more than just a renamed Counter-Strike (Seeing as Le Minh created this along with Counter-Strike). I think the feature that really made me realize the true potential was when I was playing the mission mode and I was a Terrorist, I was staying with the hostages that my team needed to hold hostage when one of the hostages ran out of the room. Instead of shooting him I told him to stay where he was and he did just that. I really appreciate how to the devs took what some people would consider a gimmick and made it useful. Another example would be the map Skyrise, I was the "Counter Terrorists" (I forgot what they are called) in the beginning of the match you have two options. Number 1 was to run straight ahead and proceed down the stairs. The second option was to rapple down the side of the building you are on top of. Number two obviously stands out rappling down the build sounds like a gimmick like it was put there for fun...nothing else right? WRONG rappling down the building not only allows you to get to the lower floor faster but you also get to surprise the enemy by shooting at them while rappling into the building (this is funny because you do the same thing in a Call of Duty: Black Ops campaign level too!).
FINAL VERDICT
* = good
^ = bad
*Team work and strategy wins the game.
^Lack luster animations.
*What appears to be gimmicks are actually strategically useful.
*New and interesting gameplay mechanics.
^This game specifically shouldn't be Free to Play.

Most indie games that use retro-style graphics and sound only use them as an excuse to be lazy or because it's what's popular. Instead of honoring the great games from which the medium originated and their part in its evolution, they come off as poorly-executed parodies made by people who care more about trends than making a good game.
Thankfully, that is not the case with Shovel Knight. This game was made with love and respect for itself and video games as a whole. The Yacht Club was able to dive deep into the milestones of one of the most beloved generations of gaming and answer the question, "What made the greats, great?" Their adept team of artists, programmers, and designers took what they found and created a colorful, stylized world filled with entertaining, catchy characters and brought them together with fluid, well-paced gameplay. Top it all off with a fantastic score by the talented Jake Kaufman (Mighty Switch Force, DuckTales Remastered) and Manami Matsumae (Mega Man 1), and you have a game that delivers in being one of the greatest old-school homages ever made.
But having played the games it tributes isn't necessary to enjoy Shovel Knight. Even though the action-platformer style of gameplay was more popular years ago than it is now, history proven that it's a style that remains enjoyable and replayable over and over again as time goes on. Many games of this genre have been made, and many more will be made. But Shovel Knight will forever be remembered as one of the best among them.

Tactical Intervention is (to be very blunt and honest) a very pathetic game. With several years behind the development, one would think it would have some care put into it. Yes, I understand it's free, but I've seen a hand full of free games that SHOULD have been paid for. For example, Path of Exile. A very well-developed game with not very many devs. Anyway, back to this pile of stinky garbage. The objective HUD is smack dab in the middle of your screen. A circle around your crosshair indicating where the bomb is, where your team-mates are, etc.. Could they honestly not think of a better place to put it? Originality doesn't necessarily mean functionality. Especially in the gaming market. You find what works and stick to it. Altering already perfect HUD and objective markers is just an idiotic move on any game developer's part. The sounds in this game seem as though ripped right from a sound-effect website. The graphics are hideous even for Gamecube era games. Movement feels extremely stiff and clunky, with no real ability to get out of line of fire. If you're being shot at, you're dead. There's no moving away or any hope to get out of line of sight. Don't even get me started on aiming in the first place. The first weapon you get in the game is a rifle that should be semi-automatic, as a full auto bullet-sprayer. This weapon is horrible. I stuck with a shotgun due to it's rediculous range and damage. You can kill people from 25+ meters easily with a single shot. That's if you can even aim in this "game". The trailer looked highly promising, but is very rapidly smashed by it's horrid controls, horrid gameplay, graphics, and mechanics. The vehicles are like trying to steer a rubber tube sliding downhill on ice. There is absolutely no hope for this game, or those who play it, which are a different story entirely. I'll let you experience them for yourself.

While playing this game, I had the impression that is was "rushed out the door", as numerious bugs, AI problems and design issues were easy to spot.
When first playing the game, AI problems are not an issue, however after 2 hours or so you will be banging your head off the wall.
Here is a short list of issues I have with this game after 2+ hours of game play:
1: Hunger cycle is too short. This is a game breaking flaw.
2: If you have harvesting set as a higher priority than cooking, your peope will eat the raw food instead of cooking it.
3: If you have item crafting set as a higher priority than chopping, your people will often times not bother to chop trees in tree farm to make stiff with.
4: After a couple hours of game play, your people will only do the top 2 or 3 proprity chores, and ignore everything else.
5: Never cook anything that requires 2 or more different ingrediants. People will often times stoop what they are doing, and the ingrediants they are "holding" dissapears.

11: An infinate loop of "gathering - cooking - eating" happens WAY too often, mostly caused by the short hunger cycle. This happens reguardless how filling the food is.
12: Raw and prepared food containers do not work.

Once upon a time, Volition made an open-world game that got positive reception, yet everyone considered it to be a GTA clone. So they tried for a second time, and released a comedic sequel that, yet again, everyone considered to be a GTA clone. And thus they tried for a third time, creating a game that exceeds the absurd, and goes beyond the over-the-top. Saints Row: The Third was born. Now, it has a unique identity to call its own.
Saints Row 3 is explosive, fun, and crude. The game relishes itself in the most immature and ridiculous things that its developers can conjure; one moment, you're chaperoning "escorts" and tigers around the city; next thing you know, you're driving light cycles in VR, and shooting mascots in a murder-themed game show. Seriously, nothing ever makes sense in this game. Have you ever wacked someone with a 48" 3-pound♥♥♥♥♥♥♥bat? Make your dream come true, and stick that thing up the citizens of Steelport.
But what do you actually do in SR3? It isn't just mindless fun, is it? Well, it actually is. However, you're given the task of growing your gang, and taking revenge on The Syndicate. To do that, you need to earn - or steal - money by doing various mindless activities across the map. With enough money, you can spend it on skills, bonuses, and customization options. Only when you're strong enough, can you handle the huge mobs and vehicles that come in your way. You want to rule Steelport? Buy all of the properties, participate in the activities, and defeat your rival gangs. Better yet, do it in a gimp suit, with your co-op buddy dressed as a priest, and an army of nudists backing you. Too bad the gimp-driven pony carts only appear in one mission. Good thing we have talented modders, right?
And there you have it.

-Excellent Bosses in this game such as the axe man.

Cons:
-The AI again is very poorly implemented. The AI will run into zombies, the axe man, chainsaw man and many other enemys. The AI is also perfect at stealing items and not using them.
Overall this game is a brilliant game to grace the Resident Evil series and is a must for all Resident Evil fans and other gamers. I hope Capcom can make more Resident Evil games like Resident Evil 5 but just bring back more horror aspect to the games. By general standard this is not a "complete game"
Graphic of this game is....let's say retro.
AI in this game is poor.
Last update v14 was released in September, 2013. V13 was released in May, 2013. The changes that was implemeneted in these patches contains very few contents and minimun bug fixes. It seems like the developers just don't care or hoping that modders can fix everything for them.
LIke every other games in the same genre that's on greenlight, AI in this game is poor.
and there's a breakdown of their "about the game" info page on steam
"The game brings a fresh new take on the city building/management genre by introducing many RPG features. "
Nope, there are many others just like it, the game is heavily inspired by many other game and it offers nothing "fresh" and "new".
"n Towns you manage a settlement on top of an active dungeon. Instead of playing the hero who delves deep into the dungeon, how about playing the town that houses and caters to the hero's needs?"
Heroes don't need jack. All it takes to attract heroes is to boost your population and have an area set up as "tavern". The "tavern" area doesn't have to be enclosed. Meaning that heores will be perfectly fine sleeping on the ground looking at stars just because you painted a 3x3 block purple and called it "inn".
There is no intereaction between your townsfolk and heroes at all. They have very poor AI and die very easily if you are new to the game. Gearing up these heroes is not an easy process and sometimes random. You need to put the items on their path or "hangout" area and hope that they pick up the gear you want them to wear.
"Both the RPG and strategic aspects will be fleshed out over a series of sprawling dungeons."
The only RPG elements involved in the dungeons is "there are mobs, they drop loot". The only strategic aspect of the game is "pray to the gods that when you dig down, you don't dig directly into a group of mobs because your townsfolk are dumb and they will not flee" and "dig open dungeon walls bit by bit and hope your townsfolk don't try to engage the mobs"
There is minimun strategy and minimun RPG elements in this game. Townsfolk has a hunger bar, a sleep bar and a happiness bar and that's it. There is no "leveling" for your townsfolk and leveling for heores is meaningless.
"Attract travelling heroes that will independently explore the dungeons below, fight off monsters, gain levels, special skills and collect the best loot they can find in order to clear the land of all evil!"
Like stated above, there is no interactions between you and the heroes.
About the loots, here's the funny part. Once you clear a dungeon, it's best not to collect loot from the dungeon because there's a billion of trash loot lying on the ground. Heroes will pick up gears when they feel like it. It's best to leave those in the dungeon.
The best loot is often not dropped in the dungeon. Once you have a market set up, travelling merchants will come and they will randomly sell you the best gear in the game. So in order to get the best loot in game, you priorites a market over anything else. Regardless your progression in the game, you will be able to buy best gears purely based on luck.
"Craft unique weapons, trade with exotic items, obtain randomized loot, set up devious death traps and build a settlement capable of holding back the forces that come up from the depths!"
Mobs in the dungeon will come to your town only when a hero engages them with low health and decides to run away. Those mobs will not stop chasing the fleeing hero until one of them is dead. This normally leads to a few townies dying because of the poorly designed AI.
There is nothing unique about the weapon and item designs. They are very generic items. I wouldn't describe loots to be "randomized". 90% of them are trash loots and 99% of them are just junk on the ground waiting to be sold when a merchant arrives (if that merchant has enough money and willing to buy these crap. normally they just don't want them at all).
In summary, this game is not worth its asking price. Yes, it's about the price of a very fancy subway sandwitch in Canada but I assure you that you will get more satisfaction out of that sandwitch than this game. If you are desprately looking for a game like this, wait for it to go on sale and do not expect any updates because it's not very likely.
There is a modding scene for this game. It's small and I suggest you to go to their forum and check out more information there. Simply google "towns" and you'll be able to access their website and forum.
Thank you.
