The concept of this game is neat, but it is lacking a lot. I've played it a while ago, and I dare say it was a bit better back then than it is now. Development seems to be quite stagnant here. At the end of this review you'll read what I really recommend instead.
The tutorials are, to say the least, quite braindead. They could've made it more interactive, but as it is now it's quite dull. Some details seems to be badly written as I didn't always get the desired results.
The military in the game is kind of a joke. If I see a spider or any other enemy, why oh why can't I just go rightclick it and tell the military to go attack it? Or at least something that enables me to make more use of the military than 'patrol there' and hope that they actually will engage the enemy on their patrol routes.
The actual mining is quite non-intuitive. Somehow I wasn't able to mine certain areas until I moved up/down. It's rather hard to see what level you are at currently, and there are no size indicators in the area you're about to mark to be mined. And you can build a roof but somehow I have not managed to build a roof on top of my shacks. I might give that a try again another time, but the game seems so pointless that it isn't really motivating to.
You have absolutely no connection with those little guys you're ordering around. You can see some basic stats, but all those little peoples aren't really special. It's lacking a certain something there, and I can't quite place my finger on it. Let's just say that you don't really care who they are, as long as they get the jobs done already. There's no feel of a story attached to it.
Assigning jobs and assigning productions/stockpiles is quite a chore. So much a chore that you just leave everything up to the defaults. A quick overview is rather impossible. Sure, they do have a list of civilians, and a stockpile list. But instead of having it present a clear overview, it's rather a messy job. I think they focused way too much on iconized displays with tiny numbers inside. In cases like this, a table-format would probably make more sense. We want to know some nice numbers and some other stats, not how pretty they look in a circle with one tiny number in there.
Speaking about iconized displays.. the GUI is very clunky. It is definitely not polished and is just bare bones style. Nothing fancy about it and there are options lacking. The build icons are non-intuitive. If you want to go back a level in the menu, the 'go back' arrow is in a different location every level. So you can't just 'click click click' fast to get to the root level. No, you have to check every time you went back one level in the menu where the back button is at now. Nothing has been streamlined in this game.
If you are charmed by this kind of game, I can recommend a different one instead which is still in active development and is rather more promising. Take it from me, you want to try
. It might be in Early Access, but I've been playing it for a while (on Desura and now also on Steam), and it is way more finished than this Towns ever will be.

Possibly the only part that could be considered innapropriate is if you lose, a zombie walks into your house, and eats your brains. It doesn't actually SHOW the zombie eating your brains, just a message pops up saying, "A Zombie Ate Your Brains!" It's up to you if you think thats innapropriate, but honestly, I don't think it's something to get worked up over.
Now to talk about what this game is really about! You start out in a normal house, when suddenly zombies try to invade your home! You have to grow special plants to defend your house, such as thhe Peashooter and the Potato Mine.
This game comes with 5 chapters that each contain 9 levels. A normal PvsZ level takes aproximately 5 Minutes, I'm not sure exactly. To add on to that, they even have awesome minigames to put your PvsZ skills to the test!
This is one of the best time-consuming games i have ever played. I highly reccomend you purchase it, as in my opinion is the best tower defense game I have ever seen.

Takes the best of GTA: San Andreas--gang warfare, character personalisation, missions where you recreate scenes from cool movies, awesome music--and ditches the dating simulation and clumsy flying missions. Then it pitches everything so far over-the-top you look down on where the top used to be from the surface of Mars. You fight masked wrestlers and technogeeks in Tron cosplay and rob a bank by lifting the safe through the roof with a chopper. In GTA you’re a mobster, in Saints Row you’re a comic-book supervillain.
As comics often are it's juvenile. There’s a slider for sex appeal that determines the size of your breasts or pants bulge. But what’s shocking is that, in spite of its crassness, it’s well-written. Banter between characters is so snappy I delay finding the checkpoint to hear it. The story's as entertaining as the rampages between missions.

Definitely a game for those who like CS games. What won me over in comparison to CS was the dynamic gameplay with the destruction and abilities of the opoerators. From a more casual game like COD, expect to put some time and research on learning some mechanics if you want to better your knowledge and skill. The high skill ceiling may be off putting to some, but by playing with friends, it will make the experience of learning enjoyable together. I like that even if your characters ability is countered (very few are directly countered), but you as a skilled shooter can still carry a team (which sounds counter-intuitive with the teamwork apect, but rarely will you have to carry that hard with skilled shooting). I've only had this game for a month and I've already logged 80+ hours on it. Don't be afraid to buy the starter edition either, as the work to buy new operators is comparable to League of Legends with the grind to get good ops. If the game is on sale or you are okay with paying $40, then go ahead and buy the full game. The main difference in versions is just the amount of work you need to put for new characters, but as long as you enjoy the game, that work will still be fun. My warning to you is that there are toxic people in the game as with any game, but if you can live with some mean people on occasion you will have a good time with the nice majority, and I in particular have met good people in this game that have taught me and made my experiance very nice.

This review could be summed up as: GET THIS GAME NOW!
For those of you who want a more elaborate exposition, Shovel Knight is a retro-styled platforming game from Yacht Club Games that has an incredible appeal in terms of design, gameplay and music. If you have had the pleasure of playing the original Mega Man series, then you'll feel right at home with Shovel Knight as the creators have spent as much attention to detail as the legendary teams behind that series on this game.
Smooth controls allow you to fluidly turn a jump into a shovel-pogo on an enemy or bouncy obstacle and use the relics to chain in more awesome moves. The difficulty varies, but is challenging for both veterans and new players, the soundtrack is in a word spectacular in 8-bit style, where stages and bosses have their own theme, sometimes multiple ones. Aside from the main quest, there are so many optional bits, easter eggs and sidequests to dig into that you'll be astounded.
I could go on for quite a while longer, but let me point this out: This game has proven such an incredible experience that even at full price it's the best buy you could make this year on Steam.
Edit: Two years later and with the DLC campaigns added, its still awesome.

This review could be summed up as: GET THIS GAME NOW!
For those of you who want a more elaborate exposition, Shovel Knight is a retro-styled platforming game from Yacht Club Games that has an incredible appeal in terms of design, gameplay and music. If you have had the pleasure of playing the original Mega Man series, then you'll feel right at home with Shovel Knight as the creators have spent as much attention to detail as the legendary teams behind that series on this game.
Smooth controls allow you to fluidly turn a jump into a shovel-pogo on an enemy or bouncy obstacle and use the relics to chain in more awesome moves. The difficulty varies, but is challenging for both veterans and new players, the soundtrack is in a word spectacular in 8-bit style, where stages and bosses have their own theme, sometimes multiple ones. Aside from the main quest, there are so many optional bits, easter eggs and sidequests to dig into that you'll be astounded.
I could go on for quite a while longer, but let me point this out: This game has proven such an incredible experience that even at full price it's the best buy you could make this year on Steam.
Edit: Two years later and with the DLC campaigns added, its still awesome.

I've got to say I'm glad I got it when it was on sale. It's definitely more of a $5 game, not a $15 one. If you find this game at $5 or less, then think about it, but any more than that and you might want to find something that got finished. This review is based off of my experience and the regular price though, so overall I don't recommend it. There's no way there isn't better games out there than this.
Let me start with what I found to be good about the game though, since I did technically like it. I never played this Gnomoria that everyone else is mentioning, and with little function in Minecraft for watching a village come to life even with mods, I found it to be a great idea. Even though it was immediately obvious from opening the game that it was far from finished I found myself enjoying finding different combinations and ways of getting my limited villagers to survive.
Secondly, the zoning. By assigning a zone type to an area the area gains a particular function, while losing other functions. This makes building a city kind of cool because the buildings one makes will actually function the way that they've zoned it to. Added to the fact that, if one could figure out the menus easily, one could get the villagers to use and upkeep these zones automatically, without any help from the player.
Then there's just the world in general. Although the maps are small, they generate well, and they're fun and easy to shape. If a player shows enough patience, it actually is possible to build the kinds of places they show in the promotional material and screenshots.
The last thing I thought was really cool was being able to put writing on tombstones and books and things. I can go through my village and remind myself of the events that passed. Who died, who did the best, or helped the most – it felt like making a civilization, even though it was really just a town at best. Epic legacies in a tiny town.
Now, the wonderful negatives that ruined it. Unfortunately there are a lot of these, so I'll put a chunk of them in point form;
*Odd menu style. That took a while to get used too, and I feel like things could be implemented better.
*Moving items is a hassle, or just plain confusing.
*Can't place enough text in books, graves, signs, etc, and can't use characters like “/”, making labels and text look flat and odd, like they were written by some 10 year old that was too lazy to use any punctuation. Breaks immersion.
*The use of scaffold isn't clearly stated to be useful, and so it can be difficult to find out about it and how to use it properly to build better buildings. There isn't a lot of direct help on the internet either, so simply building can be a hassle. Also, making second floors is too tricky.
*Extremely limited character sprites. Everyone will have too many clones for you to care about them. They also all have weird french-sounding names, even if playing the English version, and though unimportant, feels like it takes away from immersion into the game.
*The armour doesn't fit on the sprites properly. Sometimes this is funny, but it just isn't proper for a game that costs $15.
*The first floor dungeons, though easy to pass, are too expansive and too full of monsters. There's no easing into it at all, making the game feel less thought-out and more slapped together. Also an immersion breaker.
*Next to no updates. These people probably don't care anymore, and it's showing. They don't update anywhere near as much as they should, and some of the bugs in the game could really use some fixes.
*The bugs. Seriously, the game is definitely not a finished product. Amusing, but certainly not finished.
And lastly, though kind of silly, what I found to be the game-breaker;
The weapons you make, buy, and find are cool and all, but it isn't hard for some "hero" to waltz by and take all your good stuff, leaving your citizens and soldiers pretty close to defenceless. Some heroes. I worked hard on that stuff. “That hat was for the blacksmith!” and “she needed that spear to save her life!” might become alarmingly common frustrations.
So yeah. Ends up under $5? It'll amuse you long enough. $15? It's cute, but it ain't that cute, just go back to your Minecraft mods and this "Gnomoria" everyone else is talking about.

I was initially hopeful for this game. It looked super interesting and I thought why not. So a few dollars later I had a shiney top-down minecraft. Similarly powered by java (woo hoo).
Sadly the game really does fall quite short of expectation.
The menus are hard to navigate. There is no tutorial to speak of. You can instruct your citizens to build things, but if you do not have the supplies to make it, instead of telling you why you can't, it will sit, forever until you produce the needed materials or manually cancel the order. You cannot change the camera angle (which gets really aggravating). The perspective makes it really difficult build a lot of the structures shown on the store page. There is exactly one music track that will drive you absolutly crazy after a few hours of playing. Your citizens are difficult to direct. For example if you task them with digging a hole. if they find water, and proceed to drown in that water. ALL your assigned citizens will continue to drown themselves until you cancel the order, which is really hard to do, when it takes 5 seconds a person to drown and about 2 minutes for you to navigate to the cancel order screen, get to the right layer, and cancel the order.
There is some good however. Once you look up on the wiki how to pretty much play the game, it becomes more of a meditative visual rather than an actual game. I stopped at about 40 citizens and just let them do their thing. They were feeding and growing and happy. They did not require any input from me. I watched them tear through dungeons and make food, build things. It was nice
You can also build some pretty neat structures if you have the patience for it. But it will drive you crazy at first due to the limited visual angles .
I will recommend this game IF you buy it on sale. However I would most assuredly not pay full price for it.

I know what you're thinking... oh, another indie retro platformer.
is definitely that, but it's also the finest example of that in the last few years.
Developed by
, This is yet another success of how Kickstarter can bring you a game that would of not otherwise been made via  traditional funding methods.
Shovel Knight takes the retro-ness to a new level though. It's incredibly faithful, whilst removing some of the limitations of the NES console (like sprite flickering, and some other limitations). The developers stuck to the original NES color palette, though they added an 1 or 2 extra colours as Yacht Club insisted that they couldn't make certain things look the way they wanted without the extra colours. It's outstounding what they did with the limitations. The pixel art is absolutely full of character, talent and is wonderful to look at.
You play as a knight that wields a shovel -  aka Shovel Knight (how awesome, right?). The story is quite simple, Shovel Knight and Shield Knight fought alongside each other, traversing across the world seeking treasure together. But for reasons that I won't spoil, you are seperated. After secluding himself and griefing for Shield Knight, he digs up his shovel again, hoping to find and rescue Shield Knight.
The sound uses a sound engine that was used in some of the Japanese Famicom console or something along those lines. You can even put the sound track onto a NES cartridge, and it would play on a NES! (Sadly, the whole game wouldn't though - as I mentioned, they removed some of the limitations that wouldn't make it possible to play it on a NES console). It definitely nails the authenticity of 8bit sound.
The music is probably why I instantly fell in love with Shovel Knight within the first 30 seconds of the first level. What a cracker of a track. Every single level has a track that you will be bopping and humming melodies to for days. This isn't music that is 'good for chiptunes', it is GREAT music that just happens to be chiptunes.
As every track has a theme, so do the levels. Every level has a themed boss (Propeller Knight, Polar Knight and Mole Knight - for instance), where the whole level will be themed around the boss mechanically and visually. Every level adds some new mechanic and challenge that keeps it fresh as you progress through the game.
The razor tight controls are why it's so fun to play (I would recommend playing with a pad). It takes elements from certain games like Duck Tales, Megaman and Mario... and combines them with some light RPG elements. What you have is a game that feels, looks and plays oldschool. But has the polish and design tendancies of a more modern game. It gets quite challenging towards the towards the end of the game too, but newgame+ is where you will find the real challenge as checkpoints are halved, enemies do more damage, and most food platters that heal you will instead, turn into bombs that will try to bury you.
I can't really praise Shovel Knight enough. It does so much right, and if it was released 20 years ago, it probably would of been hailed as a classic.

If you miss the games of the past, when platforming, tight controls, and simplistic combat were the main things you looked for in a game, Shovel Knight has got you covered, in spades. With a map screen reminiscint of Super Mario Bros. 3, 8 bosses much like those found in Mega Man games, a handful of secret weapons, and two-to-three button controls, Shovel Knight plays alot like those games from 0ver 20 years ago.
For the most part, of you like Mega Man games, you'll probably like Shovel Knight. Shovel Knight must hit enemies with his shovel instead of blasting them from afar (sub-weapons will let you, for some magic), but both his size and movements work alot like that of Mega Man.
Pros of this game include, but not limited to -
Easy to use controls that never feel punishing, if you die, it was your fault.
Awesome chiptune soundtrack that hearkens back to Mega Man games.
Fairly lengthy game the first time through. Can take from 3 - 5 hours depending on if you want to find EVERYTHING or not.
Inventive level design. One stage everything may be pitch black and having you use background lightning to see where to jump, another you're on the back of a giant, lava-immune stag beetle.
Armor and Shovel upgrades can be bought that will change the game a bit, but not necessarily be just a straight stat upgrade. An example - Conjurer's Coat, you get an extra 50 maximum mana, and enemies drop more mana, but you take twice the normal damage.
Bosses that like to attack randomly. Bosses have alot of attacks they can use, but not necessarily in a set order. Be ready for anything.
Cons of this game? Well, there are no lives, you simply lose part of your current gold, which can be regained from the flying bags. As a guy that grew up with the more challenging games of the day, Shovel Knight didn't give me much trouble.
Even while being a bit on the easy side, this game is a sure recommendation from me. Shovel Knight takes inspiration from alot of the games of old, but makes it's own unique game from it. For $15, it's a great value.

A lot of people compare this game to GTA. However, Saints Row The Third is GTA on steroids.
Gameplay: Similar to GTA Saints Row has an open world, a set of guns you can unlock, main story missions and lots of side missions. The main difference is that Saints Row is very over the top. You can go completely ham with crazy weapons, blow everything up, use goofy weapons (including a giant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, go berserk in a tank where you have to destroy as much as you can and what not. This game is purely to have fun and they made sure there are lots of way to do so.
Another thing I really loved is the character customization. You can tweak pretty much anything you want. The model can be finetuned to your personal tastes. Even small details like make-up are available to use. You can choose from dozens of different outfits. One thing however, the models are censored. Boobs and the nether regions will be blurred out if you decide to run around naked or without underwear.
Story: Sure there is a story going on, but personally I didn't really care and this isn't a story driven game. It's all about shooting and blowing things up. There are a lot of mature themes, so this is definitely not a game for younger audiences.
Graphics: The models look pretty nice to me. I'd say they look comparable to the models from the Witcher 2. (I played both games on maxed out settings). What I did find a little bit annoying is the view distance. It's pretty short. You'll see cars and buildings pop up randomly when they enter the range of vision, instead of smoothly coming in to vision like they would in real life.
Conclusion:
This is definitely a game I'd recommend. You can turn off your brain and just have fun for hours. I didn't even notice how I played 6 hours straight, thinking I had played for about 2 hours. It's a very entertaining game which will provide you with hours and hours of enjoyment. Worth every penny so far.

Here are the ingredients you will need!
Ravioli Dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 pinch salt, 1 teaspoon olive oil, 2 eggs, 1 1/2 tablespoons water.
Ravioli Filling: 1 (8 ounce) container ricotta cheese, 1 (4 ounce) package cream cheese, softened, 1/2 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, 1/2 cup provolone cheese, shredded, 1 egg, 1 1/2 teaspoons dried parsley.
Pesto-Alfredo Cream Sauce: 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 cloves garlic, crushed, 3 tablespoons prepared basil pesto sauce, 2 cups heavy cream, 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, 1 (24 ounce) jar marinara sauce.
1. Mound the flour and salt together on a work surface and form a well. Beat the teaspoon of olive oil, 2 eggs, and water in a bowl. Pour half the egg mixture into the well. Begin mixing the egg with the flour with one hand; use your other hand to keep the flour mound steady. Add the remaining egg mixture and knead to form a dough.
2. Knead the dough until smooth, 8 to 10 minutes; add more flour if the dough is too sticky. Form the dough into a ball and wrap tightly with plastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
3. While the dough is resting, prepare the ravioli filling. Combine the ricotta cheese, cream cheese, mozzarella cheese, provolone cheese, egg, and parsley and mix well. Set the filling aside.
4. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and pesto sauce and cook for one minute. Pour in the heavy cream, raise the heat to high, and bring the sauce to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the Parmesan cheese and stir until the cheese melts. Remove the pan from the heat and keep warm.
5. Meanwhile, in a separate saucepan, warm the marinara sauce over medium-low heat.
6. Preheat an oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water to make the egg wash.
7. Roll out the pasta dough into thin sheets no thicker than a nickel. To assemble the ravioli, brush the egg wash over a sheet of pasta. Drop the filling mixture on the dough by teaspoonfuls about one inch apart. Cover the filling with the top sheet of pasta, pressing out the air from around each portion of filling. Press firmly around the filling to seal. Cut into individual ravioli with a knife or pizza cutter. Seal the edges.
8. Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Stir in the ravioli, and return to a boil. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the ravioli float to the top and the filling is hot, 4 to 8 minutes. Drain well.
9. Grease a baking sheet. Place the cooked ravioli on the sheet pan and bake in the preheated oven until brown, about 4 minutes.
10. To serve the ravioli, divide them among four warmed serving bowls. Drizzle the marinara sauce over the ravioli and then top with the cream sauce.

This is a great game ruined by Ubisoft. I've never been as invested into a game as much as I've been invested in Siege. So much that I got the Starter Edition and played enough to grind for all the operators, including the DLC ones. I find myself playing Terrorist Hunt more than multiplayer because I suck at multiplayer. Still when you have a match with a team that communicates, doesn't vote kick you because you can't clutch, or if the hit registration doesn't enrage you, or you don't lose connection to the server, you can have a blast. Despite all of its problems, I find multiplayer bearable because of how intense and fun it can be. Alas, I'm not sure I could say the same about Terrorsit Hunt. First things first. No dedicated server. P2P matchmaking is one of the worst things for games. Countless times I've entered a game only for the host to leave and thus terminate the game for everyone after he dies in the first few seconds. Or the host has a questionable connection and we get pings within the 1000-3000 range. Some days are better than others. But when you get back home from a long day at work and you just want to kick back and enjoy some terrorist hunt, because you're just too tired to pay attention or plan tactics in multiplayer, beware, because this might just not be your lucky day. First match, host terminates after he dies in the beginning. Second match, connection to server lost. Next match, you get teamkilled because some retard thinks it's funny to shoot you. Next match, everyone has 3000+ ping. And you find out it's 1 a.m. and you still haven't had one successful match after an hour of playing. Not to mention the long waiting times in the lobby. In fact, when I visit the stats page my play time is only half of what steam shows. Although, to be fair, I have spent quite some time in the menus customizing, perusing etc.
TL;DR Ubisoft servers inbound. If you're mostly going to play multiplayer get it. If not, don't get it for terrorist hunt. You'll have a lot of fun, but after a while the novelty wears off and the technical issues start getting under your skin. Perhaps things will be better after Operation Health. But I think that mostly concerns multiplayer rather than terrorist hunt.

I like the concept of this game - uncensored and unrestricted gta.
Its open world, has almost unlimited possibilities and tons of fun. Amazing gameplay. No linearity in the missions, so most of the time you can use handguns or tanks and jets, whatever you like.
Everything is amazing, except the quality – you will be constantly frustrated by the AI and physics. Your AI companions will often die in the missions because they don’t know how to cover, and will catch all bullets, die, and you will need to run under fire to revive them in a short time limit. They will block your pathways, they will run in front of your rockets, etc. Sadly, they will do anything possible to ruin your gameplay. Most of the time they are useless and make everything worse, it’s very annoying.
Controls are very weird. For example you can’t change weapons while running. Or if you want to enter vehicle in the middle of the fight to cover - often you will see character casually walking to the car soaking all the bullets. Controls are unresponsive, you will be amazed how bad and wrong character movements sometimes are.
Comparing to GTA – this game is 2 years younger than GTA  IV, but it still has worse graphics. But SR has much more freedom. Surprisingly, a lot of Saints Row gameplay elements were added to GTA  V.
Despite all the blingbling, and possibilities, and fun - the poor quality ruins everything. It’s like a supermodel with broken arms and legs… Developers could spend like additional half a year for QA to make a decent GTA killer, sadly they haven’t done this. Saints Row III is the definition of disappointment. So close to be great, but released unfinished for some reason.
EDIT: I have completed it for 100%. And I'm changing review to "not recommended". Because of Mayhem minigames (screw the guns, you will never finish it properly. Just horrible, this gameplay can be acceptable for student's lab work, but not in the actual game in the market.
Go play GTA San Andreas instead.

Loved this game when I first started playing - great graphics, great physics, great "Feel" to it - you really do feel like youj're out there on the shore casting and reeling in, and when you get a strike you feel the battle with the fish.
But...
Then in the course of a day or two something changed. Where before I was pulling in a decent number of good-sized bass with my spinning rod and jigs, suddenly I go hours without a single bite. I went an entire 2 days of a rather expensive fishing trip not getting a nibble, on a lake that had always been super productive the day before, and yes I was fishing with the right bait, rod, reel, hook, and at the right time of day. I went from 3 dozen trophy bass in a few days to no fish at ALL.  Needless to say, it was obvious they had made a change to the game that decreased the number of strikes bigtime.
To make the game more "Realistic?" Maybe. After all, who can really go to a lake and catch 20 23 lb bass in 4 hours? But you know what I have to say to that? If I want super-realism, I can get in my car and drive to my local lake and stand around for half the day casting and reeling and not catch a single fish. The reason I want a fishing GAME is so I can escape to a fantasy world where I can catch a lot of fish, unlike in real life where I basically suck at it! And no I'm not saying the game should be some easy joke where anyone can just grab a pole and catch a ton of trophy fish, no skills required. But for those of us who took the time to learn the right equipment to use, the right baits that work with the right kinds of fish, the right times of day, and the right techniques to use to catch each fish (stop and go, slow and straight, lift and drop, etc.) - we should be rewarded with good catches! And yes, plenty of them!
Not sure if this is a temporary setback, or not, but time will tell. I can say that if the game mechanics have now been changed to the point where I have to sit around for hours at my monitor not catching a damn thing - just like in real life - then I probably won't play Fishing Planet any longer. Plenty of other games I can escape into for a few hours to get away from reality that provide the rewards I'm looking for in a game.

NOTE TO THE READER: THIS GAME IS BEING FREQUENTLY UPDATED SO THIS REVIEW WILL BE CHANGED ACCORDINGLY THIS REVIEW IS ALSO NOT FINISHED
AUG, P2000, M4, do these guns stir any memories of a certain game? If that game is Counter Strike, then that's a good thing; unfortunately this review isn't about Counter Strike, though you may have figured that out. Minh "Gooseman" Le was the co-creator of the original "Counterstrike" before Valve bought it. Coincidentally, Le is working on a game that is referred to as the "spiritual successor to Counterstrike". Tactical Intervention, according to Le, fills that position. Does Tactical Intervention live up to Le's viewpoint of it? Let's find out.
Factions and Game modes
Being a Free to Play game, and being similar to Counter Strike; Global Offensive, Tactical Intervention has no story mode. You may recognize the player tags: Counter Terrorist and Terrorist. Tactical Intervention is an FPS with game modes, once again, similar to Counter Strike. These include, Deathmatch, Bomb Defusal, and Hostage Rescue, as well as a new one called VIP Escort, which includes two game modes within it where the players have to escort a VIP NPC by car to an extraction, or one where the Player is the VIP and must reach an extraction poit on foot or by car depending on the map.
Playability
Controls in this game can be operated on both a controller and a mouse and keyboard. Both bindings can be found in the settings page in the controls. While having classic and popular control schemes or Spacebar to jump, WASD to move, Ctrl to crouch, SHIFT to sprint, TAB to check scores in game, and the first mouse button to shoot, Tactical Intervention also introduces some interesting and unique controls and abilities into the game such as the F button being the intercation key and the Q and E buttons alloing to lean. This is useful when leaning around corners  or cover to get a better shot at your opponent. Pressing the two keys simultaneously will activate something called Blind Fire Mode, where your character will hold thier gun above their head, this is useful when behind cover where this mode will allow you to shoot over cover without being hit, however you will not be able to see where your bullets are going. Like Counterstrike, this game is strictly a Non-ADS game, which introduces the second mouse button as a melee button and zoom in with snipers and scopes button. Pressing X will also make your character execute a roll that wil allow you to avoid fire from opponents, put out fire from Incendiary Grenades, and minimize damage if you roll from a high place as oppose to falling or jumping off of it.
Graphics
Tactical Intervention on the first day of beta apparently looked absolutely terrible; this has since changed and the game looks so great to me,  can't even run it at 60 FPS past the lowest setting(my laptop is not that good). I have cranked up the settings to max with Anti-Aliasing killing my FPS as it is known to do. On max the game looks amazing, lighting and shadows look great, character models are great, gun models are great, car look great, water looks amazing( and kills your FPS). Hostages and dogs could look better but for the most part they're fine. I can't give a total review of the graphics because like I said they're hard to run,(I can run Crysis 2 at 60 fps on the lowest setting on the lowest resolution, not so with this game). An Asus gaming laptop with an i7 CPU and a Nvidia 660 GPU can't run this at max at 60 FPS to give you an idea of the graphical capabilities of this game.
Similarities to Counter Strike: Global Offensive
Being referred to as the successor to Counter Strike, you would expect some similarites to the series, and there, to Global Offensive in particular. For example, as listed above, those are the guns available that are also in Global Offensive. Counter Terrorists VS Terrorists are an obvious similarity,mgame modes, the voting interface, and renting guns, are all the similarities I can think of, not that many huh?
Differences to Counter Strike: Global Offensive
Tactical Intervention really shines in this section, with the game being quite different from Global Offensive at this point. The first thing is the number of maps available, Tactical Intervention does not have nearly as many maps as Global Offensive enormous amount of official maps, player created maps, and workshop maps; Tactical Intervention has no Workshop page and only has 11 official maps, some of which are reused in Deathmatch and Missions. Player counts in the game are decided by the room owner, and this ranges from 4-20, with a set time limit that ranges from 10-60 minutes, with a set kill amount that ranges from 20-200. Room owners can also limit what guns can be used in Deathmatch, with checkboxes for Pistols, Snipers, Submachines Guns, Full-Auto guns, and Shotguns; the room owner can even un-check all the boxes and just have all players partake in a knife-fight. Armor, which we will get to later can also be banned from the room, friendly fire can be controlled as well with setting for Full Friendly Fire, Partial, Mirrored(your bullets hit you instead), or none at all. Collision between players is strictly limited to enemys and is always off for teammates. Finally, the room owner can choose whether or not the maps should cycle, or stay the same, though the owner can change any of these setting at any time only cetain ones will take effect immediately with many only occurring at the end of a match. Players can leave a match at any time, however they forfit all XP and  GP(game points) they might have earned during the match, there is no banning or join restrictions for leaving. Voice chat in-game is public only and there is no death restrictions on it. Type-chat can be either team or public, and there is also selective chat where the player will choose an option that will play an audio sound that is public as well as type a message in the chat that correspons to the audio, these include "Roger", "Taking Fire", "Need some help", and others. Voting in the game needs alot of work. Players can only kick players on their team, there is a time limit for votes, and a certai number of people MUST vote in order for the vote to go through, these include Kicking People, Restarting the Match(Missions only), Balancing Teams, and Turning on or off Voice chat. Renting guns in the game is done before entering a room in the shop, and guns are purchased with GP which is earned by killing enemies, shoting rival cars, killing the VIP, rescuing or capturing hostages, and delivering cases. Guns and equipement can rented or purchased permanately, with permanent take alot of GP, guns and epuipment can also be purchased or rented with real money.

Resident Evil 5 is a fun and frantic evolution of RE4's breakthrough gameplay and the series' horror themes.
Thirteen years ago, Capcom helped revolutionize the action adventure world with Resident Evil, a game that would define an entirely new genre dubbed "survival horror." In the years that followed, the series continued to build upon the standards set by the first game, Then, in 2005, Resident Evil 4 radically departed from its predecessors and broke new ground as a more action-oriented game. Resident Evil 5, the latest offering in the long-running series, expands on the action-heavy formula of its forerunner and is built from the ground up to support cooperative gameplay. Though it can no longer be considered a survival horror game, Resident Evil 5 manages to retain and effectively translate the most important aspect of that genre--tension--into its new mechanics. It crafts a fun, collaborative experience that will keep you on your toes the entire time.
Having two agents in the field lets you team them up to trade weapons or push dumpsters.
Ten years after the destruction of Raccoon City, former S.T.A.R.S. Alpha team member Chris Redfield is an agent of the B.S.A.A. This paramilitary anti-bio-organic weapons organization travels the globe to seek out and destroy Umbrella Corporation's creations, which have fallen into the hands of terrorists following the collapse of the multinational pharmaceutical company. When Chris gets a tip that a known weapons dealer will be making a big deal in the remote African nation of Kijuju, he heads there to put a stop to it and learn what he can about the mysterious doomsday project known only as Uroboros. Chris is joined by Sheva Alomar, a local B.S.A.A. agent, and together they battle wave after wave of infected villagers, horribly mutated monsters, and even series archnemesis, Albert Wesker.
The core combat mechanics haven't fundamentally changed since Resident Evil 4. The action still unfolds from an over-the-shoulder perspective, certain battles or cutscenes are accompanied by brief quick-time events, and you still have to stop moving to fire your weapon (though you gain a bit more mobility thanks to your newfound ability to walk sideways). Resident Evil 5's slow movement and gunplay take some time to get used to, and folks expecting a run-and-gun game may find the action too sluggish for their tastes. Fortunately, this slowness isn't really an issue within the game, because enemies are deliberate with their attacks and are better handled with a cool head and steady aim. Though the Xbox 360 controller is fully supported, the standard keyboard/mouse combo offers vastly superior aiming precision and control, which makes it by far the better option.
Regardless of how similar the combat in Resident Evil 5 is to its predecessor, the addition of a second character makes encounters feel quite different. Teamwork is necessary to take down more powerful enemies and bosses, and having someone to watch your back goes a long way toward keeping you alive. Furthermore, there have been radical changes made to the inventory management system. The immersion-breaking briefcase from the previous game is gone, and enemies no longer politely wait for you to rummage through your things because bringing up your armory doesn't pause the action. Each character can store up to nine items, and as long as you properly organize your inventory using the simple click-and-drag interface, all of your items are only a single keystroke away, which offers an unprecedented level of accessibility to your gear. It's often necessary to trade items with your partner, and keeping track of who has what at all times is crucial, especially during boss encounters.
Inventory management is easier than ever when you can click and drag items around with your mouse.
Sheva's artificial intelligence makes her a competent companion, though her degree of skill seems to rely more on her armaments than anything else. She is extremely good at using burst fire with a machine gun, for example, but she tends to waste ammo when equipped with a handgun. That said, at no point does she feel like extra baggage that needs babysitting (unlike some of the series' previous companions), and she can hold her own in a fight. Sheva really shines when there's someone else controlling her. Resident Evil 5 supports online co-op play through Games for Windows Live, and exploring Kijuju with a friend greatly enhances both the experience and the fun factor. Every game has the potential to go multiplayer, since other online players can join in on a free-for-all or invite-only basis if your game session is set up to allow this from the get-go.
Despite these conveniences, there are some frustrating hurdles that need to be leaped over before a partner can begin playing. Co-op isn't drop-in, so if someone joins, gameplay is interrupted and immersion is broken to some degree because the player who joined has to sit on the sidelines until the host either restarts or continues on to the next checkpoint. Another major problem is that players' main inventories are isolated from one another, and though you can trade healing items and ammunition, weapons are off-limits for exchange, making some battles more difficult if you're playing with a partner who is not as well equipped as you.
That's it for today. Be sure to read the chapter on gun maintenance--you WILL be tested!
Resident Evil 5 isn't a survival horror game, but that doesn't mean it hasn't learned a great deal from the genre. Tension is the central element of survival horror games, and in the past, tension has been conveyed by the gloomy settings, the sense of isolation, and the frustratingly clunky camera angles and controls. All RE5 does differently is convey this feeling through other outlets. Having a partner introduces new types of tension, because you're forced to rely on each other's support, find ways to manage both of your inventories during battles, and cover larger areas since enemies can appear from almost anywhere. Waves of enemies wax and wane with just the right frequency, and while the brightly lit environments make them less scary, they can be tough to deal with because they attack in large numbers and are smarter, faster, and stronger than their counterparts in previous games. Major encounters and boss fights are doled out with excellent pacing, and since you're never sure what to expect around the corner, you have to remain vigilant.
RE5 is one of the most visually stunning games available, and its huge variety of environments is meticulously detailed in every way. There are lots of large, open areas, and you'll constantly be on the move through them since there are usually so many enemies. In-game cutscenes are top-notch (though sometimes a bit over-the-top), and Chris and Sheva are incredibly well animated, especially their faces. If you happen to have the right collection of equipment, you can also take advantage of Nvidia's 3D Vision technology to experience Resident Evil 5 in stereoscopic 3D. The dialogue is often full of the trademark goofiness found in the series. The voice acting is competent, and when paired with the excellent facial expressions, it breathes a great deal of realism into the characters. Likewise, the fantastic orchestral soundtrack heightens the gameplay with everything from the low-key, ambient tracks that play during downtimes to the frantic, upbeat songs that accompany the massive boss battles.
THE GOOD
Beautifully detailed graphics and character animations
Having a partner enhances the fun and excitement while adding tension
Real-time menu system keeps you immersed
Plenty to do once you've beaten it
Superior keyboard/mouse controls
THE BAD
Frustrating hurdles to leap when joining an online game
Slow, deliberate movement and gunplay may not appeal to everyone
Can't swap weapons with a human teammate online

Resident Evil 5 is a fun and frantic evolution of RE4's breakthrough gameplay and the series' horror themes.
Thirteen years ago, Capcom helped revolutionize the action adventure world with Resident Evil, a game that would define an entirely new genre dubbed "survival horror." In the years that followed, the series continued to build upon the standards set by the first game, Then, in 2005, Resident Evil 4 radically departed from its predecessors and broke new ground as a more action-oriented game. Resident Evil 5, the latest offering in the long-running series, expands on the action-heavy formula of its forerunner and is built from the ground up to support cooperative gameplay. Though it can no longer be considered a survival horror game, Resident Evil 5 manages to retain and effectively translate the most important aspect of that genre--tension--into its new mechanics. It crafts a fun, collaborative experience that will keep you on your toes the entire time.
Having two agents in the field lets you team them up to trade weapons or push dumpsters.
Ten years after the destruction of Raccoon City, former S.T.A.R.S. Alpha team member Chris Redfield is an agent of the B.S.A.A. This paramilitary anti-bio-organic weapons organization travels the globe to seek out and destroy Umbrella Corporation's creations, which have fallen into the hands of terrorists following the collapse of the multinational pharmaceutical company. When Chris gets a tip that a known weapons dealer will be making a big deal in the remote African nation of Kijuju, he heads there to put a stop to it and learn what he can about the mysterious doomsday project known only as Uroboros. Chris is joined by Sheva Alomar, a local B.S.A.A. agent, and together they battle wave after wave of infected villagers, horribly mutated monsters, and even series archnemesis, Albert Wesker.
The core combat mechanics haven't fundamentally changed since Resident Evil 4. The action still unfolds from an over-the-shoulder perspective, certain battles or cutscenes are accompanied by brief quick-time events, and you still have to stop moving to fire your weapon (though you gain a bit more mobility thanks to your newfound ability to walk sideways). Resident Evil 5's slow movement and gunplay take some time to get used to, and folks expecting a run-and-gun game may find the action too sluggish for their tastes. Fortunately, this slowness isn't really an issue within the game, because enemies are deliberate with their attacks and are better handled with a cool head and steady aim. Though the Xbox 360 controller is fully supported, the standard keyboard/mouse combo offers vastly superior aiming precision and control, which makes it by far the better option.
Regardless of how similar the combat in Resident Evil 5 is to its predecessor, the addition of a second character makes encounters feel quite different. Teamwork is necessary to take down more powerful enemies and bosses, and having someone to watch your back goes a long way toward keeping you alive. Furthermore, there have been radical changes made to the inventory management system. The immersion-breaking briefcase from the previous game is gone, and enemies no longer politely wait for you to rummage through your things because bringing up your armory doesn't pause the action. Each character can store up to nine items, and as long as you properly organize your inventory using the simple click-and-drag interface, all of your items are only a single keystroke away, which offers an unprecedented level of accessibility to your gear. It's often necessary to trade items with your partner, and keeping track of who has what at all times is crucial, especially during boss encounters.
Inventory management is easier than ever when you can click and drag items around with your mouse.
Sheva's artificial intelligence makes her a competent companion, though her degree of skill seems to rely more on her armaments than anything else. She is extremely good at using burst fire with a machine gun, for example, but she tends to waste ammo when equipped with a handgun. That said, at no point does she feel like extra baggage that needs babysitting (unlike some of the series' previous companions), and she can hold her own in a fight. Sheva really shines when there's someone else controlling her. Resident Evil 5 supports online co-op play through Games for Windows Live, and exploring Kijuju with a friend greatly enhances both the experience and the fun factor. Every game has the potential to go multiplayer, since other online players can join in on a free-for-all or invite-only basis if your game session is set up to allow this from the get-go.
Despite these conveniences, there are some frustrating hurdles that need to be leaped over before a partner can begin playing. Co-op isn't drop-in, so if someone joins, gameplay is interrupted and immersion is broken to some degree because the player who joined has to sit on the sidelines until the host either restarts or continues on to the next checkpoint. Another major problem is that players' main inventories are isolated from one another, and though you can trade healing items and ammunition, weapons are off-limits for exchange, making some battles more difficult if you're playing with a partner who is not as well equipped as you.
That's it for today. Be sure to read the chapter on gun maintenance--you WILL be tested!
Resident Evil 5 isn't a survival horror game, but that doesn't mean it hasn't learned a great deal from the genre. Tension is the central element of survival horror games, and in the past, tension has been conveyed by the gloomy settings, the sense of isolation, and the frustratingly clunky camera angles and controls. All RE5 does differently is convey this feeling through other outlets. Having a partner introduces new types of tension, because you're forced to rely on each other's support, find ways to manage both of your inventories during battles, and cover larger areas since enemies can appear from almost anywhere. Waves of enemies wax and wane with just the right frequency, and while the brightly lit environments make them less scary, they can be tough to deal with because they attack in large numbers and are smarter, faster, and stronger than their counterparts in previous games. Major encounters and boss fights are doled out with excellent pacing, and since you're never sure what to expect around the corner, you have to remain vigilant.
RE5 is one of the most visually stunning games available, and its huge variety of environments is meticulously detailed in every way. There are lots of large, open areas, and you'll constantly be on the move through them since there are usually so many enemies. In-game cutscenes are top-notch (though sometimes a bit over-the-top), and Chris and Sheva are incredibly well animated, especially their faces. If you happen to have the right collection of equipment, you can also take advantage of Nvidia's 3D Vision technology to experience Resident Evil 5 in stereoscopic 3D. The dialogue is often full of the trademark goofiness found in the series. The voice acting is competent, and when paired with the excellent facial expressions, it breathes a great deal of realism into the characters. Likewise, the fantastic orchestral soundtrack heightens the gameplay with everything from the low-key, ambient tracks that play during downtimes to the frantic, upbeat songs that accompany the massive boss battles.
THE GOOD
Beautifully detailed graphics and character animations
Having a partner enhances the fun and excitement while adding tension
Real-time menu system keeps you immersed
Plenty to do once you've beaten it
Superior keyboard/mouse controls
THE BAD
Frustrating hurdles to leap when joining an online game
Slow, deliberate movement and gunplay may not appeal to everyone
Can't swap weapons with a human teammate online

Be warned, your early days in this game will challenge you to be good. Some things you want to know:-
Bullet drops over distance,
Different calibre gives different bullet velocity,
Bullets can penetrate through walls/objects (depending on calibre)
Communication is essential
Blending with the environment makes you invisible but staying there will make you killed by random shots as enemies gives away your position via bearing and map coordinates (even if you're a sniper camper from 1.5 KM away).
Role as fighter jets doesnt make you invincible. There are many ways to shoot you down.
Being a medic role doesnt grant you have unlimited supplies of medkit.

I'm trying to be nice about this review but I'm sorry I have to be honest and say this game is horrible for a Resident Evil title. I couldn't even stand the first 20 minutes without taking a break. First off, it's not Resident Evil. It's some game that was originally about gangs and cannibals in Africa and they snatched it up and tweeked it and slapped the name on the box. The more you play the more obvious it becomes. There are so many situations where you "use cover" and it really feels like a light gun game on rails. It's not Resident Evil, it's Shooting Gallery starring Resident Evil characters. If you hate zombies, you're in luck because you won't find a single one in the entire game. Lame.
I want to start by saying I really hate hate Quick Time Events and even if you know what buttons to press half the time the game doesn't pick up on your input properly. If you like QTEs and dying instantly for no reason other than to die and restart at the same QTE again, well, it's your lucky day. This title is chock full of QTEs and they really would be unecessary if the game was structured better. If you're expecting that good old inventory management feel that revolves around ammo management and semi-survival, forget it. This game has a million bazillion weapons and ammo/health everywhere. Then to make it worse in several places they stick you on a turret with infinite ammo. You already had infinite ammo/weapons a shop to buy stuff every five seconds and now you're on a turret with infinite machine gun bullets and rockets? Wtf? I don't know why sticking a player on a turret is so freaking popular in videos games these days but it's really overplayed. This game has an identity crisis that falls somewhere between Halo, Tomb Raider and Call of Duty and it really doesn't work.
The difficulty is easy and the graphics while dated for 2015 aren't too bad aside from some of the 3D models that look outright horrible, ie. the zombie dogs. Progression is very linear and sadly you won't familiarize yourself with areas or double back at all. You won't have your nice little storage box. You won't have fancy keys or items you build, you won't be solving puzzles. Do you remember progressing through areas with eerie well made environments and great ambience where each new room was unsettling or suspenseful? Digging up journals and finding bits of manuscript that creepily progress the storyline? Forget it, none of that here, you'll get a taste of it toward the end of the game but mostly you'll be running around like Modern Warfare with infinite revives PEW PEW! It just disgusts me.
The camera movement in this game gives me a headache. The camera movement speed is inconsistent when standing still compared to when moving and it's headache inducing. The quick menus for inventory management are nice but they are incomplete. I actually like the old pause menus in the originals and I understand eliminating them can create suspense but since there's little danger or scare factor there's no point. You can split stacks in the item menu but you can't do it efficiently, so you end up playing with a stack of 20 grenades instead of two. Why restrict inventory management like this? It doesn't make sense to do that because allowing the player to split item stacks exactly how they want has absolutely no negative impact on the challenge and having an inventory system that's advanced while neglecting completed features only frustrates the player.
Resident Evil games have always utilized the melee weapon as a huge factor in both survivability and ammunition management. Using melee to conserve ammo while gambling a risked close encounter and possible exchange on hp recovery items is essential to generating part of the fear and suspense that all good early RE games had. Unfortunately in this release it's thrown out the window completely. You don't need to conserve ammo so it doesn't even matter. There's a basic karate combo system that enhances immersion but that's not Resident Evil. Something about shooting everything once then punching it across the room like Kazuya from Tekken is out of place.
What's singleplayer? Chris said it best in game, "partner?" Oh yes that's right they stick an AI team mate up your @** the entire game. She constantly walks in front of you, combines green herbs, jams ammo into your inventory and constantly breathes heavily for no reason. You never feel alone or stranded with such unnecessary company. That trademark sense of despair that always floursihed in RE games is gone. Even the great feeling you had when you encountered an NPC in the older games was ruined because there's no solo progression. Your trusty partner is always there chatting it up and getting in the way. Sometimes she's helpful but most of the time she's just kind of there and if the partner dies you lose and start over. Why?! Let me play singleplayer as singleplayer and co-op as co-op. This game nearly drove me to tears it's so bad and then you have to deal with this.
What's sad is the overall feel of the game. One half feels like a reasonable attempt at the continuation of the saga and the other half feels like some completely different game mashed into one another. You press start and you're going straight from point A to point B with a load screen shop. There is little exploring, zero backtracking areas with new monsters, and not one dang typewriter/sanctuary room. Other games in the series are linear but you are dropped into a semi-open world and are left to explore and find keys, events, puzzles and bosses with a little room for discovery. There's a DLC pack called "Lost in Nightmares" that is a seperate quest that looks to be more like the original RE format and playstyle, I have yet to try it out, but it's probably better than the main game.
I kept thinking my opinion would change the further I progressed but it was only confirmed. The voice acting is good the graphics are pretty and some of the bosses are cool but the basic synopsis is simple. You're Chris Redfield, you're in Africa, and it sucks. You click start, Chris yells in the hand radio, "Come in HQ" text is displayed on the screen "This device has no power" he looks at his partners chest, there's a Quick Time Event, the end credits roll. Congratulations you just beat Resident Evil 5, I saved you the struggle. If you do decide to endure this misery I can say that the one thing you might have to look forward to is cleavage and side-boob. Every time you go through a door Chris will spin around and look right at his partner's sweater puppies. Being that this is a mature title and there's been practical nudity in previous titles, mainly Code Veronica, you can be comforted in knowing that this title will fall short leaving you only a fading memory of Chris Redfield's beard stubble and beautifully rendered sideboob.

но продвижение по карьере рыбака без доната застопорится - и тогда придется платить.
В итоге сложная ситуация:
играть иногда, просто для расслабона - рекомендую.
Но по итогу не рекомендую, ввиду жесткой механики доната.
Если разработчики заменят механику и будут монетизировать игру через взносы за входы в турниры - заработают меньше, но игра будет принята игроками гораздо лучше, чем в текущей версии, где механика заточена на донат.
Gameplay:
Fishing Planet - nice fishing simulator in the mechanics of F2P.
Given the stagnation of the genre - epic win.
However, the system of monetization is very tough - yes, the first dose is really free,
but progress on the career fisherman without donation very hard - and then have to pay.
As a result of the difficult situation:
i recommend play sometimes, just for fun.
But ultimately I did not recommend, in view of the rigid monetization mechanics.
If the developers replace the mechanics and the game will be monetized through fees for entries in tournaments - earn less, but the game players will be accepted much better than the current version, which is tuned mechanics to donations.

Saints Row: The Third is the third in the Saints Row series WHAT A SHOCKER RIGHT ? Well since it's the only surviving GTA clone it is surprising to some.
As a big fan of the first two games, I was excited to play 3 and to be honest ? I absolutely loved it.
Now before we begin, I got to say something. I think that the first Saints Row game was a very stiff game, but had tons of great ideas which were all fixed in the sequel which I though was amazing.
Saints Row 3 begins almost as soon as 2 ends. The Saints are now international superstars and have tons of merchandise like a clothing line and an energy drink. They can't even rob a bank without getting mobbed by rabid fans wanting an autograph. Saints getting so many fans brings them new enemies called the Syndicate. They push the Saints out of Stilwater and push them into Steelport a town they're not that familiar with, but they will do everything in they're power to take it over.
Now when I first bought the game I was pushed away, by Angry Joe who called the game a massive disappointment and other people calling it a massive misstep in the series. I finally decided to sit down and play and I got to say, I don't understand how the game is disappointing.
Gone are the reputation points, the stiff shooting is gone, the stiff driving is gone. The only bad things is that there's no gang missions. There's no separate gangs anymore, just a big gang which takes away the interesting characters in all gangs.
The comedy is also highly improved in this game. I felt the comedy in the first one worked well and fun jokes when they happened. I felt 2 had funny jokes, but they were trying too hard to be emotional and funny at the same time which didn't really mesh with the tone of the game. 3 fixes this problem and just goes off rails and it works charms for the series.
The soundtrack is also pretty decent. Nothing too special, I still think the second game had a better soundtrack, but it's still pretty decent.
Graphically this game looks amazing. I like the neon visuals and I feel they fixed the problem in saints row 2 which was that it was colorful and at the same time colorless.
The game took me 15 hours to finish the main story and all the story DLC's. I feel it was a good amount of time for what I paid for it and you can get the game pretty cheap on sale.
Overall I loved Saints Row 3. The wacky world of Steelport while might seem boring at first has things to do and you can do them in the most Action packed ways possible which provides hours of fun.
Final Rating:
8.5/10

I watched the trailer and passed on this game, then someone told me how funny and expansive it was.  It's not just a run around shooting everything game.  There is lots of shooting to be had for sure, but there are other activities to do to, flying, driving, playing in traffic to defraud insurance, car surfing, streaking, buying different clothes, weapons, tattoos, ect.
It's a lot like Grand Theft Auto, but not so serious.  Take a break and work on a challenge.  Kill people people dressed as various mascots.  Steal cars, customize them, and add them to your fleet.  Maybe do some windshield topedo by crashing into something and launching yourself through the windshield.  Carjack a vehicle and take the passengers on a wild hostage ride.
Good graphics, good physics, and good dialog.  A lot of entertainment for the money.  After playing this I went back to GTA 4 and I much prefer SR 3.  The graphics are better, more vibrant.  The controls are better.  Controlling cars with power slides is much easier making driving recklessly at breakneck speeds that much more satisifying when you have better control.
It might be an old (and dare I say wierd) game, but it's definitely well worth the money if you haven't gotten the chance to try it!

But the important thing to add here is that finally, after about 5 years, the long-awaited Gold Edition content has made its way to PC (and GFWL has been replaced with Steamworks integration). Lost in Nightmares, Desperate Escape, Mercenaries Reunion, Versus, and most importantly, Warrior Chris / Heavy Metal Chris, all in 60fps here on the PC version.
A giant majority of my total hours spent in this game have been in the extra game mode, Mercenaries and Mercenaries Reunion; this is a unique time attack mode where you aim to kill a set number of enemies, breaking time bonuses and getting melee kills for additional time as you progress to complete the stage. With 18 characters / costumes across both Mercenaries and Mercenaries Reunion, as well as three variations of each of the 8 stages (Merc, Reunion, and No Mercy), there is plenty of content to keep you playing and having a good time, single player. But throw that all in with the option to play Duo for these modes (as well as the game's feature co-op campaign), and you've added hundreds of hours of additional gameplay with a co-op partner.
Lost in Nightmares, one of the Gold Edition campaigns which takes place in the flashback sequence where Chris loses his partner Jill Valentine, is one of the many highlights of the game. Like a love letter to their fans, Lost in Nightmares includes a handful of throwbacks and references to old-school Resident Evil flare (cranks, traps, a piano, and an easter egg featuring classic fixed-camera angles for the beginning segment of the campaign, to name a few). It makes me hopeful for the future of the Resident Evil franchise, and it's the most enjoyable add-on content I've ever played.
I have nothing bad to say about this game, and endless good things to say. Since its release in 2009, I've been in love with Resident Evil 5, and I don't think the love for this game will ever die.

So, another retro-style 8-bit game pops up. Many may think that the style is horribly overdone today and will pay no attention to Shovel Knight.
I have a message for those of you - if you like platformers at all, DO NOT IGNORE THIS GAME.
Shovel Knight takes place in an unnamed kingdom, under threat by the Enchantress and the 8 Knights of her Order of No Quarter. Sounds familiar, doesn't it? Yeah, the Mega Man comparisons can be pretty plentiful, especially since the Mega Man series is what I usually see as the best platformers ever made.
STORY:
The story is pretty run of the mill, protagonist (Shovel Knight) and his companion/lover (Shield Knight) roamed the land in search of adventure, until one day, Shield Knight was taken from him by the dark power of a magic amulet. Don't roll your eyes just yet, because it gets good. While the story is simple, it deepens as he game goes on, through little bits of dialogue you may come across here and there.
-----MINOR SPOILER - KEEPING IT AS VAGUE AS POSSIBLE-----
There's a sequence near the end that shows that Shield Knight is not a flat, boring character used just to provide a love interest for the main character - she has her own merits, and is an equal, and that sequence shows just how well they work together and how much worse off Shovel Knight is without her. All that is shown through gameplay that lasts...about 3 minutes, 5 tops.
----------
So, the story actually stands up pretty well.
MUSIC:
Holy hell, this soundtrack is incredible. The tunes are extremely catchy, and, strangely enough, I would actually encourage you NOT to listen to any of the music outside of the game until you've heard it inside. That's right, I'm counting music as spoilers for this game. Jake Kaufman has done an amazing job as always.
Mega Man 2 always had my favourite 8-bit soundtrack. Up until I played this game.
MINOR SPOILER: There is one track in the game that has taken my place of best sad 8-bit song from Mega Man 3's Proto Man Theme - Shield Knight Requiem. You'll know which track this is when you play the feels inducing sequence it goes with.
GAMEPLAY:
The game plays brilliantly, the jumping is precise, the controls, while a bit weird at first (A and D for left and right, W and S for up and down, J to attack and K to jump) work very well once you get used to them. The level designs are all done very well, with specific mechanics and enemies being used in each of the Knight Lairs, and in each specific Lair alone, keeping the game fresh and interesting and, most importantly, challenging, as you have to learn new adversaries and mechanics to deal with. Almost all deaths in the game feel like your fault, something you can improve on.
The bosses work differently than most bosses I've seen in platformers like these. In other platformers, the bosses will have an attack pattern, performing attacks in a pre-determined sequence. Learn the pattern, and you can take the boss down with ease.
Not the case here - the bosses in Shovel Knight have set attacks, but completely lack any pattern. This makes the bosses do their job MUCH better - testing the player's skill. You have to learn their attacks, not the pattern - you need to learn their attacks and make sure you know how to counter them.
The checkpoints are a point of interest, because, save for in the first level and the final level, checkpoints can be broken to yield vast amounts of money, rendering the checkpoint beyond use. Death does not punish you by knocking off a life, leading you to an inevitable and frustrating Game Over. Instead, dying takes away some of your dosh, which you must then recover in the next life if you want it back. Sometimes these flying bags can end up in awkward or downright unreachable places, which, while annoying, could be viewed as punishment for messing up, encouraging you to improve. This checkpoint system means skilled players can receive a large monetary bonus if they so decide. Of course, getting cocky and then messing up after destroying checkpoints can send you from any length through the level all the way back to the start, so choose wisely.
LENGTH:
The game lasts around 5 to 6 hours, depending on your skill, on the first playthrough, an ample length, but it's packed full of secrets to find, one of the most notable being the Music Sheet collactables. 46 sheets are out in the world, hiding wherever, which can be returned to the village bard, who will pay you 500 gold for each, who can then play them for you - the music sheets in question form the game's soundtrack, so you can listen to your favourite tracks (provided you found the sheet) while scurrying about the village.
On top of that, there's a New Game +, unlocked after beating the game for the first time. This makes checkpoints much more scarce, about 2 per level, where once there may have been 3 times as many, healing items are almost never found, the most healing you'll get is the Ichor Of Restoration (given by the Troupple King (I could explain what a Troupple is, but you're better off finding out for yourself)). Trying to beat the game like this is even harder, and would probably add a fair bit of length to the game (I say would; I've not actually been able to finish New Game + yet.)
VISUALS:
The design of the levels and foes, aesthetically, is brilliant, with each stage's looks, features and enemies having their own style, keeping the game looking new and interesting. The game was designed with a limited colour palette, to mimic the NES's restrictions. Of course, not all parts of the game, such as the parallax scrolling or a few colours the NES's limits prevented here and there, but overall, the game stays very close to the 8-bit era it's based on, with the UI looking like it's come straight out of Castlevania, and the overworld map being very reminiscent of that from Super Mario Bros. 3.
OVERVIEW:
Shovel Knight is an 8-bit platformer that has elements from previous games of the era, and uses them magnificently. it excels in all areas. It's not just a retro 8-bit platformer aspiring to be like the classics - it's better than the classics.
It's challenging but enjoyable, and has enough of its own merits to stand tall, without needing to use nostalgia as a crutch - the NES era was not my childhood, that was the PS1 era. So if Shovel Knight's not sucking me in with nostalgia, then it must be something else giving me this rampant love for the game.
The early Mega Man games used to be what I considered the best platformers.
That title now belongs to Shovel Knight.
This game is EASILY worth the £11 (or reigonal equivalent) price tag.
If you enjoy platformers, are looking to get into the genre, or are a veteran of platformers, you owe it to yourself to buy this game.

An open world game that features hilarious plots and stuff. You play as the leader of a gang, doing quests and defeating rival gangs or the government to gain control of the city. Cutscenes, plots, even weapon and vehicle are hilarious. This game makes no sense (in a good and fun way)!
Although you are able to start roaming the entire city very early in the game, the story progression, game difficulty, as well as your equipment and arsenal are well balanced and not overwhelming.
(Note: Don't use the DLC vehicles too early in the game, or it will be too over-powered and ruin some of the fun. But feel free to use them to cause mayhem to the town if you just want to blow some stuff up. xD)
This game also have some of the best musics featured in the in-game radio stations. My favorites are the classical musics. It is fun to watch how the main character drive a huge tank, causing carnage to the city, while listening to soothing slow classical music. LIKE A BOSS!
This game features a drop-in drop-out co-op mode. Your friends can join your game anytime, and playing with friends will make this game even more fun!
I have only encountered one problem with this game. During startup, the game asks whether you want to use DirectX 9 or 10. DirectX 10 will always crash my system 20 minutes into the game. While DirectX 9 will have no gameplay problem, the framerate wasn't as good.
Only the Season Pass's DLCs are worth it IMO. Those 3 DLCs are the only ones that add more contents to the main game, the rest are just reskin and early unlocks of weapons and vehicles.
The mission DLCs each adds about 5 missions worth of gameplay into the game, and each feature another set of hilarious side story, weapons and vehicles.
I highly recommends you to play these DLC missions mid to late game.
The following DLCs are required for 100% completion.
It'll be cheaper to buy the full package, or the Season Pass DLC.
Some of the achievements are missable, and some non-missable ones are very hard to obtain when you have cleared 100% of the in-game progression. So it is best to do some research and unlock some of those achievements before perfecting the game.
My score: 9/10 (Must play!)
